items.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
items.summary: The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.

scraped.title: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
scraped.description: The discount chain has fallen into administration after its owners failed to find a buyer.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: Poundland collapses putting 11,000 jobs at risk
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Watch: Why has Poundland collapsed into administration?

Poundland has collapsed into administration, putting 11,000 jobs at risk, after its owners failed to find a buyer to keep it in business.

The retailer's shops and distribution centres will remain open and continue to trade during the administration process with the business likely to be broken up and some of its stores sold off to rival retailers.

Poundland's US owners held talks with several bidders over a last-minute rescue deal, but no agreement was reached.

Poundland boss Barry Williams said in a note to staff that the board had "no alternative but to take this decision", but was making it with "sincere sadness and intense regret".

He said the US owners Gordon Brothers had removed "all borrowing facilities and access to our bank accounts" on 27 October, and adequate funds had not been released since then to keep the business solvent.

"Under these circumstances, it is impossible for the board of directors to see how Poundland can continue to operate as a going concern," he added.

Kelvin Blake, pictured at a protest in Walsall, has worked for Poundland for 25 years

Kelvin Blake, 62, who has worked for the firm for 25 years, and whose partner has been there 29 years, said he was feeling "down, depressed", and because of his age, feared he would not find a job elsewhere.

"We didn't want it, but it's come so now we've just got to face it and see what the future holds.

"My income's gone," he added. "Obviously, we'll be working until we're told to leave."

Prime Minister Andy Burnham said Poundland was "part of the fabric of high streets and communities up and down the country".

He said the news of it going into administration just weeks before Christmas would be "deeply concerning for workers and their families".

He added: "While it is worrying, going into administration does give other potential buyers the opportunity to engage and we will work hard with all the relevant parties to ensure the best possible outcome."

Alix Partners, which has been appointed as administrator, said they would look at all options for the business, "including sales of the business and its assets, either in whole or part".

"We appreciate this is a deeply concerning time for all involved - customers, suppliers and, in particular, Poundland colleagues," they said.

Gordon Brothers has been criticised over how it handled a potential sale of Poundland, with accusations the investment firm hoped to profit from selling off the chain's 600 shops and stock piecemeal after running it into the ground.

Gordon Brothers, which specialises in buying and restructuring distressed companies, has denied such claims.

On the funding question, Gordon Brothers said it had loaned the firm £85m over a year to help save it from insolvency.

But insiders critical of the US firm have said it stands to make its loans back and more from the insolvency process.

Previously, Gordon Brothers netted millions from liquidating the stock of fashion retailer LK Bennett, and in insolvency fees.

Labour MP Liam Byrne told the BBC the House of Commons' Business, Innovation, Science and Trade Committee will recall Gordon Brothers before Parliament - two weeks after Gordon Brothers representatives last appeared at the committee to answer questions about Poundland, and where MPs said they were "deeply concerned" about the business.

Byrne said: "I am really worried that a 'greed is good' approach to business by its owners has forced [Poundland] into an administration."

He added the committee wants to know "how much money they're ripping out and crucially, how do we make sure, as a country, that we don't have this kind of scenario unfold again".

What's gone wrong at Poundland?

Gordon Brothers met Business Secretary Jonathan Reynolds on Monday to update him on the progress.

The firm said on Wednesday that despite the Poundland management bringing about a turnaround over the past year, the firm was "still vulnerable" to inflation and any downturn in sales or profit margin, and it had faced "several years of instability".

A spokesperson added the firm's "thoughts are with Poundland colleagues".

It said it had stepped in to take over the retailer in 2025 when it was struggling, and when "no-one else was willing to finance the business".

One of the central stumbling blocks in negotiations to keep the business afloat was a shareholder loan Gordon Brothers inherited when it bought the business for less than £1 last year.

Gordon Brothers was owed £22.5m of that loan, while the previous owner Pepco was owed £7.5m.

Gordon Brothers rejected various offers to buy the business as a going concern with deals to pay off that loan.

Irish firm Martin Property Group offered to pay off £5m of the loan up front, and defer the rest of the payments to 2030.

London-based Xyra group offered £12.5m up front but ran out of time to get a deal over the line.

German investment firm Zachert Private Equity is also understood to have made a late offer.

All of these were rejected.

The crisis at Poundland really came to a head over the past few weeks after Gordon Brothers restricted access to funds for day-to-day operations.

This meant that stock at the retailer was not being replenished at the necessary pace in the vital run-up to the festive period.

Are you a Poundland employee? Tell us your story. Get in touch.

items.summary: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.

scraped.title: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
scraped.description: The new levies would hit many of America's biggest trading partners, including China and the EU.
scraped.author: https://www.facebook.com/bbcnews
scraped.h1: US announces new tariffs on host of countries including China
scraped.body_text:
This video can not be played

Watch: What we know about Trump's Thanksgiving tariffs

The US has announced a fresh raft of tariffs as President Donald Trump pushes ahead with his signature trade policy.

The new taxes charged on imports to America are set to hit many of the country's biggest trading partners - China, the European Union and 12 other jurisdictions.

The move follows the White House's investigation into the trade practices of other countries in March after the US Supreme Court ruled Trump's previously announced Liberation Day tariffs were illegal .

China is facing the highest rate of up to 40%, followed by Vietnam at up to 35% and then others facing either 20% or 25%.

The new duties are not expected to take effect until next year.

Tariffs are taxes levied on imported goods. The amount is typically calculated as a percentage of the good's value and paid to the government by businesses importing the products from abroad.

Some of these rates will be effectively reduced because of caps on tariffs Trump has agreed to. Individual countries also face different levies.

The proposed tariffs will affect China, the European Union, Singapore, Switzerland, Indonesia, Malaysia, Cambodia, Thailand, Korea, Vietnam, Taiwan, Bangladesh, Japan, and India.

US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer said the latest tariffs issued would "level the playing field for American workers and chart a new, more sustainable course for the world economy".

He claimed that many of America's trading partners had "for decades" adopted industrial strategies which included "targeting manufacturing, wage and labor suppression" as well as "other market distorting practices that tilt the trade balance in their favor while eroding America's manufacturing base".

But economists have warned tariffs can fuel inflation and push prices up for consumers if businesses pass on higher costs, as well as dampen global trade.

Trump has repeatedly threatened or imposed tariffs during his second term, arguing they will boost US manufacturing and create jobs.

Despite a poor result for the Republican party in the midterm elections, the president has continued to press on with his flagship trade policy.

Trump is also seeking to cut the US trade deficit - the gap between the value of goods it buys from other countries and those it sells to them.

Trump's so-called Liberation Day tariffs were struck down by the Supreme Court earlier this year

However, Stephen Brown, chief North America economist for Capital Economics, said the latest tariff announcement was "not as alarming as it looks", due to the taxes "essentially replacing" previously announced tariffs made in the summer.

"The increase in the effective tariff rate looks set to be a touch lower than we've been assuming for our forecasts, although the new tariffs will still provide a marginal boost to prices," he said in a note.

"The key message is that the additional tariff burden is likely to be small, especially as various goods... are also not subject to these new tariffs."

The announcement is likely to increase tensions between the US and China, the world's two biggest economies, who remain locked in a trade dispute and the AI race.

The two countries have also been embroiled in a tit-for-tat tariffs war, which is currently on hold.

Despite last week's meeting between Trump and China's President Xi Jinping, the two sides made no announcement on the trade war truce, which is set to expire on 10 January.

The European Commission rejected the new US tariffs, saying it would investigate the US's reasons for bringing them in. It pointed out that tariffs are limited to the 15% previously agreed.

scraped.title: At least 30 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
scraped.description: Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 25 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred
scraped.author: Associated Press
scraped.h1: At least 30 killed as fuel tanker crash ignites large fire on Cairo highway
scraped.body_text:
Blaze on ring road surrounding Egyptian capital injures at least 25 people and leaves cars and motorcycles charred

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a huge fire on a highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday, killing at least 30 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on the ring road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the public prosecutor’s office said in a statement.

The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the health ministry.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video showed firefighters working to put out the fire spreading among the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.

The Egyptian president, Abdel-Fattah al-Sissi , expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The public prosecutor’s office said DNA investigations were under way to identify the victims.

The health minister, Khaled Abdel Ghaffar, said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic incidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January, 21 people were killed and 16 were injured in a multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

scraped.title: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
scraped.description: Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/rachel-savage
scraped.h1: Swiss tourist killed and British and Americans injured by elephants in Cameroon
scraped.body_text:
Alain Throo, insurance executive based in London, reportedly gored and later died on hike near Mount Cameroon national park

A Swiss tourist has been killed and British and American tourists have been injured when a group of hikers encountered a herd of elephants in Cameroon .

The group of six tourists, four British, one Swiss and one American, accompanied by local guides, were hiking near the village of Bakingili in the south of the Mount Cameroon national park on 19 November, on a path used by elephants to access a nearby lake, when they encountered the herd of about 15 animals, according to media reports.

The elephants attacked the group and Alain Throo, a Swiss insurance executive based in London, was reportedly gored and one of the guides tossed into a ditch on top of Throo, while the others hid in trees.

Throo had a black eye and was initially responsive and complaining about an injury to his arm, one of the British female hikers told Cameroonian media, which said they had feared he was bleeding internally.

“He said that the elephant attacked him,” an unidentified Cameroonian man added, according to a video posted by CBS Radio Buea FM. “It smashed him.”

Throo later died of his injuries and his body was carried out of the park by a combined team of park staff and the military to a mortuary in the town of Limbeon 21 November. The American hiker was treated at the same hospital and later discharged, according to local media .

One of the British tourists, who said he had hid in a tree stump for two hours, recalled the moment the elephants attacked their group. “I saw these elephants almost next to me. And I thought, if I go down this path as well, I’m going to get hit. So I just moved to the opposite direction. They ran down the path, I ran and hid in a bush. And I heard some screaming.”

Sean McGovern, the UK chief executive of the insurer Axa XL, where Throo had worked for 13 years, confirmed the death, saying Throo was a “valued member of our team, respected colleague and friend whose contribution, professionalism and warmth touched many people”.

Cameroonian media reported that clashes between elephants and local people had been happening for the past 10 years.

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

Mount Cameroon is the highest mountain in west and central Africa, at more than 4,000 metres. The African forest elephant was declared critically endangered by the International Union for Conservation of Nature in 2021. There are about 195,000 left in the wild, less than 15% of its population 50 years ago, according to the World Wildlife Fund .

Just 5% of forest elephants, which are smaller than their savannah-based counterparts, are found outside central Africa. In Cameroon, there are about 6,000 forest elephants, according to the NGO Global Conservation , which said the species was at risk from poaching syndicates.

A spokesperson for Britain’s Foreign Office said: “We offered assistance after a number of British nationals were injured in Cameroon.”

scraped.title: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
scraped.description: Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections
scraped.author: https://www.theguardian.com/profile/rachel-savage
scraped.h1: Sri Lankan asylum seeker killed himself after being sent by UK to Eswatini
scraped.body_text:
Kishanth Peramalya was denied entry due to sexual assault convictions and sent to Africa where he had no connections

The UK sent a Sri Lankan asylum seeker who had been convicted of sexual assault to Eswatini, a southern African country to which he had no connection and where he killed himself.

Kishanth Peramalya was part of a group that set sail from India hoping to reach Canada and claim asylum there. The boat was rescued by the Royal Navy in October 2021 when it got into difficulty and brought to Diego Garcia in the remote British Indian Ocean Territory, which hosts a US-UK military base.

In November 2024, the UK allowed 61 migrants to enter from Diego Garcia after a damning UN report about conditions in the camp. However, the then home secretary, Yvette Cooper, denied Peramalya entry to the UK due to his criminal convictions while he was on Diego Garcia for four counts of sexual assault, one count of assault occasioning actual bodily harm and one count of arson. Cooper’s decision was upheld by UK courts.

Peramalya had been granted protection from being returned to Sri Lanka, having been tortured and sexually abused by Sri Lankan military personnel as a teenager. In late March, the Maldives said it would take him for 30 days, according to the BBC . He was then transferred to Eswatini, a country landlocked by South Africa and Mozambique and formerly known as Swaziland, where he killed himself on 13 September.

A draft deal between the UK and Eswatini governments would have committed Downing Street to cover the costs of Peramalya’s resettlement there for three years, according to the BBC, which said the UK was also finalising arrangements for Peramalya to live in Eswatini permanently.

The Guardian has not seen the draft deal. Thabile Mdluli, a spokesperson for Eswatini’s government, said: “The initial arrangement was temporary in nature and intended to safeguard Mr Peramalya’s safety while the government of the United Kingdom worked towards a long-term solution regarding his circumstances.”

She said that no formal agreement was ever reached over Peramalya’s long-term residency status with the UK and declined to comment further on the specific arrangements of his stay in Eswatini or the circumstances around his death.

Mdluli said: “Eswatini has not received any other similar request from the government of the United Kingdom. The government of the Kingdom of Eswatini remains committed to ensuring that any agreements entered into with external partners safeguard national interest as well as the safety and security of Emaswati [Swazi people].”

A UK government spokesperson said: “Keeping the British public safe will always be our first priority, and we will continue to take the decisions necessary to protect the British people. That includes taking steps to ensure high harm foreign criminals cannot enter the UK. We continue to work with the Eswatini authorities in relation to this case.”

Peramalya had post-traumatic stress disorder and attempted suicide multiple times on Diego Garcia, according to a UK high court judgment in February 2025.

Peramalya’s family told the BBC he was initially housed alone in an isolated guesthouse in Eswatini. “My brother did not want to go there at all,” said his sister, speaking from India. “He couldn’t manage being there alone, he was very lonely.”

Sign up to Breaking News UK

Sign up for the Breaking News UK email to get newsletter alerts direct to your inbox

after newsletter promotion

She said he had called her four times a day and was initially having weekly psychiatric appointments, which were made daily when his mental health deteriorated, as well as having someone brought in to prepare his food.

Peramalya’s relatives said they were not aware of his convictions for sexual offences or any plan to make his transfer to Eswatini permanent.

Eswatini has accepted dozens of third-country deportees from the US since July 2025. In November 2025, its government confirmed it had received $5.1m in exchange for taking up to 160 migrants from the US.

items.title: At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
items.summary: The bakers behind these pop-up pastry drops aren't raking in the profits, but they are building a space for people to come together in polarized times. The bakers behind these pop-up pastry drops aren't raking in the profits, but they are building a space for people to come together in polarized times.(Image credit: Michael Minasi)

scraped.title: At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
scraped.description: The bakers behind these pop-up pastry drops aren't raking in the profits, but they are building a space for people to come together in polarized times.
scraped.h1: At this Little Free Bakery in Austin, neighbors come for the pastries and stay for community connection
scraped.body_text:
By

Wynne Davis

Nick Ruiz, who arrived at 7:15 in the morning to line up for the Free Bakery North Loop event, walks up to the table being run by baker and organizer Sarah Mason during the monthly gathering on Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, in Austin, Texas. Michael Minasi/KUT News hide caption

AUSTIN, Texas— When lines form in parks they're usually for the playground. Kids taking turns on slides. Runners waiting to get a drink from a water fountain. But the line that forms in the Bruning Green park in Austin's North Loop neighborhood happens only once a month, always on the first Sunday, and includes people of all ages. They're all here for Sarah Mason's bakery.

Unlike other bakeries in town where a pastry can run upwards of $7, everything here is free.

Mason's popup is one of countless Little Free Bakeries across the country. The idea is similar to Little Free Libraries, the small boxes that are often set up in front yards where passersby can leave or take a book as they please. Instead of books, it's baked goods that are up for grabs.

The bakers behind these Little Free Bakeries make everything from classic chocolate chip cookies to croissants all at no cost to their neighbors. Some have different reasons for starting than others, but what many inadvertently created is a space for their community to come together and get to know one another.

The menu for the September event included chocolate chip cookies with mini M&Ms, croissants, pickle and sharp cheddar scones and other pastries. Michael Minasi/KUT News hide caption

Sarah Mason is the baker and organizer behind Free Bakery North Loop. She started holding the month events in September 2025. Michael Minasi/KUT News hide caption

Mason started the Free Bakery North Loop last September when she was working on improving her technical pastry skills. She was handing out baked goods at her job as an office leasing representative for WeWork, but soon she had more than she could give away.

For her first free bakery, Mason made around 150 items, ranging from coconut chocolate chip cookies to bacon cheddar chive scones.

She thought people would happen upon the event as they were walking through the neighborhood. But just in case, she posted on social media. That post took off and since then there has always been a line.

"I have a friend who jokes that waiting in the line is the most fun part, because everyone's excited and talking about what they're going to get when they get to the front of the line and you can meet people," Mason said.

People love a free treat, but Mason said she is pleasantly surprised at how many people stick around and hang out.

"It was unexpected," she said. "My observation of other free bakeries, it's more of a grab and go situation. But because we were in this park, it felt like there was room to spread out and room for other activities. It became more of a community event than just a free pastry."

Sarah Mason started the free bakery in her neighborhood after she found herself with a surplus of pastries when she was working on improving her baking skills. Michael Minasi/KUT News hide caption

For people like Sara and J.R. Almanza, the event hearkens back to old Austin, a time before the tech boom when the skyline had fewer skyscrapers and when the pace of life felt slower and it was easier to strike up a conversation with strangers. After attending the free bakery once, the Almanzas decided to come back and enjoy the sense of community.

"Right now it seems like people are becoming more divided. It feels like everything's so polarizing these days," J.R. said. "There's so much out there to kind of distract us from meeting people and engaging with other people, that events like this are important because it brings people together."

That sense of community is part of what led Lanne Stauffer to create the very first Little Free Bakery in Seattle in 2021.

Stauffer got the idea for a Little Free Bakery after she experienced a small act of kindness.

"We were still in the pandemic and the mood was scared and nobody was coming out of their houses and just a lot of fear in the air and there was a bouquet of flowers on my front step," Stauffer said.

Receiving those flowers created a shift in how she was feeling inside.

"Just the joy of finding that bouquet of flowers on my front step changed my day and I wanted to know what I could do to change other folks' day in the same way," she said.

But Stauffer isn't a florist. She's a baker. She thought of Little Free Libraries and asked her husband to build her a pick-up box.

"It gives me so much joy to bake for people," she said. "It's the way I say I love you, and so even if nobody came that day, just knowing I was baking for the community made me feel good."

That Tuesday, people did come though — and in an hour all 50 little apple pies were gone. By the time it was over, Stauffer decided she would do it again the following week.

It's been five years since then, and Stauffer has noticed a couple of things. Chocolate and lemon sweets are more popular than others. And the treats aren't the only reason people stop by.

" People are always grateful to have a place to come and meet their neighbors and have conversations often about what's going on in the news," she said. "We stand around and hug each other or laugh or cry, share our fears, and it's just added another gathering spot in our neighborhood."

Some neighbors even plan their weeks around the pastry drops.

Erin Creighton Tozier has lived in Seattle's Magnolia neighborhood for five years, but didn't know about the Stauffer's Little Free Bakery until a year ago.

"It's just like the anchor in our week," Creighton Tozier said. "I have a demanding job, but it's like a 3 p.m. calendar marker … a break in the day to get some fresh air. Even if it's raining, no matter the weather, like my dog and I go, we have a sweet treat, we chat with our neighbors."

Lanne Stauffer created the very first Little Free Bakery in Seattle in 2021. She celebrated five years of baking for her neighbors in October. Anna Marie Yanny/KNKX hide caption

For her five-year anniversary celebration, Lanne Stauffer made a 5-foot-long cake white cake, with orange curd filling, a cardamom cream cheese frosting and a pomegranate molasses drizzle. She and her family decorated it with fall fruits. Anna Marie Yanny/KNKX hide caption

To celebrate her neighbors coming out for five years, Stauffer baked a 5-foot-long white cake, with orange curd filling, a cardamom cream cheese frosting and a pomegranate molasses drizzle.

Her family helped decorate it with fall fruits before they put it out in the driveway.

"I have learned that folks need to feel connected and they can feel comforted by me just baking them something," she said.

It only took a couple months after Stauffer started the Little Free Bakery Seattle for another one to open up.

"Then it started to snowball from there, and I was having somebody reach out to me every month for a while opening a new little free bakery," Stauffer said. "I didn't know that I was starting a movement but that has been one of the biggest delights."

Now little free bakeries exist in Nashville, Tenn.; Salt Lake City, Utah; Fredericksburg, Va. and other cities.

Stauffer recently took a road trip to visit some of the other bakeries and collect stories and recipes from her fellow bakers for an upcoming book, The Little Free Bakery Book: Recipes for Sharing & Building Community, written with Jill Lightner.

Stauffer, like Mason in Austin, hopes that the movement continues to grow. "I think every neighborhood should have a little free bakery," Mason said.

In Austin, other free bakeries have popped up since Mason started hers. But the reach goes farther. In Chattanooga, Tenn., her sister plans to start a free bakery there.

"I think she just saw how much fun we're having here and thought that she wants a little slice of that in her own neighborhood," Mason said.

Maddy Helton, first in line for the Free Bakery North Loop event, receives a pastry from baker and organizer Sarah Mason during the monthly event on Sunday, Sept. 6, 2026, in Austin, Texas. Michael Minasi/KUT News hide caption

items.title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
items.summary: Several Democratic senators have been signaling this move, saying the party needs to acknowledge the diverse class of incoming freshman that catapulted the party to victory in November. scraped.title: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
scraped.description: Several Democratic senators have been signaling this move, saying the party needs to acknowledge the diverse class of incoming freshman that catapulted the party to victory in November.
scraped.h1: Group of Senate Democrats push to add freshman to leadership
scraped.body_text:
By

Barbara Sprunt

U.S. Senate Majority Leader Charles Schumer (D-NY), center, is seen here meeting with newly elected Democratic Senators, (L-R) Senator-elect Andy Kim (D-NJ), Senator-elect Ruben Gallego (D-AZ), Senator-elect Angela Alsobrooks (D-MD) Senator-elect Adam Schiff (D-CA) Senator-elect Lisa Blunt Rochester (D-DE) and Senator-elect Elissa Slotkin (D-MI) at the U.S. Capitol Building on November 12, 2024. That group of senators is pushing to add an incoming freshman senator to the leadership ranks. Chip Somodevilla/Getty Images/Getty Images North America hide caption

A group of Senate Democrats elected in 2024 sent a letter to colleagues Tuesday proposing to add an incoming freshman to the leadership ranks.

"The Freshman Representative to Leadership would be elected by members of the incoming freshman class and confirmed by the Conference," the letter said. "We intend to request a vote on this proposal."

The letter, first reported by Politico , is signed by California Sen. Adam Schiff, Maryland Sen. Angela Alsobrooks, Michigan Sen. Elissa Slotkin, Arizona Sen. Ruben Gallego, Delaware Sen. Lisa Blunt Rochester, and New Jersey Sen. Andy Kim.

The letter nods to the diverse class of incoming freshmen who helped catapult the party to controlling both chambers of Congress.

"These freshmen have their fingers on the pulse of long-time Democratic voters, those who voted for Democrats for the first time this past Election Day, and everyone in-between," the letter reads. "The deserve a seat at the table."

Senate Democrats have been signaling a desire to uplift new voices in the party.

"On election night, people voted very clearly for a new generation of leadership. That was very, very clear," Slotkin said during remarks at a conference of Democrats after the midterms .

New Jersey Sen. Cory Booker told MS NOW that leadership extends beyond the top post.

"This is a time for new leadership," Booker said, mentioning wanting to see more of incoming Sens. Annie Andrews of South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas. "I want to see them out front, I want to see them taking issues, I want to see them running on the field."

The proposed rule change comes ahead of the leadership election next week. Maryland Sen. Chris Van Hollen is challenging Senate Minority Leader Chuck Schumer , D-N.Y., for the majority leader.

Senate leadership is comprised not only of the top position of Majority leader but of additional conference officers. Both Van Hollen and Schumer support the idea of adding a position for a freshman to that leadership group.

"Leader Schumer was already planning to do this and is incredibly supportive of the idea," a spokesperson told NPR.

On Tuesday, Van Hollen posted to social media: "There should be a freshman senator on the Senate leadership team. As I've said, we need a new way to organize so we can deliver for the American people."

items.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
items.summary: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation. The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.(Image credit: Eddie Raynes)

scraped.title: How American Thanksgiving took root -- and evolved -- in Liberia
scraped.description: The first settlers of Liberia were African Americans who brought along the holiday of Thanksgiving — which has evolved to reflect the history and identity of this new nation.
scraped.h1: How American Thanksgiving took root — and evolved — in Liberia
scraped.body_text:
Ari Daniel

Yvonne Capehart Weah's family routinely gets together in the township where she grew up in Liberia. In early November every year, they gather to celebrate the Liberian version of Thanksgiving. Eddie Raynes hide caption

Yvonne Capehart Weah is from Liberia, a country in West Africa, and she's one of twelve siblings.

"I'm the second to the last one — I'm the eleventh," she says. "We have large families in Liberia."

Every year on the first Thursday in November, Weah's family gathers in Caldwell, the township where she grew up, to celebrate Liberian Thanksgiving.

"When we come together, the group become [so] large that you are not able to sit around a dining table," she explains. "So we do it outside under the tree. And when we meet, it's almost like we're having a party."

The Liberian holiday dates back to the first half of the 19th century when the American Colonization Society established the community that would grow into the country. It was founded by Black Americans — both those born free and enslaved people who had been emancipated — whose departure was sometimes voluntary, sometimes forced. "The settlers from America brought that Thanksgiving Day tradition to Liberia," says Weah. Once transplanted, the holiday evolved over time in response to national events.

Liberia gained its independence in 1847 but the British continued trying to take swaths of territory. In 1883, President Alfred Francis Russell, an Episcopalian priest, called upon God to help halt the incursions.

That invocation was a "prayer of protection against the intruders, preventing intrusion into our territory," says Weah.

The Liberians managed to maintain their sovereignty. And that year, the legislature officially established Thanksgiving as a national holiday steeped in the religious gratitude of the moment.

Weah summarizes Liberian Thanksgiving this way: "It's giving thanks to God for our freedom, for divine protection. It's giving thanks to God for unity and for the harvest."

Weah says that her family's celebration, like that of many others in Liberia, starts in the morning at church. But the holiday's for people of all faiths, and other religious communities mark the occasion as well

"The Muslims, they go to the mosques and pray," says Sekou Muhammad Sheriff , a YouTuber who travels his home country of Liberia to showcase its offerings and cultural heritage, including Thanksgiving . "And Muslims, Christians, and others — everybody observe this day as a holiday."

When Sheriff was a boy, this was the day that he counted on to get a new outfit.

"What my dad used to do for me," says Sheriff, was to purchase a "shirt-trouser suit, and then he'd buy me slipper." His favorite suit was a white one.

Over the years on Thanksgiving, he's grown accustomed to eating different stews, including one made with sweet potato leaves and another with snails collected from the garden.

"We call it king's meat," Sheriff says with a chuckle. "It is very, very nice."

The mid-afternoon meal varies from household to household in Liberia.

Yvonne Capehart Weah's nieces and nephews fill their plates at a family gathering in Caldwell. Rebecca Blapoh Weah hide caption

"We don't do turkey," says Weah, "but we do chicken. We do fried chicken, smoked chicken, roasted chicken."

Weah's family also serves jollof rice, watermelon, pineapple and a variety of stews, including one called fufu and soup. It's a mix of cassava, fish, chicken, okra, chili pepper and more. "That makes the soup very tasty," says Weah. "It has to be [at] every Thanksgiving."

(Weah doesn't especially like to cook, however. "If you tell me, 'Go in the kitchen to cook or sit in the living room and read,'" she says, "I will sit in the living room and read.")

This year, Sheriff didn't have the resources to host Thanksgiving. But he says that he remains thankful to God for keeping him healthy and for keeping Liberia peaceful after civil conflict tore his country apart from 1989 to 1997 and 1999 to 2003.

Weah is also grateful. "When I go for Thanksgiving," she says, "I'm thanking God for where I have come from, where I am now, and I'm also thanking Him for where He will take me because I know He holds the future."

Weah is the program manager at the We-Care Foundation , an education nonprofit that, among other things, teaches children literacy. "A reading child will become a reading elder," she says.

"And we expect informed adults to make informed decisions that affect both their social and economic life" — in ways, perhaps, that they will one day be thankful for.

items.title: Famed NFL agent reveals potential consequences for Steelers, Mike McCarthy after public Aaron Rodgers rupture
items.summary: Famed agent Leigh Steinberg says Aaron Rodgers' public accusations against Steelers coach Mike McCarthy could deter future free agents from Pittsburgh. scraped.title: Famed NFL agent reveals potential consequences for Steelers, Mike McCarthy after public Aaron Rodgers rupture
scraped.description: Famed agent Leigh Steinberg says Aaron Rodgers' public accusations against Steelers coach Mike McCarthy could make agents question advising players to join Pittsburgh.
scraped.author: Jackson Thompson
scraped.h1: Famed NFL agent reveals potential consequences for Steelers, Mike McCarthy after public Aaron Rodgers rupture
scraped.body_text:
Famed NFL agent Leigh Steinberg says Aaron Rodgers’ public rupture with the Pittsburgh Steelers and his allegations against coach Mike McCarthy could prompt questions from agents advising potential players about joining the Steelers.

Famed NFL agent Leigh Steinberg says Aaron Rodgers’ public rupture with the Pittsburgh Steelers and his allegations against coach Mike McCarthy could prompt questions from agents advising potential players about joining the Steelers in the future, and tarnish Rodgers' lasting memory in the NFL.

"This is about as far away from an ideal parting as can be imagined," Steinberg told OutKick.

This page may contain affiliate links to legal sports betting partners. If you sign up or place a wager, FOX News may be compensated. This content was created by a team that works independently from the FOX newsroom.

Steinberg, whose former clients include Steelers quarterbacks Ben Roethlisberger , Kordell Stewart and Neil O’Donnell, criticized Rodgers for taking the dispute public, saying the quarterback was undermining the kind of farewell most accomplished players hope to have.

"But for Rodgers to have this long, illustrious career and then go out this way is certainly not ideal because his critique of the team, whether accurate or not, is exposing dirty laundry to the world," he said.

Steinberg also suggested Rodgers understood exactly how much attention his comments would attract.

"Pat McAfee didn’t have to do much interviewing," he said. "He just, he asked a couple questions and Aaron took it from there."

"So he knew what he was doing."

STEELERS COACH MIKE MCCARTHY INJURES HIMSELF AND IT WAS SERIOUS ENOUGH HE NEVER GOT TO HALFTIME LOCKER ROOM

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers listens to head coach Mike McCarthy during NFL practice in Pittsburgh on May 20, 2026. (Gene J. Puskar/AP)

Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep and snoring during meetings and missing team events during a Wednesday appearance on ESPN’s "The Pat McAfee Show." The interview followed Pittsburgh’s announcement that Rodgers would be inactive for Friday’s game against the Denver Broncos, with Mason Rudolph starting. NFL Network subsequently reported that Pittsburgh was waiving Rodgers.

But Steinberg said the public nature of Rodgers’ accusations did not absolve Pittsburgh of examining them.

"The Steelers have to look at themselves and ask, are any of these allegations true?" he said. "Is there dysfunction in the coaching ranks?"

Steinberg stressed that he could not independently determine whether Rodgers’ account was accurate.

"Only the people involved know," he said.

The consequences could extend beyond Rodgers’ departure, according to Steinberg, who said the allegations would warrant questions from agents helping players evaluate Pittsburgh as a destination.

Asked how he would advise a high-value client considering signing with the Steelers, he said he would seek answers directly from team leadership.

"You would certainly have discussions with their front office as to whether or not these allegations are true," he said.

Steinberg said Rodgers had described a distant, uninvolved coach, making it necessary for agents to establish the facts rather than simply accept either the quarterback’s account or the franchise’s reputation.

SUPER BOWL CHAMPION JOE THEISMANN REVEALS KEY FACTOR IN AARON RODGERS DECISION TO RETURN TO STEELERS

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers walks off the field after an NFL football game against the Cleveland Browns, Sunday, Dec. 28, 2025, in Cleveland. (AP Photo/David Richard)

That would mean weighing the allegations against Pittsburgh’s history of stability, including its limited coaching turnover.

"So you certainly want to understand the facts," he said.

Steinberg’s own experience with the organization offered a favorable view of its leadership. Over years of representing Pittsburgh quarterbacks, he said, the front office consistently emphasized players’ interests and the franchise’s future.

"Every discussion I ever had with their front office, they were looking to the long view. They cared about players," he said.

He also praised owner Art Rooney II and general manager Omar Khan.

"I’ve dealt many times with Omar Khan and many times with Art Rooney, and they’ve been nothing but classy."

That history, Steinberg suggested, makes the current controversy particularly difficult for an organization that has long prided itself on its culture.

"They’ve always had a reputation as the epitome of stability, class, a unique culture," he said. "When people put on the Steelers uniform, they tend to play better."

Steinberg described the deterioration of Rodgers’ relationship with McCarthy , who previously coached him in Green Bay, as "stunning."

For Steinberg, the issue was not simply that a quarterback and coach disagreed. It was that a dispute ordinarily handled inside a franchise had become a public spectacle.

He said teams generally want to work through internal criticism while presenting unity to the outside world.

Asked whether McCarthy should be held responsible for the situation, Steinberg declined to assign blame solely to the coach.

"I don’t have the inside information," he said, adding that the stories Rodgers told were "disturbing stories for a franchise."

"I’m sure they’ll take a look at the conduct and evaluate it."

Pittsburgh Steelers quarterback Aaron Rodgers listens to a question during a news conference after an NFL football game against the Miami Dolphins in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania on Dec. 15, 2025. (AP Photo/Gene J. Puskar)

His broader assessment placed responsibility on the fractured relationship.

"I think it’s a mutual breakdown," he said.

Asked whether he had seen a comparable situation involving such a high-profile player publicly criticizing his coach, Steinberg answered, "No."

"First of all, it’s shocking that Aaron Rodgers gets benched. Then it’s even more shocking that he goes public and tells the world that the coach is just not effective," he said.

Steinberg contrasted the episode with the more appreciative farewell he said players typically want, pointing to Tom Brady, Troy Aikman and Peyton Manning as examples.

Still, he expressed sympathy for Rodgers’ frustration .

"Aaron Rodgers is a proud player. He obviously has had a storied career. This was not the way he wanted to go out, so I can understand his unhappiness."

Steinberg was skeptical that another team would pick up Rodgers before the season ends, pointing to the practical challenges of joining a new organization without an offseason or training camp together.

"The difficult thing with that is he would not have had training camp with that team," he said.

Even for an accomplished quarterback, Steinberg suggested, a late-season move leaves little time to prepare and develop familiarity with a new team.

"Does a team pick him up this late in the season? Probably not," he said.

But asked whether he would drop Rodgers as a client if the quarterback wanted to continue playing, Steinberg answered: "No."

"There’s a loyalty factor there," he said.

He was more optimistic about Rodgers’ opportunities after his playing career, suggesting broadcasting, coaching or potentially team ownership as possibilities.

"I think at a certain level this will blow over. And Rodgers will be remembered for the best facets of things," Steinberg said.

Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

THE CRAIG CARTON SHOW–UNFILTERED, UNAPOLOGETIC AND UNMISSABLE. DOWNLOAD HIS DAILY PODCAST NOW!

He said Rodgers could be an intriguing broadcaster because of his insights and opinions, while noting that coaching can be a difficult transition for former players.

"He’s forgotten more about football than most people will ever know," Steinberg said.

Still, he cautioned against reaching a final judgment based on the quarterback’s account alone.

"We don’t know what the reaction will be to this, because we’ve only heard one side of the story," he said.

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We haven’t heard from the Steelers."

Duran Duran guitarist Andy Taylor has died at age 65 of prostate cancer, Fox News Digital confirmed.

Taylor died peacefully at home surrounded by family on Monday, according to a joint statement from his family and former bandmates.

"To the world, Andy was a brilliant guitarist, but to us, he was the most wonderful husband, a loving dad and the proudest grandfather," his wife, Tracey, said on behalf of the family.

In a tribute on the band's website, lead singer Simon Le Bon wrote, "There’s a massive Andy Taylor shaped hole in my heart."

Because now-former signal caller Aaron Rodgers went scorched earth on Steelers coach Mike McCarthy during an appearance on "The Pat McAfee Show," even claiming that the coach has been known to doze off in meetings.

Now, players like tight end Pat Freiermuth found themselves in front of microphones just minutes after Rodgers' bombshell interview and in a brutal spot.

AARON RODGERS NOT RETURNING TO STEELERS, SAYS MIKE MCCARTHY FALLS ASLEEP IN MEETINGS AND IS 'UNWELL'

"Yeah, listen: anything I say about the situation is going to be tough, and obviously (the situation) is tough," Freiermuth said. "Y'know, I'm here, and we're just focused on trying to get a win against Denver."

The former Penn State Nittany Lion was then asked if he had confidence in the Steelers coaching staff and the team's current direction.

Steelers tight end Pat Freiermuth did his best to toe the line when it came to questions about the Steelers' split from quarterback Aaron Rodgers. (Bill Streicher-Imagn Images)

WHAT’S YOUR TAKE: WILL AARON RODGERS PLAY ANOTHER SNAP THIS SEASON?

"I'm confident," he said.

Freiermuth was especially in a bind, as Rodgers claimed that the tight end was the one who broke the news that he was being benched in the first place. He was asked about the conversation he had with Rodgers over the phone.

"I was just checking in on a close friend, from what I heard," Freiermuth said. "That's all I have to say about that."

Freiermuth also steered clear of a question about whether the situation between Rodgers and the organization could've ended differently.

Aaron Rodgers and head coach Mike McCarthy of the Pittsburgh Steelers chat before an NFL football game against the Philadelphia Eagles at Lincoln Financial Field in Philadelphia, Pa., on Nov. 22, 2026. (Getty Images)

CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"Again, I'm sorry, but I'm just going to focus on Denver," he said.

It's a wise choice to put as much focus on the Broncos as possible. With the Steelers already facing a Black Friday meeting with the top team in the conference, the last thing they need is some noise creating distractions.

And, boy, is there a lot of drama here, and likely more to come.

Matthew Reigle is a writer for OutKick.

scraped.title: Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after he blasts coach Mike McCarthy in fiery exit interview
scraped.description: The Pittsburgh Steelers released quarterback Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday shortly after he described his head coach Mike McCarthy as “unhealthy” in a critical interview following the Steelers’ decision to deactivate Rodgers for the team’s upcoming game.
scraped.h1: Steelers cut Aaron Rodgers after he blasts coach Mike McCarthy in fiery exit interview
scraped.body_text:
For You

Settings

news Alerts

There are no new alerts at this time

The Pittsburgh Steelers released quarterback Aaron Rodgers on Wednesday shortly after he described his head coach Mike McCarthy as “unhealthy” in a critical interview following the Steelers’ decision to deactivate Rodgers for the team’s upcoming game.

Speaking to ESPN’s Pat McAfee on Wednesday, Rodgers accused McCarthy of falling asleep during team meetings and missing walkthroughs in the weeks leading up to his benching.

“Last Thursday, I was in a quarterback meeting and in 10 minutes I heard snoring,” Rodgers said of his head coach. “Thursday, he misses an offensive meeting. Friday, he misses walkthrough... Saturday, he misses the team meeting.”

Added Rodgers: “If you’re sleeping in meetings, you’re unhealthy.”

Following the interview, the team announced Rodgers had been released.

The Steelers are 6-4 and have lost their last two games. On Tuesday night, the team announced that Rodgers would be inactive for the team’s game Friday against the Denver Broncos.

The Steelers did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Rodgers’ interview.

Rodgers blasted McCarthy while speaking to McAfee, alleging his coach even broke down a team huddle with a “one, two, three, Packers!” last week, confusing players. (McCarthy was previously Rodgers’s coach in Green Bay from 2006 to 2018.)

“Everybody knows what’s going on. He’s missing walkthroughs, you don’t think everybody else knows?,” Rodgers said. “Does any other quarterback have these issues?”

Rodgers added: “It’s a very delicate situation, the coaching staff is worried about their job security, the players are worried about their money and jobs security.”

Rodgers said he is willing to speak out about McCarthy because of the financial security his long career has afforded him.

Rodgers also claimed McCarthy hasn’t connected with Pittsburgh’s defense, and rebuffed Rodgers’ efforts to get him to connect with players on that side of the ball.

Rodgers also said McCarthy has not been watching film and lacks an intimate knowledge of the team’s week-to-week game plans.

“I don’t expect people to come out strong in my defense even though everybody knows the truth,” the quarterback said.

Rodgers said issues with McCarthy began in training camp, and he also accused his coach of harboring ill will over his dismissal from the Packers.

“In Mike’s mind, I got him fired in 2018. He told a staff member he still doesn’t forgive me for getting him fired in 2018,” Rodgers claimed.

In the hours before his benching, Rodgers said he brought up his issues with McCarthy in an in-person conversation and delivered him an ultimatum to either address the problems or grant him a release. Rodgers claimed McCarthy did not admit to sleeping during team meetings, and the idea of his benching was not raised.

“I found out that I was going to be inactive on a phone call last night from Pat Freiermuth,” Rodgers said, referring to the tight end.

The quarterback repeatedly said his stories are not “hyperbole” or “opinion,” but instead first-hand accounts and facts.

Rodgers, 42, has said on several occasions the 2026 season would be his final one in the NFL. A four-time MVP and a former Super Bowl champion, Rodgers in recent years has become equally notable for his willingness to speak freely, opining on topics from the Covid vaccine to the benefits he feels of taking psychadelic drugs .

Rodgers is also a frequent guest on McAfee’s ESPN show, and was previously paid for weekly appearances on the program.

As he’s become a lightning rod for his public comments, Rodgers’s play on the field has slipped in the late stage of his career. He’s averaging a career-low 6.2 yards per attempt this season, and Rodgers has not posted a passer rating higher than 95.0 in five seasons after doing so 12 times between 2008 and 2021.

McCarthy spoke with reporters at a press conference in the wake of Rodgers’ comments, and refuted multiple claims. McCarthy said it was “not accurate” that he held a grudge with Rodgers over his firing in 2018, and also said he made multiple attempts to reach Rodgers to inform him of his benching.

But the coach also largely avoided getting into the finer details of Rodgers’s accusations.

“We are focused on beating Denver,” McCarthy said.

Rohan Nadkarni is a sports reporter for NBC News.

scraped.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed until Saturday due to weather for first time in its 100-year history
scraped.description: For the first time in history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to weather, Macy's said Wednesday.
scraped.h1: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade postponed until Saturday due to weather for first time in its 100-year history
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 25, 2026 / 5:18 PM EST / CBS New York

For the first time in history, the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has been postponed due to weather, Macy's said Wednesday.

The 100th annual parade will now kick off Saturday at 8:30 a.m.

The historic move comes as a powerful coastal storm is set to impact the area Thursday.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our city and agency partners, we've made the decision to move the celebration due to expected severe weather," Macy's said in a statement. "Thank you to the thousands of volunteers, performers and partners who create the magic millions enjoy each year. We look forward to celebrating together on Saturday."

The watchword for the mayor's office, the NYPD and Macy's is safety, and there's ample reason for concern. Past parades have seen balloons tear, deflate or collide with overhead wires.

In 1997, high winds pushed several balloons out of control. The Cat in the Hat balloon struck a lamppost near Central Park West, which brought down a heavy fixture, injuring four spectators. A woman suffered a fractured skull and coma. Barney and the Pink Panther balloons also ran into trouble and had to be deflated.

In 1993, Sonic the Hedgehog was driven by high winds into a lamppost, injuring spectators and an NYPD officer. Dudley the Dragon hit a lamppost in Columbus Circle in that same parade, ending glass showering down on the crowd.

In 1971, balloons were grounded because of high winds, but even during COVID, the parade went on.

The operational challenges involved in shifting the date of the parade are substantial. The parade involves plenty of marching bands and other performers who had been expecting the event on Thursday, and now will need to make alternative arrangements.

Fans who came into New York City to see Wednesday night's balloon inflation seemed alright with the decision to postpone the parade.

"So much goes into the parade each year. It's like a tradition each year to watch, get up early and watch the parade with my whole family," one person said. "I'm really excited that they're changing it because so much work goes into it every year, and people come from all over to help with the balloons. So I'm really excited that they're still making an effort to do it. Even on a different day, it's still just as special."

The parade was previously suspended from 1942 to 1944 during World War II when officials needed the helium used to inflate the balloons for the war effort. It has never been postponed due to weather.

items.summary: Iran's U.N. envoy claims the U.S. military used Palantir and Anthropic AI systems to select some 2,000 targets over just four days.

scraped.title: Iran War Updates: Tehran denounces U.S. for using AI in strikes it claims violate international law
scraped.description: Iran's U.N. envoy claims the U.S. military used Palantir and Anthropic AI systems to select some 2,000 targets over just four days.
scraped.h1: Iran War Updates: Tehran denounces U.S. for using AI in strikes it claims violate international law
scraped.body_text:
Watch CBS News

Updated on: November 25, 2026 / 5:03 PM EST / CBS News

Yemen's Houthis said Wednesday they had targeted the Saudi ports of Jeddah and Jazan in response to Saudi strikes on a Yemeni port controlled by the Iran-backed group as their conflict further escalated.

The attacks came after the Saudi-led military coalition fighting the Houthis said it had struck Yemen's Red Sea port city of Hodeida, drawing threats of retaliation from the Yemeni fighters.

"Both operations resulted in damage to the targeted sites," Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree said.

An explosion was later heard in Saudi capital Riyadh, according to an AFP journalist and residents, after authorities issued an alert warning of a "hostile aerial threat," which was lifted shortly after.

The Saudi coalition said on social media Wednesday that its air defenses intercepted and destroyed two Houthi-launched ballistic missiles that were heading toward Riyadh. Earlier, the coalition said its air defenses also intercepted and destroyed a cruise missile launched toward the western region.

CBS/AFP

The Iranian Foreign Ministry has called out Republican Sen. John Cornyn for a post on X criticizing Iran's alleged pursuit of nuclear weapons, however, the quote cited by the senator was actually about North Korean nuclear ambitions.

The Texas senator cited International Atomic Energy Agency chief Rafael Grossi raising concern "about a rapidly built extension at the Yongbyon gas centrifuge uranium enrichment plant."

Cornyn wrote on X, "Doesn't sound like the Iranian regime is giving up on its nuclear weapons aspirations."

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei correctly pointed out Grossi was speaking about Yongbyon, North Korea, and nothing to do with Iran.

Cornyn serves on the Senate Committee on Foreign Relations, one of the governing body's most important posts. Cornyn is on his way out of the Senate. He was soundly defeated by Ken Paxton in the Republican primary this spring. Paxton would eventually lose earlier this month to Democrat James Talarico.

The post on X remains live 24 hours after the senator shared it.

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said Wednesday that Israel was trying to drag the United States into another war after an Israeli minister alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons.

"This warmonger shamelessly accuses Iran ... of developing and concealing such heinous weapons in pharmaceutical factories. The objective is audacious: to deceive the US into fighting yet another war on its behalf," he wrote in a statement posted on X .

Israel has for years accused Iran of trying to acquire nuclear weapons, but Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Tuesday alleged Tehran is building chemical weapons and vowed to stop the Islamic republic from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons but has not yet reached the capability to attack Israel with them," said Katz in a statement published by his Likud party on Telegram. He also left open the possibility of preemptive strikes against Iran.

"We must not allow this to proceed," he said.

President Trump mentioned the same thing to Fox News earlier this month on his Asia trip, saying, "Well, there is indication that Iran is looking at gases, looking at bio, because we've shut them out with the nuclear. ... Nuclear is much harder, and they're looking at gas and they're looking at the bio, the biological weapons."

CBS/AFP

A projectile fired by the Houthi militia struck Jazan port in southwestern Saudi Arabia, causing minor damage but no civilian casualties, the Saudi-led coalition said on Wednesday .

It said efforts were underway to determine the type of projectile.

The Iran-backed Houthis reiterated earlier on Wednesday their threat to target Jeddah and all Saudi Arabian ports on the Red Sea if Saudi Arabia followed through on its threat to target Yemen's Hodeidah port, which is held by the rebels.

Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and other essential supplies into Houthi-held northern Yemen.

Shortly after the Houthis' warning, the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV network reported a Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah.

Iran's Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps claimed Wednesday that a liquified natural gas carrier exploded after striking a sea mine while transiting what it calls an unauthorized route through the southern Strait of Hormuz — shipping lanes the U.S. military insists are free of mines and safe for travel.

The IRGC statement, carried Wednesday by state television network IRIB and other Iranian media, did not provide any further information about the ship purportedly impacted, and there was no immediate report from independent monitoring agencies of a vessel being hit Wednesday.

Iran has repeatedly warned vessels not to ignore its restrictions on the Strait of Hormuz, saying ships must only use northern shipping lanes through the waterway, close to its shores, and only with authorization from Iranian authorities.

The IRGC said Wednesday that ships being "deceived by the plundering U.S. military" were at risk of striking naval mines.

Iranian army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said Wednesday that Iran's forces had tightened their control over and monitoring of the Strait of Hormuz.

U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said Wednesday that the Iranian regime was a "sinking ship."

In a brief social media post, Bessent said Iran had failed to load a single oil tanker since the Treasury launched Operation Economic Outcast in August, which he called at the time an "unprecedented campaign against the Islamic Republic of Iran and its enablers."

The initiative is aimed at using economic tools - including secondary sanctions against countries and entities that do business with Iran - to force the regime to halt its threats to shipping in the Strait of Hormuz and to end the war.

While neither of those objectives has been met, Bessent said in his post on Wednesday that "Iran doesn't have a drop of oil on the water left to sell."

Iran's First Vice President Mohammad Reza Aref said Wednesday that Tehran is not concerned about the U.S.-imposed naval blockade of Iranian ports, claiming an increase in exports and the clearance of goods via other routes, according to state news agency IRNA.

Aref was quoted as saying increased commerce across Iran's "northern and other non-southern borders" demonstrated the Islamic Republic's ability to maintain supplies despite maritime restrictions.

The U.S. military announced earlier this month an expansion of its naval blockade, as Central Command heralded a new task force aimed at disrupting the illegal shipment of prohibited items such as military technology or illegal revenue streams over ground transportation routes into and out of Iran.

"The establishment of Task Force Iron Gate reinforces the success of our ironclad blockade against Iran at sea," U.S. Central Command chief Adm. Brad Cooper said in Nov. 7 a statement. "Strengthening CENTCOM's collaboration with U.S. interagency partners will further constrain Iran's ability to finance terrorism, rebuild weapons factories, and replenish their military."

Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi said Monday that a land blockade of Iran would be "almost impossible" given the country's vast territory, numerous provinces and extensive ties with neighboring countries.

Britain's air force is moving planes into hangars and hardened shelters overnight to protect them from drone threats, The Times and Sky News reported Wednesday. The two U.K. media outlets also said the Royal Air Force (RAF) is planning to install anti-drone nets around warplanes that remain exposed.

The Ministry of Defense did not immediately confirm the reports, but British authorities have issued warnings recently about the rising threats posed by Russia and Iran, and the government has urged citizens to be prepared for various contingencies that could make access to fresh food, water and other essentials difficult for days.

In October, the head of Britain's domestic spy agency MI5 warned that Iran had made a "major shift" in its efforts to attack the U.K., including going after harder targets such as military bases,

He spoke weeks after authorities thwarted an alleged Iran-backed plot targeting the U.K. air base RAF Fairford . That incident, for which two men have since been charged with serious national security offenses, led the U.S. to withdraw all of its bomber aircraft , which had been used in strikes on Iran, from the base.

CBS/AFP

The Iran-backed Houthis reiterated on Wednesday their threat to target Jeddah and all Saudi Arabian ports on the Red Sea if the Saudis follow through on their threat to target Yemen's Hodeidah port, which is held by the rebels.

Hodeidah is the main entry point for food and other essential supplies into Houthi-held northern Yemen.

In a statement posted online , Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree called on "employees and workers at these ports, as well as those present in their vicinity, to evacuate them immediately and move away."

Shortly after Saree issued the warning, the Houthi-affiliated Al-Masirah TV network reported a Saudi attack on the port of Hodeidah.

The rebel group said earlier Wednesday that it had carried out two operations targeting the Ras Tanura refinery in Saudi Arabia's Eastern Province, as well as the financial center in Riyadh.

Saudi Arabia's Civil Defense agency said Tuesday that a skyscraper in the financial district had been targeted by a Houthi attack, injuring 11 people.

United Nations humanitarian relief chief Tom Fletcher said Wednesday that half of Yemen's population is in need of aid, as he arrived in the war-torn nation that has become the most active front in the intertwined Middle East conflicts.

Fletcher warned in a statement shared online that "renewed fighting has forced over 364,000 people from their homes since August, including tens of thousands this past week alone."

He repeated his demand for Yemen's Iran-backed Houthi rebels to "immediately and unconditionally release our detained UN colleagues " and other humanitarian workers and said the U.N.-led relief efforts in the country were overstretched, underfunded and under attack.

"Yemen is where we are furthest off track on our ambition to reach 87 million people with lifesaving support this year," Fletcher said. "We will not allow the people of Yemen to slip off the world's radar."

Iranian army spokesperson Brig. Gen. Mohammad Akraminia said the military had tightened its control and monitoring of the Strait of Hormuz on the orders of the army's commander-in-chief.

Ships attempting to transit the waterway without coordinating with Iran's armed forces have faced greater risks in recent weeks, including sea mines, Akraminia was quoted as saying Wednesday by the semi-official Tasnim news agency.

President Trump has dismissed Iran's claims attacks on ships and sea mines being laid in the strait as lies intended to inflate global energy prices, and the U.S. military declared international shipping lanes through the waterway free of mines at the end of October.

Without offering any evidence, however, Akraminia claimed Iranian forces had upgraded their monitoring capabilities by introducing new systems, improving existing ones and strengthening their combat abilities, and he said the measures would continue.

Iran's Persian Gulf Strait Authority (PGSA) said Tuesday that 26 tugboats had been added to the country's "Non-Compliance List," for providing services to non-compliant vessels, indicating they could be targeted.

Iran issues daily claims of commercial vessels striking mines in and near the strait, few of which are ever corroborated, but independent monitors do report frequent incidents involving "unknown projectiles" striking ships in the region.

Iran has denounced the U.S. military's use of artificial intelligence to plan and carry out attacks.

Speaking at a U.N. Security Council meeting Tuesday, Iranian Ambassador Gholamhossein Darzi said the weaponization of AI "raises serious concerns."

Darzi claimed U.S. forces used the technology to deploy more than 2,000 munitions to hit 2,000 distinct targets within 96 hours. He said Palantir's Maven and Anthropic's Claude system were used to analyze intelligence, identify and prioritize targets and provide strike coordinates.

"Neither advanced technology nor the involvement of private companies can shield the United States or the Israeli regime from accountability for flagrant violations of their obligations under international law," Darzi told the council meeting.

"Those responsible for the commission of atrocious crimes against Iranian people, including deliberate attacks against civilians and civilian objects, must face individual criminal accountability," he added.

In March 2026 , the Commander of U.S. Central Command Adm. Brad Cooper confirmed American forces had used a "variety of advanced AI tools" in order to "cut through the noise and make smarter decisions faster than the enemy can react."

While the Pentagon has not said exactly how AI tools are being deployed, CBS News spoke in March with several experts with knowledge of military operations who described the likely scenarios.

"The military is now processing roughly a thousand potential targets a day and striking the majority of them, with turnaround time for the next strike potentially under four hours," said retired Navy Admiral Mark Montgomery, senior director of the Foundation for Defense of Democracy's Center on Cyber and Technology Innovation. "A human is still in the loop, but AI is doing the work that used to take days of analysis — and doing it at a scale no previous campaign has matched."

Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis on Wednesday claimed attacks targeting the financial district in the Saudi capital and the sprawling Ras Tanura refinery in the kingdom's oil-rich east, in retaliation for strikes on their territory.

Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree described the attack targeting the refinery as "accurate and direct", saying it "caused fires to break out at the facility". He said the attack on Riyadh was "carried out in three phases, with strikes hitting their targets accurately".

In separate attacks, Saudi's forces said they had struck the city of Hodeida on Wednesday, after the Houthis said they would retaliate if that attack took place.

The Houthis have been locked in grueling, more than decade-long civil war against Yemen's government forces, who are backed by Saudi Arabia. Recent Houthi gains have consolidated the group's control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, which the group has tried to use to disrupt Saudi oil exports.

CBS/AFP

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz said on Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons, and vowed to stop Tehran from obtaining them.

"Iran is in the process of developing chemical weapons," Katz said in a briefing to Israeli reporters, according to public broadcaster KAN and other national outlets. "The state of Israel will not allow them to reach that capability."

In his briefing on Tuesday, Katz floated the possibility of a preemptive strike against Tehran, if necessary.

"If we recognize that the Iranians intend to attack Israel, can't we tell the army to attack earlier and thwart the threat?" he said, according to a transcript from Israel's Channel 12. "If the Iranians attack us first, it will be a failure."

Katz's comments came at the same time as Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi criticized the U.S. government for not funding the Organisation for the Prohibition of Chemical Weapons, the international body that monitors and combats chemical weapons use at The Hague. The organization is facing a budget crisis because the U.S. has pulled funding, according to a Reuters report.

"The U.S. is so concerned about chemical arms that it's crippling the world's chemical weapons watchdog," Araghchi wrote Tuesday on X. "OPCW may be forced to suspend work and scale back vital programs. By obstructing its mandate, the U.S. is deliberately putting global peace and security at risk. Shameful."

The OPCW won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2013 for its work in Syria.

CBS/AFP

A U.S. jury convicted Chinese tech giant Huawei Technologies on Tuesday of conspiring to steal trade secrets and doing business in countries subject to U.S. sanctions, including Iran.

In all, Huawei was convicted on 10 of 12 counts. The case in Brooklyn federal court involved no human defendants, but the company could be made to pay billions of dollars in penalties when it is sentenced next September.

The Department of Justice said Huawei and its subsidiaries assisted an Iranian intelligence apparatus called Zaeim in monitoring and censoring internet access. The company also provided surveillance cameras that helped Tehran monitor protest activity, according to the DOJ.

"Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the U.S. government that it did not assist Iran's government, military, or intelligence community; that it began restricting its business in Iran in 2011; that Skycom was a business partner, rather than a wholly-owned subsidiary; and that Huawei complied with all applicable sanctions," the DOJ said. "Huawei knew that all of those statements were materially false and misleading."

CBS/AP

scraped.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade postponed due to weather
scraped.description: New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's have decided to postpone the annual Thanksgiving Day parade, sources familiar with the decision told ABC News.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Macy's Thanksgiving Day parade postponed due to weather
scraped.body_text:
The parade will take place on Saturday, the department store said.

New York City officials, the NYPD and Macy's have decided to postpone the annual Thanksgiving Day parade due to unfavorable weather , the department store said Wednesday.

The forecast for New York City Thursday called for sustained winds between 20-22 miles per hour and gusts up to 40 miles per hour at 9 a.m., along with heavy rain. The approaching storm threatened to ground the balloons and drench spectators.

"The safety of our participants and spectators is our top priority, and after close consultation with our City and agency partners, we have made the decision to move this year's celebration," Macy's said in a statement Wednesday.

The parade will now take place on Saturday at 8:30 a.m., according to the department store.

The iconic balloons for this year's parade, the 100th parade, began to inflate Wednesday.

A city official told ABC News the balloons will be deflated beginning at 7 p.m. and will be re-inflated on Friday afternoon.

The parade has only been cancelled three times, in 1942, 1943 and 1944 due to the restrictions on helium and rubber for World War II efforts.

High winds grounded the balloons in 1971, and they have flown in the parade ever since.

Rough weather during the 2006 and 2019 parades forced the balloons to fly at lower heights.
