items.title: Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast
items.summary: The Army detonated several tons of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa.

scraped.title: Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast
scraped.description: The Army detonated several tons of lead azide at an ammunition plant in Iowa.
scraped.author: ABC News
scraped.h1: Federal officials say 'zero' airborne lead detected after Iowa munitions blast
scraped.body_text:
Several tons of lead azide were detonated on Wednesday.

Federal officials said preliminary reports on the Army's planned detonation of nearly five tons of lead azide at an Iowa ammunition plant Wednesday morning have found "zero" levels of airborne lead in the air, as smoke from the blast moves through communities.

The two controlled detonations of 68 barrels containing lead azide occurred simultaneously at approximately 9 a.m. CT/ 10 a.m. ET on Wednesday at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown, according to the Army.

Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, the commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said in a video statement later in the day that the blast "exceeded expectations."

"Every indication is that all of the munitions that were employed absolutely reduced the lead azide threat," he said.

The Environment Protection Agency said in a statement that "real-time air monitors are reporting ZERO detection of airborne lead."

"EPA monitors never stopped collecting data throughout the event," the agency said.

Robert Cekada, the director of the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms and Explosives, said in a video statement that the blast drove the explosion into the ground "and followed a blast channel that was designed to go down the right path to minimize any sort of dispersion of lead into the atmosphere."

The controversial plan raised concerns from the public, environmental organizations and medical groups over the potential impacts of the blast's anticipated lead dust plume.

According to the Army's latest guidance, the surface deposition of the explosive material's hazardous dust and materials may cover a 148 square-mile zone outside of the plant.

Missouri Gov. Mike Kehoe said in an X post after the explosion that "initial analysis shared with us by federal partners and Iowa Homeland Security and Emergency Management indicates that the mitigation measures appear to have been successful and the explosion was well-contained."

The detonation comes eight months after the Army said it discovered that the explosive bomb-making material had become unstable.

Due to the risks of an accidental, uncontrolled detonation in packing and moving the stockpile, the Army said it determined that the safest way to dispose of the degraded lead azide was to destroy it in place.

Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley, commanding general of the U.S. Army Sustainment Command, said that months of research determined there was no other way to safely get rid of the barrels.

"Inaction is no longer an option," Shirley said during a press conference on Tuesday.

The Army worked with experts to mitigate the effects of detonating nearly 9,700 pounds of the toxic and volatile substance, including using a waterwall, foam barriers and gel blocks to contain the explosion, according to acting Army Secretary Adam Telle.

Though mitigation efforts will be in place, a public advisory released by the Army on Tuesday recommended that Middletown residents and those in surrounding areas evacuate their homes ahead of the blast "out of an abundance of caution."

Those who evacuate will be updated by phone once the all-clear has been given, the advisory said.

The Environmental Protection Agency will be monitoring levels of lead, a neurotoxin, in the area "for as long as it takes that we have the comfort that the levels are back to safe levels," Tom Croci, the associate administrator for national security and operations coordination at the EPA, told reporters Tuesday.

Lead azide is the primary explosive used to detonate munitions, such as grenades and artillery shells.

The planned detonation of the degraded stockpile was originally scheduled for Friday, but the Army postponed it twice amid public concerns and a legal challenge.

The Iowa Environmental Council and Sierra Club Iowa Chapter filed an emergency motion on Thursday arguing that the detonation could spread lead dust across a large area, potentially reaching communities more than 100 miles from the plant.

In an order filed late Thursday night, the Eighth Circuit Court of Appeals granted an administrative stay of the permit while the federal appeals court considered the emergency request to formally halt the detonation.

President Donald Trump said Monday that he believes the "proper course is to get rid of this long term problem," but left the decision to the appeals court and incoming Iowa governor-elect Rob Sand.

The federal appeals court ultimately denied the emergency motion and lifted the administrative stay, allowing the operation to proceed.

"We are mindful of the very real risks presented by the Army's planned detonation of the stores of degraded lead azide. However, we must acknowledge the realities of the situation: the degraded explosives present a risk of an uncontrolled and unplanned explosion, which would occur without the benefit of the safety measures that the Permit puts in place," the opinion stated.

The two environmental groups said they would not attempt to further block the detonation following Monday's decision, but pushed the federal government to remain transparent about the operation with the public.

Sand, a Democrat, deferred to the Trump administration on moving forward with the federal operation while also calling for greater transparency.

The governor-elect said in a statement after the blast that he was grateful.

"The lead-up to the detonation should never have been so chaotic and unclear," Sand said in an X post Wednesday.

"Iowans across the state are understandably alarmed and scared. There must be immediate transparency to understand how and why this situation became what it did. And any Iowans who have been impacted in any way must be taken care of fully, right away," he added.

The Army said Wednesday morning will "allow for optimal weather conditions and all mitigation measures to be emplaced."

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) activated an emergency response to assist with the Iowa detonation, the agency said Tuesday.

The CDC said it is supporting Iowa's health department to help protect people from potential lead and air pollution exposure, as well as activating a team with expertise in toxicology, communication and public health emergency response.

Ahead of the detonation, Iowa Gov. Kim Reynolds issued a disaster emergency proclamation for several counties to activate the "disaster response and recovery aspects" of the detonation.

Illinois and Missouri were also bracing for potential impacts, though officials in both states said they expected them to be minimal.

Reynolds' office said Tuesday up to 100 federally activated Iowa National Guard soldiers would assist with evacuation efforts, including outreach to approximately 150 households identified by local and federal authorities.

Federal officials recommended that residents in the impacted area -- in particular pregnant women, children under the age of six and those with a chronic illness -- evacuate due to the potential lead exposure.

Some Middletown residents taped up their windows and garage doors to protect from the blast and dust plume and could be seen evacuating with their families ahead of the planned detonation.

Alec Patterson told ABC News ahead of the detonation that he and his pregnant wife were planning to leave.

"We just want to do everything we can to make sure that she's safe and the baby is safe," he said.

"It's terrifying," Patterson said, adding, "The lead dust stuff is the biggest concern, I think for everybody."

ABC News' Steve Beynon and Mason Leib contributed to this report.

items.title: Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double
items.summary: Bruno Fernandes nets twice in Lisbon, but referee's decisions in spotlight as Mauricio Pochettino denied first win.

scraped.title: Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double
scraped.description: Bruno Fernandes nets twice in Lisbon, but referee’s decisions in spotlight as Mauricio Pochettino denied first win.
scraped.h1: Man United denied at Sporting as referee overshadows Fernandes double
scraped.body_text:
Bruno Fernandes nets twice in Lisbon, but referee’s decisions in spotlight as Mauricio Pochettino denied first win.

Save

Share

Mauricio Pochettino must wait for his first win as Manchester United coach after a wild 2-2 Champions League draw at Sporting Lisbon on Wednesday, with the hosts equalising thanks to a goalkeeping error from Senne Lammens.

The Belgian stopper’s poor handling allowed Luis Suarez to complete a brace for the hosts, cancelling out United playmaker Bruno Fernandes’s double against his former side.

United gave away two penalties in the first half, the second converted by Suarez, before Fernandes equalised from the spot early in the second half.

Fernandes sent United ahead with a lucky bounce taking his effort over the Sporting goalkeeper, before Suarez’s acrobatic effort levelled the game.

United midfielder Youri Tielemans was sent off in stoppage time for a second yellow card to end a compelling and often erratic match.

A crushing 4-0 defeat by rivals Liverpool in the Premier League at the weekend, leaving United 19th, was a disastrous first game at the helm for Pochettino after replacing Michael Carrick.

Pochettino brought Harry Maguire into the three-man defence as he shuffled his pack, as well as starting Joshua Zirkzee in place of the suspended Matheus Cunha.

Neither side took many risks in the opening stages, with few chances of note until the game burst into life midway through the first half as United lost control.

Lisandro Martinez brought down Geny Catamo in the area and Sporting were awarded a penalty.

The hosts blew their chance from the spot, with Suarez’s scuffed effort easily saved by Lammens, but the Red Devils gave away another spot kick just a couple of minutes later.

Goalkeeper Lammens came flying off his line and clattered Maxi Araujo, and this time Colombian striker Suarez made no mistake from the spot.

– United unhappy with disallowed goals –

United thought they had equalised when Amad Diallo hit the crossbar and then nodded home the rebound, but the goal was disallowed to their dismay.

Youri Tielemans was ruled to have fouled Goncalo Inacio, although he seemed to win the ball, upsetting United further after Leny Yoro’s controversial red card against Liverpool on Sunday that was later rescinded.

Fernandes pulled United level early in the second half from the spot after Eduardo Quaresma brought down Martinez.

The former Sporting playmaker calmly stroked his penalty beyond the dive of Kaique Pereira into the bottom left corner.

Fernandes said on the eve of the game he had stopped contract talks because he wanted to focus on helping United improve their form after a dire start to the season.

The midfielder soon had his second goal, with the help of a bizarre bounce off a divot on the pitch.

Fernandes’s low effort from distance seemed bound for Pereira’s hands, but suddenly bounced up off a patch of uneven turf and fortuitously over the goalkeeper’s head.

The Portugal international bent a free-kick narrowly off target as he looked to complete his hat-trick.

Lammens saved well from Sergi Altimira to protect United’s lead as Sporting battled to find an equaliser.

It eventually came from a howler from Lammens, who failed to claim a cross dropping out of the sky, spilling the ball in front of Suarez, who produced a hooked acrobatic effort to score.

Moments later United had the ball in the net at the other end after another goalkeeping error by Pereira, who mishandled Fernandes’s corner, pushing the ball into his own net.

However what would have been the winner was disallowed for an elbow by Patrick Dorgu on the goalkeeper, a decision the visitors were also unhappy about.

items.title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
items.summary: About 200,000 tents need replacing, Gaza’s municipalities say, as the EU urges Israel to reopen all crossings.

scraped.title: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
scraped.description: About 200,000 tents need replacing, Gaza’s municipalities say, as the EU urges Israel to reopen all crossings.
scraped.author: Al Jazeera Staff
scraped.h1: Winter rains threaten 1,000 Gaza shelter sites, councils warn
scraped.body_text:
About 200,000 tents need replacing, Gaza’s municipalities say, as the European Union urges Israel to reopen all crossings into the territory to aid.

Save

Share

Gaza’s municipalities have warned that winter rains could flood about 1,000 camps and other sites hosting displaced Palestinians in the war-torn enclave, adding that damage to drains and sewers, and a shortage of pumps, have left their crews with little means to clear the water.

After a meeting in Gaza City on Wednesday, the Union of Gaza Strip Municipalities singled out al-Mughraqa and al-Zahra in central Gaza, where water levels in Wadi Gaza could rise suddenly. Across the territory, about 200,000 tents need replacing, and more than 2,000 damaged buildings are at risk of collapse, the union said. Gaza’s Government Media Office had warned on Tuesday that it expected another storm within days.

This is Gaza’s fourth winter since Israel launched its war in October 2023. The union said storms in early November flooded about 70,000 tents and affected more than 350,000 displaced people. During a winter storm this November, families piled sand at tent entrances to keep out the rain. Others carried their children out and salvaged what belongings they could.

One displaced mother said she had cut up the burial shroud she had bought for her son and used it to patch her tent. She wanted to keep the family’s bedding and clothes dry. “I couldn’t get a tarpaulin,” she said.

When the first rains hit, Gaza’s civil defence crews reached only a minority of those who called for help. Most of the other callers received advice by phone, Al Jazeera reported .

In Brussels on Wednesday, the European Commission called on Israel to reopen all Gaza crossings to humanitarian aid. Commission spokesperson Eva Hrncirova said tents were waiting on trucks outside Gaza because Israel had not allowed them or the equipment needed to put them up to enter.

The UN said earlier this month that more than 150,000 tents were awaiting entry into Gaza.

Al Jazeera’s open-source unit (Ar.) measured a queue of trucks stretching about 1.1km (0.7 miles) along the Egyptian road to the Rafah crossing in a November 17 satellite image, up from about 460 metres (1,510 feet) on October 6. The images do not establish what the trucks carried. Freight from Egypt is routed through the Karem Abu Salem crossing, known as Kerem Shalom in Israel, for inspection rather than entering Gaza through Rafah.

COGAT, the Israeli military body that coordinates aid, said that nearly 100,000 tents had entered Gaza since the start of a winter aid programme. It said Israel would allow reconstruction equipment into Gaza only after Hamas had fully disarmed.

Inside Gaza, aid workers have cleared drains, installed flood barriers and reinforced shelters. The UN’s humanitarian affairs office reported on November 20 that teams had recorded such work at 162 of the 356 flood-prone locations they had identified. Gaza’s municipalities are asking for pumps, backup generators and fuel before the next storm, as well as 10,000 tonnes of cement for emergency repairs and mobile homes that can withstand wind and rain.

items.title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
items.summary: Virginia schools face scrutiny after revelations of abuse and widespread failures in mandatory staff background checks.

scraped.title: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
scraped.description: Virginia schools face scrutiny after revelations of abuse and widespread failures in mandatory staff background checks.
scraped.author: Umar Farooq
scraped.h1: US Education Department probes Virginia schools after sexual abuse scandal
scraped.body_text:
Virginia schools face scrutiny after revelations of abuse and widespread failures in mandatory staff background checks.

Save

Share

The United States Department of Education says it is launching an investigation and withholding funding from a district in the state of Virginia after local officials shut down all of its schools in the wake of a child sexual abuse scandal involving its employees.

“Parents should never have to question whether their child’s school is aiding and abetting child predators,” US Secretary of Education Linda McMahon said in a statement on Tuesday. “The Trump Administration is taking decisive enforcement action to hold those responsible accountable and ensure Virginia schools are safe places for children to learn.”

Officials in Albemarle County, Virginia, announced they were closing all 29 schools in the district last week, after learning that more than 500 staff had not been subjected to a routine background screening for a history of child sexual abuse. The school system has about 2,800 employees, and only a fraction of its $284m budget comes from the federal government.

Local officials emphasised that none of the 524 employees is suspected of abuse.

Approximately 14,000 students attend the schools, and parents have scrambled to find childcare, while many who depend on free school meals for their children have had to look for other sources of food.

Bob Beard, a member of the Albemarle school board, told Al Jazeera that families were struggling to deal with the shutdown, but schools would reopen on Monday.

The child abuse allegations have shaken the county and caught the attention of the Trump administration.

A former elementary school teacher was arrested for possession of child sexual abuse material earlier this year, while a counsellor at another school was put on leave and later indicted on 20 counts of sexual crimes involving seven different children, according to the Albemarle County Police Department.

Two county school officials and a school principal were later charged with failure to report child abuse, and the county’s superintendent of schools resigned.

Jason Grant, a spokesman for Albemarle County Public Schools, told Al Jazeera that none of the individuals implicated in those cases was among the 524 employees who were hired without the proper screening required to check for a history of child sexual abuse.

“This was not about having the policies in place, this was about processes that were not followed,” Grant said. He said officials were working with the state to “make sure the processes are in place to make sure this doesn’t happen again.”

Grant said all employees in the district undergo several stages of vetting, including a criminal background check and an attestation that they have no history of child abuse or neglect. Then the school system submits their information to the Virginia Department of Social Services to verify that they are not part of the agency’s abuse and neglect database.

For three years, it appears that vetting procedures were not consistently applied. Putting employees hired over that period on leave to carry out background checks meant schools would not be able to run, so officials decided to close them until next week.

“Those were for every range of employee, from teachers to bus drivers to substitutes and across the division, so we couldn’t get coverage for that amount of people,” Grant said.

All but three of the 524 employees have now been properly vetted, and none had background issues, Grant said, adding that the county will reopen schools on Monday.

The Trump administration has long called for the dismantling of the Department of Education. The US president signed an executive order last year that tried to set that in motion.

The department, which distributes federal funding to states for use in schools, also traditionally investigates whether local officials are complying with civil rights laws banning discrimination against minorities and marginalised groups.

Since returning to office in 2025, the Trump administration has cut more than half of the department’s staff and subjected it to wider changes it says are aimed at rooting out “diversity, equity, and inclusion” (DEI) policies.

items.title: Egypt: At least 31 dead after fuel truck overturns on highway
items.summary: The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances are responding to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.

scraped.title: Egypt: At least 31 dead after fuel truck overturns on Giza highway near Cairo
scraped.description: The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances are responding to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.
scraped.h1: Egypt: At least 31 dead after fuel truck overturns near Cairo
scraped.body_text:
The accident occurred on the packed Ring Road in Giza near Cairo. Dozens of ambulances are responding to the crash, and Egyptian health authorities say the death toll could rise.

A fuel truck overturned on a packed highway in Giza, Egypt, on Wednesday, killing 31 people and injuring 21 more, according to Egyptian authorities.

The fuel tanker crash ignited a massive blaze on Ring Road in Giza's Waraq district. The Ring Road encircles the greater Cairo metropolitan area.

Egyptian Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were transported to nearby hospitals and added that the death toll could rise further. He said 39 ambulances are responding to the accident.

A massive fire broke out after the accident, with rescue workers pulling people from their vehicles. A large crowd gathered in the densely populated Waraq neighborhood amid the rescue efforts.

The blaze left at least 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, charred.

An investigation has been launched into the crash, according to Egypt's public prosecutor. DNA tests are being carried out to identify badly burned victims of the blaze.

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his deepest condolences and sympathy to the victims and directed relevant authorities to provide necessary support to the families of the victims and the injured.

Other countries also reacted to the crash in Giza.

Italian Foreign Affairs Minister Antonio Tajani said he extended his "deepest solidarity to the victims' families," Egyptian Foreign Minister Badr Abdelatty "and to the Egyptian people, whom I count as friends, at this tragic time."

The Algerian Ambassador to Egypt, Mohamed Sofiane Berrah, also said the Embassy of Algeria in Cairo extends "its deepest condolences and heartfelt sympathy to the sisterly Arab Republic of Egypt."

Car accidents are frequent in Egypt due to poor road conditions, reckless driving and lax enforcement of safety rules.

items.title: Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
items.summary: Nigeria's anti-drug agency said Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern state of Enugu.

scraped.title: Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
scraped.description: Nigeria's anti-drug agency said Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern state of Enugu.
scraped.h1: Nigeria detains 5 Mexicans, confiscates over $220 million of meth
scraped.body_text:
Nigeria's anti-drug agency said Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern state of Enugu.

Nigeria's National Drug Law Enforcement Agency (NDLA) said Wednesday it had arrested five Mexicans and confiscated over $220 million (around €200 million) in methamphetamine as part of a significant drug bust.

The agency said the Mexican experts were allegedly recruited by a Nigerian national to run a meth laboratory in the southeastern Nigerian state of Enugu.

"A total of 1,512 kilograms of methamphetamine, finished and in production, with an estimated value of $226.8 million was recovered from the clandestine factory," NDLA spokesperson Femi Babafemi said.

Nigeria first rejected the entry of the Mexicans into the country in August. They later entered Nigeria again in September via neighboring Benin using forged passports, with authorities then putting them under surveillance.

On November 11, the Mexicans were taken into custody at the Enugu lab after their movements were tracked by the Nigerian government. A Nigerian was also arrested in a nearby hotel.

The latest drug bust comes after Nigerian authorities in May also detained 10 people in a anti-meth operation in the southwest, including three Mexicans.

The arrests raise concern that Mexican cartels are getting a foothold in Africa for international drug trafficking. In addition to Nigeria, South Africa is another country where Mexicans have been arrested for being involved in a meth lab.

According to Vanda Felbab-Brown, an expert at the Washington DC-based Brookings Institution, Mexican cartels such as the Sinaloa Cartel and the Cartel de Jalisco Nueva Generation (CJNG) have expanded their operations into other continents such as Africa.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In a June testimony to the US Senate Caucus on International Narcotics Control , Felbab-Brown said the cartels find "desirable partners" for production in countries such as South Africa and Kenya due to factors such as "limited law enforcement capacities and entrenched criminal and corrupt networks."

According to the UN Office on Drugs and Crime, criminal networks often take advantage of porous borders in the West and Central Africa region to carry out activities such as illicit drug trafficking.

"Many countries in the region have vast territory and borders are located either in very remote or densely populated areas, thus making law enforcement activities particularly difficult to conduct in an efficient manner," the office said. "The porous nature of the borders in West and Central Africa is a major factor of insecurity: the borders are neither demarcated or sufficiently controlled."

scraped.title: Magyar meets Zelenskyy: Hungary and Ukraine make a fresh start after the icy relations of the Orban era
scraped.description: After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.
scraped.h1: Thawing of relations: Hungary and Ukraine turn a new page
scraped.body_text:
After years of frosty and hostile relations under Hungary's Kremlin-friendly former PM Viktor Orban, his successor, Peter Magyar, and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy seek to reset their countries' ties.

The location and the gesture were carefully chosen: Hungarian Prime Minister Peter Magyar and Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy stood side by side, laid flowers and bowed their heads at the military cemetery in the center of the Ukrainian city of Uzhhorod.

One of those buried there is an ethnic Hungarian who was one of the first soldiers killed in Russia's full-scale war of aggression against Ukraine .

Magyar intentionally chose not to begin his first visit to Ukraine as prime minister at a government building. Instead, his Tuesday afternoon visit began at a place where he could demonstrate his solidarity with Ukraine more clearly than anywhere else.

Uzhhorod, known as Ungvar in Hungarian, is the capital of Ukraine's Transcarpathia region, which is home to around 80,000 members of Ukraine's Hungarian minority. Thousands of ethnic Hungarians are fighting Russian occupying forces on the front lines.

For Hungary , where ethnic Hungarian minorities in neighboring countries traditionally play an important role, the war is therefore closer to home than it is for other European countries.

Magyar described his visit to Ukraine as a "historic day" in a Facebook post. Before the ceremony at the cemetery in Uzhhorod, he said: "I bring with me the solidarity of the Hungarian people. We stand with Ukraine against the Russian aggressor."

Zelenskyy responded on X, saying "We appreciate this gesture of respect toward those who sacrificed their lives for Ukraine's independence."

The meeting between Magyar and Zelenskyy marked a turning point in Hungary's approach to Ukraine.

The two leaders repeatedly shook hands throughout the day. Such scenes would have been unthinkable just a few months ago. The propaganda of Magyar's pro-Russian predecessor, Viktor Orban , portrayed Ukraine as a "mafia state" and "lawless country" on an almost daily basis.

Under Orban, relations between Hungary and Ukraine reached a historic low .

Now the two countries are seeking a political reset, which is important not only for Hungary and Ukraine but for Europe as a whole. After all, Orban's repeated obstruction of support for Ukraine drove the EU to the brink of despair.

During talks in Uzhhorod, the two leaders also agreed to closer economic cooperation.

The talks centered on Hungarian diesel supplies to Ukraine, greater use of Ukrainian gas storage facilities by Hungarian companies, and joint infrastructure projects, including the opening of new border crossings and a direct rail link between Budapest and Kyiv.

Nevertheless, no formal agreements were signed on Tuesday.

At a subsequent news conference, journalists asked questions about sensitive issues between the two countries: minority rights, Ukraine's EU integration and a new EU loan for Ukraine.

Throughout the day, the two men were visibly keen to avoid any discord.

Magyar, for example, described his angry outburst over Ukraine's "Carpathian Eight" initiative in parliament in late September as a "misunderstanding" and suggested that Hungary might, after all, take part.

Zelenskyy's cautious replies to journalists suggest that he knows his country's path to EU membership also runs through Budapest.

One of Magyar's statements on Tuesday was key: "We've finally put a stop to this completely unnecessary and inexplicable political escalation."

Even before taking office in early May 2026, Magyar had promised to reset relations with Ukraine. But the process has not been entirely smooth.

In many respects — but certainly not all — Magyar is distancing himself from his predecessor. He has made no bones of the fact that he sees Russia as the aggressor, but he rejects both arms deliveries to Ukraine and even the transit of weapons across Hungarian territory.

Magyar previously accused Ukraine of treating ethnic Hungarians as second-class citizens — a claim that is not borne out by the facts. He pressed for greater minority rights and for a time blocked the opening of negotiating chapters in Ukraine's EU accession talks.

Magyar also departed from diplomatic convention by choosing the location of his meeting with Zelenskyy in Ukraine: Indeed, it was Magyar who invited Zelenskyy to Transcarpathia.

Magyar's sometimes confrontational tone toward Ukraine can also be explained by the need to avoid appearing too pro-Ukrainian to the Hungarian public.

According to a November 2026 poll conducted by the think tank Globsec , 33% of Hungarians would now support their country providing military aid to Ukraine. Although this is much more than during Orban's time in office, many Hungarians remain skeptical of Ukraine.

That's why Olena Halushka, a Ukrainian political scientist at the International Centre for Ukrainian Victory (ICUV), sees some aspects of Magyar's visit as a concession to public opinion in Hungary.

"Magyar has taken over a deeply polarized country," she told DW's Ukrainian Service. "A visit to Transcarpathia is more of a step for the Hungarian population than for Ukraine."

Ukraine accommodated not only Magyar's choice of location but also Hungary's demands for better protection of minority rights, which were set out in a 10-point plan in June. That's because EU integration is one of the country's top political priorities.

After planned restrictions on the use of minority languages were withdrawn in late 2023, Ukraine's parliament in early October passed a law on minority language rights that in some respects goes even further than European standards.

Hungary subsequently dropped its obstruction of the opening of negotiating clusters for Ukraine's EU accession.

Laszlo Zubanics, chairman of the Hungarian Democratic Federation in Ukraine (UMDSZ, one of two Hungarian political parties in Transcarpathia), told DW that the Magyar-Zelenskyy meeting was "historic."

He particularly welcomed the fact that Ukraine will probably implement practical improvements in the protection of minority rights "not only by the end of 2027, but much sooner, within just a few months."

A Hungarian diplomat who spoke to DW on condition of anonymity also called the meeting "historic," adding that after the Orban government's anti-Ukrainian policies, trust now needs to be rebuilt, and that personal meetings between the two leaders play an important role in that process.

The diplomat went on to say that Hungary not only wants to ensure that the rights of the Hungarian minority are protected, it also has a strong interest in being involved in Ukraine's reconstruction.

Overall, the diplomat concluded, both sides are very keen to expand economic cooperation.

Hungarian political scientist Daniel Hegedus of the Institute for European Politics ( IEP ) in Berlin told DW that while the meeting was a "symbolic milestone," it will be important to see "how the two political leaders capitalize on the symbolic political capital generated by this meeting."

No observers have suggested that this is the grand finale of reconciliation between Hungary and Ukraine.

Nevertheless, Tuesday's reset sends an important signal to Europe, namely that if the political will is there, a deep gulf that has existed for years can be transformed into a set of diverging interests that can be addressed through negotiations.

Or, as Zelenskyy put it, now there are "all the opportunities to build hopefully constructive relations."

This article was originally published in German.

items.title: NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon
items.summary: NATO's deputy commander offers a markedly different assessment of Canada's military than the Pentagon, praising its contribution to European deterrence and efforts to rebuild its forces in an exclusive broadcast interview with CBC News.

scraped.title: NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon | CBC News
scraped.description: NATO's deputy commander offers a markedly different assessment of Canada's military than the Pentagon, praising its contribution to European deterrence and efforts to rebuild its forces in an exclusive broadcast interview with CBC News.
scraped.h1: NATO's No. 2 commander strikes different tone on Canada than Pentagon
scraped.body_text:
The deputy commander of NATO said he's happy with Canada's contribution to the Western allies' deterrence mission in Eastern Europe and offered qualified praise on Wednesday for the country's efforts to rebuild its forces.

British Air Chief Marshal Sir John Stringer sat down with CBC News in Ottawa for an exclusive broadcast interview amid the ongoing political fight between the Pentagon and the government of Prime Minister Mark Carney over defence spending and military readiness.

Senior officials at the U.S. Department of War have been waging an increasingly public campaign to force Canada to spend more on defence in the short term, saying the country is not meeting its NORAD and NATO commitments because of a poor readiness among its forces.

Separately, a senior U.S. Department of War official, speaking on background, warned the Pentagon was prepared to "up the ante" on recent restrictions it had imposed on interaction with the Canadian military unless Ottawa took Washington's concerns more seriously.

Canada 'spending well' on NATO commitments: NATO's 2nd in command in Europe

"I won't get drawn on what other nations may say," said Stringer.

"What I do look at in Canada now is a nation putting significant forces into Europe, most obviously, but not exclusively the multinational brigade in Latvia. I look at a nation that is recapitalizing its investments in its forces."

Asked directly whether he was satisfied with the readiness of the Canadian-led brigade in Latvia, Stringer responded: "I'm happy when I look at Canada."

At the moment, there are roughly 2,200 Canadian troops in Latvia with a plan to increase the number to 2,600 in the near term.

As Pentagon blasts Canada's defence spending, Carney says Trump hasn't raised concerns

Aside from contributing a battle group, Canada serves as the commander of the 3,000-strong NATO multinational brigade, a deployment which Carney recently extended until 2031 .

The commitment to Operation Reassurance, according to the recent federal budget, will amount to $7 billion during that timeframe.

Canada isn't alone in terms of where it is on the curve of rebuilding its forces and is making the necessary investments, said Stringer, who is next in line to NATO Supreme Allied Commander Europe (SACEUR), U.S. Gen. Alexus Grynkewich.

"Everybody had that wonderful moment of — we won the Cold War and it created both physical disinvestment and it also created a bit of conceptual disinvestment," Stringer said.

"A bunch of nations now are coming out of some relatively low spends and I look at Canada as one of those nations that's spending well."

On Monday, the Pentagon publicly released a "fact sheet" that said Canada is not a credible defence partner and that military spending is unfocused. The document pointed to subpar Canadian military readiness statistics and deferred modernizations of key equipment.

Pentagon takes aim at Canada's military readiness

"Ottawa's prioritization of parochial economic and commercial interests over military optimization introduces further uncertainty for NORAD and will further burden our Joint Force and the American taxpayer," the fact sheet said.

But Canada is hardly alone among NATO allies in struggling with military readiness, including the United States itself.

The U.S. Government Accountability Office told Congress in March that American military readiness had deteriorated over the past two decades. Twenty-five of 27 types of its army and air force aircraft failed to meet their operational availability targets in 2024.

A separate audit, published in June, found the mission-capable rate for the American F-35 fleet had plunged from 67 per cent in 2021 to 44 per cent last year. Only 25 per cent were capable of performing all their assigned missions.

Senior U.S. Navy officials said last year that readiness across their fleet of ships, submarines and aircraft hovered between 67 and 70 per cent.

Britain, meanwhile, refuses to publicly disclose detailed military readiness figures, citing national security. Parliamentary research published this year showed all three branches were below their trained personnel targets.

France has similarly restricted publication of readiness data. Its 2023 figures projected operational availability of 69 per cent for combat aircraft, 59 per cent for frigates and 87 per cent for battle tanks.

Germany has also classified detailed equipment readiness figures, making direct comparisons with Canada's military particularly difficult.

"If I look at where Canada is in that mix, it looks a lot like a lot of other nations," said Stringer.

"Readiness can always be improved. You can always be better tomorrow than you are today. And indeed that's one of the focuses we've got with all the nations in the alliance."

Going into a meeting of the Liberal caucus on Wednesday, the prime minister weighed in and dismissed the controversy with the Pentagon.

Carney says Trump 'has not raised' Canada's military investments in conversations

"I can assure you that in my discussions with the president of the United States, we're focused on conflict resolution around the world and he has not raised issues such as has been reported recently," Carney said.

"Canada is taking responsibility for our defence. We're at the front lines of NATO's defence, Operation Reassurance in Latvia. We're working with our NATO partners, including the U.S. but very much with the Nordics — with Germany, with France — through the High North, the Arctic."

As Canada and the U.S. debate commitment and investment, Stringer and the rest of NATO's supreme command has focused on Russia's rising campaign of grey zone warfare in Europe.

Uncertainty is the point: The growing drone campaign stalking NATO’s skies

Last week, t hree Russian KH-101 cruise missiles crashed in southeastern Poland during a large-scale overnight Russian attack on Ukraine. There were no injuries or infrastructure damage. One missile landed about 35 kilometres from where troops from 11 allied countries were conducting military exercises to prepare for a potential postwar mission in Ukraine.

Polish Prime Minister Donald Tusk called the airspace violation an "intentional provocation" by Russia.

Stringer was not prepared to go that far, saying an investigation was still being conducted.

"What we're really looking at is, why did they go there? And fundamentally … was it deliberate or was it accidental?" Stringer told CBC News.

"And by the way, even if it's accidental, what does it tell us about a recklessness in warfare five years into their three-day special military operation?"

He said Russia is always seeking to provoke. The question for NATO is how to respond.

"What we don't need to do is do Mr. Putin's job for him by overreacting," Stringer said. "What we need to do is be calm and measured and resolute in the approach to provocations. And by the way, not every military act needs, even warrants, some form of military response."

Senior reporter, defence and security

Murray Brewster is the senior defence writer for CBC News, based in Ottawa. He has covered the Canadian military and foreign policy from Parliament Hill for over a decade. Among other assignments, he spent a total of 15 months on the ground covering the Afghan war for The Canadian Press. Prior to that, he covered defence issues and politics for CP in Nova Scotia for 11 years and was bureau chief for Standard Broadcast News in Ottawa.

items.title: At least 31 dead after fuel tanker fire in Egypt
items.summary: Thirty-one people were killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned on a major ring road in Egypt, authorities said on Wednesday.

scraped.title: At least 31 dead after fuel tanker fire in Egypt | CBC News
scraped.description: Thirty-one people were killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned on a major ring road in Egypt, authorities said on Wednesday.
scraped.h1: At least 31 dead after fuel tanker fire in Egypt
scraped.body_text:
Thirty-one people were killed and 21 wounded in a fire after a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned on a major ring road in Egypt, authorities said on Wednesday.

The fire broke out above a tunnel in Giza's Al-Warraq district, the public prosecution said. Preliminary estimates found that 27 vehicles, including cars and motorcycles, had been charred, it said, adding that casualty figures and damage were still being assessed.

The prosecution ordered DNA samples to be taken from the bodies of victims who had not yet been identified to establish their identities.

Thirty-nine ambulances took part in rescue operations, the health ministry said.

People look at the charred remains of a vehicle at the crash site. (Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters)

Videos circulating on social media showed thick plumes of smoke billowing from the scene.

Reuters verified the location from the buildings and road layout, which matched archive and satellite imagery of the area. The date was confirmed through the original file's metadata. The date was also confirmed through local media reports and a statement from the health ministry.

"The cars were charred, with people inside them. They did not have time to get out," Ali Youssef, who was at the scene, said. "The fire burned the vehicles and the people inside."

Another burned vehicle at the crash site on Wednesday. (Amr Abdallah Dalsh/Reuters)

Reuters footage from the scene in Giza showed firefighting vehicles, charred cars and minibuses, burnt motorcycles and debris scattered across the major ring road, while people and security personnel inspected the aftermath and a bulldozer moved damaged vehicles.

The ring road connects key highways across Greater Cairo, linking the governorates of Cairo, Giza and Qalyubia.

Road accidents are common in Egypt due to factors including speeding, weak enforcement of traffic regulations and poor road conditions.

Death toll rises to 39 after migrant boat capsizes off Senegal

Tanker ship collides with riverboat carrying 129 people in New Orleans

The number of people killed in road accidents rose 10.8 per cent to 5,829 in 2025 from 5,260 a year earlier, according to the state statistics agency CAPMAS.

Egypt has expanded its road network in recent years, building highways and bridges under a broader infrastructure program aimed at easing congestion and accommodating rapid population growth and urban expansion. The projects have improved traffic flow in some areas, but concerns over road safety persist.

items.title: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government
items.summary: As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the provincial government with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.

scraped.title: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government | CBC News
scraped.description: As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the provincial government with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.
scraped.h1: Suspected North Korean computer programmers did contract work for B.C. government
scraped.body_text:
Four computer programmers who did contract work for the British Columbia government were likely North Korean operatives, CBC's the fifth estate has learned.

Between 2023 and 2025, the four were hired to work on the province’s business registry platform.

As part of a contract worth hundreds of thousands of dollars to supply the province with software developers, an IT staffing firm based in B.C.’s Lower Mainland facilitated the hiring of a man calling himself Kevin Zhang.

"Kevin's resume was ideal for the situation that I was dealing with," said the owner of the staffing firm. He spoke with the fifth estate on the condition that he and his company not be named. He said due to the nature of remote hiring, he was completely unaware he hired likely North Koreans.

Over the last year, the fifth estate has been investigating North Korean IT workers and how they, like Zhang, have been able to infiltrate Canadian businesses and government.

"With Zhang, he's pretty known," said Michael Barnhart, a former U.S. Army intelligence officer who investigates North Korea for the private sector.

"I had tracked him before. There's a couple crypto companies that had tracked him before. A couple of other just different industries that had been tracking him. And everyone had a different piece of the puzzle."

The photo from Kevin Zhang’s website, left, does not match that of the passports saved to his GitHub account, right. (kzdev420/GitHub)

Alongside the confirmation of experts like Barnhart, the fifth estate found multiple online clues that point toward North Korean IT worker tradecraft:

In an online profile Zhang used to do work for the B.C. government, he stored two fake Chinese passports. The place of birth for the holder is the Chinese province of Liaoning, which directly borders North Korea. The U.S. Department of the Treasury has previously sanctioned companies operating IT worker cells in Liaoning.

The names on the passports appear to have been modified, with neither matching the name on the bottom stripe of the document.

A resumé-style website for Zhang contained a headshot that did not match the photo on the passports.

"This is the same guy that also goes by Kevin Chang, too," Barnhart said. "Sometimes he’ll only go by that.

"Chang, Ching or Zhang, just different variations of the beginning or ending name."

As time went on, the B.C. government hired three more remote developers via the same IT staffing firm. The owner of the firm told the fifth estate that each was recommended by Zhang, who said they were former colleagues.

The owner said the B.C. government made the ultimate decision to hire them and would have conducted a 30-minute interview focused on competency.

The fifth estate reached out to multiple people and entities within the B.C. government, but received no response or was told that because of the provincial election, which concluded Oct. 24, the government would not be able to provide a response.

In response to a freedom of information request, the fifth estate was told that the ministry where Zhang worked could not locate an employee by that name, despite having been provided the account details that logged his specific contributions to a ministry software project.

Beyond the fake Chinese passports and differing headshots, an investigation of Zhang and his colleagues conducted by the fifth estate revealed numerous other oddities.

For instance, a resumé for Zhang found online, which listed the B.C. government as a prior employer, stated his address was "Main St. E, North Bay, ON," with the street number absent.

In email correspondence provided to the fifth estate by the B.C. staffing firm, Zhang and the other developers can be seen repeatedly changing their banking information.

"In retrospect, there's a highly unusual situation to have somebody change their bank, change their company," the B.C. staffing firm’s owner said. "I think in the years that I've been doing this, right, this happened once before, twice before."

This is a red flag, according to cybersecurity expert Barnhart.

"I’ve had the same bank account at my employer for decades. I’ve never told my company to change it, ever. If I have, it would have been once. If I’d have done it twice, that would have been like: 'What are you doing?’"

At one point last year, Zhang asked to be paid to the bank account for a company called Dev Dragon Inc. Corporate records show Dev Dragon , now defunct, was registered by a James Zhang at a derelict building in Dawson City, Yukon.

The registered address for DevDragon Inc. was a long-abandoned bank building in Dawson City, Yukon. (CBC)

One of the other remote workers, Brandon Galli, had a similarly confusing digital footprint. On the account connected to his position working on B.C. government code, Galli’s profile photo is of an Asian man. However, his closely linked personal website provides a photo of a Caucasian man.

In an email obtained by the fifth estate , Galli asked for his pay to go to the account of an Ontario company called Luk Castle Investments, registered to a home in Markham by a man named Kenny Luk.

According to his LinkedIn, Luk did computer programming jobs for a number of Canadian banks before starting a software development consultancy.

When the fifth estate contacted Luk to ask about Brendan Galli and the money paid to him, he said that "Luk Castle Investments does not participate in media inquiries or respond to unsolicited questions regarding its business activities. Neither I nor anyone associated with the company will be providing comment on this matter."

It is a common practice for North Korean IT workers to use a real person’s identity to commit their fraud. (GitHub/Brandongalli.io)

The fifth estate tracked down the real Brandon Galli in New Jersey. When told that someone using his identity had worked for the B.C. government, he said his identity might have been stolen.

But pressed further, he admitted he gave his identity to someone he was working with online. He said this person continues to use his identity without his permission, causing him a host of problems.

Ontario architect's seal forged by remote worker believed to be North Korean fraudster

Binance says $6.3B US hacked in what could be largest cryptocurrency theft ever

"It was before the pandemic. We were working together on upwork and freelancing platforms and I was receiving small payouts for a short time while I was in college just to pay for food," Galli told the fifth estate in a WhatsApp message.

Barnhart has seen this same pattern play out before.

"You'll see them targeting college students a lot that might need some money," he said.

"Where it's like: 'Hey, I don't want anything from you, I just need — can I use your LinkedIn profile? Can I use your driver's licence to try to get this job one time?’ And then once you [let them use it] one time, they have it forever."

Audience Relations, CBC P.O. Box 500 Station A Toronto, ON Canada, M5W 1E6

items.title: Plan for 200ha kelp farm off NSW coast sparks debate
items.summary: A proposal to build the state's first commercial kelp farm south of Eden is being considered by the NSW Independent Planning Commission. The proposed farm would see Golden Kelp grown on underwater lines, like in this photo.

scraped.title: Plan for 200ha kelp farm off NSW coast sparks debate
scraped.description: A proposal to build the state's first commercial kelp farm south of Eden is being considered by the NSW Independent Planning Commission.
scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/jacinta-counihan/105895042
scraped.h1: Plan for commercial kelp farm near Eden debated at public hearing
scraped.body_text:
Emergency

Backstory

Newsletters

中文新闻

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

TOK PISIN

ABC South East NSW

Topic: Fishing and Aquaculture Industry

The proposed farm would see Golden Kelp grown on underwater lines, like in this photo. ( Supplied: Jo Lane )

NSW's Independent Planning Commission has held public hearings about a proposal to build the state's first commercial offshore kelp farm.

More than 50 people spoke for and against the 200-hectare project south of Eden.

A decision about whether the State Significant Development should be approved is now with the commission.

Strong debate continues over whether a small bay south of Eden should host NSW's first commercial kelp farm.

The 200-hectare offshore project at Disaster Bay, off Greenglade Beach in Wonboyn, was conditionally approved by the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure (DPHI) last month.

But because the State Significant Development received more than 200 objections, the application was referred for determination to the NSW Independent Planning Commission (IPC).

More than 50 people voiced their views at hearings held on Tuesday and Wednesday at the Seahorse Inn Hotel.

Disaster Bay, south of Eden on the NSW south coast. ( Supplied: AusKelp )

Among those to speak was Wonboyn resident and Melbourne University emeritus professor in sustainability and land administration, Ian Williamson.

He told the IPC that while he did support kelp farming, he did not approve of the proposed location.

"The nature, the natural character, the isolation and the scientific qualities of this location are major environmental and community assets.

Ian Williamson has lived in Wonboyn for 20 years and his home overlooks Disaster Bay. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro )

"Why should this unique and exceptional marine environment bear the additional uncertainty and risk associated with establishing a new commercial industry untested at scale?"

But for South Coast Sea Urchins co-founder Ryan Morris, the project would be a chance to keep staff in the area year-round, because they could work on the kelp farm outside of the sea urchin harvesting season.

"We struggle to get the right amount of staff to process products, and it's only because it's a seasonal product that we have problems," he said.

The kelp farm is proposed for the south end of the bay, about one kilometre offshore. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro )

"If we could retain our staff throughout the whole season, we'd manage to hold onto them.

"In our respect, from an economic point of view, we can only see benefits to this farm going forward."

The Eden-1 Kelp Aquaculture Farm proposal by Auskelp involves a 200-hectare lease area about one kilometre offshore.

When fully operational, an ocean rig with longlines sitting about one metre below the surface would cover an area of about 100 hectares.

Four yellow navigation buoys would be located on each corner of the lease, and 260 partially submerged floats would be attached to the rig.

The project would be built in three stages: 25 hectares in phase one, 75 in phase two, and a maximum of 100 hectares in phase three.

The proposal also includes a hatchery at Eden and a processing facility in Edrom, but they would need to go through separate approval processes.

According to the Department of Planning, Housing and Infrastructure's assessment report, golden kelp does not require any input.

This photo shows what an ocean rig would look like, with golden kelp growing on dropper lines that reach down 8 to 10 metres. ( Supplied: Auskelp )

It said that harvested kelp could be sold for food, supplements, bio-stimulants and animal feed.

The report said that if approved, Eden-1 would be NSW's first active commercial offshore seaweed farm, and one of the first in the world to grow Ecklonia radiata (golden kelp), which is a native species.

It is estimated the development would cost $8,783,000, create up to 10 jobs during construction and 18 once operating.

Greenglade Beach, where the farm is proposed, sits between the Nadgee Nature Reserve and Ben Boyd National Park. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro )

According to the assessment report, the development application and the environmental impact statement were put on public exhibition in April and May this year.

More than half of the 208 unique public submissions objecting to the proposal were from people living interstate, with the majority from Victoria.

The proposal was sent to the NSW Independent Planning Commision after receiving 208 unique objections during the public consultation phase. ( ABC News: Mikayla McGuirk-Scolaro )

Lyn Pool owns property in Wonboyn and splits her time between there and Melbourne.

She told the IPC the project would be devastating for the local tourism industry.

"Eden-1 will only provide 18 ongoing jobs … but how many jobs in tourism will be lost?" Ms Pool said.

Alecia Bellgrove says seaweed will be important for future food production. ( Supplied: Dr Alecia Bellgrove )

Alecia Bellgrove is the head of the Deakin Seaweed Research Group at Victoria's Deakin University.

She expressed support for the project and said it would play a major role in future food production.

"We really need to look to the oceans to increase the potential for opportunity for food production, and to be able to do that in a sustainable way," Dr Bellgrove said.

"I really believe that seaweed aquaculture is well placed to help bridge this gap."

Christopher Ride is the CEO of AusKelp, pictured here at Disaster Bay, near Eden. ( Supplied: AusKelp )

Auskelp CEO Christopher Ride said in a statement that he "sincerely appreciated everyone who has taken the time to provide feedback to the IPC, including those who have raised concerns".

The public has until midnight on December 2 to make a final submission.

The IPC will then decide.

scraped.author: https://www.abc.net.au/news/giulia-bertoglio/101618808
scraped.h1: WA man drives 1,000km to make medical appointment after flight cancellation
scraped.body_text:

Backstory

Newsletters

TOK PISIN

By Giulia Bertoglio

ABC Kimberley

Topic: Air Transport Industry

John Barnes had an arduous journey to medical care after a flight cancellation. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio )

A man in WA's north was forced to drive more than 1,000km to make a "lifesaving" medical appointment.

Airnorth cancelled John Barnes's flight to Perth, meaning he had to drive to Broome to get to hospital the next day.

The local shire president says the community is losing faith in Airnorth and that the WA government needs to step in.

A West Australian man was forced to drive more than 1,000 kilometres to make a "lifesaving" medical appointment after his commercial flight was cancelled earlier this month.

Wyndham resident John Barnes was due to fly from Kununurra in the remote Kimberley region to Perth on November 11, but Airnorth cancelled his flight at the last minute.

Instead, Mr Barnes embarked on a 1,000km, 11-hour drive to Broome to catch a flight to Perth the next day.

Mr Barnes said it was a family effort just to get to Broome, with his wife and brother-in-law taking turns driving throughout the night.

"I take things in my stride, and I like challenges, but that's just not a fair challenge," he said.

John Barnes prepares to fly to Perth from Broome after driving over 1,000km overnight. ( Supplied: John Barnes )

Mr Barnes said he made it to Royal Perth Hospital just in time for his appointment.

He has suffered from gallstones and sepsis in recent months.

As a result, Mr Barnes said he could not risk rescheduling his medical review to the following week.

"I'm basically a time bomb waiting to go off," he said.

"If another gallstone goes where it shouldn't … they've saved my life once, and I don't exactly need that to happen again."

John Barnes says he almost missed a "lifesaving" medical appointment due to a flight cancellation in Western Australia's north. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio )

Mr Barnes said he understood flight cancellations happened, but the regularity in the East Kimberley was unsettling.

"I felt really let down. It took the mat from underneath my feet," he said.

Kununurra resident Sharon D'Aietti said she factored flight unreliability into her travel planning.

"We always go [to Perth] at least a day in advance just to be sure we can take other [onward] flights … sometimes two days in advance," she said.

Ms D'Aietti said her parents visited her in Kununurra earlier this year but were shocked by the cost of flying to the Kimberley region.

When booking, a flight from Darwin to Broome that stopped in Kununurra cost about $500; the Broome to Kununurra leg alone cost nearly $1,000.

Sharon D'Aietti says expensive and unreliable flights are taking a toll on her young family. ( ABC Kimberley: Giulia Bertoglio )

"It's half of the kilometres … but costs double the money," Ms D'Aietti said.

"It was the same plane. The same flight that is stopping here [in Kununurra].

"So why would you add $500 to the price? It just didn't make sense to me."

The WA government has extended a scheme to cap airfares for regional residents to Perth until 2031.

Flight delays and cancellations at the East Kimberley Regional Airport in Kununurra have had an impact on residents. ( ABC Kimberley: Rebecca Nadge )

But Ms D'Aietti said in Kununurra people were "limited on the flights you can get," with residents still forced to buy full-price fares for specific travel dates.

She said expensive fares and cancellations were putting her and other families in the East Kimberley under strain.

"We love the place," Ms D'Aietti said.

"But I understand why people don't want to come and don't want to live here."

Airnorth has a monopoly on flights to and from Kununurra, after rival airline Nexus halted services last year .

Shire of Wyndham East Kimberley president David Menzel said flights were crucial for the region's development.

"Livability, retention of staff, attracting new staff … it's near impossible if you're this far from anywhere and people haven't got confidence in the air service," he said.

"People are just losing confidence in the air service we've got.

"It feels like we're at the end of the line and get the leftovers."

David Menzel says more competition and government support are needed to rectify unreliable air travel in WA's north. ( ABC Kimberley: Dunja Karagic )

Cr Menzel said he hoped to restart conversations with carriers and the government to find better solutions.

"The market is broken, really," he said.

Airnorth was contacted for comment.

WA Transport Minister Rita Saffioti earlier this year labelled the East Kimberley Regional Airport as a gateway to the region, while also providing a critical supply chain link for local communities and industry.

scraped.description: Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.
scraped.h1: Andy Taylor, lead guitarist of Duran Duran, dies aged 65
scraped.body_text:

Backstory

Newsletters

BERITA BAHASA INDONESIA

Topic: Music

Andy Taylor (far right) was the band's original guitarist. ( Getty Images: Michael Putland )

Andy Taylor, the original guitarist of the 1980s English new wave band Duran Duran, has died aged 65.

Taylor's death was confirmed by his family and bandmates in a statement posted on social media and Duran Duran's website.

He died after a "long and courageous battle with prostate cancer", the statement said.

"From the moment he arrived in Birmingham from the North East with a guitar and an unshakeable belief in what we could become, he brought an indelible fire and swagger to our music," the band said.

"His playing drove the songs that took us around the world, and with a dry wit that was matched only by his wonderfully unsentimental, no-nonsense outlook on life he kept us grounded and gave the band its edge through the extraordinary years that followed."

Andy Taylor, seen here circa 1985, died following a prostate cancer diagnosis. ( Getty Images: Vinnie Zuffante )

On the night he was inducted in the Rock & Roll Hall of Fame in 2022, Taylor revealed that he had been battling stage 4 metastatic prostate cancer for several years and was unable to attend.

"I would like to thank each of my brothers in this great band," he wrote.

"You can dream about what happened to us but to experience it, on one's own terms, as mates, was beyond incredible."

The band's pop hits include Hungry Like the Wolf, The Reflex and Rio. The rise up the charts of Hungry Like a Wolf was inextricably linked to the launch of MTV.

The two-time Grammy Award-winners had nine gold and six platinum records, with 20 top-20 singles in the UK and 18 in the US.

The two-time Ivor Novello Award winners are also MTV Video Visionary Award recipients.

"Many families have experienced the slow burn of this disease and of course we are no different," Taylor wrote.

The band's imperial stage came through a trio of hit albums between 1981 and 1983 that delivered dance-floor anthems as Girls on Film and Union of the Snake, and the moody ballads The Chauffeur and Save a Prayer.

Their cemented their popularity when they recorded the James Bond theme song A View to a Kill and earned a slot at Live Aid in 1985.

Mixing fashion, pioneering synthesisers and glam-pop swagger, the telegenic band were all over radio and young people's walls, with bassist John Taylor and singer Simon Le Bon becoming heart-throbs and the band being labelled part of the New Romantics.

Princess Diana was known to be a fan, and that meant a lot to the band.

"It worked well for us," drummer Roger Taylor told Rolling Stone.

"It was genuine. I don't think it was some sort of PR stunt. It was massive for us because she was the number one icon of the early 80s."

MTV success and love from Princess Diana propelled their profile. Seen here in 2004, with Andy Taylor on the far left. ( AP: Lo Sai-hung/ File )

The band's success was in large part to their videos, including their Antigua-set song Rio, which featured shots of the band in pastel suits sailing confidently on a yacht.

For the album Rio, they shot three music videos in Sri Lanka and two in Antigua, feeding MTV's need to have a stream of visuals, something classic rock did not have.

"A lot of the success of the album is down to the power of the videos and the way it made the band omnipresent around the globe," Le Bon told The Daily Beats in 2012.

Andy Taylor agreed: "I don't think we could have done it without MTV."

John Taylor and keyboardist Nick Rhodes started the band as teenagers in the northern city of Birmingham in 1978.

The group's name was inspired by a character in the Jane Fonda-starring sci-fi movie Barbarella.

Roger Taylor, Le Bon and Andy Taylor joined soon after, with the British press referring to them as the Fab Five.

Andy Taylor answered an ad in Melody Maker music magazine for a live-wire guitarist. (None of the Taylors were related.)

"We all grew up on the same vinyl records and live gigs, from David Bowie to Roxy Music, The Sex Pistols and, of course, Chic," Andy Taylor wrote in a letter read by the band during their Rock Hall induction.

"I could go to all those places as a player and developed a hybrid guitar style that fitted this amazing concept of a band."

WhatsApp’s 3 billion users are getting an option that Meta says is one of the most requested features, with the ability to schedule messages in advance for both private conversations and group chats. Most messaging platforms have had this for a very long time, but now it’s on WhatsApp too.

If you think of a text at an inconvenient time or don’t want to forget to fire off a birthday message at 4AM, you can draft it and set it to send anywhere from 10 minutes to two weeks later. The feature works with photos and videos, too.

Meta:

To schedule a message, press and hold the send button and pick the date and time you want it to arrive. It will look like any other message to the person receiving it. You can see all future messages you have lined up, and delete them beforehand if you change your mind.

Even if your phone is off or out of battery, your scheduled message will still show up at the time you chose, and it remains end-to-end encrypted like all your personal messages, so no one else can read it, not even us.

Scheduled messages work with text, photos and videos, and are rolling out globally over the coming weeks. It’s one more way to show up for the people who matter to you, now at exactly the right time.

See All by Andrew Liszewski

Saying it was necessary to prevent the possible spontaneous explosion of a stockpile of material used in igniters and blasting caps, the US Army conducted a controlled detonation of over 9,700 pounds of lead azide today at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant (IAAAP) in Middletown, Iowa. Videos of the detonation showed plumes of smoke several hundred feet high drifting south before quickly dissipating.

Following the explosion, the Army confirmed that all of the barrels at the plant had been destroyed without any secondary explosions or infrastructure damage. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced, as close to zero as it’s absolutely humanly possible, the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa,” said Maj. Gen. Eric Shirley during a press conference held two hours after the blast, according to the Associated Press .

The US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) has been monitoring the area around the ammunition plant leading up to today’s event. According to a statement from the EPA following the detonation, “real-time air monitors are reporting zero detection of airborne lead throughout the region” an hour after the detonation. The data collected by EPA employees, contractors, and monitoring equipment is shared here .

The Army has used lead azide in munitions for nearly a century but began transitioning away from the material around 15 years ago because it can be difficult to transport and store. Over time, the material can degrade and crystallize and eventually become unstable enough to detonate at ambient temperatures. The Iowa ammunition plant housed 68 barrels containing about 9,700 pounds of lead azide, representing the country’s remaining stockpile. For safety reasons, the material was stored in liquid form embedded in sawdust and burlap bags while water and ethanol were added to prevent freezing. However, the decision was made to detonate the stockpile after an inspection by the Bureau of Alcohol, Tobacco, Firearms (ATF) discovered “significant crystallization on the exterior of the barrels” last March.

Ahead of today’s detonation, the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) supported a recommended, but voluntary, temporary relocation of all the residents of Middletown and immediate surrounding areas that began yesterday. A cone-shaped evacuation zone extends about five miles southwest of the ammunition plant to account for the post-explosion dispersion and deposition path of dust. Displaced residents will be lodged until Friday, November 27th, and can return home once the all-clear has been given.

To reduce the amount of lead dust released into surrounding areas and the environment, the Army said it took several additional precautions as part of today’s detonation. Walls made of four 16,000-gallon water tanks were installed to capture lead particulate, while the aging earth-covered magazines holding the barrels were covered with tarps and lead containment screens and flooded with foam.

1Password says a hacker stole customer names and email addresses after gaining access to its backend systems. The breach didn’t expose passwords or other information stored in customer vaults, but could put users at risk of phishing attempts, according to a post disclosing the incident . It’s unclear how many users are affected.

The password manager began investigating the incident on November 19th, after an attacker gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. Using the compromised account, the hacker accessed 1Password’s source code and pushed malicious code to backend services to download customer data. Along with customer names and emails, the leaked data included public keys, as well as account and user identifiers.

It also included tokens from certain emailed invitation or account recovery links. According to 1Password, attackers can’t use tokens alone to gain access to an account, as they would need to pair them with a single-sign-on method or a six-digit numeric code sent to a user’s email. 1Password has since lengthened the codes it sends to users to 10 alphanumeric characters to make them harder to guess.

The password manager also disabled the affected GitHub account, rotated internal credentials compromised by the breach, and added a new detection system for similar attacks. It warns customers about potential phishing attempts as well, saying phony emails, texts, or calls may reference 1Password invitations or account recovery attempts. The company says it will never ask customers for their account password or Secret Key, and that users should only enter this information into the official 1Password app or website.
