scraped.title: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
scraped.description: The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.
scraped.h1: Google search alternative Kagi launches Gmail rival
scraped.body_text:
The pitch is an unusual combination of privacy promises and AI features.

Kagi, a small, Palo Alto, California-based software company that provides a subscription-based search engine as an alternative to Google, has launched a Gmail-like e-mail service. Dubbed Kagi Mail, it makes many of the same claims as the search engine product: privacy, personal data sovereignty, customization, and control.

Additionally, Kagi is rolling out a calendar as part of the mail service. Right now, both the email and calendar interfaces are web-only, but native Android and iOS apps are planned for the fourth quarter of next year.

The email interface, currently in public beta, is minimalist. It emphasizes keyboard commands, as well as a private and ad-free experience. (You can see more details in Kagi’s blog post about what they mean by private.) Other feature offerings include unlimited aliases and domains, an anti-lock-in policy for user data, 50GB of storage, rule-based filtering with Sieve, an MCP server, and several optional, off-by-default AI features, like chatting with an agent to search email history, do large-scale re-labeling, or define additional filtering rules.

Some major features are still missing, though. As noted, there are no native apps yet. Critically, there is no contacts address book, but that is also coming in 2027 (Q1 in this case) according to the roadmap.

Like the search engine, Kagi Mail is a paid service. It’s not included in the $5 per month basic Kagi plan, nor is it in the $10 per month unlimited search plan. It is, however, included in the $25 per month Kagi Ultimate subscription, which also offers frontier AI models.

If you want to get Kagi Mail without the $25 per month subscription, you can subscribe for $9 per month or $99 per year, and there’s a 60-day trial right now.

That’s a lot to pay for email when Gmail has historically been such a strong product. To most people, it seems ridiculous to imagine paying for a subscription, and that’s understandable.

According to the company, Kagi Search has just over 75,000 paying subscribers. Compared to the number of people using Google Search or even Bing or DuckDuckGo, that’s not much. But the pitch is that with Google, the user is the product, not the customer, and that paying anywhere from $5 to $25 per month (there are multiple plans; unlimited search queries is in the $10 per month plan) helps users escape from that devil’s bargain.

Kagi also argues that Google’s search results—and increasingly its email as well—are polluted or corrupted by ad sales incentives. On that, several Ars staffers agree—my colleague Lee Hutchinson wrote at length about why he ditched Google Search for Kagi a year ago. A couple other Ars staffers have since made the same move, myself included—but to be fair, search is a very big part of our day-to-day work, and that’s not true to the same degree for everybody.

The pitch for email is a little harder, because most people probably don’t perceive as much impact of Google’s business incentives on Gmail. That has maybe changed recently, as Google has begun inserting Gemini into Gmail aggressively, but Kagi has AI features, too—the difference is that they’re generally more conservative and sensible. (You can disable either Gemini in Gmail or Kagi’s AI features in Kagi Mail, too.)

Email is also different because there are already more direct competitors to Kagi Mail. The most popular in this category is Proton Mail, which goes even further on privacy and security with end-to-end encryption, but that company is embroiled in controversies right now. There’s also Tuta, which Kagi specifically flags and praises in its blog post as a good existing alternative.

Based on a few hours of use, Kagi Mail seems like it’s going in the right direction, but it will need refinement to permanently unseat Gmail. Your needs may vary, but there are many good reasons to consider alternatives to Google’s business model and products.

scraped.description: Backblaze tells Ars it won't share users' backup, storage files with advertisers.
scraped.h1: Backblaze explains why it’s sharing customer information with advertisers
scraped.body_text:
Backblaze tells Ars it won’t share users’ backup, storage files with advertisers.

Some customers have raised concerns about Backblaze’s privacy policy taking effect next month, which says the backup and cloud storage company may sell certain personal information to advertisers.

Backblaze’s current privacy policy says that in addition to the personal information that users may provide, such as their email address when creating an account, it may also “automatically” collect information, such as “your software, the operating system you use when accessing our service, your Internet Protocol address, and the date and time of each request you make to Backblaze.”

The current policy adds: “Under no circumstances do we rent, trade, or share your address or e-mail address with any other company for their marketing purposes without your consent.” It also makes no mention of advertisers.

On December 1, a new privacy policy takes effect. It includes a table listing the types of “general personal information” that Backblaze says it has been collecting and sharing with third parties, including “advertising and marketing partners” since December 1, 2025, This information includes identifiers (such as “name, address, Internet Protocol address, [and] email address”); commercial information (such as “records of personal property, products or services purchased, obtained, or considered, or other purchasing or consuming histories or tendencies”; geolocation data that “can be used to determine a device’s physical location”; and “sensory or surveillance data” (which includes “call recordings or other audio, electronic, or visual monitoring or surveillance”).

This has concerned some users, but a Backblaze spokesperson told Ars Technica that “Backblaze does not sell or share sensory or surveillance data, such as call recordings, for targeted advertising, and we do not disclose it to advertising or marketing partners.” They added:

Notably, no “sensitive personal information,” such as social security numbers, credit card numbers, or “precise geolocation,” is shared with advertisers, the policy states. However, identifiers, commercial information, “Internet or Other Similar Network Activity,” and “geolocation data” may be “sold or shared for targeted Advertising”

Critically, the upcoming policy “only applies to the information collected in respect of your account and not to the content that you store on our system.” Backblaze’s broader terms of service also state that : “Files stored using Backblaze Computer Backup are encrypted prior to being sent to us.”

However, some customers remain concerned that the privacy policy doesn’t more clearly and distinctly explain that Backblaze won’t share or sell content from customers’ backup files. In response, Backblaze’s representative explained:

This is because the Privacy Notice’s sale and sharing disclosures relate to website and marketing data, such as information collected through cookies and similar technologies on our site. They do not apply to files customers store with us.

Renatta Siewert, Backblaze’s director of communications and brand programs, reiterated to Ars that Backblaze doesn’t share the contents of backup or storage files with advertisers:

Backblaze takes the privacy and security of our customers’ data seriously. We updated our Privacy Notice to keep pace with the changing legal landscape, which increasingly requires companies to spell out how they collect and use marketing-related information. This update gives customers a clearer, more specific view of what we collect and why. These disclosures are separate from the files customers entrust to Backblaze for backup and storage, which we do not sell or share with advertisers, data brokers, or analytics partners.

Customers can use this link to opt out of the selling or sharing of their personal information for cross-context behavioral advertising.

scraped.title: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
scraped.description: This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.
scraped.h1: The FCC has authorized SpaceX to deploy 1 million satellites
scraped.body_text:
This constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

In an extraordinary decision, the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday granted SpaceX conditional authorization to deploy a constellation of up to 1 million Starmind satellites designed to serve as orbital data centers.

If fully deployed, this constellation would increase the number of satellites in orbit by roughly 50-fold.

“The United States is moving decisively to ensure that this breakthrough technology creates opportunity, drives investment, and delivers lasting benefits for the American people,” FCC Chairman Brendan Carr said in a statement on Wednesday. “This action opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

The decision, announced a day before the Thanksgiving holiday in the United States, represents a major regulatory victory for SpaceX and its founder, Elon Musk, who has allied himself with the Trump administration.

This announcement clears a major hurdle to deploying data centers in space, although it does not establish that orbital data centers are technically or economically viable. Nevertheless, the FCC authorization appears designed to give the company wide latitude as it works through these remaining issues.

For example, SpaceX has seven years to deploy a single operational Starmind satellite under the order. SpaceX has until November 2035 to deploy 100,000 operational satellites, and November 2040 for the full constellation. SpaceX, therefore, has a 14-year regulatory runway to deploy the most ambitious industrial project ever approved for spaceflight.

The authorization includes some conditional aspects. SpaceX has proposed operating in six orbits, ranging from 550 km to about 1,000 km. The company sought a waiver from FCC rules to allow satellites above 600 km to be disposed of into “Earth disposal orbits or heliocentric orbits.” That is, instead of burning them up in Earth’s atmosphere, SpaceX wants the flexibility to move retired satellites into other orbits around Earth, or potentially into orbit around the Sun.

The FCC did not grant this waiver request “because SpaceX has not provided sufficient information for the Commission to determine whether its alternative disposal methods are compliant with the Commission’s requirements.” The company will need to obtain a waiver before deploying any Starmind satellites that are not intended to be disposed of via atmospheric reentry.

However, in other ways the FCC appears to have been incredibly lenient with SpaceX. This is particularly the case with environmental concerns raised by numerous parties that commented on SpaceX’s application to the FCC.

Half a dozen organizations, such as the Secure World Foundation and American Astronomical Society, raised concerns about deploying so many satellites into orbit, citing collision risks, orbital debris, atmospheric pollution from so many satellite reentries, impacts on astronomical observations, and more. The FCC also received approximately 1,500 public comments concerning SpaceX’s application.

Some of these environmental issues, the FCC said, lay beyond the scope of its review. For example, on concerns about the environmental implications of thousands or potentially tens of thousands of rocket launches, the FCC said, “Potential concerns related to the emissions of rocket launches and the subsequent impacts on the human environment as an indirect result of the Starmind system are outside of the Commission’s purview.”

The FCC also rejected calls for further environmental scrutiny of pollution from satellite reentries, including concerns about aluminum oxides and their potential effects on the ozone layer. “Other concerns, including impacts on the atmosphere caused by satellites burning up on re-entry, remain speculative and not supported in the record,” the FCC authorization states.

As part of its decision, the FCC cited a significant policy change adopted in October, when the agency concluded that space-based activities generally fall outside its obligations under the National Environmental Policy Act. The FCC reasoned that as these activities occur beyond US territory, they don’t constitute federal actions requiring environmental review. As a result, the agency declined to conduct a comprehensive environmental assessment of SpaceX’s Starmind constellation.

SpaceX was given conditional approval by the Federal Communications Commission on Wednesday to deploy and operate a constellation of up to 1 million satellites for its orbital data center business, a regulatory victory for Elon Musk and his bid to move AI data centers into space.

The FCC authorization was granted despite objections from Amazon, Viasat, and the American Astronomical Society, which flagged concerns over orbital debris and congestion, radiofrequency interference, and environmental consequences. Amazon, which is building a competitor to SpaceX’s Starlink service, argued in its petition that the application lacked basic details and described it as a “lofty ambition rather than a real plan.” Despite that lack of detail, Amazon also said the proposal “risks real harm.”

The FCC dismissed some of the key concerns raised by opponents, including potential threats to scientific research, because the agency determined they fell outside its regulatory authority.

FCC Chair Brendan Carr said in a statement that the action “opens a bold new frontier for the computing infrastructure needed to power America’s leadership and growth.”

Musk thanked Carr in a post on X , writing “Much appreciate. This will be a great asset to America and the world.”

This initial regulatory approval doesn’t mean orbital data centers are imminent.

SpaceX faces a number of technical and economic challenges, including how to dramatically reduce the cost of manufacturing and launching satellites, cool processors in space, and even how to secure financing for chips that are destined for orbit.

The company must also clear other regulatory hurdles. The FCC has not yet approved SpaceX’s plans to handle orbital debris for satellites that would operate above 600 kilometers, for instance. SpaceX requested a waiver of existing FCC rules, which requires satellites ending missions below 2,000 kilometers reenter Earth’s atmosphere within five years of completing those missions. The company is interested in moving some of these retired satellites into other orbits around Earth or even around the sun, according to the FCC authorization document .

SpaceX has said it plans to deploy the satellites, known as Starmind, at altitudes ranging from 500 to 1,002 kilometers. The FCC’s approval gives SpaceX the authority to use radiofrequency communications to maintain contact with and control its orbital data centers from Earth if their primary communications systems fail. The Starmind satellites would primarily communicate using lasers to connect with other satellites, including SpaceX’s Starlink.

The FCC has given SpaceX time to sort out these issues. Under the approval, SpaceX has seven years to get its first operational satellite into orbit and 14 years to deploy the entire constellation.

OpenAI has started rolling out a unified Chat and Work experience in ChatGPT to a few of its users, amid criticism from some subscribers that the merger could restrict their usage.

The ChatGPT maker began introducing the update to a small group of Pro subscribers, product lead Thibault “Tibo” Sottiaux said in a post on X on Tuesday. The rollout follows OpenAI’s earlier announcement of the merger in an email to users. An OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch that while most users are not expected to face more frequent usage resets, a small fraction of its heaviest users may hit their limits sooner.

That’s among the concerns raised by some ChatGPT subscribers on social media and OpenAI’s community forum recently. The users fear that merging the usage limits for Chat and Work could leave them with less access to advanced reasoning models than they currently have, even as they continue paying the same subscription fees .

Under the new system, Chat and Work will share a single usage meter across ChatGPT, the OpenAI spokesperson told TechCrunch. Conversations using the Instant model will, however, remain unlimited and will not count toward the shared allowance. Users can also continue using Instant after exhausting their usage limits. The spokesperson added that OpenAI would continue working to improve efficiency so subscribers could get more out of their plans.

While the rollout has started for a small group of users, OpenAI plans to bring shared usage limits more broadly in December, per its support page.

Similar to OpenAI, rival Anthropic also moved to bring its conversational chat service Claude and work-focused Cowork under one interface in September.

The changes come as AI companies face mounting infrastructure costs and growing demand for increasingly capable models, putting pressure on their computing resources. Bringing conversational and work-related tools into a single interface could also make AI chatbots simpler to use, allowing users to move between chats and more complex tasks without switching tabs.

When Jensen Huang gave his first all-hands address since returning as CEO, there was an odd emphasis on Nvidia’s code of conduct. He admitted to violating the code, then emphasized that no one was exempt from it. But that “does not mean, the moment you violate a code of conduct, we walk you out the door,” Huang said, according to Wired . “Facts, circumstances, a lot of assessments” still matter. In other words, the code applies to everyone, but breaking it doesn’t automatically cost anyone their job, including, apparently, the CEO.

It’s an awkward stance for a company whose CEO has admitted to breaking its rules. A central part of modern human resources, a code of conduct can seem like a quasi-legal rulebook that lays out unacceptable behavior. But experts say most codes are better understood as a reflection of corporate culture. When an infraction goes unpunished, the main risk isn’t legal but cultural — that employees will feel embarrassed or even angry about the company they work for. That’s the risk Huang now faces at Nvidia.

Matt Plass, chief market strategy officer at LRN, an ethics and compliance training outfit, recently surveyed more than 2,000 workers across different industries for a study on workplace codes of conduct . As Plass sees it, the biggest risk is that employees will become ashamed of their workplace.

“People coming into the workforce now, ethics is incredibly important to them,” he told TechCrunch. “They’re really mindful of the ethical standards of their company. They’re really embarrassed and angry when senior leadership lets them down.”

The consequences of violating the rules aren’t always tangible, but they’re definitely real. Plass gave one example of a company that banned corporate travel to cut costs — only to have its CEO turn up in a VIP box at the Olympics.

“For over a decade afterwards, ‘the Olympics’ was used within that company as an example of the worst thing an employee could do. People would say, ‘Yeah, I shouldn’t have done that, but it’s not like I went to the Olympics.’”

Plass says companies that remove an executive typically do so after an investigation, then try to win back employees. “In most organizations they make a change at the top based on what’s happened,” he said, “and then they will have a hearts-and-minds initiative, to go out to their employee base and their customers and their investors and everybody else, and say, we get it. We’re sorry. We’ve changed. That’s essentially what they do.”

Of course, that playbook is harder to follow at a company like Nvidia, where Huang left without a clear succession plan, and there are serious doubts about whether the company could continue to thrive without him. In cases like that, Plass acknowledges there’s no easy answer.

“I would draw a distinction there between the kind of companies where the CEO is a kind of godhead figure … where the person and the company are almost impossible to separate,” he said. “There it’s much, much harder to deal with.”

In that context, Huang’s stutter-step over the code of conduct is easier to understand. Judging by the employee campaign for his reinstatement, Huang’s return hasn’t created a morale problem so far. But as the coming months put more pressure on Huang and his colleagues, sidestepping the code could end up costing Nvidia something harder to measure — its employees’ pride in the company.

items.title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
items.summary: Whether the Trump administration has investigated Jensen Huang for potential national security risks has been the subject of questions.

scraped.title: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
scraped.description: Whether the Trump administration has investigated Jensen Huang for potential national security risks has been the subject of questions.
scraped.author: Kif Leswing
scraped.h1: Vance says he was assured Jensen Huang was not under DOJ investigation
scraped.body_text:
In this article

Vice President JD Vance said Wednesday that Attorney General Todd Blanche told him Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang was not under investigation.

"I was told by the Department of Justice and multiple officials in our national security apparatus that he was under no investigation," Vance told reporters in Ohio on Wednesday after being asked what assurances he had gotten that Huang was not under investigation. "Not even that he was about to be prosecuted; that he's under no investigation."

Vance spoke two days after President Donald Trump told CNBC in an interview that an investigation had been done.

Trump was asked what Blanche had told him about potential criminal liability for Huang and the question of whether Nvidia chips had ended up in China in violation of U.S. export laws.

"They did a pretty good investigation, and they felt that he, himself, was exonerated," Trump said Monday.

Reuters reported Wednesday that the Department of Justice did not conduct a formal investigation into Huang before Trump pushed for his reinstatement as CEO.

Blanche had concluded there was no evidence Huang had broken any laws based on investigations into Nvidia clients Super Micro Computer and Megaspeed, according to the report.

The DOJ did not immediately respond to a request for comment on the Reuters report. And the White House didn't immediately respond to a request for comment on Vance saying Huang was under no investigation when Trump had said there was one. Nvidia didn't immediately respond to a request for comment about Vance's remarks.

Blanche on Tuesday dodged questions about whether there had been an investigation.

"What the president said is that he talked to a lot of people going into the decision that he made to encourage the board to reinstate him," Blanche said after being asked whether the DOJ had investigated Huang and, if so, what were the results of the probe.

Huang was reinstated as CEO of Nvidia on Monday, after the chipmaker's board of directors said it had received "input from senior levels of the United States government" that Huang was not a national security risk. Trump took credit for Huang's reinstatement in the interview with CNBC shortly after Nvidia's announcement.

Huang resigned following The New York Times reporting multiple affairs , including one with a Chinese businesswoman who is alleged to be a spy for Beijing and who was an executive for the Singapore-based cloud provider Megaspeed.

The reporting added fuel to allegations that Nvidia should have known its artificial intelligence chips were being diverted to China and being used by Chinese companies, violating U.S. export laws.

"The product they create is a very important part of us staying ahead of the SI arms race with China. We really do care about ensuring those chips do not fall into the wrong hands," Vance said, using the Trump administration's preferred acronym for AI, which the president calls "super intelligence."

"We actually see this is an opportunity for Nvidia to focus on complying with American export controls, and we think Jensen Huang is going to take that very seriously," Vance continued.

"We received the assurances that he was not under any significant — he was under no investigation — and the accusations against him were based on anonymous reporting, not on actual evidence," Vance said.

On Tuesday, Trump left the door open to pardon Huang in an interview with the New York Post , but Vance said on Wednesday that the CEO doesn't need one.

"I don't think he needs a pardon at all," Vance said. "I haven't seen any evidence again that he committed a crime. And if there is evidence that he committed a crime, then that's up to relevant authorities to actually bring a prosecution against him."

Huang is scheduled to appear for a closed-door interview with House committees about his dealings with Megaspeed on Tuesday. At the same time, Nvidia will hold its annual conference where it showcases new technology in Washington.

— Kevin Breuninger contributed to this report.

items.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
items.summary: SpaceX won approval from the FCC to put 1 million orbital data center satellites into space, a proposal that was opposed by Amazon and other groups.

scraped.title: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
scraped.description: SpaceX won approval from the FCC to put 1 million orbital data center satellites into space, a proposal that was opposed by Amazon and other groups.
scraped.author: Lora Kolodny,Annie Palmer
scraped.h1: SpaceX wins FCC approval to deploy 1 million orbital data center satellites
scraped.body_text:
In this article

The Federal Communications Commission has authorized Elon Musk 's SpaceX to put 1 million artificial intelligence computing satellites in orbit, Chairman Brendan Carr announced on Wednesday.

Carr said in a post on X, the social network owned by SpaceX, that the company's Starmind constellation, and "competitor constellations will use solar power to extend America's lead" in AI.

Musk said in a reply, "Much appreciated. This will be a great asset to America and the world."

The FCC, in its authorization filing , noted that SpaceX's application "received a substantial number of comments from the public, including petitions to deny filed by Kuiper Systems LLC ( Amazon Leo), Viasat Inc. (Viasat), and the American Astronomical Society (AAS)."

In a March petition urging the FCC to deny SpaceX's application, Amazon had labeled the company's Starmind project as a "lofty ambition rather than a real plan."

The e-commerce and cloud computing giant is building a competitor to SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet service, and said it would take SpaceX "centuries" to build the constellation, adding that the company provided scant details about how it would "deliver on these grand claims."

The petition resulted in a rebuke from Carr , who said Amazon "should focus on the fact" that it's falling short of its own satellite deployment milestone.

Amazon declined to comment on the FCC's approval.

Other companies have also set their sights on orbital data centers. Google last year announced Project Suncatcher , which it describes as a "moonshot to put AI in space," and launched its first chips into space on a SpaceX rocket and Planet Labs satellite in October.

In March, Jeff Bezos ' Blue Origin petitioned the FCC to let it launch up to 51,600 satellites as part of a low Earth orbit satellite constellation dubbed "Project Sunrise." The constellation would work in tandem with Blue Origin's planned TeraWave satellite internet service, announced in January.

Astrophysicist and author Adam Becker was critical of the FCC move in an email to CNBC on Wednesday.

"Any serious attempt at this is going to further pollute the night sky and runs a serious risk of a cascading chain reaction of space junk collisions, which would be a disaster for all of humanity," he wrote. "Musk and Carr are either profoundly stupid themselves, or hoping the rest of us are too stupid to notice this is nonsense."

SpaceX did not respond to a request for comment.

The FCC said in its authorization that it dismissed "comments and concerns raised regarding topics over which the Commission has no authority, including environmental concerns," and concerns about its impact on "optical astronomy."

items.title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
items.summary: Alan Greenspan famously held the line on interest rates because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet boom. Why can't Kevin Warsh do the same?

scraped.title: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
scraped.description: Alan Greenspan famously held the line on interest rates because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet boom. Why can't Kevin Warsh do the same?
scraped.author: Steve Liesman
scraped.h1: Liesman: Why Greenspan could bet on productivity — and Warsh needs to hike
scraped.body_text:
In a discussion on CNBC's Halftime Report Wednesday, the question came up: Why can't Federal Reserve Chairman Kevin Warsh hold the line on interest rates the way his icon Alan Greenspan did at the beginning of the dot-com era?

Greenspan famously leaned against inflation hawks on his committee in 1995 and 1996, holding the line on interest rates amid strong growth, because he believed in the productivity promise of the internet revolution.

It would be nice if Warsh could follow the same playbook amid the artificial intelligence build-out and keep rates steady until the productivity arrives. Unfortunately, a quick look at the numbers shows just how different the situation is for Warsh when it comes to inflation , the magnitude of the capital-investment boom and the monetary and fiscal stimulus boosting the economy.

Bottom line: the Fed looks like it has to hike — and maybe substantially — to be anywhere close to the position where the Fed was in Greenspan's time at the dawn of a major technological revolution.

Here are some key points:

It may be that the massive capex spending on AI will mean more productivity and less inflation down the road. But the front-end build-out is proving to be more inflationary, and more challenging, to a Fed already dealing with high inflation. In many ways, that's the opposite of what Greenspan had to handle.

Two unhoused men have been charged with breaking into the country home of Prince William and Princess Catherine in eastern England after they stole cufflinks and a clock, Norfolk police said on Wednesday.

The suspects were arrested close to the property after a search using police dogs, drones and a helicopter, the Associated Press reported.

In a statement Wednesday , police said officers were called Monday evening to a report of “suspicious activity” at an address on the royal family’s rural Sandringham estate in the county of Norfolk. No members of the family were on the property at the time of the break-in.

Investigators said Mirgen Doku, 34, and Arilen Ndoci, 32, were charged with entering a dwelling with intent to steal and trespassing on a protected site. Neither man has a fixed address, the police statement said.

Prosecutors said during a hearing at Norwich Magistrate’s Court that the suspects, both Albanian nationals described as being unhoused, scaled a drainpipe, broke open a window and entered the home through a dressing room. They ran off with a clock and six pairs of cufflinks, including one described in court as “Duke of Edinburgh cufflinks.”

A Sandringham staff member, who was on patrol at the time of the robbery, said he was using a thermal spotter when he noticed two men jump through a hedge and run towards a wooded area, the Associated Press reported.

The suspects were later arrested and taken into custody; a third suspect has not been caught.

Both men, who do not speak English, were aided by an Albanian interpreter in court, where they spoke to confirm their names and dates of birth. They did not enter pleas and will stay in custody until a scheduled court appearance on Monday.

The suspects broke into Anmer Hall, which was gifted to the couple by the late Queen Elizabeth II as a wedding a present.

The 10-bedroom house, located on the Sandringham estate about 171 kilometres north of London, is used by the couple as a country retreat. The family spend the majority of their time at Forest Lodge in Windsor.

scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

Microsoft has issued a “Code Red” in order to “quickly implement lessons learned” following a 24-hour outage earlier this month, a spokesperson said.

Microsoft said this work is its “top priority.”

“Our customers and partners depend on our services, and we owe it to them to not only fix problems when they occur, but to do everything we can to keep them from happening again,” the spokesperson told Global News.

The Nov. 12-13 outage disrupted Exchange Online, its cloud-based email service, as well as Outlook, Teams, its Copilot AI assistant and other Microsoft 365 products. It affected governments in Canada, the U.S., Australia and Japan, as well as businesses, hospitals, trading firms and airlines.

Microsoft cited a network strain in their outage, and said it was not related to artificial intelligence or a cyberattack. CEO Satya Nadella publicly apologized for the disruption.

Ritesh Kotak, cybersecurity and technology analyst, told Global News the declaration of a “Code Red” means an “all hands on deck situation.”

“From an engineering perspective, when there’s a code red, it’s the highest level of severity. It means that something is absolutely critical and needs to be addressed immediately,” he said.

Kotak said outages are bound to occur, especially as we rely more and more on new technologies.

Charles Lamanna, Microsoft’s executive vice president of Copilot, Agents and Platform, told a Code Red review that the affected component had experienced “roughly ten years’ worth of acceptable failures,” according to a memo seen by Reuters.

The Code Red will allow Microsoft to prioritize testing redundancies and solidifying a backup plan that can be put in place should a system failure happen again.

But Kotak said just because a backup plan is in place, does not mean it will be foolproof.

“No plan is actually 100 per cent foolproof unless it’s been tested. And if there isn’t going to be an actual test that can simulate exactly what happened with all these outages, we won’t know until the next outage happens,” he said.

Microsoft is not the only company that has been hit with major outages recently. Before Microsoft was up and running, the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration issued a nationwide ground stop . Three days later, customers of several major U.S. banks reported online banking problems , and United Airlines reported a system outage that same day causing flight delays.

While authorities have not linked any of the incidents to each other, Kotak said they reaffirm the importance of having proper cybersecurity measures in place.

“Cybersecurity or information security, it cannot be a checkbox exercise,” he said. “It needs to be much more continuous, evolving, and real-time, and as we’ve seen, these threats are increasing.”

He said the more we rely on digital systems, the greater the consequences will be should those systems fail.

“Hospitals were impacted. Individuals couldn’t communicate. Businesses couldn’t take payments in some cases if they’re dealing with e-transfers and sending invoices. Invoices out, it had a ripple effect on individuals, on society, on the economy, on governments, on critical infrastructure and their ability to do business and provide service,” Kotak said about the Microsoft outage.

While ensuring that cybersecurity remains a top priority is the responsibility of tech conglomerates, Kotak said people can also help to protect themselves by diversifying the services that they use.

“It should always be a concern and in the back of the minds of individuals and what I tell them is don’t put all your eggs in one basket. Make sure you have some sort of business continuity contingency plans in place,” he said.

– With a file from Reuters

items.summary: Jensen Huang has found himself at the centre of a string of extraordinary developments at Nvidia, where he is CEO, with implications reaching far beyond Wall Street.

scraped.description: Jensen Huang has found himself at the centre of a string of extraordinary developments at Nvidia, where he is CEO, with implications reaching far beyond Wall Street.
scraped.h1: Explainer: Nvidia CEO and ‘AI Godfather’ Jensen Huang and his ties to Trump
scraped.body_text:
Instructions:

3 comments

My parents were siblings, I dropped out of grade 5 because it was too tough, and I hate Ben because I ain’t Ben. I voted for Poilievre cuz I closely identify with the guy who’s done nothing productive with his career.

Jensen Huang has found himself at the centre of a string of extraordinary developments at Nvidia , where he is back as CEO , with implications that reach far beyond Wall Street and into public discourse.

As the head of the company, Huang has become increasingly intertwined with developments in Washington over the last few years, where U.S. President Donald Trump has prioritized policies surrounding AI, semiconductor manufacturing and competition with China.

Governments worldwide, including Canada, are embracing AI’s potential to transform industries and society while grappling with the significant security risks that come with it.

Amid these rapid changes, Huang and Nvidia have become household names in the AI industry.

“It’s not just Nvidia, it’s the whole sector. He has an outsized footprint there. With him gone, I think a lot of companies were worried,” says Richard Powers, an associate professor at the Rotman School of Management.

From romantic affairs to national security concerns and trillions of dollars on the line, here’s a look at the key developments involving Huang, Nvidia and Trump.

1993 – Huang co-founds Nvidia and becomes president of the company, which makes hardware that powers both consumer and industrial computer systems.

Nvidia’s increasingly advanced processor chips help power newer AI innovations at technology companies throughout the 2000s and 2010s, including OpenAI later on.

Nov. 30, 2022 – OpenAI launches its large language model chatbot known as ChatGPT.

Nvidia soon came into the spotlight as companies like OpenAI launched new AI tools and features, driving demand for the physical computing infrastructure needed to power them.

Since the launch of ChatGPT in 2022, Nvidia’s stock price climbed over 1,300 per cent to a recent peak on Oct. 6, 2026.

Jan. 13, 2025 – Nvidia makes a $1 million contribution to Trump’s inaugural committee, according to FEC documents.

Jan. 31, 2025 – Trump meets Huang at the White House to discuss concerns about AI developments in China, according to government documents.

April 2025 – The U.S. imposes sales restrictions on Nvidia’s H20 chips to China over concerns they could be used for the Chinese military.

July 14, 2025 – Nvidia confirms Huang met with Trump and U.S. policymakers to promote domestic AI infrastructure, alongside a government agreement granting Nvidia licenses to sell some H20 chips to China.

Oct 29, 2025 – Huang confirms to reporters that Nvidia is contributing to Trump’s White House ballroom project, saying, “I’m delighted to be part of it.” Huang did not disclose the amount at the time.

Nov. 3, 2025 – Senator Richard Blumenthal sends Huang a letter seeking details on the ballroom donation, including the pledged amount and whether there were any conditional agreements. Similar letters were sent to other suspected donors.

Oct. 15, 2026 – Leaked documents obtained by The Washington Post indicate Nvidia committed US$25 million for Trump’s White House ballroom project and was one of several other donors named.

A spokesperson confirmed Nvidia made the donation to a nonpartisan trust independent of business interests. Nvidia has a strict policy prohibiting contributions to political candidates, parties and political action committees (PACs), though lobbying is permitted.

Oct. 29 – The New York Times reports that Jensen Huang had an alleged affair with Alice Huang (no relation), an executive at Singapore-based AI company Megaspeed, and that U.S. intelligence officials had investigated or assessed her over suspicions of passing intelligence to Beijing and aiding efforts to bypass U.S. chip restrictions.

The report says that Trump was briefed on these details in 2025, and again by Marco Rubio in May 2026, including the connection to Jensen Huang, but took no action.

Nov. 3 – The U.S. midterm elections result in a Democratic blue wave, which lays the groundwork for possibly massive policy changes, including AI regulation and data centre development.

Nov. 5 – Top Republican lawmakers in the House of Representatives call on Jensen Huang ​to brief Congress about the alleged affair with a Chinese businesswoman suspected of passing information to Beijing, according to a letter seen by ​Reuters.

Nov. 8 – Huang sends a message about his infidelity without naming the specific person involved.

“I was unfaithful to my wife. My actions hurt her and our children. There is no excuse for what I did. I am deeply sorry,” he wrote in a letter emailed to company employees and posted to the company’s website.

Nov. 10 – Nvidia announces it is launching its own independent investigation into reports that Jensen Huang has been targeted by a foreign intelligence effort, sometimes referred to as a “honey trap.”

Nov. 11 – The New York Times reports another alleged affair, in which Huang was involved with Kimberley Powell, one of Nvidia’s executives who reports to him.

Nov. 12 – Huang announces his resignation as CEO of Nvidia, although he suggests he could eventually return.

In the days that followed, many investors began selling Nvidia shares and other AI stocks.

“He’s a great leader. That’s an argument I think people can make. I’m not sure it overrides the ethical missteps along the way,” says Powers.

“He’s been sort of like the godfather of the AI industry, so now you have the idea that the godfather was gone. I think that impacted a lot of firms.”

Nov. 17 – Huang agrees to deliver testimony to U.S. lawmakers in December in relation to reports that China was able to purchase Nvidia chips through supposed loopholes despite restrictions.

On the same day, Nvidia reports blowout earnings, and executives tell analysts on a conference call that they will not take questions about Huang’s departure . Separately, Nvidia’s board issues a statement slamming the door on the possibility of Huang returning as CEO.

Nov. 20 – Trump tells reporters at a news conference that he “would love to see Jensen be given a second chance.”

Nov. 23 – Nvidia announces Huang is reinstated as CEO of Nvidia after the company received input from U.S. government officials. The board also announced a National Security and Export Control Committee in response to concerns about China’s access to Nvidia’s chips.

“We have said Nvidia is a US$300 stock with Jensen and a $225 stock without him, and with the board’s unanimous vote, announced this morning (Monday), the founder is back in the driver seat,” said analyst and partner Dan Ives at Yorkville Ives Monday in a statement.

“In our view, the board reversed itself because the alternative, a founder-less Nvidia with a CEO search running into next year, was the bigger risk to shareholders.”

Trump then says in an interview with CNBC that he personally intervened and convinced Nvidia’s board to reinstate Huang.

“I spoke to ‘em. Let me just put it that way, and I convinced ‘em. And I must tell you, it was a lot easier to convince them yesterday than it was a week and a half ago,” said Trump, adding: “I believe my intervention was very important.”

Democratic Party leaders in the U.S. Congress then vow to launch investigations into the decision when they take control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in January.

For now, it’s business as usual for Nvidia, but questions remain about the board’s decision to reinstate Huang and the potential national security implications.

This also comes as the International Monetary Fund has warned the global economy is “standing on one leg” and underscored broader uncertainty in the AI sector.

Despite long-term uncertainty or risk, investors may feel more confident in Huang at the wheel in the near term than anyone else.

“Our stress test stands: assume 20 per cent of the data centers do not get built, the Asia loophole revenue is shut off, and financing is curtailed by 25 per cent, and we are still bullish on the thesis into the next two to three years,” said Ives.

– with files from Global News’ Sean Prevail, Uday Rana and Reuters

scraped.description: Beijing urged the United States on Wednesday to "uphold the stable development" of trade relations, after media reports said Washington was planning to announce new tariffs on China and other countries.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: China warns US against imposing new tariffs
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Beijing urged the United States on Wednesday to “uphold the stable development” of trade relations, after media reports said Washington was planning to announce new tariffs on China and other countries.

The reports said that Washington’s new levies would affect major US trading partners including China, the European Union, Japan and South Korea.

“Tariff wars and trade wars are not in anyone’s interest,” Chinese foreign ministry spokesman Guo Jiakun said, when asked about Washington’s reported plans.

He told a regular briefing that the world’s two top economies, which in 2025 agreed a tenuous truce in their trade war, “should resolve relevant issues through consultation”.

He added that accusations of overcapacity — mass production at a loss to flood overseas markets and undercut local rivals — was a “false premise” and a “pretext for political manipulation”.

“China and the United States should work together to effectively implement the important consensus reached by the two heads of state and uphold the stable development of China-US economic and trade relations,” he said.

President Donald Trump has long criticised China’s yawning trade surplus with the United States, which he has blamed for a decline in local manufacturing prowess and jobs.

After starting a second term in office last year, Trump imposed new tariffs on Chinese goods, kicking off a tit-for-tat escalation with Beijing that at one point saw duties soar as high as 145 percent.

The trade ceasefire struck by Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping in October 2025 is due to expire in January, after a two-month extension was agreed in September.

The two men met last week at an APEC summit in Shenzhen in southern China and are due to see each other again in December at a G20 summit in the United States.

During their meeting at APEC, which came just before a historic trilateral with Russian President Vladimir Putin, Xi hailed China’s “stable and improved” ties with the United States.

The Chinese leader also said that his country should cooperate in the field of artificial intelligence, keeping the technology “under human control” and guarding against safety risks.

scraped.title: Beijing slams US for 'suppressing' Chinese firms after Huawei conviction
scraped.description: Beijing lashed out at the United States on Wednesday for "suppressing" Chinese companies, after a US jury found tech giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and lying to regulators over its work in Iran.
scraped.author: AFP
scraped.h1: Beijing slams US for ‘suppressing’ Chinese firms after Huawei conviction
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Beijing lashed out at the United States on Wednesday for “suppressing” Chinese companies, after a US jury found tech giant Huawei guilty of stealing trade secrets and lying to regulators over its work in Iran.

Huawei, the world’s leading telecom equipment manufacturer, has been targeted by President Donald Trump’s administration, and was convicted on Tuesday in a New York federal court after a three-month trial.

The ruling comes at a politically sensitive time for the United States and China, whose leaders sought to project what Trump called a “fantastic” relationship when they met in Shenzhen last week.

Jurors found Huawei guilty of 10 of the 12 criminal counts facing it — including bank fraud, conspiracy to steal trade secrets and conspiracy to defraud the United States.

China hit back on Wednesday, saying it “firmly opposes the US suppressing and containing Chinese enterprises and firmly supports Chinese enterprises in safeguarding their legitimate rights and interests.”

Trump’s administration has long alleged a risk of Huawei spying on behalf of the Chinese government, and previously urged countries not to use the company’s infrastructure in new 5G mobile networks.

“No person or company is above the law,” US Attorney General Todd Blanche said in a statement after the conviction.

“For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft.”

Huawei rejected the conviction on Wednesday, saying in a statement it was “without legal or factual merit.”

“We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” it added.

The jury did, however, acquit Huawei of racketeering conspiracy and obstruction of justice, a move the company said it “welcomed,” adding that it “confirms that these allegations lack factual basis and vindicates our consistent position over the past eight years.”

“We believe the government’s remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit… We will thoroughly review the relevant verdicts and take all necessary legal actions to defend our rights and interests,” the statement continued.

The charges in part involved Huawei’s business dealings with the government of Iran.

“Huawei repeatedly lied about the nature of its business in Iran, falsely telling banks, journalists, and the US government that it did not assist Iran’s government, military, or intelligence community,” the DOJ said.

“Huawei lied about its activities in Iran to banks to obtain billions of US dollars and access to US-dollar clearing services, which enabled Huawei to be a sophisticated participant in a global marketplace for telecommunications services — in part because of its lies.”

The equipment manufacturer was also accused of attempting to recruit employees of US telecoms firms and obtaining technological information from them in the process.

That data allegedly enabled Huawei to develop products similar to those of its competitors, which it then sold at lower prices, according to the original indictment.

“The misappropriated intellectual property included trade secret information and copyrighted works, such as source code and user manuals for internet routers, antenna technology, and robot testing technology,” the DOJ said in a release.

Huawei even launched an internal program offering bonuses to employees who obtained industrial secrets from competitors, prosecutors claimed.

“Today’s verdict sends an unmistakable message: America will defend its businesses, protect its workers, and safeguard its national security against corrupt foreign corporations that lie, cheat, and steal to get ahead,” Assistant Attorney General A. Tysen Duva said in a statement.

scraped.title: Hong Kong rules out gov't-run matchmaking services amid low birth rate
scraped.description: Hong Kong authorities will not follow countries like Singapore in launching matchmaking services to address delayed marriages and low birth rates, a government official has said.
scraped.author: Hillary Leung
scraped.h1: Hong Kong rules out government-run matchmaking services amid low birth rate, delayed marriages
scraped.body_text:
Hong Kong Free Press HKFP

Hong Kong news, breaking updates – 100% Independent, impartial, non-profit

Hong Kong authorities will not follow countries like Singapore in launching matchmaking services to address delayed marriages and low birth rates, a government official has said.

Secretary for Home and Youth Affairs Alice Mak said in a written reply on Wednesday to lawmaker Roy Chu’s questions about family policies that the government was aware that other jurisdictions had launched “official or quasi-official matchmaking activities.”

“Given the differences in social backgrounds, demographic structures, and institutional systems across different places, the relevant experience may not be necessarily applicable to Hong Kong,” Mak said.

She added that the move from dating to marriage involves “many different factors and personal considerations.”

“The ultimate decision on whether to start a family does not necessarily hinge on whether matchmaking activities are organised,” she said.

Like many developed cities, Hong Kong has seen a trend of marriage postponement in recent decades. The percentage of unmarried men aged between 25 and 29 was 81 per cent in 2006. By 2021, it had increased to 87 per cent.

For women of the same age group, the figure rose from 68 per cent to 76 per cent.

The number of people who have never been married has also increased, while the number of registered marriages has fallen.

In September, the Singapore government piloted a matchmaking service for government workers.

Named FirstDate, the platform promised an end to “swipe fatigue” and a “different approach” to dating. It was open to people aged between 21 and 45 who work for the government.

According to FirstDate’s website, users must sign up with their government-issued identification and fill in a questionnaire that asks about their “interests, habits, values and preferences.”

Chu asked if Hong Kong would also organise “matchmaking festival activities and allow participants to claim reimbursement from the Government for part of their dating expenses.”

He also suggested the government could combine such initiatives with Valentine’s Day, as well as subsidise non-profit-making and district groups to offer dating activities.

The quality of “private dating services” in the community varies, Chu said, adding that this undermines the “confidence of single persons in using them.”

Hong Kong’s falling fertility rates have been a policy focus for the government in recent years. In 2023, it introduced a “baby bonus” scheme, giving HK$20,000 to families for every newborn.

In September, the government raised the incentive to HK$30,000, and also increased tax concessions for parents.

A 2024 survey by the Hong Kong Public Opinion Research Institute found that the city’s education system and politics were the main reasons why Hongkongers did not want children.

A fire burns at the site where a vehicle carrying petroleum products overturned and caught fire on a major ring road in Cairo, Egypt, November 25, 2026, in this screengrab obtained from social media video. | Photo Credit: Reuters

A crash involving a fuel tanker ignited a massive fire on a major highway surrounding Cairo on Wednesday (November 25, 2026), killing at least 30 people, Egyptian authorities said.

The blaze on Ring Road, a key artery that encircles the Egyptian capital, also injured at least 25 people and left more than two dozen cars and motorcycles charred, the Public Prosecutor's office said in a statement.

The stretch of the highway where the crash occurred was in Waraq, a densely populated neighbourhood in Giza, part of the Greater Cairo area, according to the Health Ministry.

At the scene, rescue workers were pulling people out of burning cars. An Associated Press video shows firefighters working to put out the fire spreading amongst the cars. Hundreds of people gathered near the scene in the Warraq district of Imbaba, a Cairo suburb.

Egyptian President Abdel-Fattah el-Sissi expressed his condolences to the victims in a statement. The Public Prosecutor's office said DNA investigations were underway to identify the victims.

Health Minister Khaled Abdel Ghaffar said the injured were taken to nearby hospitals and that he would head to the scene himself. He said the death toll was preliminary, raising concerns it could rise further.

Deadly traffic accidents claim thousands of lives every year in Egypt, which has a poor transportation safety record. Speeding, bad roads and poor enforcement of traffic laws are the main reasons behind most of the crashes.

In January, 21 people were killed and 16 injured in a massive multicar pileup on a road near the southern province of Beni Suef.

A Bench comprising Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana asked Solicitor General Tushar Mehta to seek instructions on the issue by November 30. File | Photo Credit: S. Subramanium

The Supreme Court indicated orally on Wednesday (November 25, 2026) its inclination to set aside a Calcutta High Court order that put on hold the Kolkata Municipal Corporation (KMC) elections over a delimitation exercise, and requested the High Court to hear the dispute afresh.

A Bench headed by Chief Justice of India Surya Kant made the suggestion while hearing an appeal filed by the West Bengal government against the High Court order of November 6. The High Court had directed the West Bengal State Election Commission to not notify the elections until a petition challenging the delimitation of municipal wards was decided.

Chief Justice Kant said the apex court was inclined to set aside the order of the High Court after taking into consideration pertinent legal and factual issues raised by the State government. The writ petition could also be transferred from the Single Judge Bench to a Division Bench, which would consider the entire dispute afresh and pass appropriate orders.

“And till the Division Bench forms a view the polls can be held off,” the court suggested orally.

The lawyers for both the State and former CPI(M) councillor Dipu Das, who had filed the petition in the High Court against the delimitation exercise, sought time to take instructions. The court listed the case for further hearing on November 30.

The Bench reasoned that its proposed “ad-hoc arrangement” would place both parties on an “even keel” without the Supreme Court expressing any opinion on the merits of the dispute.

The KMC had undertaken a revision of municipal ward boundaries ahead of the civic polls. As part of the plan, the number of wards in the civic body may rise to 209 from the current 144.

A Division Bench of the High Court had stopped the State Election Commission from issuing the election notification till the Single Judge Bench hearing Mr. Das’s petition decided the legality of the ward delimitation exercise.

Mr. Das had questioned the delimitation, arguing that the expansion of the municipal wards was void. He had sought a quashing of the September 11 gazette notification on expansion of wards as bad in law. He had contended that the delimitation happened on the basis of electoral rolls instead of the actual population, resulting in the alleged exclusion of a substantial number of residents.

After the Single Judge Bench had refused his pleas for an interim stay of the elections, Mr. Das had moved the High Court’s Division Bench.

scraped.author: News On Japan
scraped.h1: Japan Debates Nuclear-Powered Submarines at 1 Trillion Yen Each
scraped.body_text:
TOKYO - Japan is debating whether to introduce nuclear-powered submarines costing an estimated 1 trillion yen each as the government moves toward revising three key national security documents by the end of December, potentially marking a historic departure from the country's longstanding policy of restricting nuclear energy to peaceful purposes.

The Maritime Self-Defense Force recently unveiled its latest submarine, the Jingei, offering a look inside its command center, torpedo launch facilities and engine room housing its diesel engines. The submarine cost approximately 70 billion yen to build. Japan currently operates 25 submarines, all conventionally powered by diesel-electric propulsion. The government is now considering whether nuclear-powered vessels should be added to its fleet as part of a broader effort to strengthen the country's defense and deterrence capabilities. The three national security documents establish Japan's fundamental diplomatic and security policies and outline the future development of its defense capabilities. Originally scheduled for revision in 2027, the process was brought forward by Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi. "As the world enters an era of upheaval and Japan faces numerous difficult challenges, the revision of these three documents is an important undertaking that will determine the fate of our nation," Takaichi said. The possible introduction of nuclear-powered submarines has emerged as a major focus of the review, alongside defense spending and potential revisions to Japan's Three Non-Nuclear Principles. The most significant difference between nuclear-powered and conventional submarines is their propulsion system and the operational capabilities it provides. Conventional diesel-electric submarines must periodically approach the surface to obtain oxygen for their diesel engines and recharge their batteries. Nuclear-powered submarines, by contrast, generate energy using onboard nuclear reactors, allowing them to remain submerged for extended periods without needing to surface for air. They can also sustain higher speeds underwater, cover greater distances and potentially accommodate larger missile systems, depending on their design. However, nuclear-powered submarines are considerably more expensive to build, with estimates reaching 1 trillion yen per vessel. Introducing the technology into Japan's fleet is also expected to take around 10 years. China is believed to possess more than 10 nuclear-powered submarines, while North Korea claims to be developing its own nuclear-powered vessels. Against this increasingly challenging regional security environment, the Japan Innovation Party has emerged as a leading advocate for introducing nuclear-powered submarines. Senior party politician Seiji Maehara, who personally delivered a policy proposal to Takaichi, pointed to developments in the United States, South Korea and Australia. "The United States has nuclear-powered submarines, and South Korea and Australia are also moving toward acquiring them. Japan must think extremely strategically about what capabilities it should possess," Maehara said. Defense Minister Shinjiro Koizumi, asked in parliament whether nuclear power was being considered as a next-generation submarine propulsion system, indicated that the government was open to examining the technology. "Whether diesel or nuclear power, I believe it is necessary to consider propulsion options without excluding any possibilities," Koizumi said. However, successive Japanese governments have avoided acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, citing the Atomic Energy Basic Act, which restricts the use of nuclear energy to peaceful purposes. Asked about other countries moving toward acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, Takaichi said, "We will deepen concrete and realistic discussions while taking into account developments in our ally, the United States, and like-minded countries, including South Korea, as well as increasing military activity among neighboring countries." The debate stems partly from Japan's decision during the previous revision of its national security documents to acquire counterstrike capabilities through the deployment of long-range missiles capable of targeting enemy bases. Japan has since pursued the deployment of ground-based missiles, but concerns remain over their vulnerability to attack. Other countries have increasingly developed submarine-based missile systems, prompting discussions in Japan over the need to acquire similar capabilities. While Japan's existing diesel-electric submarines primarily carry torpedoes, nuclear-powered submarines can be designed to carry larger, long-range missiles. Their ability to remain submerged for extended periods also makes them potentially valuable as a deterrent. However, opinions remain divided within the ruling coalition. While the Japan Innovation Party actively advocates nuclear propulsion, the Liberal Democratic Party has stopped short of explicitly endorsing nuclear-powered submarines, instead referring to the use of next-generation propulsion systems. The biggest obstacle is cost. Japan would need at least three or four nuclear-powered submarines to maintain continuous operations through a rotation system, requiring an investment of several trillion yen. Opposition has also emerged within the Maritime Self-Defense Force itself, with senior officers questioning the need for nuclear-powered submarines and pointing to a shortage of personnel with the technical expertise required to operate nuclear reactors. Even some members of the Japan Innovation Party have expressed reservations, arguing that rapid advances in artificial intelligence and unmanned military technology could leave nuclear-powered submarines outdated by the time Japan introduces them. Public opinion is also divided. While some surveys show that more than half of respondents support increasing defense spending in response to the deteriorating security environment, opposition to acquiring nuclear-powered submarines exceeds 50%. The figures suggest that many Japanese are questioning whether the enormous expenditure would deliver sufficient benefits compared with alternative investments. Conventional submarines can be built at a fraction of the cost of nuclear-powered vessels, while investment in artificial intelligence and unmanned systems could potentially provide more cost-effective defense capabilities. Some Maritime Self-Defense Force officials have suggested that rather than spending 1 trillion yen on a single nuclear-powered submarine, Japan could allocate 500 billion yen to acquiring large numbers of underwater drones, reducing the need to send personnel into conflict zones while improving their safety. Australia's nuclear-powered submarine program illustrates the potential scale of the long-term financial commitment. According to estimates released by Australia's Parliamentary Budget Office in 2023, the total cost of acquiring and operating eight nuclear-powered submarines over approximately 30 years amounts to around 33 trillion yen. Such a program would constitute a national undertaking spanning several decades, imposing financial obligations on future generations. Calls are growing for the Japanese government to provide detailed estimates of the overall cost and explain how the financial burden would be distributed across generations. The government aims to secure Cabinet approval for the revised national security documents in December. Given the potentially significant domestic and international repercussions of acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, the revised documents are considered unlikely to explicitly commit Japan to their introduction. scraped.h1: 70-Year-Old Man Stabbed to Death at Fukuoka Station Bike Parking
scraped.body_text:
FUKUOKA - A 70-year-old man was fatally stabbed while working at a bicycle parking lot near a railway station in Fukuoka City on November 25th, with police later arresting a 49-year-old man on suspicion of assault in a separate incident and investigating his possible involvement in the killing.

The victim, Yoshiaki Ishikawa, was attacked while on duty at a bicycle parking facility beneath the elevated railway tracks of JR Kyudai-Gakkentoshi Station in Fukuoka's Nishi Ward. He was rushed to hospital but was later pronounced dead. Investigative sources said Ishikawa had sustained numerous stab wounds. Police arrested a 49-year-old man surnamed Kawatani, whose occupation is unknown, after questioning him as a person of interest in the murder investigation. Kawatani is suspected of striking a male station employee on the head inside Nishijin Station on the Fukuoka City Subway shortly after 11:30 a.m. on November 25th. During questioning, Kawatani admitted to the assault, telling investigators, "There is no doubt that I assaulted the station employee." Police have yet to establish whether Ishikawa and Kawatani knew each other. Numerous police vehicles gathered near the bicycle parking facility around midday, with investigators cordoning off the area and covering the crime scene with blue tarpaulins. A witness who saw Ishikawa being transported by emergency personnel said his face was covered in blood and that he appeared to be in no condition to speak. An acquaintance described Ishikawa as a diligent and efficient worker, saying they had met him several days earlier but had heard nothing about any trouble he might have been experiencing. Police subsequently discovered what appeared to be a knife near the bicycle parking facility, which investigators believe may have been used in the attack. The incident caused widespread disruption at the Aeon Mall shopping complex directly opposite the station, where customers and employees were evacuated as a precaution following concerns that the attacker might have entered the building. Emergency announcements instructed everyone inside the shopping center to evacuate, with employees directing customers out of the food court and other areas. "I was eating at the food court when an announcement said an emergency had occurred and everyone in the building needed to evacuate," one customer said. Another shopper described the evacuation as frightening, saying the emergency announcement was different from those previously heard during fire alarm incidents or evacuation drills. Customers whose vehicles were parked in the mall's multistory parking facility were directed along an external access road after movement through the building was restricted. The shopping center resumed operations at around 3 p.m., approximately two and a half hours after the incident, after safety had been confirmed. Forensic investigators were also seen examining a public restroom and its surroundings at a park about 200 meters from the crime scene, although any connection to the killing remains unclear. The area surrounding the station is largely residential, with numerous nursery schools, elementary schools and junior high schools nearby. Following the attack, the Fukuoka City Board of Education instructed all public elementary and junior high schools in Nishi Ward and neighboring Sawara Ward to implement safety measures, including having students return home in groups or arranging for parents to collect their children. Residents expressed shock and concern over the killing in what they described as a normally quiet neighborhood. "It's always peaceful around here, and it's not the kind of place where something like this happens," one resident said. "I'm shocked, frightened and worried." Police suspect Kawatani may be connected to the fatal stabbing based on similarities between his clothing and descriptions of the attacker, as well as other circumstances surrounding the two incidents. The murder investigation remains ongoing.

scraped.h1: Japan's Ski Resorts Prepare to Open as Winter Weather Intensifies
scraped.body_text:
HOKKAIDO - Heavy snowfall blanketed northern Japan on November 25th, with the Japan Meteorological Agency's 5 p.m. forecast indicating that snow would increasingly turn to rain across Hokkaido and Tohoku on Thursday, bringing the risk of thunderstorms and hail ahead of a weekend when many of Japan's major ski resorts are scheduled to open for the 2026-2027 winter season.

A winter pressure pattern brought strong winds and snowfall to areas along the Sea of Japan on Wednesday, with snow extending from Hokkaido and Tohoku to mountainous areas of Hokuriku and central Japan. In the 12 hours through 9 a.m. on Wednesday, Hijiori in Yamagata Prefecture recorded 23 centimeters of fresh snow, followed by Matsurube in Iwate Prefecture with 22 centimeters and Iwamizawa in Hokkaido with 19 centimeters. Aomori city received seven centimeters. Weather conditions across northern Japan are expected to change significantly on Thursday, November 26th, as cold air near the surface gradually retreats, causing snow to turn to rain in many areas. Despite the presence of a high-pressure system centered to the south of Japan, a shear line, where winds from different directions converge, is expected to develop across northern Japan, contributing to atmospheric instability. An upper-level trough carrying cold air with temperatures of around minus 24 degrees Celsius at an altitude of approximately 5,500 meters is also forecast to move across Tohoku and Hokkaido during Thursday morning. The combination of these weather systems is expected to increase the likelihood of thunderstorms, with the risk of lightning gradually rising from around 3 a.m. and remaining elevated through the morning before subsiding around midday. Locally heavy rain, thunderstorms and hail are possible even as temperatures rise and snowfall changes to rain. Residents are advised to remain alert to sudden changes in precipitation and intensity. Snowfall is expected to continue in some mountainous areas of Hokkaido, with up to around 20 centimeters of additional snow forecast for northern Kamikawa. Temperatures in Sapporo are forecast to reach 7 degrees Celsius on Thursday, rising to 10 degrees on Friday and 12 degrees on Saturday, before dropping sharply to around 2 degrees on Sunday, November 29th. Another low-pressure system is expected to bring widespread rain on Saturday, followed by renewed snowfall in parts of Hokkaido as colder air returns from Saturday evening into Sunday. The temporary warming could accelerate snowmelt at lower elevations, creating slushy road conditions and increasing the risk of snow falling from roofs. Subsequent freezing temperatures could make roads and sidewalks particularly hazardous. Further rain and snow are possible in northern Japan from November 30th through December 1st, although temperatures are forecast to fluctuate considerably during the period. sapporotenki.jp+2 Despite the unstable weather, preparations for the winter sports season are accelerating across Japan. Niseko Tokyu Grand Hirafu officially confirmed on November 25th that it will open on Saturday, November 28th, with snow grooming and safety preparations underway. The resort plans to operate its Ace Gondola and Ace No. 3 Quad Lift from Saturday morning, with the Center and Shirakaba courses confirmed for opening day. Three additional courses could become available depending on snow conditions. Grand Hirafu is scheduled to operate through May 5th, 2027, with night skiing running from December 12th through March 22nd. Elsewhere in Hokkaido, Niseko Hanazono, Niseko Village, Niseko Annupuri, Niseko Moiwa, Rusutsu, Kiroro and Furano are also targeting November 28th for their season openings. Sapporo Kokusai and Sapporo Teine began their winter seasons on November 22nd, although unfavorable weather has already interrupted operations. Sapporo Teine suspended skiing on November 24th and 25th after rain reduced snow coverage. ニセコ東急 グラン・ヒラフ〖公式〗+2 In Nagano Prefecture, Hakuba Happo-one, Hakuba Goryu and Hakuba47 began limited operations on November 21st, along with the Kumanoyu and Yokoteyama ski areas at Shiga Kogen. Hakuba Happo-one was reporting a snow depth of 166 centimeters on its slopes on Wednesday, while Hakuba Goryu was reporting 130 centimeters, with both resorts offering limited skiing. Nozawa Onsen is targeting November 28th for the start of its early skiing season, ahead of its official opening festival on December 19th. Tsugaike Mountain Resort is scheduled to open on December 1st, followed by further sections of Shiga Kogen on December 4th and 5th. In Niigata Prefecture, Kagura and Okutadami Maruyama are scheduled to open on November 28th, benefiting from their high elevations and relatively favorable early-season snow conditions. Naeba is targeting December 18th, followed by Gala Yuzawa, Maiko Snow Resort and Myoko Suginohara on December 19th. In the Tohoku region, Akita Hachimantai began operations on November 23rd, while Tengendai Kogen in Yamagata Prefecture is planning a preliminary opening on November 27th. Geto Kogen in Iwate Prefecture and Nekoma Mountain in Fukushima Prefecture are targeting November 28th, followed by Appi Kogen on December 5th and Zao Onsen on December 12th. Further south, Gransnow Okuibuki in Shiga Prefecture began operations on November 13th using artificial snow, while Washigatake in Gifu Prefecture opened on November 21st and Osorakan Snow Park in Hiroshima Prefecture followed on November 22nd.
