scraped.title: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
scraped.description: A ProPublica investigation last year found the Food and Drug Administration failed to regularly test generic medications that doctors warned about or drugs coming from factories with serious quality and safety violations.
scraped.author: Naisha Roy
scraped.h1: FDA to Expand Prescription Drug Testing After ProPublica Revealed Safety Concerns
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Rx Roulette

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

The Food and Drug Administration will test more prescription drugs for impurities and other dangerous quality lapses under an expanded program described by safety experts as a critical step to better protecting America’s drug supply.

About 90% of prescriptions in the United States are for generic drugs, many manufactured thousands of miles away in countries that include India and China. Until now, the FDA has only periodically tested a sampling of those drugs to see if they were safe or worked as effectively as the brand-name medications they are meant to replicate.

Last week, the FDA announced it will test more often and identify poorly performing drugs for further study.

The agency said it will buy the medications from retail pharmacies and wholesale distributors, but it did not say how many drugs it plans to test or how frequently. A spokesperson did not answer questions about how the FDA would select drugs for testing or how it would hold manufacturers accountable for inferior products, beyond posting the results on its website. Still, drug-safety experts said the expansion helps address long-standing concerns that some suppliers sacrifice quality to keep costs low — and that the FDA has for years looked the other way.

“All drugs, regardless of where they are manufactured, must meet the same FDA standards for safety, effectiveness and quality,” the FDA spokesperson told ProPublica.

A ProPublica investigation last year found the agency routinely relied on the drug companies themselves to do their own testing even as doctors, researchers and the Department of Defense warned that essential medications were contaminated or ineffective. On its website, the FDA said it has relied on a “more targeted, risk-based” approach to testing since 2018, choosing samples of drugs that have safety, effectiveness or quality concerns. The agency publicly reports the results on its website and notes that a majority of the tested drugs meet its standards.

ProPublica, however, found the agency for years failed to regularly test both the generics that have worried outside experts and drugs coming from factories that amassed so many serious quality and safety violations they were ultimately banned from the U.S. market. ProPublica later used FDA data to create Rx Inspector , a first-of-its-kind tool that allows consumers and doctors to look up the inspection records of the factories where more than 40,000 generic drugs are made.

Researchers have repeatedly urged the FDA to test more often. In fiscal year 2025, the FDA reported testing 46 different drugs, and for 29 of those drugs, the agency only tested one manufacturer . All but one passed every test.

The FDA’s new testing regime is “a huge validation of the research that we’ve been doing raising concerns about the quality of generic drugs,” Dr. Kevin Schulman, a professor of medicine and health policy at Stanford University, said of the FDA’s new testing program. “This is a great effort on their part.”

In February, senators also introduced a bill targeting transparency in the drug supply chain process, in part because of similar public concerns.

In response to questions about how it would decide which drugs to sample and how results would drive future enforcement, the FDA spokesperson said the initiative will “help the FDA identify potential drug quality issues faster and will provide more information the agency can use to decide if further action is needed.”

Experts say they ultimately hope the FDA’s program will work alongside independent testers to shift the generic drug market to be competitive on quality rather than price. While the agency can focus on weeding out the worst actors, independent labs can test manufacturers against one another to find the most effective products, said retired Col. Vic Suarez, a former medical supply-chain commander. A similar system is already used at the Department of Defense.

“It’s an important thing because they will probably catch extreme violators of regulatory standards, so that’s a good thing,” Suarez said. “But you also need to have a complementary system where you’re actually raising the bar.”

ProPublica previously engaged an independent lab, Valisure, to test several generic versions of three of the most prescribed drugs in the United States and in two cases identified irregularities that experts said could compromise their effectiveness.

“I think, high level, the idea that we should be doing more testing is fantastic,” said David Light, the co-founder of Valisure. “I think there’s so much growing energy behind that.”

Debbie Cenziper contributed reporting.

scraped.title: Democrats Vow to Shield Smithsonian From Any Trump Overhaul
scraped.description: Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, wrote a letter to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents on Tuesday citing ProPublica’s recent reporting on draft plans by a White House staffer.

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up to receive our biggest stories as soon as they’re published.

A top congressional Democrat announced she will investigate the Trump White House’s potential overhaul of the leadership and curatorial decisions at the Smithsonian Institution, the independent agency that oversees 21 national museums.

In a letter sent on Tuesday to the Smithsonian’s Board of Regents, Rep. Chellie Pingree, D-Maine, cited ProPublica’s recent story on the draft plans by a White House staffer targeting one of the Smithsonian’s most prominent museums, calling the reporting “extremely concerning.”

Pingree, who is slated to lead the subcommittee that controls the Smithsonian’s funding in the next Congress, said the plans revealed in the ProPublica story align with the administration’s broader efforts to interfere with the Smithsonian, which receives federal funding but is governed by a 17-person Board of Regents whose members include the chief justice of the United States, members of Congress, the vice president and private citizens.

In an interview with ProPublica, Pingree said that she intended her letter to put the Smithsonian governing board on notice that the incoming Democratic majority in Congress is monitoring the institution to make sure the board upholds its responsibility to keep the agency independent from political pressure.

“No White House employee riding on the Metro gets to design a plan for what future exhibits look like or gets to veto staffers or exhibits at the Smithsonian,” Pingree said. “That’s not how it works.”

Pingree told ProPublica that she plans to use her powers as chair in the next Congress to aggressively look into what she called the Trump administration’s meddling with the Smithsonian and to expose those efforts to the broader American public.

“We fully intend to dig deeper than has been done in the past,” she said.

Pingree’s letter comes in response to ProPublica reporting on a 25-item list of possible changes that, taken together, would amount to an unprecedented attempt by the White House to control the content and personnel of the Smithsonian’s National Museum of American History, which attracts nearly 2 million people a year.

Those reforms include firing many of the museum’s top officials; rolling out a new permanent exhibit called “The Riches of Our Western Civilization Inheritance”; introducing new K-12 learning materials such as a “Founders-focused curriculum titled something like Architects of Liberty: The Heroic Journey of America’s Founders OR Profiles in Liberty: Washington and America’s Heroic Men of Courage”; and unveiling a new “Colossus Statue” of George Washington for the museum’s entrance.

The draft plans were visible on the laptop and in handwritten notes of a White House staffer who was riding a D.C.-area Metro train in late October. A nearby commuter took pictures of the materials and sent them to ProPublica reporters, who in turn verified the information. It’s unclear what kind of reception the plans have received inside the Trump White House. The staffer and White House did not respond to requests for comment for the story.

Also on Tuesday, Lonnie Bunch, the Smithsonian Institution’s outgoing leader, responded to ProPublica’s reporting in a message sent to employees. “The intended use of this list is unclear,” Bunch wrote in his letter . “What remains clear is that the Smithsonian is an independent institution with the responsibility and privilege to present accurate information to millions of visitors through our scholarship and educational programs.”

Pingree was not the only member of Congress who responded to ProPublica’s reporting with a pledge to defend the Smithsonian’s independence.

Sen. Alex Padilla, D-Calif., said on social media that if he becomes chair of the Senate Rules Committee — which has jurisdiction over the Smithsonian — in the next Congress, “we will protect it from Trump’s interference and overreach.”

“The Smithsonian is NOT a federal agency, it is an independent, nonpartisan organization overseen by Congress – not the White House,” Padilla wrote .

Incoming Congressman Fred Wellman, a Democrat elected this month to represent the suburbs of St. Louis, responded even more forcefully to ProPublica’s reporting on social media.

“Over my dead body,” he wrote .

scraped.title: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
scraped.description: Records show that Andrea Bell was personally involved in discussions about state funding of a large apartment project that would pay her husband’s employer $2 million if built. Project backers want $17.5 million from Bell’s agency.
scraped.author: Rob Davis
scraped.h1: Oregon Housing Leader Met With Officials Who Are Seeking Money for a Project Her Husband’s Employer Is Developing
scraped.body_text:
Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

Investigative Journalism in the Public Interest

ProPublica is a nonprofit, investigative newsroom that exposes corruption. We report in all 50 states and partner with local newsrooms . Our work spurs real-world impact and has received numerous awards, including nine Pulitzer Prizes.

How Abortion Bans Lead to Preventable Deaths

How Recent Arrivals at the Border Have Changed the Country and Its Attitudes

SCOTUS Justices’ Beneficial Relationships With Billionaire Donors

Sign up for ProPublica's Big Story newsletter and get our latest stories delivered straight to your inbox.

Co-published with Oregon Public Broadcasting and The Oregonian/OregonLive

ProPublica is a nonprofit newsroom that investigates abuses of power. Sign up for Dispatches , a newsletter that spotlights wrongdoing around the country, to receive our stories in your inbox every week.

When Oregon’s Housing Stability Council met by Zoom in early October, the state’s top housing official told the oversight board that she wanted to address a story ProPublica published that morning .

The story revealed that the official, Andrea Bell, hadn’t clearly disclosed her husband’s work for a small consulting firm that helps housing authorities develop apartments, sometimes with money from Bell’s agency. Nor had she notified Gov. Tina Kotek about it, something Oregon law requires of a governor’s appointee when an actual or potential conflict arises.

Council members, who award hundreds of millions of dollars in housing subsidies, affirmed their support for Bell, who told them she wanted to be clear: “None of the projects that are coming from the council impact my household income.”

Newly obtained records, however, show a clear financial connection between the council’s decisions and her husband’s employer. The records also show that Bell was personally involved in meetings and internal discussions about state funding of a large apartment project, Aloha 209th, which her husband’s employer is helping to develop.

Backers of the Aloha 209th project in Portland’s suburbs are seeking $17.5 million from the housing council, which receives funding recommendations from Bell’s agency.

JH Brawner, the consulting firm that employs Bell’s husband, Joshua Crites, will earn a $2 million fee from the housing authority in Washington County if the transaction closes. If not, JH Brawner gets nothing.

A separate project outside Portland, the Park Place apartments in Clackamas County, already received money through Oregon’s housing agency. Five months after Oregon awarded $36 million to the project in May 2025, Clackamas County’s housing authority paid JH Brawner a $2.4 million consulting fee, the new records show.

Like the Washington County contract, the one with Clackamas County says that if funding fell through for any reason and the project didn’t move forward, “no fee shall be due” to the firm.

JH Brawner said Crites, the firm’s director of strategic initiatives, has not worked on the Aloha 209th project but was one of five staffers assigned to Park Place. JH Brawner pays employees, including Crites, a fixed salary that is not tied to any project closing, according to managing director Zak de Gorgue.

Bell, executive director of Oregon Housing and Community Services, said in a statement that she is “committed to transparency, accountability, and compliance with state law.”

“At no point in my tenure as executive director have I used my position to influence or benefit myself or anyone related to me,” she said. “To be clear, I made no efforts to influence funding, and the Aloha 209 project has not received funding from OHCS and remains on the waitlist.”

Bell’s public agency sits in the middle of the state’s effort to combat a homelessness problem that is among the nation’s worst. Kotek, the governor, has made building more housing a pillar of her time in office. Oregon Housing and Community Services has distributed billions of state and federal dollars to subsidize the construction of apartments intended to have affordable rents.

Norman Williams, a law professor at Willamette University College of Law who teaches about government ethics, said Bell should have reported to the governor that she had a possible conflict and stayed out of any discussions about the projects her husband’s employer helped develop.

“It may all be an innocent mistake on her part,” Williams said, “but she knows who her husband is working for and she doesn’t report that. It makes it look like she’s trying to conceal this.”

De Gorgue said in a statement that the Aloha 209th project is still in development and the company had “no knowledge of Andrea Bell taking any action to move the project forward, nor has JH Brawner & Company engaged in any advocacy to secure funding approval” from Bell’s agency. Funding applications were submitted by the local housing authorities, not by JH Brawner.

“We have no indication, nor any reason to believe, that any project on which we have consulted has been the beneficiary of inappropriate influence,” de Gorgue said.

Separately, he said Clackamas and Washington counties chose JH Brawner as a consultant years before the company hired Crites in 2023.

Crites did not respond to an emailed request for comment.

After ProPublica asked Bell about her husband’s employment in September, she amended three years of ethics disclosure forms, explicitly naming JH Brawner as his employer. (The one time her state filings alluded to Crites’ job before that was in 2025, with a misspelling: “Spouse serves in an advisory role for a developmen.” It showed only the company’s street address, misspelled, and not its name.)

Bell also asked the Oregon Government Ethics Commission for a formal opinion about her potential conflict at the direction of Kotek’s staff. That evaluation was paused after the commission opened a preliminary review in response to a citizen complaint about her lack of disclosure. The preliminary review is ongoing.

ProPublica obtained the new details about Bell’s involvement through county contracts and emails to and from Bell, which were released under Oregon’s public records law. Bell’s agency initially said the emails would cost $612.50 to produce but eventually provided them for free. Washington County charged $364.25 for contracts, invoices and other documents.

Though backers say the Aloha 209th housing development is ready to be built, it’s on a waitlist to receive money from the state. Its turn is not likely to come until at least late 2028. By then, local officials worry that the delay will jeopardize its other funding sources and the project may need an even larger subsidy.

ProPublica previously reported that Molly Rogers, head of the county housing agency seeking money for Aloha 209th, spoke publicly about contacting Bell and said the state agency director was receptive to talking further.

The new records contain Bell’s recollections of the phone conversation she had with Rogers. The same morning the two spoke, in June, Bell told another department official by email that Aloha 209th had “a unique dimension of urgency and angst” because it was one of the last projects funded by a 2018 voter-approved housing bond administered by the Portland area’s Metro regional government.

Natasha Detweiler-Daby, who leads the state housing agency’s affordable rental housing division, responded to Bell that it could be “responsive and logical” to have lawmakers “add nuance” next year by dedicating some portion of funding for housing authority projects on Oregon’s waitlist. Detweiler-Daby did not respond to an email from ProPublica seeking comment.

Behind the Aloha 209th discussion was the way that Oregon awards its housing subsidies. Since 2024, Oregon has given the money on a first-come, first-served basis. When funding runs out, Bell’s agency places applications on a waitlist in the order received.

Bell spoke with Washington County officials about Aloha 209th during a 45-minute Zoom meeting in August, records show. Internal notes summarizing the conversation say that the county would send an updated report to the state agency to “inform movement of 209.” The summary said the groups involved would have a follow-up conversation about the project.

Bell went on to discuss the project with regional government officials in early September. About two weeks before the meeting, she emailed her deputy with two possible ways to get the project funded: a legislative “carve-out” or Metro consolidating its subsidies so it could fully pay for the project. “I want to do everything we can to help the metro projects be successful and the resources, like ours, are nearly depleted,” Bell wrote. She acknowledged that Metro might not find the solution appealing.

Bell told ProPublica that she met with Metro and Washington County at the other agencies’ request. She said her agency “does not have and is not pursuing a ‘legislative carve out’ for any project.”

“My approach is to listen to partners’ concerns and explain our funding process,” she said in an email. “I have no role in deciding whether projects should receive funding as part of this process, and I do not advocate for individual projects. Characterizing these routine discussions and legitimate concerns as something improper fundamentally misrepresents their purpose and context.”

A spokesperson for Washington County’s housing authority told ProPublica that Bell did not make any commitment to alter the prioritization of Aloha 209th. Another Washington County spokesperson said the August meeting with Bell was mainly focused on the housing authority’s desire for “clearer criteria” for how projects on the state’s waitlist get funded.

A Metro spokesperson said the regional agency requested the September meeting with a goal “for the two agencies to strengthen our working relationship and coordination.”

“Metro does not, and did not, advocate for any specific project,” the spokesperson said. “We clearly indicated this at the meeting and in writing ahead of the meeting.” The agency has advocated for a group of remaining projects, including Aloha 209th, to get money so Metro can fulfill commitments made as part of its affordable housing bond, the spokesperson said.

Oregon’s Government Ethics Commission has until early December to complete its preliminary review of the complaint over Bell’s financial disclosure, which will help the agency decide whether to open a full investigation.

Bell said she will “continue to remain responsive to the Ethics Commission” as it completes its examination.

Kotek’s office, provided with a list of ProPublica’s latest findings, said in a statement that the governor “holds all agency leadership to consistent and high ethical standards” and that her office “is closely following” the ethics panel’s review.

scraped.title: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
scraped.description: It’s not always like you see in the movies. Sometimes it’s slow and gradual – but inexorable.
scraped.author: AJ White
scraped.h1: Ancient Cahokia was transformed amid droughts and flooding – climate change is reshaping modern communities in similar ways
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

More than 800 years ago, a combination of environmental and societal challenges led some Mississippian people to leave Cahokia, a massive archaeological site that was once home to 20,000 people near modern-day St. Louis. Just south of Cahokia, another archaeological site is taking shape at Centreville, Illinois, as modern-day people abandon their homes in the face of 21st-century climate and cultural changes.

My anthropology colleague Sissel Schroeder and I studied both sites to learn how people react to climate change when it hits home.

During the 1960s and 1970s, economic downturns and the movement of white residents out of diversifying neighborhoods made Centreville into a majority-Black community that faced challenges such as mismanaged drainage infrastructure . Yet in interviews with a community group, residents reported that people had no major problems with living there until the floods came.

From the 1960s to the 2020s, average annual rainfall in the St. Louis region has increased by 10 inches (25 centimeters) to 44 inches (112 cm) a year. That has led to more frequent flooding , including in Centreville, where stormwater and sewage systems have not been significantly updated since they were built in the 1960s. The rains bring floods, which back up raw sewage into people’s kitchen sinks, and seep up through the ground, covering residents’ lawns as well as public streets and sidewalks.

Many people who can afford to move away from Centreville have done so, leaving a mostly older population and many abandoned homes . Essentially, a community is becoming an archaeological site before our eyes.

Nine hundred years ago, Cahokia occupied the same floodplain as Centreville does today. At its population peak around 1100 CE, over 100 burial, residential and ceremonial earthen mounds stretched from one end of the valley to the other, with its core centered on Monks Mound.

Monks Mound is the largest prehistoric earthwork in the Americas. It is 950 feet (290 meters) long and 775 feet (236 meters) wide, and its platform rises 100 feet (30 meters) above the floodplain. Decades of archaeological excavation show that surrounding Monks Mound are plazas that held great feasts and possibly sporting events – including chunkey, something like bocce ball with spears – timber monuments likely for ritually observing astronomical events, and other mounds containing elaborate burials .

Possibly up to 20,000 people lived at Cahokia at the start of the 12th century, but by the end of the century, the city had entered a population decline that continued for 200 years . Archaeologists have long debated the cause of Cahokia’s depopulation before European explorers and colonists arrived, putting forward a range of societal and environmental theories .

In other research, several colleagues and I previously found that Cahokia experienced several natural disasters during a warming period known as the Medieval Climatic Anomaly . In the second half of the 12th century, Cahokia experienced a large Mississippi River flood and drought conditions that stretched for several decades. Our study argued that the site’s depopulation was related to those climatic changes .

Climate change at Cahokia didn’t look like catastrophic scenes in movies like “The Day After Tomorrow .” There’s no evidence to suggest widespread destruction or death. Departures began at a time that coincided with climatic changes of the 12th century, but people continued to gradually leave the site through the 13th and 14th centuries.

As people left, life in Cahokia changed. After 1200 CE, archaeological evidence suggests Cahokians ceased or reduced communal feasting and mound building. They also contributed less to public granaries, moving agricultural surplus to private spaces. But it only became harder to live there for some people: Larger houses and status symbols became more prevalent, perhaps indicating a larger gap between the rich and poor.

To understand the relationship between social and environmental changes at Cahokia, I look at what is happening at Centreville in the 21st century.

People are not leaving all at once; instead, the accumulation of years of flooding-related failing infrastructure, repair costs and health problems have pushed some away from the community. Others have stayed, like resident William McNeal, who told a local news outlet, “ I’m not going to abandon my house . It’s all I got.”

Additionally, what’s happening in Centreville reveals that climate change is experienced unequally – some people are more affected than others. All of the St. Louis area has received increased rainfall and flooding in recent decades, but the residents of Centreville face some of the worst consequences because they live in a floodplain with outdated infrastructure.

At Cahokia, people would have also experienced the environmental events of the 12th century in different, unequal ways. Those with farms in the lower floodplain were most exposed to crop loss from flooding , but plots in the uplands were safer. During drought conditions, fields in well-drained soils likely retained less moisture and fared worse than plots with poorly drained soils.

People who lost crops may have struggled to contribute to communal feasts and shared food storage . I believe some may have become indebted to neighbors whose resources remained intact, while others may have decided to leave. Over time, these individual responses could have changed the relationships and inequalities that structured Cahokian society.

If that’s what happened, climate change did not cause a sudden and dramatic exodus from Cahokia. Instead, its uneven effects altered the social status quo; some benefited, some lost , and some left .

Today, some consequences of climate change can be major and immediate, such as sudden massive floods . But in communities like Centreville, the effects of repeated flooding accumulate over years, producing gradual societal changes that are harder to recognize than the aftermath of a sudden catastrophe.

Climate models are useful for estimating future conditions, but they reveal nothing about how people might experience or respond to those conditions. Events and people’s reactions may unfold quickly, even suddenly, or they may play out quietly over long periods of time.

Regardless, the result may be the stillness of an archaeological site.

Assistant Professor of Anthropology, Indiana University

scraped.title: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male-dominated art world by mocking it
scraped.description: Critics have attributed the repetitive, labor-intensive nature of Kusama’s work to be a product of mental illness. But a closer look reveals deliberate choices and gender dynamics at play.
scraped.author: Midori Yamamura
scraped.h1: Sewing an infinity of phalluses – how Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama confronted the male‑dominated art world by mocking it
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

Japanese artist Yayoi Kusama’s installations are big, bold and controversial. From the time she burst upon the pop art scene in the 1960s until her death on Aug. 14, 2026, at the age of 97, she challenged the Western, male-dominated art world. She also upended assumptions about mental disorders, which many people have uncritically seen as the source of her creativity . Her phallic sculptures and confounding mirror rooms are still popular, and they defy artistic classifications.

Kusama’s resistance to categorization raises an intriguing question: What is her lasting effect on the art world?

Kusama took a major step into the global art scene after sending two canvases for display at Amsterdam’s Stedelijk Museum on Feb. 5, 1962. After that, she shifted her direction to avant-garde sculpture. She created Accumulation No. 1 , her first work in a series that employed sewn phallic protrusions. The series thrust her into New York City’s pop art scene and would lead to her fantastical Infinity Mirror Rooms installation.

A major retrospective of her work is on view at the Stedelijk Museum through Jan. 17, 2027.

The specter of her mental health issues, however, still undermines her art’s significance. Critics often link the repetition in her work to obsessive-compulsive disorder. But as an art historian who has studied Kusama extensively, I argue that she intentionally used compulsivity to examine gender issues in the art world. A close look at Accumulation No. 1 reveals how she pulled this off.

Kusama’s emphasis on gender came into focus when she arrived in the male-dominated New York art world . During the 1940s and 50s, while abstract expressionism reigned in New York, women in the scene were treated as wives and assistants.

Painter Grace Hartigan had to adopt the pseudonym “George” to gain recognition. By the 1960s, that was starting to change. Venezuelan sculptor Marisol Escobar’s May 1962 exhibition at the Stable Gallery bucked the trend of gender conformity by integrating self-portraits into her sculpture series.

Kusama’s Accumulation No. 1 emerged as New York artists were seeking to move beyond abstract expressionism . The gestural paintings of this art movement were what some critics saw as an existential struggle toward originality coded as masculine . Pop artists refused this model : They turned instead to ready-made objects and impersonal repetition, evoking factory production.

Kusama procured furniture and egg cartons for her Accumulation sculptures, as well as a wooden rowboat for another sculpture that became Aggregation One Thousand Boats Show . She decided to focus on sewing — an art rooted in her female Japanese education — and she ordered a sewing machine.

Kusama embraced femininity by using phalluses – a symbol of patriarchal authority – made from assorted fabrics sewn into tubular shapes, filled with cotton and painted white. She upholstered an armchair with these protrusions, colonizing an eerie domestic scene with phalluses made through a traditionally feminine craft.

In this way, she transformed furniture into a vessel of complex meaning, with gender as the key component to interpretation.

Art critics and scholars have often interpreted the time-consuming process of creating these phalluses as evidence of obsessive-compulsive neurosis . But this assumption overshadows Kusama’s careful planning and deliberate choices in her art. Intensive manual labor is a common component of Kusama’s work.

In 2008, filmmaker Heather Lenz interviewed Kusama’s friend Helen Yrissary, who helped sew the protrusions on the armchair. She noted that while there were always five assistants who crafted the phalluses, only Kusama herself secured them to the chair. In Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, obsession was more of a calculated aesthetic and conceptual choice than a compulsive action.

Kusama knew about obsessive-compulsive disorder and the anxiety it can cause. Drawing on Sigmund Freud’s psychoanalytical theories, she explained in her autobiography that she developed the phallic image while she was exploring “kyōfu” – fear, or feelings of the uncanny – in the Accumulation series. According to Freud, the potential for the uncanny is rooted in a child’s first awareness of the anatomical differences between the sexes. He postulated that female children are traumatized when they realize they lack a penis, creating what he called penis envy .

Kusama’s Accumulation series may have functioned as a satire of penis envy . And it may have led her to the idea of vanquishing men’s authoritative power.

In one of her self-portraits from 1966 , Kusama flaunted a phallic protrusion near her crotch. This gesture suggests that the protrusion might be her own penis, that she might be bisexual or that she might not fall under the category of “female.” Such efforts to redefine female sexuality inspired many female artists at the time. Toward the late 1960s, artist Louise Bourgeois , who admired Kusama’s work, created several sculptures, including Fillette (Little Girl) , that employed phallic shapes as commentary on psychological complexes and gender.

But when Kusama premiered Accumulation No. 1 and Accumulation No. 2, The New York Times gave her work only a brief mention . When, three months later, sculptor Claes Oldenburg showed his similarly sewn “metamorphic” sculptures, he received rave reviews in numerous art magazines, bringing him to the attention of the international art world. It was only much later in the 2010s, after Kusama gained global prominence, that Oldenburg admitted her influence on his work.

Kusama’s popularity today stems from works that are both visually expansive and socially subversive. Aggregation: One Thousand Boats Show was her first all-over exhibit – an exhibition in which a repeated motif covers the gallery’s four walls, drawing the audience into the work rather than asking them to view it as a separate object. On display at the Gertrude Stein Gallery from December 1963 to January 1964, it featured a sculpture of the phallus-embedded boat surrounded by its image repeating across the wall.

Although Kusama sought to subvert male authority, she appears nude in a photograph of the phallus boat installation , her back to the camera, trapped between the real and the illusory. Rowing the boat seems like the only way to escape the omnipresence of masculinity.

She seemed even more entrapped by patriarchal symbolism in her Infinity Mirror Room — Phalli’s Field, where she lays among an array of phalluses covered in red polka dots.

In 1966, Kusama found a way to break away from male domination through her “ Peep Show ” at the Castellane Gallery in New York. In it, she reduced the towering phallus to a small dot of light. It was her first work of psychedelic art , a category the curator Christoph Grunenberg characterized as both “ artistic experiment and dissenting politics .”

Incorporating Beatles music, flickering strobe lights and mirror reflections, “Peep Show” was intended to produce effects similar to those of psychoactive drugs such as mescaline, psilocybin and LSD, liberating users from established social norms and opening the possibility of alternative values. The exhibit, later known as “ Love Forever ,” also aimed to alter perception by inducing synesthesia — a neurological state in which stimulating one sensory-cognitive pathway triggers involuntary experiences in another.

Kusama remembered attending a lecture by Timothy Leary , a former Harvard University psychology professor and psychedelics advocate, at the Village Theater in New York, a hub of psychedelic culture. In 1968, she collaborated with light artist Joshua White on Self-Obliteration , a fusion of sound, lights and images that Leary claimed “would demonstrate what an LSD session is like.”

Kusama’s ability to transform any neurosis she may have had into liberation began with Accumulation No. 1 and continued through Fireflies on the Water (2002), Soul Under the Moon (2002), Infinity Mirror Room—Aftermath of Obliteration of Eternity (2009) and Infinity Mirrored Room—The Souls of Millions of Light Years Away (2013). The ethereal visions embodied in her psychedelic mirror rooms stand in for the mind-altering drugs that release people from the rationality of society and fuel the desire to change.

Through Kusama’s Accumulation and Infinity Mirror Room series, I argue that she turned the human body into what philosopher Herbert Marcuse described as “ an instrument of pleasure .” By making the body an instrument of pleasure rather than labor, Kusama subverted the age-old patriarchal order.

Associate Professor of Art History, City University of New York

scraped.title: Georgians mark 2 years of pro-EU demonstrations – defying campaign to wear protesters down
scraped.description: So far, the government has not crushed the protest movement. But in critics’ eyes, it has used psychological weapons to help create opposition burnout.
scraped.author: Regina Smyth
scraped.h1: Georgians mark 2 years of pro‑EU demonstrations – defying campaign to wear protesters down
scraped.body_text:
Share article

Print article

For months on end, Georgians have braved the elements and long odds to protest their government’s suspension of the former Soviet country’s bid to join the European Union. On Nov. 28, 2026, those pro-democracy campaigners will mark a milestone – two years of sustained, if declining, protest.

Hailed as a beacon of democracy following its independence from the Soviet Union in 1991, Georgia has of late been increasingly held up as an example of democratic backsliding : the slow, persistent erosion of democratic institutions. Indeed, the 2025 Economist Democracy Index — an annual benchmark of global democratic health — found that Georgia had fallen 20 places on the list since 2017.

The formal hallmarks of democratic systems remain visible: Elections are held, parliaments vote and political parties organize. At the same time, democratic institutions are compromised by political leaders, parties, police, courts and legislators – who use their resources to stifle dissent and compromise democratic institutions .

These leaders commonly target electoral fairness without committing blatant fraud. For example, public sector workers such as teachers are threatened with job loss if they do not vote for the government, or local governments are rewarded for producing votes during elections. Critics allege that biased laws and politicized court cases eliminate independent media and jail opposition leaders.

Backsliding governments also use disinformation and rhetoric to create confusion and fear. Using these tactics, critics allege, the ruling populist right, pro-Russian Georgian Dream government continues to undermine the fragile democracy. With many feeling unable to fight back through elections and parliamentary debates, Georgians have taken to the streets .

I am a member of a research project that explores how national protests in countries with fragile democratic institutions create legacies that can influence politics over the long term. In Georgia, that work is based on interviews with leaders from across civic and political life. These interviews point to a widespread view that the government is actively attempting to erode protest just as critics of the government feel it has eroded institutions. So far, the government has not crushed the movement with a campaign of lethal force. Rather, it has tried to use lower-level, but sustained, suppression tactics in hopes of inducing burnout in the opposition and getting civil society to disengage .

In Georgia, the roots of protest are deep in the struggle for independence from the Soviet Union and the influence of Russia under the leadership of Vladimir Putin. In 2003, Georgians launched the Rose Revolution – the first in a series of actions across the former Soviet states called the Color Revolutions – to support democracy and autonomy from the Russian Federation.

The Georgian Dream emerged as a socially conservative opposition party in 2012 under the leadership of the billionaire Bidzina Ivanishvili and won a majority of seats in parliamentary elections. Many analysts at the time saw the party as a new chance to consolidate democracy. Yet unable to provide economic gains , the party instead embarked on a platform consistent with pro-Russian security policies, which critics allege were rife with political manipulation, and false rhetoric that undermined democracy. In 2019 , Georgians took to the streets to contest failed electoral reforms and growing Russian influence through Ivanishvili’s governance.

By 2023, tens of thousands of Georgians filled Rustaveli Avenue in the capital of Tbilisi to oppose a law designed to shutter civic organizations and independent media. The so-called Russia Law borrowed heavily from the Kremlin’s tactics to eliminate opposition to the Putin government in Russia. Many Georgians understood the law as an attack on democracy and celebrated when the ruling party, Georgian Dream, withdrew its bill .

A year later, as new elections approached, the party reintroduced the law, provoking renewed protest. This time it passed. A few months later, preelection polls showed the opposition parties leading, but expectations of victory evaporated when Georgia Dream secured 54% of vote – an outcome that critics raised as a possible indicator of electoral manipulation .

Then, on Nov. 28, 2024, the new government put Georgia’s European Union bid on hold until 2028. Many Georgians have long seen EU membership as a path forward to economic growth and democratic protections . In light of Russia’s 2008 occupation of Georgian territory and 2022 full-scale war in Ukraine, Georgians also perceived EU membership as a bulwark against Russian intervention.

Fueled by feelings of betrayal over the reversal on EU membership, crowds poured back onto Rustaveli Avenue, reaching a peak of 170,000-200,000 protesters. Several hundred activists have returned every day since.

Over the course of two years, Georgian protesters have faced chronic and unpredictable violence rather than a decisive crackdown. By Amnesty International’s count , thousands have been arrested, hundreds beaten in the streets or abused in custody, and more than 150 imprisoned after politically motivated trials.

In general, however, the Georgian government’s tactic for countering the protest movement has been to avoid mass violence in lieu of targeted attacks on protest leaders and subtler means to discourage new activists. Fines for protest rose tenfold between 2024 and 2026 to double the average Georgian’s monthly income, leading Amnesty International to conclude that Georgia’s courts have become tools for “financially exhausting protesters.” Meanwhile, repeat offenses for participating in a demonstration have become crimes.

These actions have steadily increased the costs of protesting, driving activists from the streets due to a multitude of reasons related to risk, personal safety and fear. In our research, we protect the people we interviewed from state retaliation by making them anonymous.

The effects of these costs are clear in their statements.

“We don’t say it openly,” an investigative journalist and editor told us. “But the truth is, we were exhausted, depleted — and that’s the state we were in when the election campaign started.”

Another pro-European student movement member said, “Human resources are exhausted. You can’t expect 300,000 or 100,000 or even 20,000 people to march from Ilia University to Parliament every single day for 200 or 300 days straight. People have jobs, lives, personal struggles, and you can’t ask them to drop everything every day.”

Overall, our interviews with a variety of civil society leaders and protest supporters found that exhaustion was widespread and that a declining amount of people had the physical, financial or emotional capacity to stand every day.

Still, leaders remain hopeful that the nightly protests will provide a platform for renewed activism when the next opportunity for challenging the government presents itself. As the same pro-European student movement member argued: “I believe that will change. Let’s say Georgians are just on a kind of protest vacation. I hope we’ll be back out there again, all together, very soon.”

For now, there exists an effective stalemate between the protest movement and the government. The movement endures but has not broken through, and I believe the government cannot crush it because it fears the student leader is right — and the protest vacation might end.

For a generation of Georgians invested in building democracy, the past two years have shown how quickly democratic gains can be undone.

Still, as the anniversary of nightly protests approaches, many Georgians point to Serbia, where student protesters also took the streets in November 2024 and forced an early election on Oct. 25, 2026. The same Serbian students formed an opposition bloc that won a parliamentary majority that unseated an entrenched and increasingly autocratic leader .

Georgian Dream understands this threat and has proposed a ban on opposition parties, closing the route that Serbia’s students used.

Yet a policy of attrition has its risk, as ruling in that manner can further erode legitimacy and incur the high costs of keeping elites loyal. In the meantime, the protests continue, which could yet provide oxygen for renewed opposition when a new crisis arises.

Tinatin Genebashvili, a U.S.-based Georgian researcher and founder of Research Hub, contributed to this article.

Professor of Political Science, Indiana University

scraped.body_text:

The U.S. Army detonated five tons of degraded lead azide explosives in southeast Iowa this morning, following delays and legal challenges over concerns about toxic dust generated by the blast.

Shortly after 9 a.m. local time, a series of explosions ignited the bomb-making material, sending two plumes into the air that were visible for miles. Cars passed along the north end of the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant in Middletown a minute before the detonation, with more traffic passing soon afterward.

After the blast, Environmental Protection Agency administrator Lee Zeldin said initial air samples collected downwind of the explosion showed no detectable lead. “It looks like it caved inward perfectly,” he told CNN. At an 11 a.m. briefing, Army officials also said initial air monitoring had detected no airborne lead.

But some scientists cautioned against drawing broad conclusions from the initial results, questioning whether the Army’s monitoring could totally rule out lead exposure from a blast of this scale.

Measuring airborne lead is more complicated than a single reading might suggest, said Bruce Lanphear, an expert on lead exposure and professor of health sciences at Simon Fraser University in British Columbia. The monitoring methods used, the size of the particles being measured and the height and location of monitoring equipment can all affect the results.

“The failure to detect an increase in airborne lead from preliminary samples does not establish that no lead was released or that no one was exposed,” Lanphear said in an email exchange with Inside Climate News on Wednesday. Lanphear submitted an expert witness statement in support of an emergency lawsuit filed last week on behalf of the Iowa Environmental Council and the Sierra Club’s Iowa Chapter.

“We need to know how lead was measured and the detection limits of the sampling methods. We should also await the results of other environmental samples before drawing conclusions.”

After the blast, wind gusts traveled southwest.

The force of the blast could be felt at least four miles away , according to a KWQC-TV reporter observing the detonation from a field north of the ammunition plant. The haze from the plumes dissipated quickly, but officials are tracking air quality into Missouri.

The Army says that extensive mitigation reduced the release of lead.

“I would characterize the controlled detonation as exceeding expectations,” said Major General Eric Shirley. “I believe, absolutely, that we reduced as close to zero as is absolutely humanly possible the risk to the health and safety of the people of Middletown and the extended communities throughout Iowa.”

The EPA’s air monitoring results are being rounded to one decimal place, said Alexander More, a professor of urban public health at the University of Massachusetts Boston and a researcher at Harvard University’s Initiative for the Science of the Human Past. In an email to Inside Climate News, More said the website’s code shows values less than 0.05 micrograms per cubic meter, one third of the federal air quality standard for lead, are rounded down to 0.0.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

More added that seven non-zero readings registered in the EPA’s website code as of noon on Wednesday after the blast. There were three non-zero readings before the detonation.

Soil monitoring in the days ahead will reveal how much lead dust settled in the environment, and where. Blood lead levels in children will also be important to monitor.

The EPA and Army will continue monitoring the blast site and surrounding communities.

After delaying the detonation by five days while a court weighed a challenge to the military’s plan, the Army and EPA say they used the extra time to collect more than 1,000 soil, dust, water and air samples and take additional mitigation measures.

In a post early Wednesday morning, the Army wrote that personnel in Middletown implemented measures including “a water wall filled with more than 100,000 gallons of water, earth berms, sand filled blocks, expert dispersion modeling, and temperature-regulating tarps.”

The Army also used a PFAS-free retardant foam to contain the blast. General Shirley attributed the plumes visible for miles following the explosion to the 3,600 gallons of liquid foam they’d applied to the site.

The Army believes these actions limited the spread of lead after the detonation.

Lanphear said detecting little or no lead is a sign that the delay and additional safeguards the Army took ahead of the operation were necessary and successful. “The public outcry prompted additional safeguards, and we should commend the Army, EPA and other agencies for taking steps to better protect surrounding communities,” he said.

Lanphear hopes the situation in Iowa will help draw more attention to other sources of lead exposure for Americans, such as the use of leaded aviation fuel by small aircraft.

Ahead of Wednesday’s detonation, the Army encouraged residents up to five miles southwest of the site to evacuate with support from the Federal Emergency Management Agency, a change from earlier plans.

While Middletown residents learned of the planned explosion at an October town hall, most Iowa residents, including state agencies and Gov. Kim Reynolds, weren’t notified until just five days before the operation was set to take place. The detonation was originally scheduled for Friday, Nov. 20.

At the time, the Army advised members of the public in the plume’s projected path to “consider avoiding the affected area” and keep windows and doors closed. It also suggested cleaning indoor and outdoor surfaces after the air exposure period ends.

Health and safety advice took on a more urgent tone this week. Ahead of this morning’s detonation, federal officials strongly urged community members to evacuate the affected area and advised those in areas with lead deposition to wet-clean surfaces that infants and children may touch.

On Tuesday, the EPA reported dispatching 200 staff to Iowa with plans for over 300 personnel on the ground Wednesday. As of late Tuesday night, the EPA said it had collected over 1,200 environmental samples.

The agency will compare those with others taken during and after the blast to track the range and amount of lead generated by the detonation. Minutes after the detonation, NASA aircraft circled the area to collect air samples.

scraped.body_text:

The first day of the United Nations’ COP31 climate talks in Turkey focused on the nexus of food, agriculture and health, setting a hopeful tone for negotiators and advocacy groups that have been pushing to make food systems a bigger priority at the annual gatherings.

Even before the talks wrapped up Sunday, those hopes had faded. Despite the increasing evidence that cutting emissions from agriculture and the land it occupies represents the most expedient path to lowering climate pollution in the short term—an emergency break on global warming—negotiators left the event with little action on the farming front.

Farmers in the world’s most vulnerable countries will pay the price, advocates and researchers warn, pointing to this year’s “super” El Niño as a case in point.

As the event got underway, a new report from the International Fund for Agricultural Development and Turkey’s Ministry of Agriculture and Forestry said the weather phenomenon could cost the global economy $11 trillion.

“The weather shock is becoming an economic shock, and it is arriving at the worst possible time,” said Jahan-Zeb Chowdhury, the fund’s lead technical specialist for the environment and climate. “Farmers are already vulnerable because of the two other shocks they have experienced—fertilizer and energy.”

The report noted fertilizer prices skyrocketed in 2026 as its main ingredients were stalled in the Strait of Hormuz due to the war in Iran. Fuel prices also soared because of the blockage of the strait. These financial pressures, along with expected volatile weather over the next several months, could push tens of millions more people into acute food insecurity by the end of next year, the report said.

In its latest analysis , the U.N. Food and Agriculture Organization projected that the El Niño could cause major droughts across much of Africa, Central America and parts of South and Southeast Asia.

A separate FAO analysis submitted to the conference found that 86 percent of countries include food systems and agriculture in Nationally Determined Contributions, their roadmaps for meeting the goals of the 2015 Paris climate agreement. If those countries executed those contributions, emissions from agriculture could shrink more than 40 percent within four years and 76 percent by 2035, compared to 2019 levels.

Yet negotiators at the conference failed to produce any meaningful measures to address the climate crisis through agricultural practices. Governments did not reach any agreement on a cover decision, the concluding statement of the conference, which not only omitted any reference to fossil fuels, but also lacked any mention of food systems or agriculture.

“At a time when urgent and ambitious action is needed, commitments fall far short of what is required to protect our planet and support the hundreds of millions of smallholder farmers who are already bearing the brunt of unpredictable weather, declining harvests and increasing hardship,” said Surita Sandosham, president and CEO of Heifer International, in a written statement.

Countries first developed an agriculture-specific negotiating track at the conference held in Egypt in 2022. The intention was to bring a greater focus on agriculture and, ultimately, more financing for farmers to adapt to changing weather conditions.

But the FAO points out that financing for food and agriculture has fallen by 10 percent since 2024, and receives about 5 percent of climate-related development finance, despite needing nearly 20 percent .

“In their new climate plans countries clearly recognize the opportunities for actions that can build resilience while also reducing emissions significantly from the agricultural sector,” said Kaveh Zahedi, who directs the FAO’s Office of Climate Change, Biodiversity and Environment, in a statement. “But the urgency for action is not being matched by climate finance, nor reflected in the negotiated outcomes.”

Those negotiations likely will resume at COP32, which will be held in Addis Ababa, Ethiopia.

Already, the leadership seems poised to tackle agriculture issues.

During the first week of this year’s conference, Ethiopia announced it would join the Alliance of Champions for Food Systems Transformation , a coalition of governments that are urging more robust negotiations around agriculture. Another group, the True Animal Protein Price Coalition, issued a declaration on low-emitting food systems, saying its members would explore “protein diversification”—a diplomatic term for the sensitive topic of reducing emissions from livestock through dietary shifts.

The U.N. has noted a lack of progress on reducing emissions from the livestock sector, which currently accounts for at least 15 percent of total greenhouse gas emissions and one-third of methane, the super-polluting greenhouse gas. Livestock industry lobbyists continue to show up in full force at each year’s conference, contributing to the collapsed efforts on food systems, critics said.

The CEO of JBS, the world’s largest meat company, which recently abandoned its pledge to lower emissions and emits as much methane as the world’s largest oil companies , appeared on a panel at the event, where the company’s Australian subsidiary received an award for its sustainability efforts. The award was given by the Sustainable Business COP , a private-sector initiative launched at COP31 by the Brazilian National Confederation of Industry. JBS’ business operations are largely centered in Brazil.

The company celebrated the recognition in a recent post on its website and pointed to a study showing that JBS lowered the emissions intensity of its cattle in one program in Australia by 10 percent, while also increasing production.

“That’s a key lesson: helping producers improve economic and agronomic success can also generate co-benefits for the environment,” the company wrote. “This lesson extends far beyond Australian cattle production.”

DeSmog reported that the food industry had 260 representatives at the event, including more than 40 percent who were also representatives of their respective countries.

“We cannot respond to the climate crisis without changing the models of production and consumption that are driving environmental destruction,” said Dali Nolasco Cruz, a board member of Slow Food, an advocacy group that supports small-scale farmers and food systems. “Nor can we claim to be tackling the climate crisis while ignoring food systems, both a major part of the problem and one of our greatest opportunities for change.”

scraped.title: Storm Costs Are Sending Maine’s Power Bills Soaring - Inside Climate News
scraped.description: A state with one of the highest energy burdens in the nation considers ways to rein in utility spending.
scraped.author: By Sydney Cromwell
scraped.h1: Storm Costs Are Sending Maine’s Power Bills Soaring
scraped.body_text:
The story you’re about to read is free to access—no paywall, no subscription, no ads. Readers like you make it possible.

Help our nonprofit newsroom continue delivering the independent, unbiased climate journalism you can expect from us every day.

Please give now!

Squeezing blood from a stone.

That’s how Seth Berry describes rising electricity prices in Maine. As executive director of Our Power, a coalition focused on clean energy and utility regulation, Berry talks with people all over the state who are no longer able to afford their power bills.

Combined with recent price increases for heating fuel and gasoline, he said electricity bills could create “a world of hurt” for many Maine households this winter. “People are really at their wits’ end, and I expect to see a whole lot of folks cold this winter, desperately cold in their homes,” Berry said.

Maine has one of the highest energy burdens in the country, due in part to the cost of downed power lines and other repairs after severe storms. The state’s biggest power company is currently requesting another rate increase, and Maine is now reckoning with the balance between needed grid repairs and affordable power bills.

We deliver climate news to your inbox like nobody else. Every day or once a week, our original stories and digest of the web’s top headlines deliver the full story, for free.

Our #1 newsletter delivers the week’s climate and energy news – our original stories and top headlines from around the web.

Dan Gearino’s habit-forming weekly take on how to understand the energy transformation reshaping our world.

A once-a-week digest of the most pressing climate-related news, written by Kate Waxman and released every Tuesday.

Don’t miss a beat. Get a daily email of our original, groundbreaking stories written by our national network of award-winning reporters.

An inside look at top climate news, delivered every two weeks.

A digest of stories on the inequalities that worsen the impacts of climate change on vulnerable communities.

Electricity prices in Maine increased 64 percent between 2019 and 2025, compared to an average 38 percent increase nationwide, according to the U.S. Energy Information Administration. Only Washington, D.C., and California had larger increases.

The state also has one of the highest average household energy burdens in the nation. A 2024 report to Maine’s Electric Ratepayer Advisory Council found that low-income households spend about 8 percent of their income on electricity and an additional 6 percent on other sources like propane and heating oil. Anything above 6 percent is considered a high energy burden by the U.S. Department of Energy.

Maine’s rural, heavily forested character means utility companies require more miles of power lines to reach their most remote customers, and these lines are more likely to be hit by tree branches, the most common cause of outages.

Climate change has fueled more intense storm seasons in recent years. Maine had the highest number of power outages per customer in the U.S. in 2023 and 2024, federal data shows. The state also had the highest average minutes of power outage in 2023 and the second-highest in 2024.

Central Maine Power, the largest electricity provider in the state, reported more than $600 million in storm recovery costs between 2021 and 2025, a span that included the three most expensive storm years in the company’s history.

“Storm costs have become one of the largest and fastest-growing items on customers’ bills,” said Rebecca Schultz, the senior advocate for climate and clean energy at the Natural Resources Council of Maine.

Advocates like Berry and Schultz say that the way CMP is reimbursed for its storm recovery costs incentivizes the company to overspend, leaving customers to shoulder an even greater burden.

“It’s broken, people understand that it’s broken,” Berry said.

CMP did not respond to interview requests. The company noted in comments to the state Public Utilities Commission in September that the commission’s review of its storm costs from 2023 to 2025 showed “no findings of imprudence.”

The Maine Legislature in March directed the PUC, which regulates utilities in the state, to conduct a review of energy pricing and metrics for affordability. Managing storm costs will be essential to the affordability discussion.

Power companies don’t treat storm costs like regular expenses because severe weather can be so unpredictable and costly.

CMP customers currently pay $14.1 million per year in storm recovery as part of their base rates, which goes toward a reserve account. Each storm event is classified into tiers based on how much CMP spends on the recovery.

Depending on the tier, CMP is responsible for paying up to a certain threshold of each storm’s recovery costs out of its reserves. Beyond that threshold, costs are split equally between the company and its customers—up to a point.

CMP’s share when costs exceed its storm reserve is capped at $3 million per year. The rest is charged directly to customers. The largest events, like an April 2024 storm where CMP spent more than $100 million, are billed to customers over two years, plus additional carrying costs.

CMP customers have paid for $57.8 million just in carrying costs over the last five years, according to testimony by Maine’s Office of the Public Advocate to the PUC.

Since CMP’s financial liability is capped, “it deprives the company of an incentive to control costs,” Schultz said.

Schultz said the company can contract more out-of-state line crews, which require higher hourly rates and additional housing and travel expenses, than it may actually need for storm response because there’s no reward for efficient planning.

In the past five years, CMP has hired external crews for 18 storms per year, averaging about 93 crews each time. While contractor crews are essential when major storms surpass the company’s regular capacity, Schultz said CMP’s approach creates “a huge amount of overpreparedness.”

Heather Sanborn, the state’s public advocate, said CMP’s storm response is “carefully calibrated” to be profitable, not cost-efficient or faster at restoring power.

Even in 2025, a year with less severe weather, CMP racked up $43 million in recovery costs, more than three times the base recovery costs that customers pay, according to its filings with the PUC.

“All of these costs get rolled up into customers’ bills whether the storm turns out to be a big one and whether there’s work to do or not,” Berry said.

The other major electricity provider in Maine, Versant Power, has a different storm cost structure, in which customers’ base rates include the five-year average of recovery costs.

Exceptionally severe storm recovery is reviewed and approved by the PUC separately from that budget, since Versant couldn’t financially support those expenses in a single year. But if Versant spends more on ordinary recovery efforts than that five-year average, the company and its shareholders pay for that excess through reduced returns on investments. This happened most recently in 2024.

“This framework provides accountability and transparency, but it does not limit Versant’s ability to prepare for or respond to major weather events,” Versant spokesperson Marissa McKay said via email.

Versant also brings in out-of-state crews when needed, but it “hasn’t seen this explosion of storm costs in recent years,” Schultz said.

CMP spent $179 per customer (or $4,968 per mile of power line) on storm recovery in 2021, compared to Versant’s $68 per customer (or $1,750 per line mile), according to the Office of the Public Advocate.

Our nonprofit newsroom provides award-winning climate coverage free of charge and advertising. We rely on donations from readers like you to keep going. Please donate now to support our work.

Both companies are meeting their required reliability metrics, Schultz said, so she doesn’t believe the difference in spending translates to a meaningful difference in power outages or response time.

The Office of the Public Advocate recommended to the PUC in September that CMP’s storm cost structure should be reformed to be more similar to Versant’s method, as a means to control excessive recovery costs and encourage hiring more in-state crews.

CMP’s own proposal to the PUC for lowering storm costs also includes more in-state hiring, as well as investing more in infrastructure and tree trimming.

Additionally, the company suggested raising customers’ base storm rates from $14.1 million to $53.1 million per year, based on recent years’ recovery costs. This would cause less volatility in customers’ bills since more costs would be paid upfront, though it still wouldn’t cover the entirety of CMP storm spending from the last five years.

Severe weather isn’t the only scenario where it’s possible to overspend. Maine is one of many states where regulators allow power companies to charge their customers a “return on equity,” or a certain percentage of profit, for significant infrastructure projects.

This return is meant to incentivize projects the company might not otherwise take on, like extending the power grid to the most rural areas of the country. It also attracts investors.

But that extra profit can make more expensive solutions appealing to utility companies because of their bigger returns, even if the solutions aren’t more effective, Schultz said.

Power companies are “driven to spend,” she said.

For example, Sanborn said a utility might choose to upgrade power lines or poles with more resilient versions, even though trimming back trees around the line is cheaper and often just as effective at preventing an outage. Equipment upgrades are eligible for return on equity; trimming trees is just a regular business expense.

Earlier this year, the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission ordered New England utilities to refund customers more than $1.5 billion from previous unreasonable return-on-equity rates, based on a 2011 complaint. About $130 million of that refund would go to Maine customers. CMP, Versant and other utilities lost their appeal to this ruling in November and must refund customers by May 2027.

While Maine’s Public Utilities Commission is studying electricity affordability, it’s also deciding whether CMP is allowed to raise its rates.

CMP filed in April to increase both its distribution rates and its return on equity percentage for one year, generating $189 million to pay for necessary system upgrades, additional hiring and storm costs.

CMP has stated that its proposed return on equity is in line with the rest of the industry and helps the company stay competitive in attracting investors.

The average household’s power bill would go up $18 per month.

“That seems highly insensitive to the state of its customers’ budgets at this time,” Schultz said.

CMP also requested a rate increase last year, which would have generated $1.7 billion over five years. The company withdrew its 2025 request after negative feedback from the PUC, which received a record 800-plus public comments opposing the increase.

“That was just a massive, massive proposal that would have had huge impacts on ratepayers,” Schultz said.

CMP’s current request is almost identical to the first year of the rejected 2025 request, she said. The company has stated its intent to file more multi-year rate requests in the future.

CMP’s financial health has become a major focus of the PUC’s deliberations. The company overspent its budget projections for 2022 to 2025 by $239 million, Schultz said. S&P Global gave the company a negative financial outlook in July due to significant debt and cash flow concerns.

In order to address what it described as a “profoundly impaired financial condition,” CMP also proposed a $69 million temporary rate increase while the PUC considers the main request.

The PUC unanimously rejected the temporary increase in early October. CMP responded by removing all job listings from its website, and company officials stated that the rejection could mean re-evaluating its current employment levels and deferred projects.

One expert witness, a former utility executive from California, testified to the PUC that rather than raise CMP’s return on equity as requested, that percentage could be cut by a third or more without harming the company’s finances, based on internal financial documents that CMP’s parent company, Iberdrola, was forced to release.

“That was a very powerful breath of fresh air,” Berry said.

Schultz said that lower percentage would save customers about $62 million out of CMP’s requested rate increase, even if it caused a downgrade in the company’s credit rating that would make it more expensive to borrow.

The PUC will announce a decision on CMP’s rate increase in April 2027, and it will report its findings on affordability back to the state Legislature before December 2027.

Sanborn said these two cases dovetail into an opportunity for Maine to make big changes in the way its power grid operates.

“Maine households are really feeling squeezed from all sides by increasing costs,” Sanborn said. “It’s absolutely critical that we take a look at what levers we have available to us at the state level to reduce those costs where possible.”

scraped.author: Vivian La
scraped.h1: Michigan just hit pause on a plan to update the controversial Line 5 oil pipeline
scraped.body_text:

Michigan Governor Gretchen Whitmer said Tuesday that she’s pausing both pending and issued state permits for the plan to replace a segment of the Line 5 oil pipeline beneath the Straits of Mackinac.

Whitmer said regulators at the Michigan Department of Environment, Great Lakes and Energy, or EGLE, need to answer questions about the full scope of the plan’s threats to the environment.

Those questions, according to Whitmer, were raised by a Michigan Supreme Court ruling this summer on a related Line 5 tunnel permit. Justices tossed out a permit issued by a separate state agency, saying their review of environmental harms was too narrow.

Line 5 has been transporting oil and natural gas liquids 645 miles between Ontario and Wisconsin since 1954. A 4-mile segment passes through the Straits of Mackinac, the narrow waterways that connect Lake Michigan to Lake Huron, separating Michigan’s Lower and Upper peninsulas. Sensitive coastal and wetlands habitats are found in the straits, and the area is sacred to Anishinaabe peoples , featuring prominently in their creation story and serving as burial grounds for their ancestors.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

“I have always said my ultimate goal is to get Line 5 out of the water,” Whitmer, whose second and final term will end January 1, said in the announcement. “Just one spill threatens irreparable damage to our water, our economy, and our way of life.” The permit pause comes weeks after regulators in Wisconsin had been dealing with a spill on the portion of Line 5 that crosses that state.

It’s the latest setback for pipeline owner Enbridge Energy, which first proposed the plan to replace an aging portion of the pipeline with a new one, buried in a tunnel beneath the straits, almost a decade ago .

Enbridge maintains that the pipeline is safe. In a statement, spokesperson Ryan Duffy pointed to the company’s record of permit approvals — including the pending EGLE permit, which would have been a renewal of one it received in 2021.

Line 5 delivers the energy people depend on every day, Duffy said. “At Enbridge, we remain committed to that purpose and equally committed to safeguarding the Great Lakes,” he said.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The permit freeze is a win for Line 5 opponents who have protested for years against the tunnel project and have fought to shut down the entire pipeline.

“I think this is a really, really excellent step in the right direction,” said Ashley Rudzinski, climate and environment program director for the nonprofit Groundwork Center for Resilient Communities. “We’re seeing the Whitmer administration, finally, putting some real strength behind the words that she had already spoken.”

The Line 5 tunnel project has received federal approval , but with the remaining state permits in question, it’s unclear what its future looks like. Separately, Line 5 faces legal challenges from groups that have fought to shut down the entire pipeline for years, including the Whitmer administration.

Lawyers representing Michigan tribes in their fight to shut down Line 5 said they hope this momentum continues into the administration of Governor-elect Jocelyn Benson, who, like Whitmer, is a Democrat. All 12 federally recognized tribes in Michigan oppose the pipeline.

“No matter who the governor is, it’s in all of our interests to keep the Great Lakes free of oil and to transition away from Line 5,” said Laura Berglan, senior attorney with the legal nonprofit Earthjustice, which represents the Bay Mills Indian Community, the Sault Ste. Marie Tribe of Chippewa Indians, and the Little Traverse Bay Bands of Odawa Indians. “We need to protect our shared resources and our tribal resources for the future.”
