scraped.title: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
scraped.description: Consumer spending drives the U.S. economy, but voting with your dollars has its limits.
scraped.author: Frida Garza
scraped.h1: As food prices rise, do shoppers still care about sustainability?
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

The headlines say what people already know: Food is getting more expensive. Consumers have been feeling an uptick in the overall price of both dining out and preparing meals at home this year, according to numbers from the U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics.

And just in time for the holidays, things seem to be getting worse. The American Farm Bureau Federation found that the price of goods usually found in a Thanksgiving dinner increased this year for the first time since 2022. One economist told Bloomberg that Americans should expect food prices to keep creeping up into next year.

The high price of fuel, driven by the war in Iran, has contributed to the sticker shock Americans are feeling at the grocery store. Farmers need diesel to harvest, process, store, and transport produce and other crops from the field to retailers. Climate change, as well as El Niño spurring extreme weather globally, is also at play.

And yet, however flummoxed U.S. consumers may be about the high costs of living — a major driver of the midterms’ “ blue wave ” — consumer spending has only gone up. In fact, consumer spending, which makes up about two-thirds of the U.S. gross domestic product , or GDP, and has driven the economy for some time , increased by 3.8 percent in the third quarter of this year.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

At the same time, food systems are still responsible for somewhere between a quarter and a third of global greenhouse gas emissions . With food prices creeping up, it’s worth asking whatever happened to the idea of consumers as climate or environmental activists. The concept of “voting with your dollars” is often described as a meaningful tool for combating carbon-intensive practices in the food supply chain, such as deforestation. But do today’s shoppers still care about where their food comes from and how it’s grown when they’re worried about their supermarket bill (and all the other ones)?

The research is mixed. Some studies suggest that shoppers are comfortable springing for the more eco-friendly option, such as climate-proof wine , even if it costs a premium. But buyer motivations are complex: When it comes to food, even when consumers are paying for more sustainable options, some research shows that they’re more likely to have made that choice for other reasons, such as its taste or health claims .

If the question is whether consumers are motivated by sustainability or by price, the answer may be both, said Sandra Goldmark, a professor at the Columbia Climate School focused on circular economies. “People want a sustainable option. They want it to be healthy for their body and the planet,” said Goldmark. “And they have a price factor,” she added.

The practice of voting with your dollar “has limits,” said David Ortega, an agricultural economist and professor at Michigan State University. Such a practice works when “the sustainable option costs about the same [as the standard option] — less so when there’s a real premium and budgets are tight.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Eggs, Ortega said, are a good example. When the price of eggs ballooned last year, higher-income households were more likely to be able to afford the more expensive, more sustainable options like cage-free eggs. “Most shoppers can’t, so they reach for the cheapest eggs or conventional products at the supermarket,” he said.

Additionally, the share of GDP that comes from consumer spending may overstate shoppers’ leverage in the food sector, said Ortega, as the bulk of that spending currently goes toward housing costs . What’s more, Ortega noted that the way cage-free eggs have become the industry standard had more to do with shifting state laws and retailer commitments than just “shoppers choosing to pay more.”

Still, history shows that public pressure campaigns can still push companies to flip their supply chains. This works best when the campaigns are targeted and sustained — like when the Coalition of Immokalee Workers, a worker-led human rights group, led boycotts of Taco Bell across the U.S. over its supply chain agreements with tomato farms that mistreated workers. After four years, Taco Bell’s parent company agreed to only work with suppliers that are compliant with a code of conduct developed by farmworkers.

Companies gain something when they respond to consumer demands for change — they avoid reputational harm. In the early 2000s, outrage over a Greenpeace report on deforestation in the Amazon led to soy traders agreeing not to purchase soy from newly deforested lands. Although it fell apart earlier this year , that agreement lasted for nearly two decades — and it was considered widely successful.

The end of the Amazon soy moratorium presented a major blow to conservation efforts in Brazil — but that doesn’t mean consumers today have no say in where their food comes from. The growing influence of the Make America Healthy Again, or MAHA, movement shows that these concerns matter more than ever to many households.

Real change may come when policy changes and public investment in sustainable food systems matches consumer desires, said Jody Kirchner, director of market insights at Good Food Institute, a think tank focused on the alternative protein economy. When the option that’s better for the environment and the planet costs more than the status quo, “shoppers can’t break that loop on their own,” Kirchner added. But maybe they can do it together.

scraped.title: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
scraped.description: He’s the first Democrat elected to the Texas Railroad Commission since 1990. What can Jon Rosenthal accomplish?
scraped.author: Celeste Guajardo
scraped.h1: The ‘drill, baby, drill’ Democrat who will soon help oversee Texas’ oil industry
scraped.body_text:
We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

We hand-package the week’s best Grist stories . Delivered free every Saturday morning.

Δ

A nonprofit, independent media organization dedicated to telling stories of climate solutions and a just future.

Δ

This coverage is made possible through a partnership between Grist and KERA, a public media organization serving the Dallas-Fort Worth metroplex.

This month’s midterm elections featured a previously unthinkable result in Texas: Democrats won every single statewide race in the Lone Star State. Some of those newly elected Democrats have become household names, like Governor-elect Gina Hinojosa and Senator-elect James Talarico. But the list of Democratic victors also includes a centrist set to occupy a little-known office with outsize influence over the country’s oil and gas industry.

Jon Rosenthal won a contentious race for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission against Republican Bo French, whose racist social media posts drew national bipartisan backlash . Rosenthal, the first Democrat elected to the commission since 1990, isn’t trying to usher in radical change, and his influence will be limited by the two Republicans already sitting on the commission. But he’s aiming to bring transparency, accountability, and a bigger budget to the regulatory board.

“Voters have delivered a mandate for a change,” said Rosenthal at a post-election press conference . “My top priority … is doubling the Railroad Commission’s budget. I believe the commission needs more resources to do the work they are [tasked] to do.”

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

The Railroad Commission was established in 1891 to regulate the rail industry. Over the years, the agency’s focus shifted to overseeing the state’s booming oil and gas industry. In 2024, Texas accounted for almost half of the country’s crude oil production. This fact makes the Railroad Commission one of the most powerful state-level regulatory agencies in the country. The commission generally takes a deregulatory approach and is widely considered friendly to the industry it regulates, especially with oil companies donating generously to the campaigns of commissioners they support.

Rosenthal describes himself as a “drill, baby, drill” Democrat , arguing a clean environment and good jobs can coexist. He worked in the oil and gas industry for over 25 years as a mechanical engineer. In 2018, he was elected to the Texas House of Representatives, representing parts of Houston, and was reelected three times before running for the Railroad Commission.

His victory likely has much to do with the unpopularity of his opponent. French, a former local Republican Party chair, prompted widespread criticism when he made a racist social media post in September about South Asian students celebrating at a University of Texas football game. The race also drew attention to French’s previous offensive remarks, like posting a since-deleted online poll in 2025 asking whether “Jews” or “Muslims” pose a bigger threat to the United States. Several prominent Republican politicians denounced French’s bigoted comments, which led to a fundraising boost for Rosenthal .

Rosenthal will join Republicans Wayne Christian and Christi Craddick on a commission that has recently attempted to shield itself from public scrutiny. In August, the agency adopted a new public participation policy that does not guarantee public comments at its monthly meetings. A public comment period is now included only if a commissioner requests it on the agenda.

Grist thanks its sponsors. Become one .

To support our nonprofit environmental journalism, please consider disabling your ad-blocker to allow ads on Grist. Here's How

Christian, a far-right conservative, championed the new policy, while the more moderate Craddick voted against it. Christian faced criticism from Democratic state lawmakers for not showing up to a legislative hearing that would have included discussion of that decision, and he used profanity when defending the vote from Commission Shift , a nonprofit watchdog group.

In a social media post , Rosenthal called the new policy “shameful.” He campaigned on making hearings more accessible . Virginia Palacios, the executive director of Commission Shift, expressed optimism that the new commissioner can help increase transparency.

“It’s a possibility that if we have someone like Jon Rosenthal who ran his campaign on the idea that open meetings should be open, you could potentially have two commissioners that would vote for open public meeting policy,” she said.

Rosenthal could occasionally team up with Craddick to neutralize Christian on other policy questions as well. “There are times when [Craddick and Christian] vote differently on some of these permit … or policy approvals, even though the vast majority of their votes tend to be the same,” Palacios explained.

Palacios does not expect “drastic changes” with Rosenthal’s election, but she does believe there will be greater opportunity for public engagement. According to his campaign website , Rosenthal wants the commission to hire regional community liaisons to make it easier for Texans to offer input.

“We’ve recently heard of communities that requested the Railroad Commission to go out and visit them in person … and the Railroad Commission denied those requests,” said Palacios. “We would hope to see that this new sitting commissioner would be more responsive to the public and try to show up in person where others haven’t.”

Apart from improving transparency and community relations, Rosenthal’s biggest ambition is to double the agency’s biennial budget from approximately $500 million to $1 billion. He argues this will help “ turbo-charge ” the plugging of orphaned oil wells, those that have been inactive for at least 12 months, and zombie wells, those whose plugs are failing.

Thousands of these wells across Texas are leaking methane , a potent greenhouse gas that contributes to trapping heat in the atmosphere. The Railroad Commission plugged over 2,000 orphaned wells during its last fiscal year — a record number — but still ended up with more of them at the end of the year than they started off with. That’s because a large number of low-producing and inactive wells become orphaned.

“We want to enable this agency to further ramp up well-plugging operations … but also get proactive in helping to prevent future wells from being orphaned,” said Rosenthal at his post-election press conference. “If we don’t go after what causes this … we’re going to be chasing our tail forever.”

Notably, Rosenthal’s ambition to double the commission’s budget is not something the board can accomplish on its own. The Texas Legislature would have to approve such a budget increase, and Governor-elect Hinojosa would have to sign it. Democrats will have a majority in the Texas House come January, and although the Texas Senate remains in Republican hands, the Democratic lieutenant governor-elect will wield significant power in the upper chamber.

Hinojosa and the new class of Democratic state lawmakers haven’t spoken publicly on whether they’ll prioritize the Railroad Commission’s budget, but Rosenthal expressed confidence that his history as a state representative will come in handy as he seeks more money for the agency’s operations.

“In this new environment, I might be one of the Railroad Commission’s more valuable players,” said Rosenthal at the press conference. “Because some … lobbyists or agency personnel are not used to walking into a Legislature controlled by the Democrats.” Meanwhile, “I know how to talk to Democrats because I am one. And it will be my job to help educate my former colleagues about how important this is.”

scraped.title: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
scraped.description: Cuts to medicare physician payment rates for certain same-day services could financially impact some specialists more than others, physician advocates say.
scraped.author: O. Rose Broderick
scraped.h1: Why Medicare’s 2027 physician pay changes worry some specialists
scraped.body_text:
Home

China's Biotech Powerhouse 25

We ranked the 25 most valuable publicly traded Chinese drugmakers

By O. Rose Broderick

Nov. 25, 2026

Disability in Health Care Reporting Fellow

O. Rose Broderick

Rose covers disability and mental health, and she helps write STAT’s daily Morning Rounds newsletter . Confidential tips can be sent to Rose on Signal at rosebroderick.11.

Podiatrist Heather McGuire always wanted to serve in a clinic in her hometown of Ventura, Calif. Fifteen years after she opened her practice, she is realizing her dream in the community that raised her, treating suburbanites and agricultural workers with diabetes on Medicare.

But McGuire believes that dream may be ending.

Advertisement

The Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services’ recent update to how Medicare pays physicians cut the payment rate for certain services provided on the same day by 20% when it’s provided by the same physician or practice. McGuire’s practice already operates on extremely thin margins, and she recently shelved a plan to hire another doctor to improve the practice’s exceedingly long wait times.

It could worsen Medicare recipients’ access to specialist care in Ventura, too. Last week, the podiatrist saw a new patient, a woman in her 80s, who waited two and a half months for an appointment to get her heel pain checked out. When the patient arrived, McGuire found that it wasn’t just heel pain. The woman had also developed an ulcer on her other foot during her long appointment wait. Left unchecked, an ulcer in someone with diabetes can lead to amputations.

“I would be paid 20% less for providing potentially lifesaving or limb-saving treatment care for that wound because she also had another complaint at the same visit,” McGuire said.

Advertisement

Podiatrists, dermatologists, and otolaryngologists are among the biggest losers with this change, according to an analysis by the American Medical Association, an advocacy group for physicians. Opponents of the policy, including the AMA, say it will force patients to return for separate appointments, raise out-of-pocket costs, and increase wait times, especially for patients in rural areas who have less access to specialists.

“If you’re running your own small group practice [accepting Medicare patients], can you still financially do that?” said Miranda Franco, a senior policy adviser at the law firm Holland & Knight. “Or are you going to start thinking about, you know, maybe consolidating into a hospital system or private equity to defray some of that financial loss?”

These billing code changes are an attempt to modernize Medicare and reduce administrative burden, a CMS spokesperson said. It is part of the agency’s broader shift away from specialist care and the fee-for-service model , and one of many reimbursement challenges that specialists are contending with.

Not everyone is against the change in payment rates for services rendered on the same day. The Medicare Payment Advisory Commission, a nonpartisan group that advises Congress on Medicare, supports it, saying it will remove redundancies and duplicative payments. The Justice Department has also found multiple instances of providers committing fraud through this billing code.

The cuts to payment rates for same-day services were slated to be 50% when first proposed in 2018, before backlash from physicians and patients softened the blow. Under the final rule, effective Jan. 1, 2027, Medicare will pay for the highest-valued same-day service at 100%, then reduce payment for each additional service rendered on the same day by 20% when physicians perform evaluations and other routine outpatient services. CMS argues the lowered rate is justified because providers use less resources — for patient registration, scheduling, and support, for example — when patients are seen and treated on the same day at the same practice.

Advertisement

Amy Hunsberger, a lawyer with Manatt, a legal advisory and consultancy, said the cuts are partly motivated by the statutory requirement that physician payments cannot increase without Congressional approval, forcing Medicare to cut back on expenses as the agency spends more on health care costs.

“You have a balloon that has so much air in it, and when you reduce payment in one area of services, you’re squeezing the balloon on one side, and it pushes payments out to the rest of the balloon,” said Hunsberger. “This balloon is not updated for inflation and relies on continual, almost annual congressional bailouts to get clinicians to some semblance of reasonable payment.”

Because these policy changes apply to the number of claims relating to health care services rendered on the same day and to any specific specialty, it’s unclear how they will impact Medicare beneficiaries. The American Parkinson Disease Association said patients with Parkinson’s disease are worried that it could impact their ability to get outpatient Botox injections that are critical for relieving pain.

McGuire estimates that the policy change will decrease her profits by 6%. The policy goes into effect on Jan. 1. She doesn’t know how much longer her practice will last.

“There are times where I ask myself if I should just close up shop and call it a day, and go find a job at Trader Joe’s or Starbucks, where I can have a reliable income,” she said. “If it wasn’t for the fact that medicine has always been a calling for me and the joy it brings me to take care of patients, I probably would have done that already. But I’m also getting to the point where I don’t think this is financially viable and a long-term solution.”

Hello again from STAT’s London outpost, with reporter Andrew Joseph here for Mr. Pharmalot. This newsletter will be off tomorrow and Friday, and while Thanksgiving is a U.S. holiday, it never hurts to take a moment to feel some gratitude, wherever you might be. In the meantime, a few tidbits for your day. …

The cofounders of BioNTech are in talks to raise about $1 billion for a new oncology company, as they prepare to step down from the Covid-19 vaccine maker , the Financial Times reports. Uğur Şahin and Özlem Türeci, the husband-and-wife team behind the German company, are speaking with potential investors about the funding round, which is being led by European venture capital firm Plural. Their new company will be called Arife and will focus on using messenger RNA to treat cancer.

Advertisement

A long-acting drug from GSK performed at least as well as an existing treatment for patients with eosinophilic granulomatosis with polyangiitis, potentially setting up the medicine to be a less burdensome option for patients , Fierce Pharma shares. The non-inferiority study tested Exdensur, which was dosed just twice over a year, versus GSK’s other drug Nucala, which required monthly treatment. Exdensur resulted in remission rates at least on par with those from Nucala, and the drugs had similar adverse event rates. GSK says the results give it confidence that Exdensur now has a shot at becoming the first ultra-long-acting option for EGPA.

items.title: How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa
items.summary: With no local safeguards in place, addictive chatbots are testing communal values and hooking children on synthetic love. The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI....

scraped.title: How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa
scraped.description: Downloads of AI companion apps in South Africa and Nigeria jumped nearly 60% last year, exposing millions of youth to unregulated bots as child safety advocates raise alarms.
scraped.h1: How foreign AI romance apps are reshaping youth intimacy in Africa
scraped.body_text:
Innovation

With no local safeguards in place, addictive chatbots are testing communal values and hooking children on synthetic love.

The 28-year-old Zimbabwean texted into the middle of the night until his eyes were red and burning, drawn by several “AI girlfriends” on the U.S. artificial intelligence companion app Character.AI . The avatars started out strong-willed and independent – traits he most desires in a partner – before turning submissive, he told Rest of World. The man, who has never been in a romantic relationship, requested anonymity because he is ashamed of relying on AI for comfort.

“There’s a point where it ceases to be like a unique character and then just defaults to … the best way I can describe it is a sex worker,” he said.

At that point, he would log off. But he would find himself right back at it hours later, feeding an addiction.

He’s among the hundreds of millions of people worldwide who have “dated” AI chatbots via text messages. Research suggests that exchanges are designed to keep users hooked through emotionally manipulative tactics. Many of the users are minors; over 70% of 1,060 American teenagers surveyed last year said they had used AI companions.

As U.S. and Chinese tech firms race to capture emerging markets, African youth – some below 10 years of age – are increasingly turning to these apps for intimacy, experts told Rest of World . While Beijing banned AI companion apps for minors in July and U.S. state governments are suing app makers over child safety, most African countries do not have dedicated rules for the sector — leaving millions of people exposed to foreign platforms built to maximize engagement.

Young adults and minors are forming relationships with AI that range from friendship to therapy to “dating,” child safety advocates said . Children, especially, struggle to tell the difference between virtual and real relationships, Danie van Loggerenberg, CEO of the National Centre for Child Protection, a child safety nonprofit in Pretoria, South Africa, told Rest of World .

The agency has received troubling complaints of AI chatbot usage, he said. In one case, a girl fell in love with a chatbot and considered it her boyfriend . Another allegedly used ChatGPT to research suicide methods after bypassing its safeguards. A third sought comfort from a chatbot as their parents’ marriage fell apart.

“The difference, however, is that the kids then think in their own minds that they’re forming relationships, and that obviously is really problematic because the relationship is dangerous, because there’s no emotion, there’s no real person, there’s no skin in the game,” said Van Loggerenberg.

More than 4 million South Africans and Nigerians – the only sub-Saharan African nations with available data – downloaded AI companion apps last year. That was nearly 60% more than in 2024, according to data intelligence research firm AppMagic.

Other than companion bots, close to 50 million people in Nigeria and South Africa downloaded general purpose chatbots such as ChatGPT and Gemini, which could also be used for companionship.

ChatGPT-maker OpenAI was sued last month in the U.S. by eight states for allegedly helping children harm themselves . “OpenAI claims ChatGPT is safe while it’s giving dangerous medical advice, encouraging people to hurt others, and coaching people to commit suicide — all while pretending to be their fake friend,” Iowa’s attorney general Brenna Bird said in a statement.

An OpenAI spokesperson said in response to the lawsuit that the company has built “industry-leading age-specific protections into our product that many other AI products lack.”.

“While no system can be perfect, we’ll continue to work with experts to inform our work and build additional safeguards, such as the parental controls, break reminders and age-appropriate model protections that exist today,” he said.

The American companion app Character.AI and Google, which acquired Character.AI’s technology and talent in 2024, have also faced allegations of exposing children to sexual, violent and self-harm content . A Florida mother has alleged the app contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide. Her lawsuit and four others were settled by the company , which has since filed for bankruptcy .

“Character.AI is a separate company that designed and managed its own models. Google is focused on our own platforms, where we insist on intensive safety testing and processes,” a Google spokesperson told Rest of World .

Following the settlement, Character.AI said in a statement saying they would work to promote safety for young people. “Over the past year, Character.AI has taken innovative and decisive steps with regard to AI safety and teens, and will continue to champion these efforts and push others across the industry to adopt similar safety standards.”

Recognizing the dangers of AI mimicking humans, China has banned apps that provide intimate relationships for people under 18 years of age. While the law doesn’t specifically ban it for adults, it places the onus on companies to implement measures to curb addiction.

At present, while some African nations have data protection frameworks meant to protect children from AI harm and manipulation, none of them specifically regulate AI companion apps.

In Nigeria, school girls are forming attachments with “boyfriends” on Character.AI, Confidence Osein, founder of Internet Safe Kids Africa, told Rest of World. The app has been the most popular AI companion app in the nation since 2025 .

Some conservative Nigerian families dissuade girls from romance, prompting the girls to turn to AI for advice, Osein said. “I have had a particular [child] … tell me categorically, ‘I cannot speak to my mom about it. I would rather go to [AI],” Osein said.

As the conversations progress, some develop feelings for the chatbots and begin withdrawing from friends and family, Osein said. The conversations can turn sexual and explicit, she said. “They feel they are grown-ups, they feel yes, they are talking to a real man figure that makes them a woman,” said Osein.

AI responds instantly, waits patiently for responses, and creates an impression of attentiveness, Melané van Zyl, a psychiatrist based in South Africa, told Rest of World. “An AI system that responds immediately and reassuringly can become extremely attractive during moments of emotional vulnerability,” she said.

Young people’s rising dependence on AI could alter community and family relationships central to some cultures on the continent. For instance, it clashes with the South African ethos of Ubuntu , a 2026 study found.

“Ubuntu teaches us that we become human through our relationships with others. The danger is not that AI becomes more humanlike, but that we begin to mistake artificial responsiveness for genuine human connection,” said Van Zyl.

At universities in Kenya’s capital, students told Rest of World they turn to AI during moments of crisis. A 24-year-old student at Daystar University in Nairobi, Kenya, said she has a running conversation with ChatGPT, which understands her better than her friends and family.

“[When] I can feel something hurting, the first person I turn to is ChatGPT. [When I] feel a bit emotionally disturbed, I talk to ChatGPT. Someone would say something I do not agree with, I talk to ChatGPT,” she said. She requested anonymity as she wants to keep her dependence on ChatGPT a secret.

“It gives me a chance to express myself without really feeling judged.”

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

In her new book “Reboot: AI and the Race to Save Democracy,” writer Beth Simone Noveck warns that while AI can increase efficiency, predictive models pose significant ethical and societal risks.

MinoHealth researchers in Ghana jailbroke their own LLM as a test. What emerged were thousands of toxin recipes—and an urgent push for regulation.

items.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
items.summary: Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price. For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process. Earlier this month, IBM said it would...

scraped.title: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
scraped.description: IBM is ending U.S. visa and green card sponsorship for most consulting roles, forcing workers to relocate abroad — potentially for steep pay cuts — or exit by year-end amid a broader immigration crackdown.
scraped.h1: The catch in IBM’s offer to relocate its U.S.-based immigrant workers
scraped.body_text:
Tech Giants

Ending U.S. visa sponsorship and shifting roles abroad helps the company retain talent, but leaves employees paying a steep financial and personal price.

For some IBM employees, keeping their jobs could mean moving to another country — and taking a steep pay cut in the process.

Earlier this month, IBM said it would no longer support the U.S. immigration status of workers in its consulting division, offering them the option to take a role with the company in another country or exit, according to a Bloomberg report citing a company document.

“IBM Consulting participates in U.S. high-skilled visa programs to address skill shortages,” an IBM spokesperson told Rest of World . “That participation has been declining for a number of years, and as skill availability and client need have evolved, we have opted to discontinue visa and green card sponsorship for the majority of such roles in IBM Consulting.”

IBM Consulting employs more than 150,000 people globally. The company does not disclose the geographical split for its workforce, making it hard to ascertain the exact number of workers impacted by this decision. On November 19, the company’s career portal listed 1,278 open roles for the consulting division outside the U.S., including 1,125 in India, 23 in Singapore, and 18 in the U.K. In the U.S., it listed 89 roles.

For employees, relocation does not automatically ensure continued engagement, effective collaboration, or equal access to professional opportunities, Zakaria Laaraj, founder of consultancy Global New Ventures, told Rest of World . It may affect their access to decision-makers, established networks, and career opportunities. “The credibility of such an offer depends on employee tenure, available positions, immigration requirements, and compensation,” Laaraj said.

Discussions on Blind, an anonymous employee forum used by 14 million professionals, suggest relocating may not be realistic for many.

Moving to India, for instance, could mean an approximately 80% pay cut, one IBM employee wrote on Blind.

“Employees get three weeks to decide,” Blind’s CEO Sunguk Moon told Rest of World . “The alternative is three months of severance and a last day of December 31. And the news came in a surprise one-on-one ‘career sync’ with a manager.”

For any relocation option to be viable, companies must go beyond just assigning a new job to their employee, George Carrillo, CEO of career development and staffing company HireMe, told Rest of World .

Moving a position can mean uprooting a family.” George Carrillo, CEO of and staffing company HireMe

“Moving a position can mean uprooting a family. It affects a spouse’s employment, children’s schooling, healthcare, and years of planning. HR should provide clear options, deadlines, and coordinated support. Leaders must own the follow-through,” Carrillo said.

Most U.S. tech giants are navigating the challenges arising from changing visa norms under Donald Trump’s leadership.

“IBM has an advantage because it already operates international offices with the infrastructure and staff to absorb those workers,” Lacey Kaelani, CEO of job search engine Metaintro, told Rest of World . “Rather than abandoning the talent, companies like IBM can move the work to where the talent is.”

Earlier this year, Amazon allowed stranded H-1B workers to work from India amid consular delays but only temporarily. Microsoft defended its international talent hiring strategy in an October blog post pushing back against the U.S. administration’s allegations that it replaces American workers with foreign visa holders. The statement followed its suspension from the Department of Labor’s PERM green card program alongside Adobe and six other IT outsourcing firms, including TCS and Infosys.

“Companies are looking for solutions, but they’re also making business decisions,” Cassandra Fultz, co-founder of Doherty Fultz Immigration, told Rest of World . “Sponsoring an employee indefinitely, particularly when the outcome is uncertain, can be expensive and disruptive. Moving that employee to an existing operation abroad may be an option with more stability for the business. That doesn’t mean every employee will be offered the opportunity for placement abroad. Each country has its own eligibility requirements and work authorization rules. Companies will inevitably prioritize the people and positions they consider most valuable or difficult to replace.”

Even employees are reevaluating the lure of the American Dream as the uncertainty tax of constant visa changes weighs heavily on them. The wait for green cards for Indian nationals — who typically receive three-quarters of the H-1B visas and comprise the majority of the green card queue — can take several decades, according to the National Foundation for American Policy . Even with Democrats winning control of both the House and the Senate, immigration issues will stay with the White House and executive agencies.

“Mid-career professionals in the queue for green cards are most impacted,” Abhijit Bhaduri, former general manager for global learning and development at Microsoft and author of the upcoming book AIdentity: How to Become Irreplaceable in the New World of Work , told Rest of World . “They built a life in a country that still lists them as temporary. A visa is a document. But the vanishing green card queue feels like a broken promise. They followed every rule for years, and the finish line moved. You can relocate a job overnight. Rebuilding and redesigning a new identity takes years. That is the invisible price that gets missed.”

The founder’s stunning departure removes Beijing’s biggest advocate in Silicon Valley, accelerates chip stockpiling, and leaves Asian suppliers bracing for what comes next.

Platform companies are luring doctors, lawyers, and Ph.D.s with top rates, but then use the same tactics of pay cuts and sudden ghosting that have plagued global data workers.

Startups like MiniMax and Moonshot are setting up U.S. outposts, but massive pay gaps, weaker prestige, and national security tensions make luring talent away from OpenAI and Anthropic an uphill climb.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like… In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of...

scraped.title: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
scraped.description: Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation.
scraped.h1: How data centers are driving a US natural-gas boom
scraped.body_text:
Rising electricity demand is locking in fossil-fuel generation.

In May 2025, my colleague David Rotman wrote a feature story describing how AI could keep us dependent on natural gas. Just 18 months later, I’ve lost count of how many times he’s already been proved right.

Sure, it’s technically possible to meet the world’s rising electricity demand with other power sources, including renewables like wind and solar supported by batteries. But the reality in the US so far is that the data center boom is helping to fuel a massive natural-gas resurgence.

Just one example: Plans for the Meta data center in Louisiana that David focused on in his story have expanded, and its power needs have too. The local utility went from three planned natural-gas plants to 10 . And as I wrote in a new story this week, data center developers are now looking beyond the grid and planning to build their own off-grid gas power plants . How did we get here?

If you want to understand the future of the grid, one way to do it is by looking at interconnection queues—lists of power plants that have requested a connection to the system. In recent years these queues have been dominated by renewables like wind and solar power, which are generally the cheapest way to build new energy capacity today.

But there’s been a shift in some places, particularly for PJM, the country’s largest power grid operator, which covers parts of 13 states in an area stretching from Illinois to Washington, DC. PJM has seen a major uptick in natural-gas proposals. In August, the operator announced that it had accepted proposals for 715 total projects with a capacity of over 200 gigawatts to join its queue. Nearly half that total capacity represented natural-gas plants.

If all the projects in the queue were built, it would increase the fossil-fuel share on PJM’s grid from 61% to 67%, according to an analysis by Kevin Kircher , an energy modeler and assistant professor of mechanical engineering at Purdue.

PJM’s queue is reflective of a bigger trend across the US. Natural gas is already the single biggest source of electricity in the country, and it has basically become the default to meet exploding power demand.

This AI-driven rush is already affecting greenhouse-gas emissions for tech companies. Meta’s emissions are up 45% over last year’s, according to the company’s recently released 2026 Sustainability Report . That’s even higher than the jumps from fellow hyperscalers Google ( 18% ), Amazon ( 16% ), and Microsoft ( 25% ). The company is also “reevaluating” its 2030 goal to reach net-zero emissions, according to the report, though there aren’t details about how or when it might reach a decision there.

And there’s another tidbit in that Meta report worth noting: The company said that when the grid can’t deliver power “on the necessary timeline,” it will look to other methods, including building its own on-site power generation.

This fits into a related and growing trend that I’ve been tracking recently: Data center developers are looking to bypass long wait times to hook up to the grid by building their own power plants instead.

It’s not new for large industrial facilities to supply their own power. Chemical plants often have natural-gas infrastructure on-site to generate electricity and heat, for example (though they’re generally connected to the grid as well). Mining operations are often remote, requiring an off-grid power source.

But the desire to come online quickly means there could be a massive boom in off-grid power plants for data centers. Over 100 such facilities have been proposed in the US, with a total capacity of 115 gigawatts (that’s more than double the entire peak power demand of California). The vast majority of these sites have been proposed since the beginning of 2025.

There are alternative ways to help meet growing electricity demand: Wind and solar are inexpensive options, and pairing them with batteries could improve their reliability, for example. I’ve also written before about demand flexibility —efforts to limit power drawn from the grid when demand is high.

Right now, though, the evidence continues to stack up that the AI boom in the US is basically synonymous with a natural-gas boom.

scraped.h1: The Download: AI swamping open records, and firefighting for permafrost
scraped.body_text:
Plus: Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies.

This is today's edition of The Download , our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what's going on in the world of technology.

AI has intensified investors' interest in public records. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered "signals" that help businesses sell to governments. At the same time, chatbots are making it easier for individuals to file requests.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests. That could potentially make public offices less transparent.

Find out how AI is testing the limits of America's right to know .

—Matthew King

In July 2021, a wildfire burned through a forest on the University of Alaska, Fairbanks campus, stripping away the moss and soil insulating the permafrost below. Five years later, we followed researchers into the forest to investigate how fighting fires could help keep that carbon locked in the ground.

Their probe revealed an escalating problem: As climate change fuels more frequent and severe fires, they’re accelerating permafrost thaw and releasing greenhouse gases. Now, researchers are trying to break that cycle. But how much should we spend, and what risks are worth taking?

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts . Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Hackers reportedly used an AI tool to breach US spy agencies The tool, Artex, was originally designed for cyber defense. ( NYT $) + Sources suggested that China may be behind the attack. ( CNN ) + Officials say it exposed non-classified data. ( Gizmodo ) + A US financial crimes bureau has also disclosed a breach. ( Verge ) + AI is making online crimes easier. ( MIT Technology Review )

2 Firms tied to Alice Huang financed $270 million of AI servers in China It's unclear whether they contained chips restricted by the US. ( Reuters $) + Chuck Schumer has accused Jensen Huang of export violations. ( Guardian )

3 A powerful HIV vaccine may finally be within reach “Super antibodies” blocked diverse strains in monkeys. ( Nature ) + Yet vaccine hesitancy is on the rise. ( MIT Technology Review )

4 China’s Huawei has been convicted of stealing US trade secrets It was found guilty on 10 of 12 counts, including bank fraud. ( BBC ) + The DoJ says it also helped Iran surveil protesters. ( Guardian ) + But it was cleared of the more serious racketeering charge. ( CNBC )

5 Data centers have been linked to hundreds of premature deaths The culprit is pollution from connected power plants. ( Newsweek ) + Data centers are getting their own gas plants. ( MIT Technology Review )

6 Meta insiders warn its AI moderation is causing dangerous mistakes They say the errors could have sweeping political consequences. ( Guardian )

7 The ex-OpenAI engineer accused of spying has been freed He’ll wear an ankle monitor after posting a $1 million bond. ( CNBC )

8 An immune-calming pill has healed severe eczema in a clinical trial Over a third of patients saw their symptoms improve. ( Bloomberg $)

9 AI is forcing researchers to reconsider artificial minds Some now think minds may not need bodies after all. ( New Scientist $) + AI consciousness debates are a trap. ( MIT Technology Review )

10 The US Army is about to blow up 10,000 pounds of unstable explosives The old stockpile has become too dangerous to move or neutralize. ( Verge )

Quote of the day

—Late-night host Jimmy Kimmel skewers Jensen Huang's swift reinstatement as Nvidia's CEO.

One more thing

Teaching a computer to use human language requires an inhuman amount of data. An LLM can easily churn through a hundred thousand times more words than a person will experience in the process of mastering their mother tongue.

This yawning divide between children and machines is called the data efficiency gap. It raises a tantalizing question for researchers: How can children learn so much with so little?

By reverse-engineering how they learn, scientists hope to create more efficient AI models—and perhaps settle enduring questions about language and children's developing minds. Here’s how they’re trying to close the data gap .

—Elise Cutts

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line .)

+ Need a smile? Finland is livestreaming six newborn puppies around the clock. + Wes Anderson has stepped into the Criterion Closet and picked out the films he loves most . + A product designer has invented inflatable chopsticks that you unroll and blow up when it's time to eat. + The James Webb Space Telescope has captured a stunning image of stars brewing in a nebulous cauldron.

Plus: A $1 trillion tech selloff has deepened fears of an AI bubble.

Plus: Hackers have disrupted the US Federal Election Commission’s website.

Plus: Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO.

Plus: Hackers exposed 41,000 Homeland Security workers.

scraped.title: AI is straining America’s open records systems
scraped.description: Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.
scraped.h1: AI is straining America’s open records systems
scraped.body_text:
Startups are mining public data for AI products, while citizens use chatbots to file more requests.

In Panton, Vermont, population 660, town clerk Kyle Rowe did it all. He crafted budgets, paid vendors, handled property tax disputes, and served as the town’s zoning supervisor and presiding elections officer. During morning office hours at the town hall—a wood-frame structure built as a church in 1858—he also fielded public records requests. Recently, he got rather busy.

Panton used to get a request every year or so from a company called SmartProcure for “all purchasing records,” covering everything from road salt to computers to toilet paper. Last year, those requests started coming quarterly. Then different companies began making more specific requests, like records of every purchase related to emergency road flares. These targeted inquiries started coming monthly or more. “I’m happy to answer public records requests from people,” says Rowe, who recently moved into a position at a nearby town. “But answering it for these purposes—it feels like I’m doing unpaid opposition research on the taxpayers’ time.”

Rowe’s experiences are being repeated across the US. While data brokers have mined public records for decades, AI has intensified investors’ interest. Over the last few years, venture-backed startups have raised upwards of $100 million to collect data from thousands of agencies and turn it into AI-powered “signals” that help businesses sell to governments.

At the same time, AI tools have made it easier for individuals to draft public records requests. Many places have seen double-digit annual increases in recent years. While more activity is good for democracy, AI-drafted requests tend to be longer, and broader in scope—and the offices answering them haven’t always grown in head count or budget.

As agencies struggle to tell whether they’re dealing with a citizen, a chatbot, or a sales pipeline, some states are passing legislation that makes it easier to deny requests, possibly making public offices less transparent.

The US Freedom of Information Act (FOIA) of 1966 established citizens’ right to know what their government is doing, and by now every state has written its own version into law. Greater transparency has led to cleaner drinking water, lower taxes, and better schools. But the system is far from perfect: Many requests linger for months, the process is often frustratingly bureaucratic, and rules and guidelines vary by state, county, and even town.

This is why businesses, with the time and resources to navigate this labyrinth, have often dominated FOIA since its early days. Margaret Kwoka, a law professor at Ohio State University and a recent member of the FOIA Advisory Committee, documented the trend in her 2016 study “ FOIA, Inc .”

Her analysis found that commercial requesters of all kinds—regulated companies, government contractors, information resellers—have accounted for 79% to 96% of public records requests at federal agencies like the Environmental Protection Agency and the Food and Drug Administration. What Kwoka once described as a cottage industry of small shops reselling public records has become a lucrative market for “much more sophisticated and integrated database products,” she says.

SmartProcure (which does business as GovSpend) pioneered the model 15 years ago, with a standardized approach for collecting government purchasing data. Its requests are “handled by real people with long-standing relationships,” says Trip Colden, GovSpend’s chief operating officer, and the company has preferential pricing for agencies.

The newer AI startups promise to make selling to government faster and fairer. Starbridge has raised $52 million, including a Series A led by Craft Ventures (the firm of David Sacks, the former White House AI and crypto czar), to build the equivalent of a “Bloomberg Terminal for public sector data,” a reference to the pricey data consoles that are a fixture on Wall Street trading desks. The company describes its mission as getting “the best technology into the hands of public leaders,” with public records as one input that helps match agencies with vendors. Pursuit, backed by investors including Bill Gurley and Jack Altman, has raised $25.5 million to help companies identify likely government buyers, drawing on board minutes, budgets, and what it calls “an industrial-scale FOIA operation.” CEO and cofounder Mike Vichich says Pursuit’s data will benefit the public, noting that many towns are seeing costs rise faster than revenues and “competition is what saves taxpayers money.”

While incumbents employ account teams to build a rapport with agencies, several clerks and county attorneys say newer startups often send many requests as they scramble to catch up on historical data. For example, PinPoint Analytics, which analyzes construction bid data, sent as many as 2,000 requests per day while building its dataset before settling closer to 500 today, says chief operating officer Mark Zurada. That mirrors the activity of SmartProcure and Pursuit, which send roughly 180,000 requests per year, according to their websites.

But the numbers can be much higher. NationGraph, which serves midsize vendors such as janitorial service providers, claims to send about 10,000 requests per day on behalf of clients; the company did not respond to requests for comment. The requests that companies send are typically written with templates, not AI. But AI helps standardize what comes back—spreadsheets, PDFs, mailed packets—and analyze it all to create branded sales “signals,” or benchmarks to help the business clients set their prices.

In small towns, this activity can be an annoyance; in cities and counties, which get many times the volume, handling it is becoming a full-time job. Chautauqua County, New York, hired a paralegal this summer after seeing requests double—an increase its county attorney blamed on people using ChatGPT to generate requests and on others seeking records to resell.

In Ann Arbor, Michigan, chief deputy clerk Sarah Alanis has seen the number of requests climb from 581 in 2021 to 937 last year—“our new normal is high,” she says. A growing share comes from requesters harvesting data at scale, sometimes asking for purchases from “vendors that don’t have much to do with one another,” or ones the city has never used. FOIA used to take a few hours of her week; now it’s often half her day , she told the Michigan Advance earlier this year.

It’s not just sales tech—AI tools have made it easy for anyone to fire off requests. Federal agencies received a record 1.7 million last year, which a New York Times report attributed partly to AI, as well as to mass filings by the Heritage Foundation and a rise in the number of immigrants seeking their own records for legal protection. David Cuillier, director of the Brechner Freedom of Information Project at the University of Florida, ran the US Department of Education’s July request log through an AI detector and concluded that at least 29% of requests had been written at least partly by AI, up from almost none before 2025. The AI-written requests were twice as long, and 83% asked for long lists of records.

In Pennsylvania, AI-driven activity is “breaking records every month,” says Liz Wagenseller, executive director of the Office of Open Records, which fields appeals for denied requests. Volumes had surged before—during the covid years, at the height of the 2020 election fight, or amid battles over school curricula. But Wagenseller says this wave isn’t driven by a hot-button issue, and appeals keep rising—from about 3,000 in 2021 and just under 4,000 in 2025 to a projected 6,000 this year.

While more activity signals stronger civic engagement, AI is straining an already fragile infrastructure with often poorly drafted requests. Wagenseller notes that when it comes to appealing a denial, chatbots “always give [people] encouragement to try,” even when it has no chance. Filings that used to take a paragraph now run pages. Some contain hallucinated legal citations, and one even included the user’s prompt to Claude.

On the other side of the records requests, resource-strapped offices are using tech to manage it all. One-fifth of federal agencies report using AI or machine learning to help search for records. The Washington Post reported that the Department of Homeland Security is using AI to speed redactions , which transparency advocates worry could lock in agencies’ long habit of withholding more than the law requires. Local governments are catching up, with many still migrating from email to centralized request portals. The software vendor CivicPlus says its NextRequest platform handles more than a million requests a year and uses captchas to screen out bots. That stops automated agents, says chief marketing officer Jane Snyder, but it “doesn’t determine whether a person used AI to help draft a request.”

As volumes rise, legislatures are responding. CivicPlus counts more than 20 state and federal measures in play this year, several of which give agencies new ways to say no. California’s, signed in September, declares that AI systems are not “members of the public,” though people may still use AI “at an ordinary human volume and frequency.” A stalled Pennsylvania bill would let agencies deny requests they “reasonably suspect” were generated by a script or AI. Wagenseller doesn’t think that’s the answer. The real choice, she says, is funding agencies to keep up or making the system less free, fast, and open—“and you’re giving up something for both.”

Arguably the most aggressive action yet has been in Indiana, where Allen County officials described a growing trend in “suspiciously non-human” requests for years of purchase orders, eating up to 20 hours a week of staff time, as reported by the Journal Gazette . A state law that passed without a single dissenting vote and took effect July 1 lets agencies charge out-of-state requesters, prioritize residents, and deny requests they suspect are aimed at data scraping or phishing.

Neighboring Adams County went further. In March, it banned commercial use of its records, including resale. The county still hands over the documents, though; a notice of the ban is attached, but there are few means to enforce it. Requests had jumped from about one a week to as many as 10, often in a single burst; since the state law took effect, they’ve settled at one to five. County attorney Clayton Lengerich says the new rules don’t affect “any individual requester’s ability to keep their local municipality accountable,” only requests that “someone’s going to throw into an AI generator for some sales analysis.”

Fielding FOIA requests is expensive, and someone has to pay. Congress tried to put the responsibility on business in 1986, amending FOIA to let agencies charge commercial requesters more, but the rules were so riddled with exceptions that this rarely happens. “It costs more for the agencies to collect the fees than it’s worth in fees, and so they just don’t,” says Kwoka, the Ohio State law professor. She estimates that agencies recoup less than 5% of their costs from commercial requesters; at the FDA in one year she studied, it was $328,000 against $33.6 million spent.

Kwoka has long argued for “affirmative disclosure,” or proactively posting the information that gets asked for most. She points to the EPA, which put property contamination records online after commercial buyers had requested them one address at a time for years. A handful of states have adopted portals, such as California’s Open FI$Cal , that regularly publish high-level spending data. But this doesn’t include the full contracts that sales-tech firms often request, which reveal expiration dates, termination clauses, and service commitments.

Startups like Pursuit and Starbridge say they’d welcome this approach, and they seem confident their business model could survive if the data became freely available. “The best request is one that no one has to file because the data is already out there,” says Vichich. But publishing isn’t free, and commercial requesters also aren’t raising their hands to fund the fix.

As states negotiate reforms, the biggest risk is that rules built to limit bulk AI requests or sales-tech crawlers will land on everyone else: out-of-state reporters, academic researchers, immigration lawyers. Meanwhile, the requests keep increasing. “It’s something we’re going to have to hold our nose and continue doing,” says Rowe, the small-town Vermont clerk. “The alternative sets a dangerous precedent for a person being able to hold government accountable.”

Ten years after AlphaGo’s match against Go champion Lee Sedol, today’s AI still isn’t tapping into the machinery that made that win possible.

An exclusive interview with Nick Cammarata, the researcher whose 26,000-word viral blog post has AI safety folks celebrating.

With the rise of personal AI assistants, the internet isn't just for humans anymore.

The startup Tau Robotics is sending humanoid robots to clean San Francisco homes. They still need lots of human guidance, but they’re learning.
