Please do your part today.

This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.

“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”

We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr , whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.

“ Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr . “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman.

We are currently awaiting an Egyptian court decision on whether the closing of Mada Masr , the independent newspaper in Egypt, will stand. We’ll go to Cairo when we hear.

But right now we’re going to turn to what happened in the last few weeks here in this country, in New York, where we are. Novelists, essayists, poets and other writers from around the world took to the stage at the 77th annual National Book Awards ceremony in New York City last week. The winner of this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction, Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, though, was notably absent from the event, after the Trump administration denied his U.S. visa application, blocking him from entering the United States.

ElGendy’s debut book is called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , and chronicles his more than six years of imprisonment in Egypt following his arrest at the age of 17, alongside his father, during the crackdown on protests after the military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2013. He and his father were in their car, and Abdelrahman was taking a picture.

This is the moment the prize for nonfiction was presented by panel chair Robert Warrior.

ROBERT WARRIOR : It’s my distinct honor to announce that this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction goes to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna .

AMY GOODMAN : Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor, Helen Thomaides, then took the stage and read a statement written by ElGendy.

HELEN THOMAIDES : If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you. Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would one day end up in a book, that the guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist, that the slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how to render on the page the torture my body was enduring. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I’d imagine that book winning an award, and deliver fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, fleetingly unincarcerated. Today, that dream should have come full circle, but like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable.

AMY GOODMAN : That was Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor Helen Thomaides reading Abdelrahman’s words after his memoir Huna won the National Book Award just last week. Ahead of the ceremony, Abdelrahman wrote a piece in The New Yorker magazine. It’s headlined “I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa.”

Abdelrahman ElGendy wrote much of the book while in the United States, where he came two years after he was released from prison in Egypt. He studied at the University of Pittsburgh, where he obtained an MFA in creative nonfiction. Then, in April 2025, following the Trump administration’s widespread targeting of pro-Palestine voices, including international students and academics, Abdelrahman ElGendy decided to flee the U.S., fearing he’d be next, that he’d be detained and possibly deported back to Egypt over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations. At the time, he wrote in The Nation magazine, quote, “I was a political prisoner in Egypt. I didn’t want to become one again in America,” unquote.

For more, we’re joined now by Abdelrahman ElGendy from Europe, where he lives now.

Abdelrahman, I just want to congratulate you on this remarkable book, which I’ve just finished. And I had the joy, flying back from Turkey, the U.N. climate summit, of listening to your book, the audio book, which you read in your own words. The magnificence, the power, the pain of this book cannot be underestimated. I want to thank you so much for sharing your life with us, Abdelrahman ElGendy. Thank you for joining us.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Thank you. Thank you so much, Amy. Thanks for having me and for these kind words. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN : So, we are awaiting word right now about whether Egypt will be forced to reopen Mada Masr , a place where you actually, I think, published your first words. You wrote throughout your six years in prison. But talk about — well, first, start with the title, and talk about what it meant to win the National Book Award in the United States, the place you wanted to stay, to be in exile, to be protected, but could not reenter for the award ceremony.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Yeah. Thank you. I mean, of course, it was a gutting thing to not be able to, you know, attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising. You know, we all know how this U.S. administration is now trying to keep everyone who criticizes policies out, especially when it comes, you know, to our region, especially when it’s around Palestine. You know, and if you’re a citizen of another country that doesn’t, you know, need a visa, they don’t want you. They just detain you at the point of entry at the airport. But if you do, like in my case, they just deny you, you know, at the embassy.

And I just — yeah, they love repeating the idea that the visa is, you know, a privilege and not a right. This is kind of the mantra that they keep, you know, repeating to everyone. But, yeah, this, I think, is just intentional distraction from the most important point here, which is that the visa process is being weaponized, and has been now for a while, as a form of transnational repression, which we’re very familiar with in Egypt, as well, because the Egyptian state also uses this form of transnational repression, you know, denying us certain paperwork and stuff like that to punish you for political speech and to keep certain bodies that you deem undesirable outside. So, same for the U.S. So, the visa denial itself being weaponized in that way is the issue, not the fact that the, yes, consul office can deny or approve, etc. So, I think this should be, yeah, the headline, really.

But it was also, like, very sad, I think, in a way that is very specific to my personal journey, you know, as a — this is not new to me. As a kid, you know, I worked my whole life to earn a scholarship to study engineering at this great school that my family couldn’t afford at the time. And then I was arrested on the eve of my first day as a freshman. This is — I speak about this in the book — before I get to live this dream. And then, when I was released in 2020, it happened straight into COVID in 2020. And I started, like, when the lockdown was being lifted, and I started slowly rebuilding community. Because of my writing with Mada Masr , actually, because I continued writing with Mada post-prison, word kind of circulated. Relatives who were well connected told me that my name is being kind of floated again for rearrest. And eventually, I was forced to flee Egypt because of that writing with Mada Masr . And since then, you know, I’ve never been able to share a room with Egyptian readers of my work, except accidentally in exile, you know, when we’re all, like, kind of shunned away from Egypt together. So I’ve had to do it from a distance.

And now, you know, this book, which I imagined writing from prison, which I wrote, you know, throughout my time in the U.S., and then, just as I was about to graduate from my MFA in the U.S., which this book was the graduation, the thesis for — right? — you know, I was forced again to temporarily leave for safety concerns of ICE targeting, as you mentioned, because of my political writing and pro-Palestine activism on campus. And so, I had to graduate from my MFA remotely, as well, witness that moment, you know, be celebrated remotely by people in the room that I was unable to be in. And I wanted to bring my family over to the U.S. to have that graduation ceremony, that prison denied us in Egypt, and we were deprived of that again.

I couldn’t do a U.S. book tour. And now the book, you know, has made it all the way into that room of the National Book Award. And, you know, to have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love who have witnessed this journey, it is gutting. But in a way, it is also just the story of my life. This is not new.

And still, I think I need to redirect all this back, you know, to Egyptian political prisoners, because as I said in my speech, a life that I’m living right now beyond prison, in which my dreams could even be crushed in this way, that was the dream back in prison. I dreamed of a day when I have these, like, unincarcerated people problems. But there are 60,000 political prisoners, you know, who don’t even have the luxury of such precarity, that at least opens into possibility, right? So, I think, yeah, I always want to redirect it to them. I am blessed, no matter what, like, everything that happened that was very sad and gutting and everything. But I always try to put that in relation to people back home behind bars in Egypt, my friends, Ayman and everyone else still behind bars. I’m still blessed to have these problems. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : Tell us why you named the book Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming .

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Yeah, I mean Huna , huna is the Arabic word for “here.” And it was inspired by a popular Arab protest song, “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which means “We Will Remain Here.” And I first heard that song, you know, up close on my third night in detention. We were in this, like, military camp in the middle of the desert, very excruciating physical conditions, where 68 of us were crammed into a tiny room, piled on top of one another. There were some people that were shot and wounded, so it was very heavy. My father was with me at the time. He was dying.

And then, out of nowhere, the guards finally allowed in the homemade food our families had brought to the gate. So, our families would come every day; they’d be sent back. But that day, they just brought in the food. And then, for the first time since the arrest, we had a taste of home.

And then something very magical happened. We just began to sing. The mood got lighter, and we began to sing. And one of the songs was “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which goes, “We will remain here until the pain subsides. We will remain here. The melody will sweeten.” And, you know, we sang together, and I started feeling those chills on my arms. You could feel that everyone in the room was entering this sort of visceral moment together.

And I found myself thinking, fascinated, that I didn’t want to remain here. Like, who wants — you know, none of us wants to remain here. We couldn’t wait to escape this room fast enough. My father was dying. We were being tortured. People were shot. So, what was this huna ? What was this “here” that we were so touched by, that we were all actively choosing to inhabit together? What were we entering?

And I think I would say my book — if I would kind of put it in one line, I’d say it is a six-year pursuit of this huna , like the question of what it means to inhabit a space that is designed to erase you in body, in language, in your very sense of personhood, and still find ways to be. So, I try to trace, you know, that sense of nonphysical hereness and witness, that repeatedly saves me from being wholly conquered by prison.

And you also mentioned the becoming part, which is important to me, because I was arrested — I think sometimes that gets lost, the fact that I was arrested at 17 years old. So, to me, this is not just prison and revolution. It is also becoming, because I say this is a coming-of-age story. And so many people come to this political awakening that I had, you know, in high school age. They start getting politically agitated or involved. And to me, it happened that I went into prison in those formative years. So, my whole history of activism was two months — right? — after the Rabaa massacre until October 6, and then I was arrested. So, incarceration, in a way, was this school in which I was thinking about the world and my positionality inside it.

So, I was just politically activated before I went into prison, and I went into prison with all those agitated questions that were so unsettled for me. I was so angry. I carried so much rage at the military dictatorship, the police state. And I felt like I had a moral compass. But it was mostly motivated not by, you know, theory or intellectual thought or engaging with political theory. It was just rage at seeing certain injustices and wanting to intervene and be part of removing them or restoring justice. So, to me, that was — you know, I see people massacred, a military dictatorship. I think, “These things are wrong, and I don’t want to be on this side. I want to be on the other side that is against them.”

But in prison, I get into a more, I think, sophisticated approach. In prison, I think you have — you know, you have nothing more than time, and you sit down, and you just question everything. And I think prison forces you to confront so many not only political questions, but also very existential questions, you know, about what it means to be here, to be human, to be in relation to other humans, to your own father, to your friends, your mom, and what kinds of obligations does that carry.

So, every day, I was encountering new things that agitated me even more, and that were forcing me, you know, to think. You’re beaten. You’re tortured. You’re being beaten by those batons every day. You see your father hit. Everything around you radicalizes you and makes you think, you know, “I cannot afford to look away from these things. I don’t have the luxury of looking away from these questions,” because the batons are beating me every single day. I just cannot not think about them and my relationship to them and to other people fighting them, and whether I think of them, again, as allies or even political enemies. So, momentarily in prison, I have to align with factions that, you know, I don’t align with politically. It forces me to think about these questions. Like, in my cell, I don’t agree with you politically. I’m very aggravated by you. But we step up outside the cell, and the same police officers are beating us. So, what does that mean in terms of, you know, allyship, mobilization, working together? So, yeah, all those questions at 17, you wouldn’t be thinking about, I think. But I couldn’t afford not to, because my survival depended on grappling with them in prison.

AMY GOODMAN : I mean, this is also a story of a father and son, a mother and son, a brother, a cousin. Talk about how you were first detained with your dad. And it’s a relationship that carries throughout the book. I mean, you go from being a son to being your dad’s protector, to having to separate from your father. My goodness, I mean, you were arrested at the age of 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Yeah. One thing I always like to bring up about this is, one of my dear friends, when she read the manuscript of the book for the first time, before it was published, she told me, “Do you know what this book is?” And I told he, “What?” And she said, “This is a love letter to Baba.” And I found that very moving, because I do think this is one of — at least one of the things that this book is, because, you know, my father was apolitical. Like, he wasn’t even involved in politics. And I was a very hot-headed teenager. I really wanted to be on the streets. I was very — again, I was — I had this awakening, and I was attending protests very — you know, every single day, maybe three protests, you know, in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening. And they tolerated — my parents tolerated that for a while.

But then, on October 6, that was a particularly dangerous day. This is the Armed Forces Day. And protesters wanted to break into Tahrir Square. And because of its symbolic value, you know, revolutionary value, the police would get very brutal when people attempt to even approach Tahrir Square. Up until today, it’s a very heavily securitized area. And so, what happens, the arrangement is my mother forced my father to basically come chaperone me, you know, to this protest, to look out for me and make sure that I don’t get harmed or arrested, which, you know, doesn’t work out as planned, obviously.

So, we go there. I start shooting a video. I’m, like, speaking enthusiastically. I leave the car. He yells at me to come back, so I go back inside. I shoot from the window. And then I don’t notice there are two plainclothes officers standing right next to the window, who kind of, from my commentary, kind of deduce that I’m aligned with what’s happening. So, they, you know, pull the door open. They wrench me out. They start beating me, take my phone. And then my father comes, and he starts trying to wrench me away, you know, from their arms. And then they end up arresting him, as well. So, my father gets arrested just because, you know, I made him be in that space, which, of course, we can always argue that it’s a structural issue, it’s a state’s issue. But guilt, you know, doesn’t — it doesn’t work like that. And so, my — the whole six year begins from that kind of inciting incident and that guilt. It’s a very guilt-ridden story, you know, toward my father.

And we’ve always, my father and I, struggled, I think, to express affection to one another. There’s also commentary about Arab masculinity in the book a lot, and specifically father-son relationships. So, we struggled to do that, and I think we carried so much and so many unsaid things inside both of us. And through prison, it was very difficult to communicate, because you’re used to seeing your father as this protective figure, right? And then, in prison, you suddenly realize he is helpless, he cannot protect you. And in a way, he does his best to protect me in all those small ways in prison, of course, but in the bigger scheme of things, he cannot get me my freedom, right? And I cannot get him his freedom. And, you know, the state loves to weaponize love, the Egyptian state, any fascist state, really. So, in prison, they used that against us. They hurt my father to get to me. They hurt me to get to him, and so on. So it was a very difficult situation.

But what I also try to explore in the book is the avenues that opened up once my father and I were not only father and son in prison. I suddenly started seeing him in all those other kind of roles. He was also a prisoner in relation to the state, a prison cellmate or, you know, a prison mate to other prisoners, which was both difficult, but I think also opened up different avenues of communication between us, because sometimes, I don’t know, we’d have a fight in the cell, and we’d fight together with — like, against people and be aligned with one another, and I think, “Oh, my father and I are co-conspirators now.” There’s that first scene in the book where we do this. And through the night, my father, for the first time ever, he rests his hand, you know, on my back and leaves it there through the night. And I remember that being one of the first instances in my life where he touches me in that way.

So, when he read the book after, you know, it was published — I gave him the Arabic. I wrote it in Arabic. It’s coming out in Arabic, and he read the Arabic version. And again, he doesn’t — he was so struck, I think, by the intensity of the love, because I couldn’t express it to him verbally. So, he just said, “You know, I understand so many things much better now,” and then went on to, like, fact-check the entire book, because that’s his — you know, his language of love. So, eventually, I think this is just the sweetest, I think, closure that could have happened to this harrowing experience that we shared together. And if he was the only reader, you know, of this book, if this was the only thing to come out of it, that would have been enough for me.

AMY GOODMAN : And, of course, he gets out before you and then tries to get you out, and ultimately does, based on the fact that you were arrested at 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Yeah, and it is — I was wrongly tried — wrongfully tried as an adult instead of a minor. And this is — again, throughout the book, you come across the absurdity and arbitrariness, you know, of the Egyptian state. I was 17 at the time of arrest, two months shy of 18, right? So I had two months to turn 18. And then, the officer that arrested me breaks my ID, or both of our IDs, delivered us to the police station. And just so randomly, because of that, I get processed as an adult, and then I just keep getting processed as an adult throughout. In the prosecution, my lawyer ends up, you know, submitting appeal after appeal. None of them gets looked into, because we’re in Egypt. We get tried as this package deal, right? All of us together in a mass trial.

AMY GOODMAN : Abdelrahman, I want to continue this conversation after the show, but I want you to stay with us, because we’re going to go to Cairo right now.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : OK, yeah, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN : This story doesn’t end, and I want you to be a part of it. We’re going to Cairo, Egypt, where an appeal was just heard in the case against Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , for operating an unlicensed website, they’re saying, though she’s been operating it for years. Late last month, she was fined $50,000 or to shut down Mada Masr , following an expedited trial where her lawyers were denied time to prepare a defense, call witnesses or submit documentation. Lina Attalah is also facing charges for publishing so-called false news, that could lead to her imprisonment. We’re going right now outside the court to Hossam Bahgat, founder and director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, part of Mada Masr ’s legal team, just outside the courthouse. And I want Abdelrahman to respond to what you report to us. Do we have a decision from the court whether Mada Masr can be reopened, Hossam?

HOSSAM BAHGAT : Thank you, Amy, for having me.

No, I mean, the defense team finished their oral pleadings and submitted the requests. The court has adjourned the session, and we should get a decision on this final appeal by the end of today. I mean, the good thing is that at least it looked more like a courtroom and more like a normal trial today compared to the absurdity that we saw in the first instance. Unfortunately, though, we don’t have any signs that there is an intent to look fairly at the situation, the position of Mada Masr . Today, the lawyers not only challenged the decision to convict Lina and shut down Mada Masr —

AMY GOODMAN : You’re breaking up.

HOSSAM BAHGAT : — and confiscate all its —

AMY GOODMAN : Hossam, you’re breaking up, but I want to tell people you can go to see our interview with Lina Attalah that I did with Anjali Kamat just as she was facing all of this, and also you can go to democracynow.org to see our visit to Mada Masr when we were in Egypt. I want to give Abdelrahman ElGendy the last word, though. You thank Lina Attalah and our former producer Sharif Abdel Kouddous for being able to find a way to get your words out of prison. Ultimately, you would smuggle them out. Is that right?

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY : Yes, absolutely. I began writing in that way, smuggling my words out in prison. And I think you just — you know, once you, as a political prisoner, get a taste of that magic of being able to smuggle your language out to the world, and then receive the world’s language back in response, you just cannot stop. And Mada were the first place to, you know, offer my words a home, is how I thank them. And they feature in the book, as well, because Mada , you know, they sent me wanting to publish, you know, some of the things that I smuggled out, and ever since I had this relationship with them, I published six more pieces with Mada Masr from prison. And that was important to me.

I think that the project of the current Egyptian military dictatorship is — it’s a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before. It was possible, and therefore it is possible. And they don’t want it to be a thinkable or imaginable thing anymore.

And I think Mada Masr is a huge part of that. I cannot understand or speak about the campaign against Mada Masr , you know, divorced from the idea of this more bigger project of erasure of the Egyptian state, because Mada carries so much of the archive, you know, of our revolutionary history. It is the place that people like me, in prison and after prison, can go write in. It is the place where, you know, Alaa El-Fattah, who published “Graffiti for Two People” with Ahmed Douma. It is the place that speaks about prison letters and communication. And so, to erase it is to erase an archive. And also, it is to erase the more, I think, intimate and dangerous thing, is we go to Mada Masr to feel less alone, to remember, you know, that we were many, and therefore we are many still today. We have not been — you know, as Alaa says, we have not been fully defeated. And that, to me, is important. Maybe we’re not — maybe we are defeated in a way, but not wholly, not fully.

AMY GOODMAN : Abdelrahman ElGendy, I want to thank you for being with us and for this incredible memoir. It’s called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming . It has just won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and we’ll link to your New Yorker and Nation pieces. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman. This is Democracy Now!

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

The U.S. Army detonated nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday, potentially sending toxic lead dust and other deadly contaminants spewing across communities and farmland throughout the Mississippi River water basin. Residents, who were first informed last week, had been ordered to evacuate or else shelter in place. “The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts,” says Pat Elder, who tracks how military activity impacts people and the planet at the Military Poisons project. “There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen.”

AMY GOODMAN : This is Democracy Now! , democracynow.org, The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman.

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. The detonation will cause a massive blast that could send toxic lead dust spewing across communities, farmland, and potentially into the Mississippi River. The detonation is scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time.

Officials have recommended residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant to evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. Men are being told to — in this farmland area, to bring their cows inside. A number of farmers have said that’s impossible.

Jeremy Atwater, a resident of Augusta, Iowa, told a reporter he plans to go west to escape the toxic plume.

JEREMY ATWATER : But now the winds are changing directions, and it’s going to blow directly south through our town, so I guess we’re going to head west instead.

REPORTER : And what’s out west? Is it hotels? Or is it just —

JEREMY ATWATER : Anything but the bomb. … My primary concern is a lot. I mean, nobody really knows. There’s never been a documented explosion like this, as far as I could find any doing my due diligence digging in the interweb. But it’s just going to be a big problem. It’s going to be a lot of lead poisoning going on.

AMY GOODMAN : The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There’s no safe level of lead exposure. Lead is a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm and is particularly dangerous to children and pregnant women.

The Army says the explosives, stored for decades in 68 drums at the Iowa Army Ammunition Plant, have deteriorated to the point that they could spontaneously explode. This is acting Army Secretary Adam Telle speaking at a press conference in Iowa Tuesday.

ARMY SECRETARY ADAM TELLE : There is consensus across the experts across the country that a controlled, mitigated detonation of the lead azide here at Iowa Army Ammunition Plant is far preferable to uncontrolled, spontaneous detonation of that substance.

AMY GOODMAN : On Saturday, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option, a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded a contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead.

Well, for more, we go to Lexington Park, Maryland, where we’re joined by Pat Elder, the founder of the group Military Poisons. He just wrote a piece headlined “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.”

Pat Elder, welcome back to Democracy Now! Iowans are panicked.

PAT ELDER : Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN : They say they have gotten very little notice about what’s about to take place. If there are hills, they’re saying people are heading to the hills. But what do they do with their cows, those who are farmers? If you could start off by saying why you see this as a warning to the world? And how on Earth did this surprise this whole community, where the governor now has declared a disaster emergency in three counties?

PAT ELDER : Well, thank you for having me, Amy. I appreciate it.

We have to go back to the words of Thomas Jefferson, who wrote in the Declaration of Independence that we must be warned of usurpations by the federal government that will strip the liberties of individual states. And so, that’s what we see today. The Army has decided to act as it wishes, and it is going against the recommendations of its own experts and experts with the EPA and experts with the Applied Physics Lab, Johns Hopkins here in Maryland.

There is no reason for this to be done, and it is a disaster waiting to happen. And I feel sorry for the poor folks in Iowa, as I do for people around the world who suffer these same sorts of fates, because the United States Army does what it wants and has acted in a Neanderthal fashion with its detonation and supposed disposal of hazardous materials.

AMY GOODMAN : Let’s talk about the effects —

PAT ELDER : I think it’s —

AMY GOODMAN : — of lead, Pat Elder. If you can talk about the health concerns for lead exposure, especially for children and fetuses? The New York Times says lead is a neurotoxin, and there are no safe levels for exposure. Can you take it from there?

PAT ELDER : Well, I can, Amy. Thank you so much. We know, all the way from our experiences with leaded gas and lead paint, and the fiasco in Flint, Michigan — we have the clinical data — we understand that lead is a killer. It is a killer in the embryo. It is a killer for young children. And it is a killer for all of us.

But the Army would pretend that this is not the case, because — well, because it’s very fond of lead in ammunition. And so, we look around the country, and we see where the Army has been absolutely irresponsible in the way that it handles lead. We look at Fort Ord in California, for instance, and entire sand dunes are loaded with lead, and campers are allowed to traipse. They built an entire campus at the University of California, Monterey Bay, over top of old Army buildings with lead pipes. The poor kids are drinking lead. The Army is irresponsible when it comes to lead all around the world. It has buried it, and it has — supposed to be following a process, that it does not follow, to safely dispose of lead.

AMY GOODMAN : So, let’s —

PAT ELDER : And I want to add, too —

AMY GOODMAN : Go ahead.

PAT ELDER : Yeah, thanks. Just, you know, we’re not just dealing with lead here. We’re dealing with lead azide. And the best way to put this into focus is that lead azide is the explosive that detonates a bomb. So, if we have a 2,000-pound bomb that is falling on Gaza, lead azide the size of a small pea is detonated, which then sends a tremendous blast into the bomb itself. So, it is the explosive agent. And this is the material the Army is getting ready to detonate. And so, we’re not just talking about lead itself. We’re also talking about contaminations like hydrogen cyanide and hydrazoic acid. These are deadly. They deprive the brain of oxygen. And this is what is getting unleashed on the people of Iowa.

AMY GOODMAN : I want to ask you about that New York Times exposé on Saturday that may have surprised many, as so much of this has just crept up on them, the people of the community. It’s not as if this is a story that broke into the whole, you know, country. But they’ve been dealing with it for a while. Many residents did not know until the last few days what was about to happen. But The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially pursued another, cleaner option: a chemical process designed to neutralize the explosives without a blast. In March, the Army awarded this contract to MuniRem Environmental, a Georgia-based company that uses a sulfur-based solution to break down explosives and immobilize toxic chemicals. Two months later, the Army canceled the contract and chose detonation instead. Pat Elder, explain.

PAT ELDER : Well, we have to go back to March of 2025 to fully understand what has transpired. The Army itself, along with experts from the EPA and experts with the Johns Hopkins Applied Physics Lab here in Maryland, sat down, and they all voted that it would be too dangerous to detonate these materials, and that the way to do it is to saturate the exterior of these barrels, and the interior of these barrels once they are opened, with a chemical compound that is made of sulfur in water. And so, we spray that over the barrels. And when the Army says, “Well, this is too dangerous,” MuniRem, the company behind this process, has said that it would use robots, as it has in decontaminating other Army ammunition sites. So, the entire process and the entire culmination in the Army deciding suddenly that they would go ahead and detonate this material is lunacy.

And the idea that way back in August of 2025, we — the Army knew that there was a problem, and MuniRem knew there was a problem, and Johns Hopkins knew, and the EPA knew. The last people to find out are the people of Iowa and the people that live in the immediate area. They didn’t find out until last week. And that’s how the Army operates.

AMY GOODMAN : Pat Elder, I want to thank you for being with us, founder of the group Military Poisons. We’ll link to your piece , “The Pentagon’s Toxic Shortcut in Iowa Is a Warning to the World.”

Coming up, Egyptian writer Abdelrahman ElGendy. He just won the National Book Award for Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , but he wasn’t at the award ceremony. The U.S. denied ElGendy a visa. While he was a political prisoner in Egypt, starting when he was 17 years old, he published his writings in the Egyptian independent paper Mada Masr . Right now we are awaiting a court’s decision, an appeal of the government’s just closing down Mada Masr . We’ll go to Cairo, as well. Stay with us.

[break]

AMY GOODMAN : “Massive Will” by Emel Mathlouthi, performing in our Democracy Now! studio. To see all the performances and interviews in our Democracy Now! studios of musicians and artists, go to democracynow.org .

Special guests Angela Davis, Bruce Springsteen, Patti Smith, Michael Stipe and more came together to celebrate 30 years of Democracy Now! at a sold out Riverside Church event in NYC on March 23, 2026.

Please do your part today.

Iowa Governor Kim Reynolds has declared a disaster emergency in three counties, as the U.S. Army prepares to detonate nearly five tons of highly unstable lead-based explosives at an ammunition plant in southeastern Iowa today. Environmental groups are warning of an unfolding public health catastrophe, with a detonation scheduled for 9 a.m. Central Time that could spew toxic lead dust across communities, farmland and potentially into the Mississippi River. Officials have recommended that residents of Middletown, where the plant is located, and anyone within a five-mile cone southwest of the plant evacuate, while people living up to 20 miles away have been told to stay indoors with their windows closed. This is Sean Kaufman, a disaster preparedness official with the Department of Health and Human Services.

Sean Kaufman : “Individuals that are in that directly affected area — which, again, we will continuously get updates based on the weather — if they are women who are pregnant, children under the age of 6, or children in general, and individuals who may have chronic disease, you definitely want to be out of that area. I would evacuate that area.”

The Army published an updated map estimating the lead plume could spread all the way to northern Missouri, more than 100 miles from ground zero. There is no safe level of exposure to lead, a neurotoxin that can cause permanent cognitive and behavioral harm. Ahead of today’s detonation, The New York Times published an investigation revealing the Army had initially hired a firm to turn the explosives into harmless waste, but then dropped the contract in favor of a so-called controlled blast. We’ll have the latest on this story after headlines.

In Gaza, at least four Palestinians were killed this morning in an Israeli airstrike on an apartment building in the al-Shati refugee camp. The strike followed Israeli attacks that killed at least 10 Palestinians across Gaza on Tuesday, including a 30-year-old pregnant mother and Khaled Walid al-Jamal, a 13-year-old boy shot dead in northern Gaza City. Another Israeli airstrike killed a senior Hamas security official, along with his wife and their two teenage daughters. The relentless attacks came as Palestinians held funeral services in Khan Younis for three people killed in an Israeli strike on a police post. Rashad Abu Loli is a relative of one of the victims.

Rashad Abu Loli : “There is no ceasefire. Throughout the days, throughout the hours, there are strikes in the streets on civilians and on vehicles. We hear about a ceasefire, but this ceasefire exists only as an agreement. On the ground and in reality, it does not exist.”

On Tuesday, Gaza’s Health Ministry declared an epidemic alert over a surge in meningitis, warning that hundreds of thousands of people are at risk of contracting the deadly condition.

Saudi Arabia’s biggest oil refinery caught fire following an attack by Yemen’s Ansar Allah movement, known as the Houthis. Ras Tanura is one of the largest refining complexes and oil export terminals in the world, with a capacity of over a half-million barrels per day. It erupted in flames hours after a Houthi strike on Saudi Arabia’s main financial district in Riyadh Tuesday that injured 11 people. That attack damaged Riyadh’s tallest skyscraper, which is home to the kingdom’s sovereign wealth fund. The Saudi-backed coalition responded by attacking the Houthi-controlled port of Hodeidah, prompting Ansar Allah to threaten Jeddah and other ports on the Red Sea.

In Moscow, President Vladimir Putin has vowed to retaliate against Ukrainian ⁠attacks on Russian energy sites. At least 14 oil refineries have been struck since the start of November, despite President Trump’s explicit request to Kyiv to halt such attacks. On Tuesday, Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky defended the strikes, as well as a drone attack on a Russian cargo ship in the Gulf of Finland.

Meanwhile, Italy has warned the conflict has spread to the Mediterranean, after a Ukrainian drone struck a Russian ship anchored at a port in Benghazi, killing two Libyan naval officers. The Libyan National Army has vowed to retaliate.

This comes as the U.N. food agency warns the war in Ukraine is disrupting grain shipments, jeopardizing food aid for 7.3 million people. Luke Lindberg is director of the World Food Programme.

Luke Lindberg : “This is one of the world’s breadbasket regions. Its grains are vital to nations, including Somalia, which is at risk of famine, and Yemen, which imports 90% of its food today. And yet, grain silos in Ukraine and Poland are full, while families in Somalia, Sudan and South Sudan suffer catastrophic hunger. This is not a problem of production. It is a political problem. Grain is available, but it is not reaching the people who need it.”

Two people who were brutally arrested by federal agents during widespread immigration raids in the Chicago area last year have filed separate lawsuits against the Trump administration. Dayanne Figueroa and Luis Jesus Acosta Gutierrez were among those detained as hundreds of federal agents descended onto Illinois for Trump’s so-called Operation Midway Blitz. Gutierrez was taken into custody following an hourslong standoff with federal agents who deployed tear gas and pepper spray on community members and neighbors who had gathered to try to protect Gutierrez. Figueroa is a single mother and U.S. citizen. She had just dropped off her 5-year-old child at school when her car was rammed by ICE agents, who then dragged her out by her legs, threw her onto the pavement and pinned her face-down using their knees. According to the lawsuit, one of the agents placed a knee near an incision from a recent kidney surgery, causing grueling pain. Figueroa was arrested without a warrant despite repeatedly telling agents she was a U.S. citizen.

In related news, the family of a U.S. citizen from Pharr, Texas, is considering legal action against the Trump administration after surveillance footage showed masked federal agents detaining Domingo Vásquez at a construction site in Alamo. His mother says he has an intellectual disability and at the time of his arrest did not have his identification. Vásquez had been working in construction with his uncle.

Meanwhile, four formerly detained immigrants, including two transgender men, say they were subjected to rape, sexual assault, anti- LGBTQ hate speech and forced labor by staff at a for-profit ICE jail in Basile, Louisiana. The group has filed a lawsuit against the private prison company GEO Group and two ex-employees at the South Louisiana ICE Processing Center, including the former assistant warden. The plaintiffs say they were also denied medical care and were placed in solitary confinement in retaliation for filing complaints against the abuses.

In more immigration news, Maryland father Kilmar Ábrego García has arrived in Spain after leaving the U.S. on his own to avoid deportation. The Trump administration repeatedly attempted to deport him to countries he had no ties to, in a legal standoff that’s lasted for nearly two years. Ábrego García, who is originally from El Salvador, became a symbol of Trump’s cruel mass deportation campaign after he was sent to the notorious Salvadoran maximum-security prison known as CECOT in March 2025. García was returned to the U.S. about two months later, following a high-profile visit to El Salvador by Maryland Democratic Senator Chris Van Hollen, who met with Ábrego García and advocated for his release.

More than two dozen Hollywood superstars are calling on New York Senator Chuck Schumer to resign from his leadership role as Democrats take control of the Senate in January. Among those calling for Senator Chris Van Hollen to instead be elected Senate majority leader are actors Robert De Niro, Marisa Tomei and Jane Fonda.

Attorney General Todd Blanche signaled Wednesday that he won’t investigate Nvidia’s co-founder Jensen Huang over potential criminal charges, following reports that Huang had an affair with a Chinese businesswoman whose former company is suspected of diverting advanced Nvidia chips to China in violation of U.S. export rules; she was also allegedly in communication with China’s top spy agency. Blanche spoke to reporters a day after President Trump publicly proclaimed that Jensen Huang was not a national security threat. Asked if he had investigated Huang, Blanche snapped, “For what?”

Attorney General Todd Blanche : “What I will say is, yes, Nvidia is a good corporate citizen. That’s not — that shouldn’t be groundbreaking. I’m not — that’s something that — that the president has talked about, that the vice president has talked about, that everybody in leadership has talked about. And I would echo that.”

On Tuesday, President Trump told the New York Post he’s willing to pardon Jensen Huang but believes that won’t be necessary.

Meanwhile, Public Citizen called for an investigation into suspiciously timed bets on the so-called prediction market platforms Kalshi and Polymarket that Jensen Huang would be reinstated as CEO of Nvidia. That includes one account that sat idle for almost a year until mid-November, when a flurry of bets earned the trader $128,000.

A leader of India’s Cockroach movement says he was stopped by immigration officials at the Delhi airport and blocked from boarding a flight to the United Kingdom. Twenty-seven-year-old Saurav Das has been one of the main organizers with the youth-led Cockroach Janta Party. This incident comes about a month after he was detained during mass protests demanding the resignation of India’s chief election commissioner.

In related news, a new report by Human Rights Watch warns Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi and his Hindu nationalist government have systematically eroded India’s democratic freedoms, human rights and civil liberties over the past decade. The report accuses Modi of weaponizing federal and judicial agencies to target and persecute his critics.

Renowned actors and directors have rallied in support of Oscar-nominated Iranian director Jafar Panahi, who last month was sentenced in absentia by a Tehran court to five years and one month in prison. Variety reported about 200 individuals and film institutions have signed on to a letter expressing deep concern over Iran’s persecution of Panahi, but that number has now soared to nearly 2,000 signatures and counting. Signatories include Mark Ruffalo, Tilda Swinton, Michael Moore and Barry Jenkins. The Cannes Film Festival also issued a letter protesting Panahi’s prison sentence, calling “for the lifting of all restrictions that prevent him from traveling, creating and expressing himself freely.”

Spanish voters head to the polls Sunday in a snap election triggered by nationwide protests over the spiraling cost of living that erupted after the eviction of an 87-year-old from her lifelong home in Madrid. The Spanish Socialist Workers’ Party led by Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez faces challenges by the right-wing People’s Party and the far-right, anti-immigrant Vox party.

A federal judge has permanently barred the Trump administration from punishing people or organizations who share evidence with the International Criminal Court or other Palestinian rights groups sanctioned by the U.S. Monday’s ruling makes permanent a court injunction that blocked the Trump administration from potentially imposing civil or criminal liability on the groups Democracy for the Arab World Now and the Taxpayer Alliance Against Genocide. The groups sued the Trump administration in July, after an executive order threatened civil fines and up to 20 years in prison for sharing evidence with the ICC , a U.N. expert on Palestine or rights groups including the Palestinian Center for Human Rights. The court ruled the executive order was a content-based restriction on speech, in violation of the First Amendment.

The post It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand appeared first on The Intercept. Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, D-N.Y., during a press conference outside of the U.S. Capitol on Nov. 19, 2026, in Washington, D.C. Photo: Finn Gomez/Getty Images The stakes in 2028 couldn’t be higher for Democrats. Americans see the party as likely to win the White House after another two...

scraped.title: It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand
scraped.description: Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand wants to lead the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee into 2028. She’s the wrong person to meet the moment.
scraped.author: Eoin Higgins
scraped.h1: It’s Time to Ditch Kirsten Gillibrand
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

The New York senator wants to lead the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee into 2028. She’s the wrong person to meet the moment.

Eoin Higgins is the author of “Owned: How Tech Billionaires on the Right Bought the Loudest Voice on the Left.”

The stakes in 2028 couldn’t be higher for Democrats. Americans see the party as likely to win the White House after another two years of Donald Trump, especially given his historic unpopularity, and Democratic leadership will look to further expand their majorities in Congress.

How the Democratic Party selects candidates and develops strategy is going to have an outsized effect on the overall results — and the direction of the country.

After Senate Democrats elect their leader for the next two years on December 1, Chuck Schumer or Chris Van Hollen will have the opportunity to name the next head of the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee. It’s a powerful role: Whoever’s chosen will have an outsized voice in what kind of candidates run in 2028 and how much support they get.

New York Sen. Kirsten Gillibrand, a close ally of Schumer and a loyal member of the party’s pro-business wing, is making her case to remain DSCC chair for a second two-year term. On the face of it, she has a lot to commend her record: nine flipped seats in the 2026 midterms and a new majority that is likely to extend to 2030. It’s inarguable that under her leadership, the DSCC saw major gains.

Yet Gillibrand’s political instincts have, at times, threatened electoral success. Her tenure at DSCC has been marked by pushing ideological preferences, and candidate choice from her and Schumer has been a mixed bag.

While Gillibrand and the DSCC can point to real success stories like James Talarico in Texas and Mary Peltola in Alaska, they also backed Haley Stevens in Michigan, a charisma void who turned on the Democratic nominee , Abdul El-Sayed, in the last days of the race allegedly over his views on Israel.

Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect.

In Maine, the DSCC and establishment Democrats recruited Gov. Janet Mills, a 78-year-old with little interest in running, whose campaign against progressive upstart Graham Platner failed to launch . That was true even despite the many glaring deficiencies that ultimately doomed Platner’s candidacy and saw him replaced with ultimate general election winner Troy Jackson (whom Mills declined to endorse outright).

Even in cases when her instincts are right, Gillibrand struggled to exercise her influence for material effect. In Florida, left-wing Democratic Socialists of America member Angie Nixon came within 2 percentage points of winning the state’s Senate seat. Gillibrand, alongside Schumer, donated $5,000 each from their own leadership PACs and urged other senators to do the same — but couldn’t get the party overall to commit cash when it could have mattered .

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion. Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free

The Democratic Party is not a monolith bringing together moderates and progressives into a general left-of-center umbrella. There are, necessarily, compromises for those in the tent, as Third Way Democrats are in coalition with DSA members.

After a blue-wave election, it’s important for party leaders to keep both sides happy as much as possible — within reason. The current push and pull and jockeying for position is leading to some dubious assertions of success metrics that the next DSCC chair will need to keep a clear head about.

Polling decisively showed Americans want action on the economy, healthcare, and the war with Iran. Over and over again, the public has made its priorities clear about accountability: Many voters in Texas were motivated this year because of the brutality of the administration’s immigration crackdown; voters also named “corruption” as a top concern .

Given those concerns, a role in leadership for someone like Gillibrand raises questions. The senator’s coziness with the crypto industry has drawn criticism as sector heavy-hitters poured over $196,000 in campaign donations to her in 2026 alone , by far the most for a candidate or officeholder in New York state.

This summer, Gillibrand’s son, Theo, started a financial exchange at age 22. He quickly took on investments from powerful financial operatives like crypto billionaire Chris Larsen and Palmer Luckey, founder of Anduril Industries, among others.

Gillibrand has legislated in lockstep with industry interests and repeatedly publicly defended crypto —even, in 2022, analyzing the feasibility of investing retirement plans in the currency market . As The Intercept reported in July , she was a lead negotiator in the crypto industry-favored legislation known as the Clarity Act, which would have allowed Wall Street to directly invest in the currency. The bill stalled out in the Senate in September despite her best efforts .

It’s hard to see a context in which it makes sense to send the message that corruption will continue, just as long as it’s our team doing it. But with Gillibrand at the head of the DSCC, that’s exactly what voters will hear in the next election cycle. The New York senator simply isn’t the right leader for the moment.

We’re independent of corporate interests — and powered by members. Join us. Become a member Join Our Newsletter Thank You For Joining! Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept? Original reporting. Fearless journalism. Delivered to you. Will you take the next step to support our independent journalism by becoming a member of The Intercept?

By signing up, I agree to receive emails from The Intercept and to the Privacy Policy and Terms of Use .

DSCC vice chairs Adam Schiff, Lisa Blunt Rochester, and Mark Kelly seem to be the three most likely alternatives , and all bring with them their own baggage. But they can plausibly claim a break with the existing do-nothing-Dem approach aimed more at personal enrichment and out-of-touch ideological commitments than Gillibrand can.

Newly elected Democrats understand the need for change and have almost uniformly rejected calls to continue the status quo by backing stale leadership in the Senate. Whether their efforts to change the face of the party in the chamber succeed or not, first-term Democrats are going to be more attuned to the concerns and priorities of the voters who sent them to Washington.

Senate leaders should listen to them. Democrats have an opportunity to show the public they heard the change message on Election Day.

Sticking with Gillibrand won’t help get that across to voters.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?

scraped.title: Trump’s Imperialist Fantasy for Latin America Is Already Failing
scraped.description: Despite an early Trump win with the Venezuelan coup, the administration's plans to expand its influence in Colombia and Brazil have stalled.
scraped.author: Sam Carliner
scraped.h1: Trump’s Imperialist Fantasy for Latin America Is Already Failing
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

Despite Hegseth’s victory lap, Trump’s “Donroe Doctrine” may already be on life support.

Last week, self-styled Secretary of War Pete Hegseth headed to Latin America looking for love. It capped off weeks of tumult in which a desperate Hegseth and his Pentagon underlings fought a pitched battle to save his job. Despite their efforts, more than 200 members of Congress gave him a vote of no confidence , and the embattled secretary remains on the hot seat, with potential impeachment looming in 2027.

Things were different in Venezuela, which Hegseth’s military invaded earlier this year, deposing and kidnapping President Nicolás Maduro. Hegseth was feted at Miraflores Palace by Maduro’s former vice president, Delcy Rodríguez, a once outspoken anti-imperialist leftist who quickly pivoted to become America’s top quisling . “I’m very thankful for your presence here,” Rodríguez gushed, calling Hegseth “very tall and very young, with a great responsibility on his shoulders.” Acting like a satrap in what is now an American protectorate, Hegseth said that he appreciated Rodríguez’s “leadership” of a country he praised as a “compliant” partner.

Hopped up on neocolonialist fantasies, Hegseth claimed that America’s invasion on “January 3 is the day that will go down in history as a day of liberation for Venezuela.” He praised it as “the single most sophisticated military operation in the history of Latin America.” After soaking in the adulation of a leader beholden to the Trump administration, Hegseth headed off to Colombia, Ecuador, and Honduras, where he continued talking tough.

“President Trump has prioritized our hemisphere and made it clear … that we will not cede our own backyard to foreign adversaries or to transnational cartels,” he said in Ecuador, where U.S. forces are taking part in “ Operation Total Extermination .” He continued, “Together, we will never back down; we will finish this fight for our citizens and for yours.”

Today, in his inaugural post for TomDispatch, Sam Carliner examines how the U.S. is attempting to impose its will on the Western Hemisphere under the so-called Donroe Doctrine. So far, the Trump administration has wreaked endless amounts of havoc and scored what it thinks are victories in Latin America. But Carliner points out that countervailing forces are rising across the region. One day, we may look back on Hegseth’s viceroy victory lap as the high point of the Trump administration’s gunboat diplomacy — and on Carliner’s analysis as one of the first to lay out what led to its downfall.

—Nick Turse, editor of TomDispatch

It would have been unimaginable for the United States and longtime U.S. adversary, Venezuela, to enter into a military alliance just one year ago. But that’s exactly what U.S. “Secretary of War” Pete Hegseth announced from its capital, Caracas, on November 18, as part of a surprise meeting with Venezuela’s acting president, Delcy Rodríguez.

The new military agreement — which will include joint training, intelligence sharing, and defense equipment capabilities — and an oil deal signed in August, which even Bloomberg has called a reprise of the industry’s “neocolonial past,” is the most significant achievement of President Donald Trump’s aggressive “Donroe Doctrine” to strengthen U.S. control over Latin America. “In the last year, the country that previously sent its oil wealth to Cuba or to China, from rigs built by Venezuelans and Americans, has now signed a historic oil deal with the United States, through the Department of War,” Hegseth boasted at a press conference last week.

That same day, however, the New York Times reported that Colombia rejected a plan to conduct joint military operations with the United States. This led Hegseth to cut a visit to Colombia short; he had originally planned to discuss military cooperation with the country’s new right-wing president, Abelardo de la Espriella. Both he and Hegseth took to X deny the Times’s claims. But de la Espriella, who campaigned by aligning himself with the Trump administration and calling for military action against drug cartels and gangs, did not have sufficient support in Colombia’s Congress to ink a military agreement with the United States that would have allowed U.S. troops to conduct counter-cartel operations inside Colombia.

The military agreement with Venezuela and the lack of one in Colombia showcase the contradictions of the Trump administration’s aggressive Latin America policy. On the one hand, the administration has greatly expanded operations in the Western Hemisphere over the past year. But a recent series of setbacks, of which Colombia’s snub is only the latest, show the limits of U.S. power projection even in a region it has treated as its backyard for hundreds of years.

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion. Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free

One year ago this month, the Trump administration published its National Security Strategy , which candidly advocated for a “Trump Corollary” to the Monroe Doctrine, invoking the policy that the United States historically used to treat Latin America and the Caribbean as the country’s exclusive sphere of influence. Just two months after releasing the NSS, on January 3, the administration carried out a coup in Venezuela , which removed its president, Nicolás Maduro, from power. A U.S. strike in southern Venezuela in June reportedly killed a leader of the Tren de Aragua gang. And last month, U.S. aircraft attacked a camp of supposed Colombian guerrillas operating inside Venezuela, killing more than two dozen people.

With the cooperation of remaining regime officials, headed by Rodríguez, U.S. Secretary of State Marco Rubio has also effectively dictated significant shifts in Venezuelan domestic and economic policy, including the oil deal which gives the United States a direct stake in more than 17 strategic oil fields and the resumption of U.S. embassy operations in Caracas.

Rubio’s influence over Venezuelan policy also enabled him to escalate an economic offensive against Cuba, which has long been a target of Rubio’s staunch anti-communist crusade. Venezuela had been Cuba’s largest oil supplier, but after the coup, Venezuela quickly cut off its supply of fuel to the island nation. The Trump administration then threatened tariffs against any country that sold oil to Cuba. By February, the United Nations was warning that Cuba faced “humanitarian collapse” from the embargo. Trump officials have also repeatedly threatened to carry out regime change on the island. As recently as November 13, Trump told reporters : “I want to get Cuba done before I leave you.”

Since last September, the United States has also conducted scores of attacks on supposed drug boats in the Caribbean Sea and Pacific Ocean. By alleging that these boats are suspected of “narco-trafficking,” the Trump administration has carried out lawless operations that have killed more than 240 civilians.

The administration had even bigger plans for Latin America. The NSS envisioned a region run by subservient governments willing to play their part in advancing policies favorable to U.S. interests. As the document put it:

Our goals for the Western Hemisphere can be summarized as “Enlist and Expand.” We will enlist established friends in the Hemisphere to control migration, stop drug flows, and strengthen stability and security on land and sea. We will expand by cultivating and strengthening new partners while bolstering our own nation’s appeal as the Hemisphere’s economic and security partner of choice.

Shifts in the region would favor this policy, with recent Latin American elections bringing U.S.-aligned, right-wing leaders to power in several countries that had previously been governed by left-wing administrations. Bolivia, Chile, and Honduras elected right-wing heads of state in 2025, followed by Costa Rica, Colombia, and Peru this year. These new governments joined staunch Trump allies Javier Milei in Argentina, Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, and Daniel Noboa in Ecuador.

On March 7, 2026, Trump and Rubio brought 13 of these allies together at a summit of Shield of the Americas , a multinational security initiative created by the administration earlier this year. The main result of the summit was the creation of the Americas Counter Cartel Coalition , which Trump described as “a pledge from military leaders and representatives from 17 countries demonstrating that the region is ready to operationalize hard power to defeat these threats [cartels and terrorists] to our security and civilization.” At an October meeting, the coalition (which has grown to 19 countries) “committed to expand information sharing, increase bilateral and multilateral cooperation, and conduct combined operations that deter and dismantle those networks, secure borders and critical infrastructure, and protect law-abiding citizens,” according to a U.S. Southern Command press release .

Under Noboa, Ecuador has been at the forefront of advancing U.S. military operations in Latin America, offering a glimpse of what might be in store as the United States seeks to expand military cooperation across the region.

In March, U.S. Special Operations forces began joint operations with Ecuador’s military against alleged drug cartel facilities. The partnership was established despite a referendum in Ecuador which saw voters overwhelmingly reject a proposal to host a U.S. military base. A New York Times investigation found that at least one of the facilities targeted in these joint operations was a civilian dairy farm. A Human Rights Watch report — based on extensive interviews and analysis of data including satellite imagery, judicial documents, and medical records — found three separate incidents implicating the U.S.–Ecuador security partnership in subjecting civilians to torture, drone strikes, and arbitrary detention. The report argues:

From a human rights perspective, this partnership is a perilous one. The two countries’ security relationship is deepening at a moment when both governments have engaged in serious human rights violations fueled by their insistence on framing their confrontations with organized crime groups as a kind of war.

On November 6, Rep. Jesús “Chuy” García and 12 other members of Congress sent a letter to Rubio urging him to suspend military assistance to Noboa, noting “Ecuador has seen the repression of opposition actors across the political spectrum, attacks on judicial independence, and restrictions on the freedom of the press.” This week, the New York Times reported the Trump administration paused joint military operations in October due to concerns about possible human rights violations committed by Ecuadorean forces during a September operation.

While the plans to expand military cooperation in Colombia suffered a setback, the Colombian and U.S. militaries have nonetheless made efforts to deepen their relationship. This month, 350 U.S. military personnel were in Colombia training alongside 400 local troops as part of a military exercise dubbed Southern Vanguard 2027. Panama and Honduras have also hosted training exercises with U.S. troops in the past year.

A recent U.S. Army press release also announced that U.S. and Colombian military leaders met for bilateral discussions about the two countries’ partnership. Even under left-wing President Gustavo Petro , who was a vocal critic of Trump and the war on drugs, U.S. military personnel were deployed to Colombia and the two countries shared intelligence.

Historically, U.S. military partnerships with Latin American leaders have been linked to human rights abuses, including the Guatemalan military’s massacre of Indigenous Maya civilians during the country’s 36-year-long civil war, and Peru’s government, under the 10-year rule of Alberto Fujimori, carrying out forced disappearances of dissidents. Considering the civilian toll of the administration’s boat strike campaign, as well as the abuses being carried out in Ecuador, it is likely that the Donroe Doctrine will lead to further human rights violations.

The administration has also increasingly meddled in the political affairs, and even the sovereignty, of various Latin American countries, including conditioning a $20 billion bailout of Argentina’s economy on the success of Milei’s party in the country’s legislative elections, pressuring Bolivia’s government to arrest its own attorney general and other officials who were investigating a Trump-friendly political strategist, and attempting to sway Brazil’s presidential election in favor of Trump ally Flávio Bolsonaro.

Read Our Complete Coverage

Despite the seemingly unrestrained advance of the Donroe Doctrine this past year, Trump’s influence over the region is already teetering. Even before Colombia rejected deeper cooperation, Trump had encountered several other key setbacks across Latin America.

Despite Trump’s efforts to sway Brazil’s presidential elections in October, incumbent President Luiz Inacio Lula Da Silva pulled off a stunning defeat of Bolsonaro, securing another term leading the largest country in Latin America . Bolsonaro’s loss, bolstered in no small part by the Brazilian public’s outrage at U.S. interference, dashed the Trump administration’s hopes of having an entirely subservient ally at the head of the largest and most politically influential country in Latin America.

This month, outrage over a banking scandal in Paraguay led to the impeachment of Trump-aligned President Santiago Peña. In Chile, right-wing President José Antonio Kast’s approval rating has plunged to new lows after just eight months in office. And in Argentina, where Milei, one of Trump’s most subordinate allies, has been carrying out sweeping neoliberal reforms, the country appears to be entering a recession just ahead of next year’s presidential election.

This year has also seen significant protests and increased left-wing activism challenge the region’s right-wing governments. In May, a peasant-led rebellion in Bolivia over austerity and government ties to the Trump administration brought the country to a standstill for over a month. President Rodrigo Paz has since enacted a state of emergency, enabling him to use the military and police to suppress dissent. Despite this, Bolivian teachers launched a strike last month over efforts by the government to privatize education. In Chile, the country’s student movement has held several national days of protests, facing off against police armed with tear gas and water cannons. Recently, Chilean truckers also entered the fray, setting up roadblocks to protest fuel price hikes.

In Argentina, Trotskyist congresswoman Myriam Bregman has rapidly grown in popularity. Recent polling has shown that Bregman, a vocal critic of Milei and U.S. influence in Argentina, now has the highest favorability rating of any political figure in the country, foreshadowing an electoral environment in which the far left is becoming a serious contender against the right and the country’s more mainstream Peronist opposition. All these trends further signal a landscape less conducive to Trump’s agenda of continued U.S. intervention.

This surge of left-wing populism across Latin America doesn’t mean that the administration will cease aggressive interventions in the region. Trump’s appointment of Stephen Miller as his new chief of staff may signal the opposite. Miller was highly involved in planning the coup in Venezuela and the boat strike campaign. But following the Republican Party’s historic defeats in the U.S. midterm elections , the administration will have to contend with a new Congress elected by a public that is souring on constant military interventions. Hegseth, competing with Miller in his zeal for employing military terror in the region, has already become the target of an impeachment effort which is likely to carry over into the next legislative term.

As the Iran war has shown, military might alone is not enough to make countries, let alone entire regions, submit to U.S. dictates. The Trump administration may well continue its efforts to revive the Monroe Doctrine, but the long history of U.S. intervention in Latin America is also a history of the region’s people defending their sovereignty from U.S. empire and local quislings. This year has been another chapter in that history.

“To the narco-terrorists who have used this as a safe haven, your time is up. We will hunt you down. We will find you. And we will kill you,” Hegseth announced last week in Caracas. He also passed along a “greeting” from Trump to Rodríguez and lauded the puppet-president who has consistently met Washington’s demands. Standing outside the U.S. Embassy, Hegseth praised Venezuela’s transformation from an enemy to a “compliant security partner.” But repeating the success in Venezuela may prove to be very difficult.

Update: November 25, 2026, 11:58 a.m. ET The article was updated to include recent New York Times reporting that the Trump administration paused joint military operations with Ecuador in October, due to concerns about possible human rights violations.

IT’S EVEN WORSE THAN WE THOUGHT.

What we’re seeing right now from Donald Trump is a full-on authoritarian takeover of the U.S. government.

This is not hyperbole.

Court orders are being ignored. MAGA loyalists have been put in charge of the military and federal law enforcement agencies. The Department of Government Efficiency has stripped Congress of its power of the purse. News outlets that challenge Trump have been banished or put under investigation.

Yet far too many are still covering Trump’s assault on democracy like politics as usual, with flattering headlines describing Trump as “unconventional,” “testing the boundaries,” and “aggressively flexing power.”

The Intercept has long covered authoritarian governments, billionaire oligarchs, and backsliding democracies around the world. We understand the challenge we face in Trump and the vital importance of press freedom in defending democracy.

IT’S BEEN A DEVASTATING year for journalism — the worst in modern U.S. history.

We have a president with utter contempt for truth aggressively using the government’s full powers to dismantle the free press. Corporate news outlets have cowered, becoming accessories in Trump’s project to create a post-truth America. Right-wing billionaires have pounced, buying up media organizations and rebuilding the information environment to their liking.

In this most perilous moment for democracy, The Intercept is fighting back. But to do so effectively, we need to grow.

That’s where you come in. Will you help us expand our reporting capacity in time to hit the ground running in 2026?
