scraped.description: A federal judge opened the discovery phase in The Intercept’s lawsuit over Trump’s scheme to enrich himself by selling early access to his posts.
scraped.author: Jessica Washington
scraped.h1: Court Orders Trump Media to Hand Over Truth Social Records in The Intercept Lawsuit
scraped.body_text:
© THE INTERCEPT

ALL RIGHTS RESERVED

A federal judge opened the discovery phase in The Intercept’s lawsuit over the president’s scheme to enrich himself by selling early access to his posts.

The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation won a crucial victory against the Trump administration in court on Tuesday in a case challenging the president’s right to sell early access to his social media posts on Truth Social.

The ruling by Judge J. Paul Oetken in the Southern District of New York allows both organizations to seek limited discovery, offering a chance to peel back the layers on the president’s scheme to enrich himself through his public office. The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation can request records from the president’s private media company on both the operation of its six-figure early-access model and whether other media companies have purchased a subscription.

Truth Social is owned and operated by Trump Media & Technology Group, a company in which the president holds the largest stake in a trust controlled by his son, Donald Trump Jr. The early-access model, known as Truth API, requires subscribers to pay $60,000 to $100,000 a month. The service offers a first look at Trump’s posts — where, as the White House has acknowledged , he often makes official policy announcements.

Most Read An Air Force Major Is Being Held in Solitary Confinement for Criticizing Trump on CNN Seth Stern ICE Spreads Misinformation About Securing Your iPhone. Here’s How to Really Do It. Noah Hurowitz, Nikita Mazurov, Karl Loftus Private Prison Told ICE Its Jail Was Worth $67 Million. ICE Bought It for Nearly Half a Billion. Jacqueline Stevens, Andrew Free

The lawsuit argues that the premium service violates the First Amendment rights of the public and the media to enjoy equal access to official government information. According to the lawsuit, Trump has published about 11,000 posts or reposts on Truth Social since returning to office.

The ruling will allow the plaintiffs “to get some answers about how this scheme works,” said Nikhel Sus, chief counsel at Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, who is representing the plaintiffs. The subscription service, he added, was “rolled out with minimal transparency as to how the actual functionality works and who has been subscribing to the service thus far.”

In October, The Intercept and Freedom of the Press Foundation requested a preliminary injunction arguing that the president should be barred from posting on his personal platform, Truth Social, as long as the premium service is in effect.

Oetken has not ruled on the preliminary injunction. But his decision on Tuesday is a “positive step forward,” Sus said. “The court didn’t explicitly say that it thinks our claims have merit, but the fact that it ordered discovery, we think, indicates that the court doesn’t think our complaint is non-meritorious because otherwise it wouldn’t have granted discovery.”

scraped.title: Grand Theft Auto Grew Up. America Didn’t.
scraped.description: The United States under Donald Trump has turned into a parody of itself, descending further and further into juvenilia. Grand Theft Auto VI, meanwhile, has turned more darkly serious and morally complex.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

The United States under Donald Trump has turned into a parody of itself, descending further and further into juvenilia. Grand Theft Auto VI , meanwhile, has turned more darkly serious and morally complex.

In Grand Theft Auto VI , the city is no longer a collection of victims waiting for you to beat up or exploit them. It’s a collection of people with their own short fuses — many of them as broke, frightened, and intoxicated as you are. (Rockstar Games)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

E arly in Grand Theft Auto VI , you and your girlfriend drive to the local branch of Fleeca bank on an errand that, by the franchise’s standards, is something of a novelty. Your job is not to rob a bank but to open an account at one.

Lucia Caminos, fresh out of prison, needs somewhere to deposit her check from her mandatory reentry job, and since her boyfriend, Jason Duval, has made it this far in life without a checking account, they’d like to open one. But after a quick financial review, the manager wonders whether they’ve considered maybe downloading an app instead, and you leave empty-handed.

There are any number of teenagers who could, with a few shakes of a PlayStation 5 controller, get these two out of a police pursuit and across three counties of South Florida without putting a scratch on the car. None, however, can get Jason approved for a checking account. As in real life, the credit score — not brute force or cunning — is the god of this universe.

It’s a telling moment, because the Grand Theft Auto (GTA) that I grew up with was two things at once. It was an adolescent male power fantasy, a sandbox where you could steal a sports car, mow down a crowd, and outrun the police with no lasting consequence beyond a few hundred dollars docked from your wallet. And it was a South Park –style satire of American life, all fake radio ads for penis pills and televangelists and talk-radio cranks. The jokes were broad, and the violence was cartoonish, and the upshot was that nothing meant anything, so everything was permitted. GTA III let you hire a prostitute and beat her to get your money back. GTA V let you torture a man with a car battery and then play golf. It all had a weightless quality.

Yet in the thirteen years since Grand Theft Auto V came out, something peculiar has happened: Rockstar, the studio that produces the game, and its subject have switched places. The United States has turned into a parody of itself, while GTA VI has turned more darkly serious. It plays less like a theme park and more like prestige television, something like HBO’s The Wire or Task crossed with It’s Florida, Man .

In VI , you alternate between the two leads: Jason Duval, an Army veteran doing errands for drug runners, and Lucia Caminos, his girlfriend and partner in crime, recently out of prison. Their relationship is the spine of the game, and a score is kept. If Jason behaves like a sociopath, Lucia notices. Push it far enough, and the game will decide you are, in its own words, “Irredeemable,” and you will be saddled with the suboptimal happy-never-after ending.

P erhaps even the idea of a happy ending is laughable. Jason and Lucia are not mafia dons or retired bank robbers in shiny new Miami mansions; they are among South Florida’s ever-growing lumpenproletariat, Karl Marx’s term for the drifting, disorganized underclass that sits below the working class and outside its institutions. They’re the deinstitutionalized, dealigned masses who hold no union card, no pension, no political loyalty, and often no permanent address. Together they must navigate the gig-work and shadow economy with one hand on their guns and one eye over their shoulders for a probation officer who could help take their young son away from them forever into the foster care system.

So, yes, you can still be a monster, and there are plenty of mindless action sequences and shoot-outs. But they’re tempered by real-world obligations (your son’s crib isn’t going to build itself) and the moral weight of your misdeeds.

Likewise, the world of Leonida, Rockstar’s faux Florida, is much more than a virtual crime laboratory. For twenty-five years, GTA’s pedestrians were furniture with legs. They walked, they screamed, they died. In GTA VI , if you accidentally bump into a man outside a gas station, he’ll square up and may throw a punch. Cut someone off on the highway, and they’ll chase you down in their own bout of road rage. Try to make small talk with a stranger, and there’s a decent chance she’ll tell you to go to hell — or worse — because in a place like this, hardly anyone talks to strangers.

The city is no longer a collection of victims waiting for you to beat up or exploit them. It’s a collection of people with their own short fuses, and many of them are as broke, as frightened, and as intoxicated as you are.

Because the city seems to have a soul, however shrunken, it’s striking what isn’t in Leonida. There are no churches, an observation by British critic Peter Hitchens, who once called GTA the Devil’s Bible. There are also no schools, no community centers, no food pantries, no nonprofits. To be fair to Rockstar, there were never caring institutions of any kind in Grand Theft Auto ; the series has always been a portrait of America with the heart surgically removed. But in the older games, the absence read as a joke, a deliberate cartoon of a godless consumer wasteland.

Here, in a world rendered with photographic fidelity, that absence feels like a statement. Every building you can enter exists to extract something from you — your money, your labor, your time. Pawnshops, payday lenders, strip clubs, car washes that launder cash. The only god in Leonida is the market, and you are a free agent navigating its moods, which are capricious and rarely in your favor.

For half a century, Florida has been where America goes to see its own fever dreams, from glamorous to gonzo. In the 1980s, it was cocaine-cowboy Miami: Scarface and Miami Vice , pastels and shoulder holsters, an image so seductive that Rockstar lifted it wholesale for Vice City in 2002. Later came Carl Hiaasen’s crooked developers and his hit man with a Weed Eater for a hand, Tom Wolfe’s Back to Blood , Harmony Korine’s Spring Breakers , the “Florida Man” headline construction, and Tiger King . From high culture to low, it all seemed insane and fun.

Not here. There were stretches early on when GTA VI made me queasy. Rockstar doesn’t open with the postcard Florida of South Beach sunsets or champagne-soaked nightlife, but with the ugly, uncinematic Florida: trash-strewn trailer parks, run-down motels with hourly rates, drug dealers too strung out to count their own money, and skeezy strip club owners who talk to Lucia like she could be part of the inventory. It’s Sean Baker’s The Florida Project , minus the Magic Kingdom glowing on the horizon. I’ve played every GTA since the series went 3D, and this is the first one in which I occasionally wanted a shower, as if the scum from the swamps I was wading through had rubbed off on me.

W e’re at a strange moment in the culture wars. In 2026, the people defending Grand Theft Auto VI ’s honor are largely progressives — even though one of its leads is a violent white man devoted to his straight, monogamous relationship — while it’s MAGA types who seem to want more anarchy and amorality in their games.

For a quarter-century, hating on Grand Theft Auto was one of the few things Washington could agree on. In 2005, Hillary Clinton demanded a federal investigation after the Hot Coffee scandal in GTA: San Andreas . After Sandy Hook, Joe Biden called video game executives in for a meeting. In 2018, after Parkland, Donald Trump held his own meeting: “The video games, the movies, the internet stuff is so violent. It’s so incredible,” he said. A year later, after El Paso, he blamed “gruesome and grisly video games” for glorifying violence.

Blaming Rockstar Games was once the bipartisan comfort food of American politics: cheap, filling, and nobody ever had to touch a gun law.

So you’d expect Grand Theft Auto VI , the biggest entertainment launch of the decade, to set off the mother of all moral panics. The timing could hardly be better: Republicans were just routed in the midterms and lost both chambers of Congress. Why not change the subject to a video game where you can rob a liquor store in a neon-soaked Florida?

Instead, we’ve mostly heard crickets, with a couple of notable outliers. Tennessee Congressman Tim Burchett told TMZ the game is “more of a how-to video” for stealing cars and shooting cops and said those who let their kids play it are bad parents. But he immediately added, “We’re not going to legislate it.” On Fox & Friends Weekend , Rachel Campos-Duffy said she was “gonna push back a little,” because she didn’t think the game was good for our culture and asked whether Lucia, one of the coprotagonists, was “the hooker.” (Surprise: sex workers are gone from this version.) Fox News Digital’s big GTA story last week was about the dangers of sleep deprivation from playing games all night.

Liberals? They gave up the video game hate beat years ago. Since the Gamergate wars of the 2010s, progressive game criticism has mostly asked who gets to be the hero and how women are depicted. How many cops you can run over hasn’t been the question, and a game with a Latina colead has largely inoculated itself on that front.

So why has the Right gone soft? Perhaps because the Trump White House is like a parody that Rockstar’s writers’ room would have rejected in 2013 for being too on the nose.

The day before GTA VI launched, the official White House account posted a montage of Donald Trump striding past fighter jets, rendered in the game’s signature font, set to Dire Straits’ “Money for Nothing” and captioned “WELCOME TO MAGA CITY XLVII.” This wasn’t shocking, because for more than a year the White House’s social media team has embraced a strategy of appealing to gamer bros.

Consider the back catalog. In September 2025, the account cut footage of Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) arrests to the Pokémon cartoon’s opening theme, then closed on fake trading cards bearing detainees’ faces under the tagline “Gotta Catch ’Em All.” When the bombs started falling on Iran in March, the White House opened its war montage with a Call of Duty killstreak animation, as if the strikes were a reward for thirty kills without dying. Then, in September this year, came Arcade.gov, a set of retro browser games in which you can build the wall and deport people.

The Pokémon Company objected; Halo ’s cocreator said a Halo -themed ICE recruitment post made him sick. The White House’s response? More or less its mission statement : “Nowhere in the Constitution does it say we can’t post banger memes.”

That line tracks with an administration that has governed as if life were a nihilistic M-rated game, with the president living out an adolescent male power fantasy: parading young blonde female aides on his arms, staging an Ultimate Fighting Championship fight card on the South Lawn for his eightieth birthday, and floating Nicki Minaj as press secretary after the previous one lasted five days in the job. Alligator Alcatraz might sound like a sick joke from GTA , but indeed, it was all too real: a dehumanizing makeshift immigration detention center in the Florida Everglades, complete with Florida Republicans selling branded merch to chuds.

Even outside of Mar-a-Lago, there are signs everywhere that America has hit a midlife crisis, descending into juvenilia — or, worse yet, psychosis. Grown men trade cartoon apes or dogs on the blockchain and lose their savings, while Hunter Biden gets in on the action with a $LAPTOP coin; bets on Jesus Christ returning for the Rapture in 2026 on Polymarket turn out to be a better wager. Even Las Vegas is dying, because everywhere in America is becoming like Las Vegas, a casino and a vape pen in every pocket.

One of our nation’s biggest young celebrities, sadly, is Clavicular , a twenty-year-old famous for smashing his own face with a hammer to “improve” his bone structure. Out on bail for rape charges, which he denies, stemming from an alleged assault shortly after a live stream, he’s complained about GTA VI being too “cucked” because it wants you to be kind to your virtual girlfriend.

The politicians and pundits worried about GTA corrupting America have it the wrong way around. These days, the game is the one that should worry about being corrupted by us.

Ryan Zickgraf is a journalist based in Harrisburg, Pennsylvania.

scraped.title: Charles Koch Has a Dystopian Plan for How to Control Workers
scraped.description: Ultraconservative billionaire Charles Koch likes to style himself as a champion of individual liberty. But his phony science of workplace management created an atmosphere that Koch’s workers compared to living in a totalitarian state.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Ultraconservative billionaire Charles Koch likes to style himself as a champion of individual liberty. But his phony science of workplace management created an atmosphere that Koch’s workers compared to living in a totalitarian state.

Billionaire Charles Koch created a system for controlling his workers that he called Market-Based Management (MBM). Koch’s employees compared the experience of MBM to life in George Orwell’s 1984 . (Patrick T. Fallon for The Washington Post / Getty Images)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

A t a conference in Orlando, Florida, in 2005, the American billionaire Charles Koch gave a speech explaining how he and his audience could protect “freedom and prosperity in the world.” While accepting an award named after potato chip magnate Herman Lay, Koch explained that he had conceived a “science of liberty,” which he described as “the study and practice of sustainably advancing liberty to create prosperity and social progress.”

The solution lay, Koch said, in economic analysis — treating every interaction between people as a market exchange. He claimed this “Market Process Analysis” helped him build not only his fortune but also his family life and interpersonal interactions.

Out of it, he created what he called Market-Based Management (MBM), a theory for managing workers and his business. The science of liberty he outlined in Orlando applied those same principles to government — in America and around the world.

W orkers at Charles Koch’s web of companies felt differently. One anonymous Koch employee in Wichita wrote that their colleagues were “walking around like they are in the George Orwell book, ‘ 1984 ,’” terrified of the Koch family, the “only major employer in the area,” who used their power “to control the employees and their movement within the other Koch entities.”

Another, in Atlanta, called Koch’s extensive training in MBM “brainwashing.” The atmosphere, others reported, was “cult-like,” and employees were “noticeably unhappy,” with fifty-hour workweeks as well as mandatory overtime and weekend work. A software engineer in Bangalore wrote that at Koch’s companies “managers are GOD. . . . They can play with anyone’s life.”

Some of these disgruntled employees, hoping to convince management to change their ways, insisted they were not “practicing what they preached” — that MBM’s values were good and simply being misapplied. But Charles Koch had worked on the system for decades.

He personally cultivated its materials, and his company forced employees to study them for upward of five hours a week, according to one review. Some of the values in Koch’s system of MBM were simply anodyne — “respect” is its ninth “guiding principle.” But the underlying purpose of the philosophy was to extract maximum profit from employees.

T he science of liberty seemed more like a science of control. Koch’s “science” relied on four connected claims about human behavior that structure economic and political life across the globe today.

First, that we should analyze society as merely a collection of individuals, an idea known as methodological individualism. Second, the claim that individuals are motivated only by self-interest, generally though not exclusively in the form of material incentives — or psychological egoism.

Third, an insistence that deliberate planning cannot be trusted: humans are too selfish, and too limited, to make or execute grand plans for society. We should trust the competitive evolution of markets over the cooperative intention of democracy.

And fourth, the belief that everything is — and should be — a market. The world consists of competing individuals, and social science exists to figure out how to structure that competition so prosperity arises out of it. This paradigm is known as market fundamentalism.

Proponents of these ideas present them as inescapable truths about the world, like gravity. If we know how human beings will act, there is no need to speak of how they should act. Thus, “there is no alternative,” as the Victorian philosopher Herbert Spencer put it, to these cruel calculations: they are an inescapable truth about human action.

B ut these ideas are not scientific truths that experts have discovered. They are political visions that ideologues have created. There are other ways we can live and work, and generally most people prefer those alternatives when asked and frequently pursue them when we are not.

From Samuel Bentham’s program of mechanized and precarious shipbuilding labor to Frederick Winslow Taylor’s floundering efforts to optimize pig iron loading, supposedly optimal methods for manipulating workers have generally failed — until their architects relied on political and economic force to impose their ideas anyway.

Four hundred years of elite scheming have failed to produce either the technocratic control that utilitarians like the Benthams wanted or the pure competition advocated by market radicals like Ludwig von Mises. Every country in the world, even those with little or no political freedom, has major movements that demand better. Those movements do not always win. But every victory builds a foundation for the next.

Today we have labor rights, voting power, and political freedoms — where we have them — because of the hard work of those who came before us. Building on their legacy, we can continue to make a better world now and to create conditions for yet more advances after we are gone.

Control science is not “human nature.” It is not “how the world works.” It is not just orthodox economics or economic common sense or advanced political discourse. Identifying the different intertwining strands that give control science its strength and naming the total result, helps us take it on. Labeling control science — and labeling it accurately as a matter of control — is all the more important because of how it works.

T he irony of control science is that it is ultimately not a theory of control by anyone at all. Control science respects no kings, no presidents, and no gods but what one of Herbert Spencer’s followers called “that awful One to whom it is profanity to pray.” This is an ideology for control by no one, of everyone. Its advocates call this freedom.

The science of control is an attempt at rule without rulers, an abstract authoritarianism, an art of excuses: centuries of elites finding themselves in positions of power and scrambling to justify that power to themselves and the world. This vast program of institutionalized apathy has been developed through, and always relies on, the forceful control of workers themselves.

Identifying this program does two things for us. First, it makes clear that cynical claims about “human nature” are social and political constructions, not an objective truth discovered by capitalists. Second, then, this intellectual history of economic thought reveals how much it has always been about control of us, not by us. We can rally against it accordingly: control science is fake, and it is wrong.

Ideas alone will not be enough, of course. Control science has succeeded by embedding itself in the legal, political, and economic structures of the world around us. It does not describe actual human nature, but it does describe how many people do, and must, act, precisely because of the way capitalists have made the world.

Selfishness is embedded in the real material relations we have with each other: the most responsible strategies for investing, for example, may include investments in oil companies. The cheapest products are produced under the worst labor conditions. Buying better or investing differently as an individual will accomplish little, and it is difficult to build collective movements around doing something that makes us, temporarily, worse off, in a world of economic scarcity and against constant competition by the preachers of selfishness.

We cannot defeat control science as individual consumers. But we can as workers, as voters, and as full human beings. Over the last four centuries, many of the greatest victories for justice, equality, and freedom have relied on mass movements of working people, from the revolutions of the eighteenth century to the New Deal and decolonization in the twentieth century.

T he twenty-first century has been, in much of the world, a period of defeat and retreat for working-class left-wing politics. But it does not have to be that way. The science of control was made in the workplace. It can be unmade there as well. Labor organizing forces idealistic progressives to ground our projects in material incentives: better wages, improved working conditions, more free time.

This is particularly necessary in the cynical world control science has made. We have been told that everyone is selfish and that an alternative world is impossible. This makes it all the more difficult to believe rousing appeals to empathy and ethics alone. Organizing within workplaces must become part of a broader movement for democracy and equality at work — control by workers, not of them.

Most of us recoil at the idea of an absolute monarch or a dictator. Yet we spend a good portion of our days, and our lives, doing the bidding of bosses over whom we have little power. We should abhor authoritarian company “presidents” and company boards the way we do dictatorship and monarchy. Working people should wield power through robust and assertive democratic unions to force our bosses to take our needs and desires and dreams into account.

A powerful labor movement alone will not end the science of control. And an economy of competing democratic cooperatives would still be one driven by markets and competition. Thus, we also need to aim for democratic control of the economy writ large. Human needs and collective desires, not the movement of markets, should determine what we make and do.

A market is a forever skewed democracy: your voting power is proportional to your wealth, and the most exploitative actors are therefore the most powerful. We should find this an offense against democracy, and we should act accordingly. Rule by market rules has only succeeded in leading us to a world that satisfies no one.

Mass working-class movements, wielding the power of democracy, can build an intentional and deliberate world that reflects our most meaningful and deeply held collective wants, democratically aggregated, rather than our individual purchasing choices, scaled by our wealth. We can build our moral principles and our material needs into the legal structure, social fabric, and collective ideals of our societies so that acting in the common good, instead of against it, becomes easier and more obvious every day.

W e know collective effort can outcompete nihilist competition, because it has done so before: an imperfect fraction of this program of economic democracy saved the world from fascism. Imagine what a full-fledged collective program could do for living standards, economic growth, and climate change.

Through public housing authorities, we can determine where housing is built and how much it costs based on our need for comfortable homes, instead of the political demand to keep housing prices up for those already locked into an expensive mortgage. With utility nationalization, we can replace hated telecommunications monopolies with less expensive, more functional infrastructure that we control.

All of this requires no promises of or belief in a socialist utopia (though it will help us move toward one). Right now, it is right-wing economics that is in the way of lower rent, higher wages, shorter hours, full employment, and economic dignity, for all of us. If we take control of our work and our lives, we can secure a better life together.

This is an extract from Control Science: How Management Made the Modern World , now available from Verso Books.

Henry Snow is a labor historian based in Connecticut. Their book Control Science will be published by Verso Books in May 2026. They write the newsletter Another Way .

scraped.title: Pregnant Workers Say Amazon Is Violating Their Rights
scraped.description: Amazon now faces a class-action lawsuit on behalf of its pregnant workers, many of whom say their rights to accommodation have been violated. They describe a pattern of being refused chairs, additional bathroom breaks, and relief from strenuous work.
scraped.h1: Jacobin
scraped.body_text:
Login

Get an introductory Jacobin subscription for just $20

Amazon now faces a class-action lawsuit on behalf of its pregnant workers, many of whom say their rights to accommodation have been violated. They describe a pattern of being refused chairs, additional bathroom breaks, and relief from strenuous work.

Pregnant workers at Amazon describe a pattern of being refused timely accommodations so that they are forced to work as normal or take unpaid leave, which rapidly runs out. They are then fired for “job abandonment.” (Leon Neal / Getty Images)

Our winter issue is out soon. Subscribe today to get your copy in our first mailing.

W illamina Barclay was working as a picker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rochester, New York, when she felt lightheaded again. “She pleaded with a manager for a seat. . . . He refused: ‘No, because you don’t have a [pregnancy] accommodation. If I give you a chair, I have to give everybody else a chair,’” he said, according to a recent lawsuit.

But Barclay, who learned she was pregnant in March 2025, had already asked managers many times for accommodations — a seat, extra breaks to drink, eat, pee (or throw up) in the bathroom, no ladder-climbing or squatting, and no heavy lifting.

Amazon — a company known for fast delivery — had failed to answer for weeks, demanding medical documentation. Even after Barclay provided it, Amazon still refused most accommodations, permitting her four breaks a day but no chair. She was moved to a different position but still required to lift heavy packages.

Amazon counted her new breaks against her unpaid time off (UPT), a leave bank that workers accumulate at five minutes per hour and that maxes out at eighty hours. She went to Human Resources several times to try to rectify the situation but stopped, because they were also counting those visits as UPT, the lawsuit says.

The heavy lifting led to sharp pains. At one point she left the warehouse in a wheelchair headed for the hospital. Amazon also counted that time against her unpaid leave bank. On another occasion, she had to leave due to uncontrolled vomiting. Despite a doctor’s note, that was also counted against her. Her UPT thus used up; Amazon fired her.

Under the law, workers cannot be penalized for taking pregnancy-related leave.

Barclay’s ordeal is detailed in a lawsuit filed September 8 by A Better Balance , a nonprofit focused on work policies affecting families. It’s a proposed class action on behalf of all US workers whose rights under the Pregnant Workers Fairness Act (PWFA) have been violated by Amazon.

B arclay’s harrowing experience is common, said Sultana Hossain, recording secretary of the Amazon Labor Union (ALU) on Staten Island: Under the law, “pregnant workers don’t have to give in paperwork,” she said. “They only have to verbally say, ‘I’m pregnant and I need to be accommodated.’ But we’re seeing Amazon systemically violate that.

“Even if workers get an accommodation eventually, it can take several weeks,” said Hossain. “So people really don’t have any choice but to keep working in their regular role, which is really dangerous if they actually need an accommodation.”

Key’Asia, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center near Wilmington, Delaware, said that Amazon management twice rejected a note from her doctor, once because it had an e-signature, and then again when she got an ink signature. (For privacy to discuss medical matters, some workers asked that last names not be used.)

Managers said the signature looked fraudulent and still refused to accommodate her pregnancy, Key’Asia said. “They are making you do the things that your doctor told you that you’re not supposed to be doing,” she told attendees at an online Jobs With Justice event in October. “They’re making you do things that are putting yourself and your baby at risk.” She said Amazon fired her twice, both times when she was pregnant.

W orkers have noticed a pattern: When they request accommodations, Amazon managers ask if they are “safe to work.” If they say yes, they are forced to continue to work without accommodations. If they say no, Amazon puts them on unpaid leave , which rapidly runs out.

Marissa, who worked at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Rossford, Ohio, said that after her accommodations were denied, she was forced out on unpaid leave, and she ended up losing her apartment. “I was out $1,700. . . . I couldn’t pay for my vehicle. I couldn’t afford to eat.

“Amazon doesn’t care about whether or not you’re in pain,” she said. “They care about whether or not you can get their packages out on time.”

Hossain said it was typical for workers to get fired for “job abandonment” because “they ran out of time-off options because they were just not given the accommodation.” (A Better Balance has also sued Amazon for this practice on behalf of a disabled worker.)

H ayat Bzezi was working at Amazon’s Staten Island JFK8 warehouse during the busy holiday season of 2024, when all workers were required to take an additional weekly ten-hour shift. She had asked for lighter duty, and management said she could use a chair, but then she was denied it.

She was “lifting heavy products, climbing up and down the stairs, despite having a high-risk pregnancy,” said her husband Wajdy, an elected ALU trustee who works at the same warehouse.

Hayat worked through pain, but it got worse and finally she had to go to the hospital, where she miscarried. It was the second time she had miscarried while working at Amazon. After that the couple decided to speak out . Since then, she has stopped working at Amazon and has been able to bear a child.

W hen the PWFA went into effect in 2023, a study found that it reduced miscarriages by 9.6 percent. This suggests that many more miscarriages could be avoided if Amazon, the country’s second-largest private employer, started following the law.

But there is every indication that Amazon is ignoring it. Last year, New Jersey’s attorney general filed a lawsuit against Amazon after reviewing thousands of worker requests for accommodations. Amazon is New Jersey’s largest private employer, with around fifty thousand workers.

“When Amazon’s pregnant workers and workers with disabilities request accommodations, Amazon stonewalls them,” the suit charges. “It forces them through a byzantine accommodations process, imposing rigid and unnecessary paperwork requirements and subjecting workers to unexplained weeks-long delays.”

Rosa, a worker at Amazon’s fulfillment center in Akron, Ohio, said she asked for pregnancy accommodations because she was working in Ship Dock, a role that requires heavy lifting, pushing, and pulling. She was hospitalized for dehydration four times, but managers still kept her in that role, she said.

“Eventually my symptoms became so severe that I had to take an unpaid leave of absence,” she said. “I found out afterwards that I could have done paid short-term disability leave, but these options weren’t told to me.”

Amazon denies this. “The suggestion that we routinely deny or don’t support pregnancy accommodations is simply untrue,” said Amazon spokesperson Kelly Nantel. She said “99.9 percent” of pregnancy accommodation requests this year had been approved.

But New Jersey investigators found that Amazon regularly fired workers for requesting accommodations, in violation of New Jersey’s Law Against Discrimination and the PWFA. New York State has also s ued Amazon for this.

Hossain said the medical forms that Amazon requires for pregnancy, injury, and disability accommodations are so comprehensive and invasive that doctors have objected that they violate medical privacy laws.

Amazon wants such detailed medical documentation, Hossain said, because “they want to claim that if workers ever get injured, it’s because of conditions they came to work with, and it’s not workplace injuries.” Asked about this, an Amazon public relations representative declined to respond.

T he worker justice group Warehouse Life has been tracking and protesting Amazon’s health and safety record since 2023, and helping injured workers who have to “fight through a lot of misinformation and lies that they received from [Amazon] managers about workers’ comp,” said Chloe Sigal, campaign manager for the group.

Sigal said Amazon’s rate system, along with “time off task” (TOT) policies, make the work unsafe: “Amazon is pushing people to work as fast, as hard as humanly possible — or really outside what is humanly possible. That’s what’s driving this injury epidemic .”

In 2021 the California legislature found that injuries in Amazon warehouses were driven by its rate system. Workers were forced to work faster and faster because if they fell into the lowest 25 percent they could experience discipline, and the bottom 5 percent risked termination.

California passed a law requiring warehouses to publish stable quotas and not constantly accelerate them. In 2024 the state fined Amazon $6 million for violating it.

Workers also accumulate TOT when surveillance detects a pause in their package scanning. Fear of too much TOT pushes workers to cut short their breaks, skip bathroom breaks (and reduce liquid consumption to match), and push on through pain. Dehydration is particularly risky during a pregnancy. “The reason that people are miscarrying at Amazon is because of this rate system,” said Sigal.

Doctors agree. Jenny Fish is a Santa Rosa, California, physician who provides prenatal care. “Prolonged standing, going the whole shift without water, lifting more than 15 to 20 pounds, working night shifts regularly,” she said, “all of this has been irrefutably linked to higher risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, increased maternal fatigue, preterm delivery, low birth weight, and just in general adverse birth outcomes.” Preeclampsia is potentially fatal.

S igal said that soon after Warehouse Life started, several Amazon workers came to the group reporting pregnancy issues. But when the group put out a call on social media for experiences working at Amazon while pregnant, it was flooded with stories. Two thousand women from forty states responded, and eighty-one described loss of a pregnancy. (Get more info on Warehouse Life here .)

Now some of these workers are leading the charge to get changes at the company. They have put pressure on New York City’s Mount Sinai Health System to terminate Amazon board of directors member Edith Cooper as a hospital trustee, given Amazon’s dismal safety record.

Warehouse Life members have also met with Amazon management. Sigal said that during those meetings Amazon claimed to have a policy on pregnancy that was only available to workers. But no workers were able to access it. “Nobody has it. We’ve heard from managers that they don’t have it either, that they don’t receive training on what to do,” Sigal said.

When Labor Notes asked Amazon for its pregnancy policy and any training materials, no documents were forthcoming. Warehouse Life counters that the company’s real pregnancy policy is “ Delay. Deny. Discipline .”

T he Amazon Labor Union organized on Staten Island in 2022, and in 2024 affiliated with the Teamsters. But Amazon refuses to negotiate with the union at the five-thousand-worker warehouse, despite being ordered to do so by the National Labor Relations Board in April.

The union can still help, though. “Just a few weeks ago a pregnant worker came to our union hall saying she wanted help getting an accommodation at work,” said ALU’s Hossain. The worker had already told her manager that she was pregnant.

The union sent several workers to accompany her to HR, saying “that should be enough, and Amazon needs to start the process of accommodating her,” Hossain said. “And they actually did listen, but only because a group of workers accompanied her.” A contract could provide additional protections.

The union isn’t waiting for workers to seek it out. Union activists distribute fliers with a QR code to a reporting form that goes to the union. Half of the reports “are unfair discipline, the other half is workers who are dealing with injuries or the accommodation process or need workers’ comp or whatever,” said Hossain. “It’s such a big issue.”

“It really does feel like we’re all just numbers,” said Rosa in Akron. “I want them to take more accountability. They make it so hard when it comes to a life-changing thing.”

Jenny Brown is an assistant editor at Labor Notes . She is author of Birth Strike: The Hidden Fight Over Women's Work . Her latest book is Without Apology: The Abortion Struggle Now .

scraped.description: The DNC wants more debates and new media voices in 2028, but its rules also threaten to disqualify candidates who join unsanctioned debates.
scraped.author: Meagan O'Rourke
scraped.h1: DNC Unveils 2028 Primary Plans: 12 Debates, Influencers, and No Dark Money
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Election 2028

Meagan O'Rourke | 11.25.2026 4:45 PM

Clear your calendar for 2027 and 2028, because there will be 12 Democratic primary debates to watch, starting in June.

The punishing primary debate schedule is just part of the Democratic National Committee's (DNC) recently announced plan for the 2028 presidential election. And while sitting through 12 Democratic primary debates seems nightmarish (think of all the corny, engineered viral moments we will be subjected to), a more rigorous primary process is preferable to a virtually nonexistent one like the Democrats pulled in 2024 .

The DNC also wants to make sure these 12 debates attract the maximum number of eyeballs, and the organization says it "will seek to maximize the viewership of the debates, including by incorporating creators and influencers into the debate process." The announcement has already caught the attention of Hasan Piker, who wrote on X, "the debate will include creators and influencers you say?" According to The Washington Post , some influencers and content creators are already considering getting involved. Brian Tyler Cohen, president of the Chorus Creator Incubator program (which tech journalist Taylor Lorenz reported was funded by a liberal dark money group), said it is "long past time for independent media and a creator" to host a debate, according to the Post.

The DNC has not clarified how exactly influencers will be involved in the debate process (tiny microphones for everyone? Best TikTok creator wins?). But it does state that candidates cannot "participate in events in which two or more candidates share the stage, whether virtually or in-person, and answer questions." Candidates who participate in such unsanctioned debates would be disqualified from future sanctioned debates. While new media and podcasters can be a democratizing force, an influencer-led debate would likely turn a political debate into an even more vapid spectacle than usual. Will candidates have to face a circle of critics on Jubilee ? Will they all have to sit down with the SubwayTakes guy? Crafting a smart social media strategy worked for a mayoral candidate like current New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani. But if candidates do not propose things that resonate with voters (even if those policies are misguided and impractical), a Brat-style, "Hotties for Harris" campaign is likely not going to land.

As another part of the DNC's efforts to run "a 2028 presidential primary process that is transparent, fair, and rigorous," the organization is also asking candidates to denounce dark money spending to qualify for these debates. While the DNC acknowledges that it cannot legally ban dark money and super PAC groups, it says that "a uniform denunciation statement will be provided for each campaign to complete upon notification of spending that violates the pledge." The pledge won't apply to the general election.

"You want to lead this party? Go earn it – with voters, not dark money," DNC chairman Ken Martin wrote on Substack Tuesday.

Earning votes in 2028 will likely be more difficult than during the midterms, when Democrats were able to win support from those dissatisfied with President Donald Trump's war in Iran and high gas prices. While adding more independent media voices to the debate process could be edifying for voters, it would be foolish for Democrats to think that social media appearances and debate performances alone will secure their nomination. Voters are results oriented. Then again, self-reflection has not been Democrats' strong suit .

scraped.title: Why prisoners continue to serve sentences that Congress has deemed unjust
scraped.description: Congress agreed that some federal sentences were too severe, but its reforms left many prisoners serving the old penalties.
scraped.author: Jacob Sullum
scraped.h1: Why Prisoners Keep Serving Sentences That Congress Has Deemed Unjust
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Sentencing

Jacob Sullum | 11.25.2026 4:30 PM

When Congress reduces the criminal penalties authorized or mandated by federal law, it usually does not make those changes retroactive. That means people sentenced before the new law took effect continue to serve prison terms that legislators subsequently deemed excessive, which makes no logical or moral sense. As Reason 's C.J. Ciaramella notes in his recent story about one such prisoner, that situation inspired a judicial solution that the Supreme Court deemed out of bounds last May in Rutherford v. United States : resentencing based on "extraordinary and compelling reasons" under the FIRST STEP Act.

The judges who embraced that approach included Ketanji Brown Jackson, whom then-President Joe Biden nominated to the Supreme Court in 2022. Jackson's legally controversial use of the FIRST STEP Act figured in the confirmation debate, and she was one of three dissenters in Rutherford . Her position on the issue highlights the perverse consequences of legislative compromises that might be politically convenient but defy basic principles of justice.

The FIRST STEP Act , which President Donald Trump signed into law in December 2018, changed federal sentencing in several ways. It reduced enhanced penalties for repeat drug offenders under 21 USC 841(b) and 21 USC 960(b) , expanded the "safety valve" that allows certain nonviolent offenders to escape mandatory minimums, and barred prosecutors from "stacking" charges under 18 USC 924(c) , which applies to a defendant who "uses or carries" a firearm "in furtherance of" drug trafficking or a violent crime. Section 924(c) prescribes lengthy prison sentences for drug offenders who own guns, even if they never use them to threaten or harm anyone.

The FIRST STEP Act passed with broad, bipartisan support. The vote was 87 to 12 in the Senate and 358 to 36 in the House . In other words, legislators overwhelmingly agreed that the existing penalties were too severe. Yet the law did not make the revised penalties for drug offenders retroactive, meaning they applied only to defendants sentenced after the law took effect.

That choice was especially puzzling because the same law retroactively applied the shorter crack cocaine sentences prescribed by the Fair Sentencing Act of 2010—a provision that benefited about 4,000 prisoners who had been convicted before Congress approved the earlier law. But the FIRST STEP Act included another provision that many federal judges saw as a solution to the disparities created by nonretroactive sentencing reforms. It allowed prisoners to seek "compassionate release" for "extraordinary and compelling reasons"—a process that previously had to be initiated by the Bureau of Prisons.

Could a striking difference between the sentence someone received and the sentence he would have received under current law count as "extraordinary and compelling"? Jackson, then a judge on the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia, thought so.

In July 2018, Jackson sentenced Keith Young, who had been convicted of possessing with intent to distribute one kilogram or more of heroin, to 20 years in federal prison. That penalty was mandatory once prosecutors noted Young's prior conviction for possession with intent to distribute cocaine, which qualified as a "serious drug felony." Otherwise, Young's sentence would have been half as long.

Five months later, the FIRST STEP Act changed the definition of "serious drug felony," excluding defendants who were released from prison more than 15 years before the new offense. That category included Young, who filed a motion for resentencing under the law's "compassionate release" provision in September 2020.

Like many other prisoners who filed such motions during the pandemic, Young argued that he should be released in light of the danger posed by COVID-19, citing his asthma and smoking history as factors that made him especially vulnerable to the disease. But he also noted that he "would not be subject to a 240-month mandatory minimum today," saying "this change in law additionally warrants compassionate release." Jackson agreed with the latter argument and resentenced Young to 10 years.

Sen. Tom Cotton (R–Ark.) grilled Jackson about that decision during her Supreme Court confirmation hearing, portraying her as soft on drug dealers. Jackson said she found it "extraordinary and compelling" that "between the 20-year sentence that I gave [Young] originally and the compassionate release motion that he filed, Congress changed the law." It decided that "the old crime was no longer eligible for the increase, so that a person who was convicted at the time of his compassionate release motion for doing exactly what Mr. Young had done would not get a 20-year sentence."

Jackson noted that "one of the things that Congress says to the judges" is that they should "care about unwarranted sentencing disparity," meaning they should "care about the fact that the person you're sentencing is being treated differently than someone else who committed exactly the same crime." Although the statutory change in the treatment of repeat drug offenders "wasn't retroactive," she said, "here I have a defendant before me, and all of the factors that Congress has asked me to take into account, and a compelling argument that there were extraordinary and compelling circumstances—that is, a change in the law—that would create unwarranted sentencing disparity if I didn't take account of it."

While Cotton was one of the 12 senators who voted against the FIRST STEP Act, critics of Young's resentencing also included Sen. Chuck Grassley (R–Iowa), the bill's chief sponsor in the Senate. As Grassley saw it, Jackson improperly substituted her policy judgment for the one reflected in the FIRST STEP Act.

"Judge Jackson said she based her 'extraordinary [and] compelling' finding on the nonretroactive change in the law," Grassley said during a meeting of the Senate Judiciary Committee. "This is a terrible and dangerous interpretation. Congress chose…which provisions of the FIRST STEP Act would apply retroactively…The Senate is currently considering legislation that I cosponsored with [Sen. Richard Durbin (D–Ill.)] that makes some of the FIRST STEP Act retroactive. But Congress must make that change."

Jackson's shortcut reflects "a radical position," Grassley said, "and it's outside of the confines of law." Yet Jackson was by no means alone in taking that position, and federal appeals courts were split on the question of whether it was valid. The U.S. Sentencing Commission lent support to Jackson's reading of the law in 2023, when it amended its guidelines regarding what counts as "extraordinary and compelling."

If a defendant "received an unusually long sentence and has served at least 10 years of the term of imprisonment," the commission said, "a change in the law (other than an amendment to the Guidelines Manual that has not been made retroactive) may be considered in determining whether the defendant presents an extraordinary and compelling reason, but only where such change would produce a gross disparity between the sentence being served and the sentence likely to be imposed at the time the motion is filed, and after full consideration of the defendant's individualized circumstances."

The Supreme Court resolved this legal dispute in Rutherford . The case involved two defendants who had been sentenced under Section 924(c) prior to the FIRST STEP Act. One of them, Daniel Rutherford, received a 32-year minimum sentence, while the other, Johnnie Carter, received a 57-year minimum.

In both cases, prosecutors charged multiple violations of the statute, which triggered the 25-year minimum for repeat offenses. The FIRST STEP Act disallowed that practice, requiring prior convictions under Section 924(c). If Rutherford and Carter had been sentenced after that law took effect, their sentences would have been much shorter: 14 years and 21 years, respectively.

"Obviously, Rutherford and Carter—not to mention the many other similarly situated prisoners—would like the benefit of the Act's amendment to §924(c)," Justice Amy Coney Barrett wrote in the majority opinion . "As a rule, however, changes to sentencing statutes apply only to offenses committed after the statute's effective date. The Act departs from this rule in a very limited respect: Its more lenient penalties apply to offenses committed before the statute's enactment 'if a sentence for the offense has not been imposed as of such date of enactment.' But for defendants sentenced before the Act, the general rule of nonretroactivity remains in place."

Federal appeals courts "remain divided over whether the disparity created by a nonretroactive change to sentencing law, like the Act, can constitute an 'extraordinary and compelling reaso[n]' that 'warrant[s]' compassionate release," Barrett noted before concluding that it cannot. "'Extraordinary and compelling' reasons for compassionate release are those that are especially unusual and convincing. The disparity created by Congress's amendment to §924(c) does not satisfy this definition."

That disparity is not "extraordinary" because "nonretroactive amendments to criminal penalties are the norm," Barrett wrote. "'Ordinarily,' we have explained, 'statutory changes to federal penalties only benefit future offenders.'"

Nor is the disparity "compelling," Barrett said: "It is hard to see how Congress's deliberate decision not to extend newly reduced penalties to those already sentenced could be a convincing reason that 'warrant[s]' a reduction. As we have explained, Congress decided to apply the lower prison sentences to some violators of §924(c)—those for whom a sentence had not yet been imposed—but not others. In doing so, Congress 'reinforced its interest in finality and avoided burdening district courts with additional litigation.' Treating the disparity resulting from §924(c)'s amendment as a compelling reason for reducing a sentence would undermine Congress's choice to leave the sentence intact."

In a dissent joined by Jackson and Justice Elena Kagan, Justice Sonia Sotomayor argued that Congress empowered the U.S. Sentencing Commission to "define what constitutes 'extraordinary and compelling reasons' for incarcerated individuals to receive a sentence reduction under the compassionate release statute." The question therefore was "whether the Commission acted unreasonably when it issued that guidance," she wrote. "It did not. The Commission's policy statement is consistent with Congress's commands and centuries of legal practice in which courts look to the totality of the circumstances when deciding whether to modify a sentence. Because the Court concludes that the policy is unlawful, and that courts may never consider nonretroactive changes in law when deciding whether someone is eligible for compassionate release, I respectfully dissent."

The majority, by contrast, agreed with Grassley that judges flout the will of Congress when they take into account "nonretroactive changes in law." Whatever your take on that legal issue, it is notable that Grassley himself favors retroactivity, as he emphasized in 2022.

If fair punishment is the main concern, it is hard to understand why Congress would decide that penalties for certain offenses are excessively severe yet force current prisoners to continue serving sentences it now considers unjust. Yet that is what Congress did, and Grassley argued that such inconsistency was the price of winning approval for the FIRST STEP Act. "The compromise that I brokered with Sen. Durbin on the FIRST STEP Act," he said , "wouldn't have been possible if we thought that the activist judge would insert their own views into the law. Decisions like [Young's resentencing] represent serious separation-of-powers concerns and will make bipartisan work harder in the future."

Such compromises may indeed be politically necessary to accomplish marginal improvements in criminal penalties, which can add up to decades even for nonviolent defendants whose offenses violated no one's rights. But at some point, legislators ought to reconsider the morally dubious "norm" that Barrett described, which entails a default contradiction between the punishment that Congress currently deems appropriate and the punishment imposed on "many other similarly situated prisoners."

scraped.title: How Montgomery County uses its alcohol monopoly to squeeze small businesses
scraped.description: Montgomery County, Maryland, marks up alcohol for private retailers by as much as 90 percent, charges its own stores nothing, and inspects the businesses it competes with.
scraped.author: Josh Pauzé
scraped.h1: How Montgomery County Uses Its Alcohol Monopoly to Squeeze Small Businesses
scraped.body_text:
Log In

Create new account

Alcohol

Josh Pauzé | 11.25.2026 4:15 PM

A bottle of Kendall-Jackson Vintners Reserve Chardonnay goes for $9.97 at Total Wine's store in Friendship Heights, Washington, D.C. Just across the D.C. line in Montgomery County, that same bottle costs Arash Tafakor, the owner of two wine and beer stores, $11.75 to stock. Like so many business owners in the county, Tafakor can thank his government for this disparity.

Unlike its neighbors to the north and south , Maryland is not a control state; residents can buy alcohol from privately run stores, and wholesalers can purchase their products at market rate. This freedom ends in Montgomery County, where state law requires stores and restaurants to buy their beer, wine, and spirits from the county, which also runs its own stores and oversees licensing and inspection of its competition.

​Montgomery County is the only county in the U.S. with full monopoly control over the wholesale distribution of beer, wine, and spirits. This system dates back to the end of Prohibition, when Maryland lawmakers created a liquor control board to manage alcohol licensing and distribution. Nearly a century later, Montgomery County's control board—renamed Alcohol Beverage Services (ABS) in 2019—has only grown and now operates 27 of its own stores. The original idea was to regulate what the state considered a potentially dangerous substance, but in recent years "they made it into a business," Tafakor tells Reason .

The county adds 5 to 35 percent markup to local businesses on wine, 23 to 60 percent on beer, and 29 to 90 percent on kegs over what it pays distributors, according to records Tafakor obtained through a Maryland Public Information Act request. County stores are exempt from that markup, allowing them to sell to consumers for far less than private stores and, in some cases, even less than what they charge private retailers. Last December, the county charged private stores like Tafakor's $226.50 per bottle of Dom Pérignon. On its website, it was selling that same bottle to consumers for only $217.59. "This practice is common by the county stores during the holiday season to attract more customers," Tafakor says.

If private stores want a product that the county doesn't already distribute, they have to wait for the county to approve the sale, which Tafakor says can take two to eight weeks, if it gets done at all. Meanwhile, ABS stores and stores outside Montgomery County can get those products in under a day. In addition to their lower prices and first dibs on new products, ABS stores are also the only off-premise sites that can sell spirits. "It's nearly impossible to compete with these stores," Tafakor says.

The government's control over the industry has been lucrative for Montgomery County. According to an ABS staff report , Montgomery County's alcohol business raked in $31.3 million in net profit in FY2024; however, this wasn't because it ran a successful enterprise. The report shows ABS stores lost more than $3.9 million that year, while their wholesale division profited nearly $50 million.

Tafakor estimates the county's inventory markups cost his two stores around $1.1 million in FY2025—and his stores accounted for just 2.23 percent of the county's wholesale sales that year, according to the county's financial disclosures .

"Essentially, they own 30 percent of our store," he says. "I don't have the basic freedom that everybody else is entitled to outside of Montgomery County in Virginia [which is a control state for spirits], D.C., and Maryland, because I am forced to buy through the county."

On top of that, Tafakor's stores are also subject to inspections from the County Board of License Commissioners, which was folded into the ABS in 2007, and is now responsible for regulating the same businesses it competes with. "They're supposed to visit us every quarter. I had an inspector that was coming in nonstop, harassing me," Tafakor says. The inspector would show up claiming he was "in the neighborhood," then "snoop around…looking for stuff." Even making remarks like "the mouse catches the cheese once in a while."

The county's dual role as a retailer and enforcement arm raises obvious conflict of interest concerns, which some county leaders have acknowledged.

In 2015, Fred Silverman, then a member of the county's Board of License Commissioners, wrote a memo to the County Council's Alcohol Policy Ad Hoc Committee warning the county about the system's economic harms and questionable legality. Silverman argued that the county made a "mistake" by stripping the board of its independence. He also said the county is "operating outside the law."

After Tafakor filed a complaint over the county's pricing schemes, Maryland's Alcohol, Tobacco, and Cannabis Commission investigated and found that county stores paid no markup on their inventory. According to Tafakor, ABS officials justify this practice by telling state officials that their stores aren't retailers but "extensions of the county warehouse," so products can be transferred without a markup. The county has a point: even if stores did pay the same markup, they would merely be transferring money between the county's retail and wholesale divisions. The retailer's balance sheet wouldn't be pretty, but the county's bottom line would stay the same.

In a March letter to the ABS director, Kathie Durbin, the commission said the practice "effectively gives the appearance of price discrimination" and suggested the county charge its own stores "the same markup applied to private retailers."

​In 2016, businesses and consumers pushed back against the county's system, with many suggesting the alcohol business be privatized. County Council member Marc Elrich outlined an alternative solution. "I would make it so the customer wouldn't know whether they were in a private liquor store or a county liquor store," he told Bethesda Magazine . "I basically would make this a system that you would think is a private system and keep the revenue," and that's exactly what they did. In 2021, the county began rebranding its "Montgomery County Liquor & Wine" stores to "Oak Barrel & Vine," giving them the look of a private retailer. Their stores run ads, offer promotional discounts, and host wine tastings.

The Montgomery County ABS was not available for comment at the time of publication.

Small businesses aren't the only ones paying the price for Montgomery County's policies; consumers feel it too. "Not only has it hurt us personally, [but] it's hurt the growth of the small businesses in Montgomery County. It's killing them." Tafakor says, "Restaurateurs, they don't open in Montgomery County. They open in Frederick, they open in Virginia, they open up in D.C. where they don't have to go through this."

scraped.title: Iran War Day 271: White House Weighs Killing Leaders, per Report
scraped.description: State of the Union: The Israeli defense minister claimed Tehran is developing chemical weapons.
scraped.author: Andrew Day
scraped.body_text:
The Trump administration is debating whether to kill top Iranian leaders, NBC News reported Tuesday. Officials who support the plan claim it would enable President Donald Trump to end the war, though how it would do so isn’t clear. Officials opposed to the plan say killing more leaders would push Tehran to dig in, further erode Iranian trust in U.S. diplomacy, and imperil American officials who could face reprisals.

Trump officials have discussed many possible paths forward in the Iran War and the president does not seem to have finalized a decision. The U.S. and Israel killed Iranian leaders in the opening strikes of the current war, but the Islamic Republic maintained continuity and, analysts say, grew more hardline.

Israel’s Defense Minister Israel Katz claimed Tuesday that Iran is developing chemical weapons. Israel’s Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has urged Trump to launch another round of war, and his government has shared with the U.S. intelligence that Iran is plotting to use chemical weapons against Americans. The Islamic Republic has denied the claims.

Israeli military and intelligence officials have assessed there is no urgent need to strike Iran, but opposition figures warn Netanyahu may seek major hostilities to tighten his hold on power following elections in which his party lost its majority.

Iran’s top diplomat at the United Nations on Tuesday accused the U.S. and Israel of weaponizing artificial intelligence in recent conflicts with Iran, including by allowing AI models to select targets.

Three oil tankers struck sea mines in the Strait of Hormuz and caught fire, Iran said Wednesday. Shipping trackers have recorded an escalation of Iranian strikes on vessels in the waterway but have not confirmed Iranian claims about sea mines. Tehran warned that ships that do not coordinate with the Islamic Republic face elevated risks.

The price of Brent crude opened at $91.06 per barrel on Wednesday and the average price of regular gasoline in America was $3.59. Gas prices have declined in recent weeks despite continued hostilities in the Hormuz.

scraped.description: State of the Union: The Chinese telecom giant was convicted on most charges, but acquitted of racketeering.
scraped.author: Luke Nicastro
scraped.body_text:
Huawei was found guilty of conspiracy to steal trade secrets, commit bank fraud, and violate U.S. sanctions on Iran Tuesday, though it was acquitted of the most serious charges of racketeering. A jury convicted Huawei on 10 of 12 counts, ending proceedings that began in 2018 with the dramatic arrest of executive Meng Wanzhou in Canada.

Federal prosecutors said that the company had made fraud and intellectual property theft a core part of its corporate strategy. “For decades, Huawei and three of its subsidiaries conducted their business in the United States on the basis of lies and theft,” Attorney General Todd Blanche said Tuesday. “Thanks to the work of the FBI and our federal prosecutors, those who engaged in these criminal activities will be held accountable.”

Huawei, a Chinese telecommunications firm with a global presence, denies wrongdoing. The company welcomed its acquittal of racketeering in a statement , and claimed that the “remaining charges are equally without legal or factual merit.”

Luke Nicastro is a senior editor at The American Conservative. Before joining the magazine, he spent nearly a decade working on defense and foreign policy in both government and industry, most recently as National Security Advisor to U.S. Senator Josh Hawley. He has also worked at the Congressional Research Service, the Department of the Navy, the National Defense University, and several defense contractors.

scraped.title: Democratic voters want Congress to cut funding for Iran war: polls
scraped.description: Eighty percent of respondents say conflict should end now, while many threaten electoral consequences for those who fail to do so
scraped.h1: Democratic voters want Congress to cut funding for Iran war: polls
scraped.body_text:
Eighty percent of respondents say conflict should end now, while many threaten electoral consequences for those who fail to do so

Democratic voters want Congress to quickly cut off funding for the Iran war and are prepared to punish lawmakers who fail to do so, two new polls suggest.

With government funding set to expire on December 11, congressional Democrats are weighing whether to withhold their support for any spending bill unless it includes restrictions on funding for the war. Such a move would leave Trump and congressional supporters of the conflict to decide whether to accept those restrictions or risk a government shutdown to keep the war going. The new polling indicates that pursuing this strategy would have considerable support among the Democratic party’s base.

Opposition to the Iran war helped fuel Democrats’ sweeping midterm victories earlier this month. Now, the question of how quickly the party should move to end the conflict has become a dividing line for the party, including in the race for Senate majority leader. Sen. Chris Van Hollen (D-Md.) has made the December 11 war funding deadline a key plank of his bid to unseat Sen. Chuck Schumer (D-N.Y.) as party leader.

A University of Maryland poll released Tuesday shows that 80% of Democratic respondents want the Iran war to end “now, regardless of the terms.” Only 14% said they would prefer to stay the course until Iran offered concessions, and 3% wanted to escalate “in an attempt to force Iran to accept US terms.” Exactly one-quarter of Republicans and 59% of independents agreed with the majority of Democrats that the war should end now.

Respondents were more split over the specifics of whether to include a cut-off for funding in a stopgap funding bill. Just over half of Democrats (51%) said they would favor such a strategy, even at the risk of a veto and potential shutdown. A mere 16% said they were opposed to the maneuver. Across all respondents, 31% supported including language to cut funding, 28% opposed, and 39% replied “don’t know.”

“As is implicit in the wording of our poll question on this issue, the Democratic public is apparently prepared to take that risk [of a shutdown],” the University of Maryland’s Shibley Telhami wrote in his accompanying analysis of the shutdown question. “On the other hand, Trump may be looking for a way to end the war, and cutting war funding may provide him with an exit ramp, while blaming Congress, especially Democrats, for the consequences.”

On Wednesday, progressive group Demand Progress released a new poll that digs further into the question of the political consequences if such a vote were to take place.

According to the poll, just over three-quarters (76%) of respondents who voted for Democratic nominee Kamala Harris in 2024 said they would be “less likely to reelect a lawmaker who votes to extend government funding past December 11 without a ban on funding for the war against Iran.” Nearly half of Harris voters said they would be “much less likely” to support a member who voted to keep funding the war, and only 7% said they would be “much” or “somewhat” more likely to vote for someone who supported legislation that did not cut funds.

Even among voters who backed Donald Trump in 2024, only 38% said they would be more likely to reelect a lawmaker who voted to extend government funding without prohibiting further money for the war. A plurality of respondents (29%) said that it would have no impact, while 19% said that they would be less likely to support a member of Congress who supported such a bill.

The Demand Progress poll surveyed 1,006 voters from November 18 to November 20.

Many Democratic skeptics of including Iran-funding-specific provisions in future funding bills have pointed to the potential political costs of being blamed for a government shutdown as a reason to avoid such a debate during the lame duck period.

But among the party’s own voters, there may also be a political price to pay for waiting.
