items.title: EU budget blackmail: fund Ukraine or else
items.summary: The European Union is engaged in contentious budget negotiations this week with spending on security and the Ukraine War competing against other priorities, pitting net contributors such as Germany against net recipients like Poland and Hungary.EU Council president Antonio Costa is trying to hasten adoption of the Multiannual Financial Framework, which runs from 2028 through 2034, because next year’s elections in France, Italy and Poland could bring Euroskeptic leaders to power who may want t...

scraped.title: EU budget blackmail: fund Ukraine or else
scraped.description: Leadership is scrambling to pass the Multiyear Financial Framework before the potential of populist wins in 2027
scraped.h1: EU budget blackmail: fund Ukraine or else
scraped.body_text:
Leadership is scrambling to pass the Multiyear Financial Framework before the potential of populist wins in 2027

The European Union is engaged in contentious budget negotiations this week with spending on security and the Ukraine War competing against other priorities, pitting net contributors such as Germany against net recipients like Poland and Hungary.

EU Council president Antonio Costa is trying to hasten adoption of the Multiannual Financial Framework, which runs from 2028 through 2034, because next year’s elections in France, Italy and Poland could bring Euroskeptic leaders to power who may want to cut their countries’ contributions.

This would include the leading presidential candidates in France — Marine Le Pen and Jean Luc Mélenchon — who both call for sharp reductions in France’s contributions.

As the budget drama unfolds, the EU is also moving toward a potential clash over a proposed €45 billion ($49 billion) loan to Ukraine, with a final decision to be taken at a meeting of heads of government on November 26-27, in which they will also work toward an agreed draft budget.

Ukraine in the mix: Merz’s gauntlet There has long been significant variation among EU member countries in their financial or military support for Ukraine. Support from the Nordic EU member countries is greatest as a share of GDP, but in absolute terms, Germany is the EU’s largest bilateral donor to Ukraine. Spain and Italy are among the most obvious laggards. The trend in public opinion across the EU is toward greater reluctance to continue funding for Ukraine. The IMF now estimates that the funding gap for Ukraine’s state budget for the coming year is €70 billion ($76 billion). The EU leadership seeks approval for a new loan of roughly €45 billion ($49 billion), with non-EU supporters of Ukraine to provide the remainder. Under current rules this loan must be approved by all EU member states. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz wrote to council president Antonio Costa on November 10 to say that all EU member countries should financially back the loan to Ukraine. He threatened a German veto of the EU budget if this condition is not met. Germany is also the largest single contributor to the EU budget, and EU institutions are the largest provider of financial assistance (budget support) to Ukraine. The draft EU budget for 2028-2034 includes generous assistance to Ukraine, but the proposed loan is outside the budget deliberations. The loan is an unanticipated response to Ukraine’s acute financing gap, presumably the consequence of damage to power and other infrastructure inflicted by Russia . This time it’s different? At the end of last year, the European Commission tried and failed to get member states’ agreement to provide aid to Ukraine from the frozen Russian reserves held mainly in Belgium’s Euroclear depository. EU members agreed instead to provide a €90 billion ($98 billion) loan to Ukraine backed by the EU budget. This loan was intended to meet Ukraine’s financing needs for 2026 and 2027. The $98 billion loan approved in December 2025 required unanimous approval by member states. To ensure the funds were made available to Ukraine, the EU allowed Hungary, Czechia, and Slovakia to be exempted from any financial obligation in servicing or repaying this loan. The leaders of Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia and Bulgaria have indicated they are unwilling to back this new EU loan commitment. Merz’s November 10 ultimatum makes clear that Germany will oppose any exemptions or reservations in approval of the proposed loan. Blowback In a November 10 press conference with Czech Prime Minister Andrej Babis, Slovak Prime Minister Robert Fico called the German ultimatum “ blackmail” and indicated that Slovakia and other EU members can also wield veto power, including over the budget. In a joint press conference with Merz on November 10, Hungarian Prime Minister Petr Magyar said Hungary did not agree with conditioning the approval of the EU budget on unanimous approval of the proposed EU loan to Ukraine. A November 23 summit of the Visegrad Group (Poland, Hungary, Czechia, Slovakia) prime ministers questioned the usefulness of further negotiations on the EU budget this week, in part because of the controversy around the loan and its relation to the budget. Consequences It is obvious in populist circles that EU leadership is speeding this along to avoid any challenges to EU priorities — including support for Ukraine — after the 2027 elections. The April presidential contest in France could radically tip the balance. Marine Le Pen, leader of the populist right Rassemblement National, has a clear lead in polls. Although Le Pen no longer advocates leaving the EU or the euro, she is outside the EU mainstream on Ukraine/Russia, enlargement, climate, and some defense and security issues. She advocates curbing the power of the European Commission and strengthening the intergovernmental European Council. Whatever the outcome, Merz’s hardball approach to the Ukraine loan has roiled the already complex budget process. His public ultimatum breaks with the customary tactful and cautious German interactions with EU partners. Typically, Germany has sought to act in concert with like-minded countries and avoided the appearance of throwing its weight around. Merz’s insistence that Ukraine is a collective European obligation risks aggravating the somewhat submerged discord among EU members over the ever increasing aid to Ukraine. It also slows the adoption of a budget that could limit the potential of populists such as Marine Le Pen to change dramatically the relations between member countries and Brussels. Merz may have hoped to please the German public by insisting others bear more of the burden of aiding Ukraine, but he did not reckon with other countries’ needs to focus their scarce resources on domestic priorities. The difficult progress toward a multiannual EU budget has been made more complicated.

scraped.title: The Quad is on life support and Trump is holding the plug
scraped.description: Their Philippines meeting was brief and awkward, the result of souring relations between the US president and individual leaders in this once promising partnership
scraped.h1: The Quad is on life support and Trump is holding the plug
scraped.body_text:
Their Philippines meeting was brief and awkward, the result of souring relations between the US president and individual leaders in this once promising partnership

Last week the leaders of the Quad (Quadrilateral Security Dialogue )— comprised of Australia, India, Japan, and the United States — met in the Philippines for the first time in two years.

President Donald Trump was in Manila for less than 24 hours with a jam-packed schedule, including his participation in the main event, which was the ASEAN Summit, as well as a bilateral engagement with President Ferdinand Marcos and the Quad summit itself. Perhaps because of this busy itinerary, the Quad was given extremely short shrift, with Trump scheduled to participate for a mere 55 minutes total.

But that was only part of the problem. Since the Quad’s last summit in 2024 during President Joe Biden’s administration, the strategic bloc’s members have grown increasingly frustrated with the lack of formal meetings. India is particularly aggrieved because Trump refused to travel to New Delhi when it hosted the Quad last year.

Indeed, India still believes that it is the rightful next host of the Quad, even though this year is supposed to be Australia’s turn. Trump’s decision to combine the Quad with the ASEAN summit, and to have the Philippines become the first third-party nation to host a Quad summit, has potentially caused otherwise avoidable diplomatic protocol frictions between New Delhi and Canberra.

Moreover, America’s bilateral relationships with each of the Quad members has soured since Trump’s return to the White House. He has strained relations with India by imposing steep tariffs, demanding a trade deal, and resetting ties with Pakistan after Indian Prime Minister Narendra Modi declined to nominate him for the Nobel Peace Prize. Japan has faced tariffs , demands to dramatically increase defense spending , and criticism for not helping to reopen the Strait of Hormuz as part of his war against Iran . Australia has similarly faced tariffs and pressure to increase defense spending.

Canberra was also kept in the dark about Washington’s decision to counter-blockade Iran, and Trump criticized its refusal to participate in his war.

Meanwhile, during the summit this week, Trump, who prides himself on building personal relationships with foreign leaders, frustrated at least one of them while on stage. Trump’s decision to hold an impromptu press conference, in effect cutting further into the already short Quad time, prompted Modi to ask “Shall we move?” Both Australian Prime Minister Anthony Albanese and Japanese Prime Minister Sanae Takaichi also stood silently and looked uncomfortable while Trump took questions.

Beyond the awkward atmospherics and limited time spent on Quad matters, the strategic bloc failed to achieve any meaningful policy deliverables. Perhaps the summit’s most significant security announcement concerned the Indo-Pacific Maritime Surveillance Collaboration, an initiative designed to improve maritime domain awareness and information sharing. Under the initiative, the Quad members pledged to deploy their P-8 and P-3C maritime patrol aircraft in a joint exercise in 2027.

But the announcement was hardly groundbreaking and in truth is a repackaging of ongoing cooperation. Rather than conducting a standalone Quad exercise, the four nations will integrate their activities into Sea Dragon 2027, an established U.S.-led multinational anti-submarine warfare exercise in which Quad members have previously participated.

Another major announcement was the launch of the Quad Business Leaders’ Forum. In truth, this is also repackaged from previous Quad initiatives. During Biden’s administration, all members in May 2022 agreed to convene a business and investment forum, and the following year, they formally launched the Quad Investors Network (QUIN) to bring together investors and executives from all four countries, leading to the Quad Investment and Technology Dialogue with then-Secretary of Commerce Gina Raimondo present. In September 2024, at the Wilmington summit, the QUIN highlighted ten strategic investments and partnerships.

Similarly, the Cable Connectivity and Resilience nor Enhanced Quad Cybersecurity Cooperation initiatives simply build upon Biden-era agreements as well. Even the Super Intelligence Accelerator initiative has strong antecedents in the Biden administration, when the Quad established joint research initiatives, worked on safeguards, and pledged funding. By contrast, Trump’s AI program seems more focused on deployment, but does not specifically pledge to do anything new beyond that.

Trump’s decision to fly to Shenzhen immediately after the Quad summit to meet with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping — two authoritarian leaders whose governments stand in opposition to the democratic values underpinning the Quad — further reinforced the perception that he does not necessarily prioritize cooperation with U.S. allies and partners over engagement with America’s rivals. This strikes at the very heart of the Quad and is likely to cause rising anxiety.

While Trump’s participation in the Quad has certainly kept it alive for now, the grouping is on life support. It is abundantly clear that he and his administration are simply rebranding past initiatives and framing them as progress, and they do not take the Quad seriously — particularly when compared to great power relationships. Trump has also made no attempt to repair strained bilateral ties with each of the members, and his personal relationships with their leaders appear to be worsening.

If current trends persist over Trump’s last two years in office, the Quad is likely to become far more symbolic than substantive — an international box-checking exercise rather than a forum for policy achievements — which will only redound to the benefit of Russia and China and diminish the value of the strategic bloc to the rest of the world.

items.title: Politico ‘Experts’: This Magical Statute Is Only Legit When Dems Use It Against Republicans
items.summary: Politico legitimized Jack Smith's anti-Trump lawfare while arguing Trump admin use of the same statute would be 'political payback.'

scraped.title: Politico 'Experts': Magical Statute Is Only Legit When Dems Use It
scraped.description: Politico legitimized Jack Smith's anti-Trump lawfare while arguing Trump admin use of the same statute would be 'political payback.'
scraped.author: Brianna Lyman
scraped.h1: Politico ‘Experts’: This Magical Statute Is Only Legit When Dems Use It Against Republicans
scraped.body_text:
Politico legitimized Jack Smith’s anti-Trump lawfare while arguing Trump admin use of the same statute would be ‘political payback.’

Jack Smith’s use of a Civil War-era “conspiracy against rights” statute against Donald Trump was a perfectly reasonable and even good application of the law, according to the “experts” cited by Politico Wednesday. But the outlet simultaneously argued that Trump world even mentioning a potential use of the same statute to prosecute Democrats — who have promised to weaponize congressional investigations — is an act of “political payback.”

Politico’s Josh Gerstein and Kyle Cheney made these skewed assertions in an article titled “‘Political payback’: Trump admin warns Dems with same criminal charge Jack Smith brought against Trump.” They began by declaring that the Trump administration is “borrowing a page from former special counsel Jack Smith’s book as it seeks to cow newly empowered Democrats conducting oversight.” (By “oversight” the authors likely refer to weaponization and lawfare, which Democrats have expressly promised to engage in once they take office).

“Smith’s use of the charge centered on the allegation that Trump’s bid to subvert the 2020 election would have disenfranchised millions of voters, violating their constitutional right to have their votes counted,” Gerstein and Cheney stated. At the same time, they framed the Trump administration’s use of the statutes in terms of grievance and intimidation.

Trump aides, readers are told, are turning to the “broadly-worded” Section 241 on Democrats because they are still dealing with “grievances that it was contorted to punish the president.”

When Gerstein and Cheney returned to Smith’s use of the statute, they acknowledged that the charge was “novel” before quickly reassuring readers the lawfare was acceptable because “many experts embraced it.”

Those “experts” apparently included former Obama White House attorney Ian Bassin and former DOJ civil rights prosecutor Kristy Parker, who wrote a New York Times op-ed in which she argued that “bringing civil rights charges against the former president is not overreach by the Justice Department.”

To bolster the case for Smith’s charge (and delegitimize the potential use by the Trump DOJ), Gerstein and Cheney also pointed to a century-old Supreme Court decision involving ballot-box stuffing. The case merely showed that Section 241 could be used in election-related crimes, but in no way did it establish a precedent for Smith’s use. Yet Politico invoked it to lend credibility to a charge that Politico itself acknowledged was “novel” (an airbrushing of what one commentator called “ outrageous “) in order to suggest any use by the Trump administration would not be backed by court precedent.

Gerstein and Cheney also gave Norm Eisen — the former Obama ethics czar and serial Trump attacker — ample space to warn about how the potential use of Section 241 follows the “Roy Cohn school of litigation” and is “just a naked tit for tat.” Eisen insisted “this is not Alice in Wonderland” and that Section 241 “requires an actual factual predicate, an actual evidentiary predicate of the kind that you had with Donald Trump’s assault on the rightful outcome of the 2020 election.” But simply denying the existence of an “evidentiary predicate” falls well short of debunking the Trump admin’s proposed application of the statute, and calling Trump’s probing of election irregularities an assault doesn’t make them one.

Politico also described Eisen’s “Democracy Defenders Fund” as a “group pressing a series of lawsuits over alleged abuses of power and corruption in the Trump administration.” Notably, Democracy Defenders Fund intervened in a lawsuit on behalf of the NAACP and other groups after the Trump DOJ sued California over potentially 20,000 noncitizens on its voter rolls. Eisen called the DOJ’s efforts “election sabotage.” Democracy Defenders Fund also threatened to sue the Trump administration in 2025 because it was seeking to fire career DOJ and FBI officials, and the group “backed lawsuits opposing Trump’s order on birthright citizenship and challenging the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE),” according to the Daily Caller News Foundation.

Eisen — an “expert” who works for a group that uses lawfare against the president’s administration routinely — conveniently found that Smith’s use of the statute against Trump was a smart legal move.

Smith actually brought a criminal charge against Trump under Section 241, and the Politico reporters reassured readers that “many experts embraced it” to legitimize the blatant lawfare. Yet when the Trump administration warned that Democrats using subpoenas to trample citizens’ rights could draw scrutiny, Gerstein and Cheney framed it as “political payback” because Politico is nothing more than a propaganda outlet for the left.

scraped.title: Sen. Chris Van Hollen Just Can't Quit Kilmar Abrego Garcia
scraped.description: Chris Van Hollen is "relieved" Kilmar Abrego Garcia will be a "free man" after self-deporting to Spain.
scraped.author: Breccan F. Thies
scraped.h1: Sen. Chris Van Hollen Just Can’t Quit Alleged ‘Human Trafficker’ Kilmar Abrego Garcia
scraped.body_text:
Kilmar Abrego Garcia, the “ Maryland father ” who was really a Salvadoran illegal alien and has been accused of being a “human smuggler, wife beater, gang member, and child predator,” self-deported to Spain on Tuesday following removal orders from the Department of Homeland Security (DHS). But Sen. Chris Van Hollen, D-Md., who jet-set to San Salvador to conduct a welfare check during Garcia’s first deportation, is just “relieved” he will finally be a “free man.”

“Kilmar is traveling to a country of his choice, a free man – unharmed and with dignity,” Van Hollen said . “While the Trump Administration had been pursuing their vindictive prosecution against Kilmar and desperately trying to ship him against his will to countries known for human rights abuses, the Administration was forced to come to this agreement that respects Kilmar’s will and the due process rights guaranteed to him and to all in our nation.”

The Maryland Democrat’s initial trip to San Salvador in 2025 was for the express purpose to “bring him home,” even though he was already back in his home country. Van Hollen’s purpose was different, as my colleague Eddie Scarry wrote : “the senator [was] attempting to re-import an illegal alien who was lawfully removed from the country.”

Van Hollen, who is currently challenging Sen. Chuck Schumer, D-N.Y., for the top Senate leadership position in the upcoming Congress, is once again expressing more interest in the well-being of an illegal alien who has been accused of multiple crimes than the American people.

Today, Kilmar Abrego Garcia is a free man. I am grateful that he finally received the due process he, and every single person in our country, is owed. We can never compromise when it comes to our Constitutional rights. pic.twitter.com/uZJYgaHMO4

To Van Hollen, it was all about “uphold[ing] his constitutional rights.”

At least the much-beleaguered Garcia “will be safe” outside the United States, Van Hollen said.

“Now, this El Salvadoran man cannot terrorize innocent Americans,” DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin said. DHS stated that Garcia paid his own way out of the country and did not receive any taxpayer dollars that have been offered to others to self-deport.

Garcia was a “known member” of MS-13, a notoriously violent gang that has been designated a foreign terrorist organization. According to DHS, he was in possession of drugs and rolls of money during his arrest and was arrested alongside two other gang members.

He was also pulled over on a highway transporting eight passengers with no luggage, for which DHS accused him of human trafficking. Garcia is also accused of being a child predator, as court documents allege he “solicited nude photographs and videos of a minor.”

Garcia has been accused of domestic violence numerous times, with his wife filing petitions with a court against him. “She alleged that Garcia verbally abused her, kicked her, slapped her, shoved her, mentally abused her kids, locking them in their bedroom while they cried, and detained Vasquez against her will. In the 2021 filing, Vasquez claimed he bruised, punched, and scratched her while ripping off her shirt,” DHS stated.

But as Van Hollen said, Garcia obtaining his “freedom” and “dignity” is a “good day for Kilmar Abrego Garcia and his family.”

items.title: The Plague Of Sports Gambling Threatens To Swallow Up A Whole Generation Of Men
items.summary: Cracking down on vice, especially when that vice has a detrimental effect on society at large, is not anti-American.

scraped.title: Sports Gambling Threatens To Swallow Up A Generation Of Men
scraped.description: The utter plague of sports gambling that has infected America threatens to ruin the lives of millions of Americans, especially men.
scraped.author: Hayden Daniel
scraped.h1: The Plague Of Sports Gambling Threatens To Swallow Up A Whole Generation Of Men
scraped.body_text:
Cracking down on vice, especially when that vice has a detrimental effect on society at large, is not anti-American.

Sports gambling is a plague.

A friend of mine told me that a 13-year-old boy at his church has a gambling app installed on his phone. Thirteen. And he’s certainly not the only one. Online gambling, especially sports gambling, has exploded among men over the last few years.

It’s a problem that’s easy to minimize given the many other, in some cases existential, problems that face the United States. But although sports gambling may at first seem like a few innocent bets here and there on the Sunday games, the sheer scale of this mass addiction should give everyone pause.

Prior to 2018, Americans bet about $5 billion a year through sportsbooks. In 2025, that figure stood at nearly $167 billion — a 3,000 percent increase almost entirely spurred by the proliferation of sports betting apps. More than a quarter of Americans have an online sports betting account that’s active. For men between 18 and 49, it’s 52 percent . On college campuses, 67 percent of students reported betting on sports, with 16 percent saying that doing so caused them financial distress, according to the House Committee on Education and the Workforce. As the committee noted, those numbers are from three years ago and almost certainly higher today as usage of the apps continues to proliferate.

A review published in 2024 found that nearly 62 percent of adults in North America gambled within the preceding year. Again, much of that was driven by online sports gambling. Diagnoses for gambling disorder have risen 60 percent in states where sports gambling is legal since 2018. The rate of diagnoses for young men aged 18-29 more than doubled, while men aged 30-49 have the highest diagnosis rate — almost double the average. Conversely, diagnoses plummeted by 30 percent in the 11 states that have not legalized sports gambling.

What caused this explosion? A Supreme Court case and the peculiar legal status of some betting markets. In 2018, SCOTUS struck down the Professional and Amateur Sports Protection Act, a federal law passed in 1992 that prohibited state-approved sports gambling (except in Nevada, of course). The 6-3 decision in Murphy v. National Collegiate Athletic Association , as the case is known, came from the court’s conservative majority, who argued that the federal law violated the 10th Amendment. Less than a decade later, 39 states and the District of Columbia allow sports gambling. Thirty-two states and D.C. allow online sports gambling.

Certain betting platforms, like Kalshi and Polymarket, don’t operate like traditional sportsbooks, which, while legal in most states, are more heavily regulated and taxed. Prediction markets, which allow betting on sports, are legal in all 50 states, even in ones that ban other types of sports gambling. These types of platforms also don’t have to obtain state gambling licenses, and revenues from these prediction markets are only subject to federal taxes, while traditional gambling sites are subject to state, tribal, and federal taxes, according to ESPN.

And the anecdote mentioned at the beginning of this article is merely the tip of the iceberg. It’s not difficult to find absolute horror stories that have resulted from online sports gambling addiction.

One 29-year-old man, featured on CBS News Sunday Morning back in September, “bets on sports every day” and by his own admission bets between $80,000 and $100,000 per year — just as much or more than his annual salary. One Illinois man bet $2 million through credit cards, 401(k) loans, and wedding money on the site DraftKings. One young man said that he started gambling at age 16 and wagered more than $100,000 before he turned 21. He was thousands of dollars in debt before he even finished high school, and he said online gambling addiction was pervasive among his peers.

The X account Degenerate Tracker chronicles a seemingly endless number of examples of people utterly ruining their lives through online sports gambling.

The rise in sports gambling, driven almost entirely by the rise of betting apps, threatens to trap millions of Americans in spirals of addiction, depression, and lifelong financial woes. Many conservatives today claim to care about these issues, especially how they affect young men. If they really do care, then now is not the time for half-measures.

It’s easy to say, “Think of the children!” on a topic like this, and it’s certainly important to think about how this affects youths who are inundated with sports betting ads. And most people can support putting restrictions on youth access to harmful and addictive materials, like we already do with tobacco and alcohol — and as we are beginning to move toward with things like smartphones and social media.

However, once someone turns 18, as has become the modern conventional wisdom, society magically becomes free of any obligation to put in place reasonable protections for its citizens. But the usual libertarian mantra of “consenting adults can do what they want” is insufficient on this issue, just as we’re beginning to recognize it is insufficient on other issues like the transgenderism delusion. When the problem becomes so widespread and so damaging that it threatens an entire generation’s financial security, the authorities have the right and the obligation to step in. In fact, not doing so would constitute gross negligence and represent yet another symptom of our nation’s apparent death wish.

The first law against gambling in what would become the United States was issued by the Puritans of Massachusetts in 1638. New Hampshire banned gambling in 1721 specifically to “prevent the unnecessary impoverishment of the gambler’s family.” In the 19th century, most states outlawed lotteries, while New York passed a law in 1851 that mandated a fine for gambling houses and required the destruction of confiscated gambling equipment. Nevada completely banned all forms of gambling in 1909.

Cracking down on vice, especially when that vice has a detrimental effect on society at large, is not anti-American. It’s the basic function of a civilization that wants to survive in the long run. If we don’t move to enact common-sense regulation or prohibition on online sports betting, it will end up destroying an entire generation of men.

scraped.title: Douglas Murray: When Writers Stop Believing in Free Speech
scraped.description: PEN America long rallied around authors facing persecution. Now its members seem more interested in policing one another.
scraped.author: Douglas Murray
scraped.body_text:
Happy Thanksgiving from The Free Press! As you travel to spend time with family and friends, we’re celebrating the holiday with our biggest sale of the year: 25 percent off everything we have to offer. That means columns from Douglas Murray (scroll down for his latest), Ross Douthat, Abigail Shrier, Niall Ferguson, Nellie Bowles, and so many more. It also means access to our livestreams, podcasts, videos, and live events.

Most importantly, it means joining a community united by the founding mission of this publication: that the truth matters, and that the only way to find it is to think for yourself. We hope you’ll join us. —The Editors

Is there anything on Earth worse than writers’ associations? I don’t mean the sort of samizdat groups that exist in closed societies, where organization is needed. I mean the sort of organizations in the West that specialize in self-congratulatory backslapping and professions of their own “bravery.” No other line of work makes such a fuss of itself. Firefighters’ associations do not endlessly applaud themselves for their courage. Police and the military tend to demonstrate their own accountability with actions, not words. Awards seasons are not rolling events in these professions. But for a certain type of writer, you can never have enough self-applause.

Which is one of the reasons why it is not endlessly sad to watch PEN America pull itself apart.

There was a time when PEN was an organization with some purpose and backbone. Memorably, when there were actual threats to the life of a writer, Salman Rushdie, PEN was an indispensable rallying point for those who wanted to defend writers against the assassins’ veto. Fast-forward a quarter of a century from the fatwa, and PEN had degraded, as all good causes do.

scraped.title: Every Angle on the Huang Scandal. How to Avoid an AI Dark Age. Does Meghan Markle Deserve an Apology? Plus. . .
scraped.description: In today’s Front Page, a recap of Jensen Huang’s scandal. Kat Rosenfield on the Melania documentary. Rod Dreher on the Christians perverting Christianity. And more.
scraped.author: The Free Press
scraped.body_text:
It’s Wednesday, November 25. This is The Front Page , your daily window into the world of The Free Press —and our take on the world at large.

On Tuesday, a day after his astonishing return as CEO of Nvidia, Jensen Huang apologized for making “some terrible mistakes,” and said he was in therapy “every day.” The story remains the biggest in the world, encompassing the global economy, the technology transforming our world, the race with China, and more. We’ve published a lot on it in the last few days. So we wanted to kick off today’s Front Page with a quick recap of what you might have missed.

There’s Joe Nocera on why Huang was too big to fail:

Aaron MacLean on whether the White House has endangered America by facilitating Huang’s comeback:

Niall Ferguson on the great man theory of AI, and whether Huang can save us from a crash:

Matt Pottinger on the logic of Huang’s return:

Ross Douthat on his own test for AI superintelligence—when can it do Jensen Huang’s job?:

And if you want to go back a little further, read Bethany McLean from last month on the warning signs of the financial trouble stored up in the AI sector:

We also have one new tech story this morning. It’s by Palantir CTO Shyam Sankar , and it’s about why everything keeps breaking and what we can do to stop it. A series of alarming outages over the last few weeks has many wondering if we’re at the start of some kind of technological apocalypse. We may well be, says Shyam. But there’s a way to fight back. Read his piece on how.

But we know that there is a limit to one’s appetite for stories on AI, foreign policy, and chip wars, especially with the holiday around the corner—and that, as you catch your plane, train, or automobile home for Thanksgiving, you may want to tuck into something a little different. And we have plenty of entertaining and illuminating writing for you on other subjects today, including Kat Rosenfield on the new Melania documentary—she was gripped— Sarah Ditum on whether Meghan Markle is owed an apology, and Rod Dreher on the Christian case against the New Christian Right. And more. Let’s get to those stories now.

—Oliver Wiseman

Get all The Free Press has to offer, now for 25 percent off.

Ross Douthat. Abigail Shrier. Douglas Murray. Niall Ferguson. Coleman Hughes. Caitlin Flanagan. Nellie Bowles. Arthur Brooks. Kat Rosenfield. Tyler Cowen. The voices you trust, all in one place.

Subscribe

Earlier this month, Meghan Markle’s father was charged with possession of child pornography. For most daughters, that news would be catastrophic, but for the Duchess of Sussex, it may be her salvation. Shortly after her father’s arrest, the same tabloids that targeted Markle are treating her as a victim, and asking whether they owe her “a collective apology.” Does the former royal deserve our pity? Should the tabloids apologize? Can she ride her father’s sex scandal into a second chance? In her column today, Sarah Ditum weighs the case.

To most, the phrase “Christ is King” is a pious expression of Christian faith. But in recent months, it’s taken on a disturbing new meaning. The term has become a rallying cry for the “New Christian Right”—a group that wants to repeal women’s suffrage, and expel anyone who isn’t white or Christian from the U.S. Today, Rod Dreher lays out what this radical faction believes, and argues that, though they may be fringe right now, that doesn’t mean they aren’t dangerous.

Last weekend, Amazon released “Melania: The Series,” a new documentary that reveals almost nothing about our First Lady. Critics are calling the show “bloodless,” “dead-eyed,” and “regurgitated slop”—but our columnist Kat Rosenfield says that’s precisely what makes it so compelling. “As fun as it is to hate-watch this show as a work of pro-Melania propaganda, the more accurate and interesting viewing is one that understands it as something else: an expression of the First Lady’s near-total indifference to what anyone thinks of her,” she writes. Read Kat’s piece on how Melania mastered the art of being a public person who reveals nothing.

This week, Pope Francis’s estate released 160 pages of his private diary. The book promises an unprecedented look into the mind of the late spiritual leader. And while it has its moments—such as Pope Francis’s three meetings with the devil— Matthew Walther says that “The Private Diary of Pope Francis” is a disappointment. “Those who are expecting a gossipy sort of book in which the late pontiff unburdens himself about Donald Trump or Benedict XVI or even Jim Harbaugh will find little to satisfy them,” he writes. So why has the book been published at all? Read Matthew’s piece on the cash-grab by the late pope’s estate—and what we all lose in treating the pontiff like a celebrity.

The Trump administration banned Singapore-based Megaspeed from acquiring advanced semiconductor chips on Monday. The new restrictions come after allegations that Nvidia and its CEO Jensen Huang used the company to funnel prohibited chips to China.

The U.S. is investigating whether the Iranian regime is behind a new wave of cyberattacks against ships in the Middle East. As many as 50 vessels carrying oil, chemical products, and potentially explosive materials have been targeted thus far as the conflict with Iran rages on.

The U.S. is reportedly planning to raise tariffs against China and dozens of other countries during this Thanksgiving week. The increased pressure comes after the Trump administration accused these nations of prioritizing their own domestic industries, rather than trading with American companies.

Iranian singer Parastoo Ahmadi received 74 lashes from her government this week. The punishment comes two years after she sang without her hijab during a 2024 virtual concert, as the regime continues to crack down on its citizens’ freedom. (For more on this story, read Masih Alinejad’s piece .)

The Pentagon is reportedly in talks with General Motors and Ford to supercharge the production of military drones. If they reach a deal, the collaboration with the private sector could signal a major step in addressing our arms shortage .

The Army is set to blow up a stash of degrading explosives in southeastern Iowa on Wednesday. Environmental groups tried to get a court to block the detonation on Monday, but the judges ruled unanimously in favor of the project, citing the old weapons’ potential to spontaneously explode.

President Trump awarded his former lawyer Rudy Giuliani the Presidential Medal of Freedom on Tuesday. The White House praised Giuliani for his crackdown on crime during his time as New York City’s mayor, and his leadership in the aftermath of 9/11.

South Korea has rolled out a new policy awarding up to $375,000 to anyone who catches a student using AI to cheat on the country’s college-entrance exam. President Lee Jae Myung equated academic dishonesty with stock market manipulation, emphasizing the need to impose restrictions early on in the AI race.

Kat or River - never sure which one is worse.

I remember at one point we were giving old ammuniction to Ukraine to use before it degraded enough to be dangerous. I guess we have stopped that, but why?

scraped.title: My all-AI Thanksgiving
scraped.author: Valerie Stivers
scraped.h1: My all-AI Thanksgiving Claude will seat your relatives now
scraped.body_text:
Among the civilizational concerns caused by artificial intelligence, the fate of the food blogger doesn’t rank high. But the new technology seems poised to dramatically change their function, if not put them out of business altogether. As most people working on their Thanksgiving menus have already discovered, if you ask Google for a recipe, “AI mode” will pop out the sum of human wisdom on the matter, no need to click through to an actual website. This is theft of user content on a grand scale, since the AI platforms trawl the cumulative product of human creativity — but who can stop them?

The more pressing question on the eve of the holiday is: can the machine cook?

In my research for my forthcoming book on famous artists and their favorite recipes, I’ve already discovered a few bewitching features of AI food wisdom. It makes short work of vexing and obscure questions that formerly required a deep dive down an internet rabbit hole and often, in my case, a trip to the library.

How did early Americans make a glaze for a cake? Powdered sugar and whipped egg white — meringue, basically, which hardens to a delicious crisp shell in 24 hours, voilà . It’s also an amazing source of ideas outside the narrow lanes of daily food practice, which is another way of saying that, as in the other creative arts, a person with the existing knowledge to use it right can wildly enhance her creative output.

Less positive for the Thanksgiving guests, however, is that AI really doesn’t know how to cook. In terms of basics like quantity and technique, it’s going to tell you something , but whether that’s the right thing is luck of the draw. When I asked Claude, ChatGPT, and Google’s Gemini for the best way to prepare a turkey, ChatGPT recommended dry-brining with herbs and then roasting, while the other two suggested the answer that’s trendy this year — spatchcocking, which means cutting out the backbone and flattening the bird.

A user with existing knowledge can make useful judgments about this information, which is a combination of incorrect (you don’t use herbs in a dry brine) and impractical (no timid cook is going to spatchcock a turkey). The suggestion is fire in the hands of a master, like the New York Times food writer Melissa Clark, who has declared spatchcocking her preferred method. But otherwise, it’s more dangerous than not.

By Valerie Stivers

I also asked for “creative” early American ideas on how to prepare sweet potatoes and discovered a different set of issues. The machine’s ideas were mouth-watering: a sweet-potato pone in the black, Southern tradition; a “plantation-and-tavern-style” sweet potato whipped with lemon and brandy; a mid-Atlantic sweet potato roasted and glazed with maple syrup and cider-vinegar; and a 19th-century sweet-potato scalloped with chestnuts. The descriptions of these dishes promised “dense, chewy, and caramelized” crusts, “nutty, velvety, and autumnal” flavors, and more. But three recipe tests exactly following the instructions produced results that ranged from mushy and insipid (the maple-and-cider glaze) to actually gross (the eggy sweet potatoes in the pone). I recognized the excess butter, unbalanced proportions, and unwise baking temperatures as I tried these dishes, but I did it for posterity. Of four dishes, three were flops, and the scallop — slightly adjusted because by this time I’d given up listening to AI — was a keeper.

Useful features such as AI’s ability to scale recipes up or down based on your number of guests or your eight-inch pan when the recipe calls for a 10-inch pan also demand informed judgment. For real beginners, AI’s advice is better than what you might calculate. For a more experienced cook: if you think it doesn’t make sense, listen to yourself.

Listening to our better instincts, I’d argue, is exactly what AI is training us not to do. Its arc of seduction bends toward evil, leading us to not use our heads when we should, yet endlessly encouraging the kind of impulse that leads brain-damaged elderly men to sell all their possessions and set off for the nearest bus terminal, clutching a photograph of a woman who doesn’t exist . For example, I lied to Google’s Gemini, telling it that I was making a multicultural Thanksgiving menu with early American recipes, and asked for advice on a chop suey, maybe from San Francisco’s Chinatown. Its reply? “An early Chinese-American chop suey (circa 1890s–1907) is a great addition to a multicultural historical Thanksgiving menu….” These words are affirming but untrue. An early Chinese-American chop suey is not a great addition to a Thanksgiving table: no one’s relatives want chop suey for Thanksgiving. (The recipe turned out pretty good, though, so I’m sharing it below.)

What this kind of query really showcases is the machine’s ability to provide the raw materials for cooking inspiration when you provide the spark of creativity yourself. Asking it directly for a multicultural, early-American menu, for example, got me a predictable — and predictably woke — response. Would I care for recipes in the black, Indigenous, or Mexican traditions? Operating on my own vague intuitions, like asking for the chop suey, or a fall version of the type of chilled fruit soup favored by Polish immigrants to Minnesota, revealed troves of wisdom I would have had great difficulty sourcing myself, that I could then use to make up my own recipes.

Minnesota Polish fruit soups are dishes of pasta in fruit purée, for example, and look about as horrifying as anything you might find in an internet search result. I tried a winter, dried-fruit version of the same soup, elevated by my knowledge that the self-harvested and homemade ingredients relied upon by the sturdy Polish pioneers aren’t fungible with the supermarket dried fruits of today. This dish should only be attempted with gorgeous dried fruit from a specialty grocer. I also knew that the liquid quantity proposed by Gemini was too little, the thickener too much, and that the dicing should be much finer than suggested, because the fruit will swell in liquid. With all my adjustments, the finished product was a bowl of beautiful multicolored confetti, floating in a delicious, chilled fruit liquor.

To be clear, some of the AI recipes are great: the point is that you just can’t tell, unless you can. Gemini’s chop suey, as written, was dour on the color palette but better-tasting in a side-by-side test than the one I’ve been developing for my book. And making it with leftover dark-meat turkey and giblets is a brilliant innovation on Thanksgiving leftovers. It’s even not-terrible paired with the smoky, meltingly unctuous glory of the roasted-chestnut-and-sweet-potato scallop.

By Kathleen Stock

Lastly, I’ve been experimenting with a random Gemini-tidbit that intrigued me months ago: early Americans baked cakes from “leftover” bread dough. In brief, most yeasted cakes enrich the basic bread dough formula with butter, sugar, and other ingredients, such as spices and dried fruit. We moderns fold the butter and sugar into the dough, then allow it to rise. As AI suggested to me, however, in homes where dough was a daily occurrence, a cook might repurpose an already-risen dough, by adding the enrichments after the rise. The significance of this can hardly be overstated, because what you’d get if you made bread from the same modern method usually used for enriched dough (just stir, no kneading required) is … bad bread. Adding enrichments to a dough handled properly in order to make good bread sounds like a game-changer.

The classic Sullivan Street Bakery no-knead bread recipe , is the best-developed, most entry-level technique I know of for a home baker to make a decent loaf. There’s an overnight rise and a round of folding; it’s not easy, but it is foolproof. I made a half-batch of dough by this method, then enriched it before the second rise, followed by baking in a six-inch tin and glazing the old-fashioned way, with meringue. The chewy, pillowy, delicately flavored results were a revelation on just how good a cake-version of bread can be.

As painful as it is for this technophobe to admit, the combination of my own knowledge and experience with the random free-association enabled by AI made for an amazing menu. Nonetheless, the process of paying close attention to what the technology can do reminded me to avoid AI when I can, especially for my creative work. I will be more careful about clicking the “AI mode” button in the future, even when I’m just cooking dinner.

This will mean giving up the benefits discussed above, which are real. The fate of the food bloggers, though, is a cautionary tale: for many years, well-meaning small-professional home cooks have been pouring their time, their personalities, their family traditions, and the best of their expertise into the machine, building businesses whose accumulated wealth is now being wiped out. They trusted the tech, or didn’t see around the corners, or in a more positive light, if you’re a techno-optimist, they were just the unfortunates whose pulped lives will be the fertile soil for the growth of other people’s new businesses.

What they were really doing, however, was making a deal whose terms they were unaware of. The new form of distribution that allowed home cooks to suddenly compete with food magazines and communicate with millions seemed free — but it wasn’t. The bloggers’ legacy now trains our robot overlords and enriches Silicon Valley. Oops. In the same vein, I don’t know which of my own skills and thoughts prolonged interaction with AI might take from me. My food is good, because I know what I’m doing from a lifetime of analog experience and decades of curating my exposure to other good cooks whose work I like and trust. How might that change when I start consuming slop instead?

Hospitality is the gift of my home to my guests and my cooking for their pleasure. It is actually free, and I want to keep it that way. Happy Thanksgiving.

Minnesota Polish Fruit Soup Serves Eight

Fill a large soup pot or Dutch oven with six cups of cold water, and add ¼ cup of raisins and the following ingredients, finely chopped: ¾ cup pitted dried plums, ½ cup dried apple rings,

½ cup dried pears. Soak for an hour to soften, then add a cinnamon stick and three cloves, and heat to a simmer. Simmer covered, on low, for 10 minutes. Fish out the cinnamon stick and cloves, then add ⅓ cup honey or sugar, a tablespoon of lemon juice, and ½ cup of heavy cream, whisked with a teaspoon of flour, and cook briefly to thicken, about three minutes. Let cool, and chill in the refrigerator overnight. Stir in a handful of cold cooked Polish kluski noodles or other decorative pasta just before serving. Drizzle each bowl with honey, and garnish with mint. Serve cold.

Gemini’s Creative Sweet Potato Scallop Serves Eight

Preheat the oven to 375°F and generously grease a 9 x 13 baking dish. Combine a cup of heavy cream, ½ cup of milk, a teaspoon of salt, ¼ teaspoon of black pepper, ¼ teaspoon of allspice, a pinch of nutmeg, and a tablespoon of maple syrup in a medium saucepan, and gently heat. Do not bring to a boil. Let it sit for 10 minutes to infuse. Peel two pounds of sweet potatoes, about three medium, and thinly slice on a mandoline. Finely chop ¾ cup of whole roasted chestnuts. Layer ⅓ of the sweet potato rounds in the baking dish and top with half the chestnuts. Repeat with another layer of sweet potato and chestnut, and top with the remaining sweet potatoes. Pour in the infused cream. Cover with tinfoil and bake for 35 minutes. In a small bowl, combine ½ cup of coarse breadcrumbs with a tablespoon of melted butter, and toss to combine. After 30 minutes, remove the foil, spread the buttery breadcrumbs evenly over the top of the potatoes, and cook 20 minutes more, until the crust is golden. Serve immediately.

Chinese-American Turkey Chop Suey, 1907 Serves Eight

Mix two tablespoons of light soy sauce, two tablespoons of dark soy sauce, two tablespoons of brown sugar, a teaspoon of sesame oil and two tablespoons of cornstarch in a small bowl and set aside. In a large bowl, toss the following together: two small yellow onions, cut in thin wedges; ½ small Savoy cabbage, sliced, about six cups; ½ jicama root, peeled, quartered and sliced in ⅛ inch wedges; two cups of mushrooms, sliced; and two cups of fresh mung-bean sprouts. Heat a tablespoon of peanut oil in each of two large skillets (or work in batches if you have only one large skillet). Add half of the vegetables to each skillet and stir-fry until just tender, then add four cups of leftover turkey meat, ideally dark meat and giblets, a cup of chicken stock, and the reserved sauce mixture, distributing evenly between skillets. Cook until the sauce has thickened, three minutes more. Serve over rice or mashed potatoes.

Early American Cake Serves Eight

First, make the bread dough. Combine 1½ cups of flour in a large bowl with ⅛ teaspoon of yeast and a teaspoon of salt, and whisk to combine. Add ¾ cup of water and stir to combine, until you have a sticky, shaggy dough. Use your hands if necessary. Cover and let rise in a warm place for 12 hours.

After the first rise, “fold” the dough by pulling up a side of it and folding it over itself a couple of times. Let rest for 30 minutes while you prepare the ingredients for enrichment. In the bowl of a stand mixer, combine four tablespoons of softened butter, ½ cup sugar, ½ teaspoon of cinnamon, ¼ teaspoon of nutmeg, and ⅛ teaspoon of ground cloves, and beat using the paddle attachment, until fluffy. Add an egg and beat again until combined. When the bread dough has rested, pull it into golf-ball-sized pieces and add to the mixer. Beat until combined, then add ¼ cup plus two tablespoons of bread flour, and incorporate. Grease a six-inch cake pan. Pour the dough into the pan, and let rise in a warm place, two more hours. Preheat the oven to 425°F. Bake for 40 to 45 minutes, until a tester in the center of the cake comes out clean. Let cool.

Make the glaze by whipping 1 egg white in a stand mixer with the whisk attachment, until foamy and forming soft peaks. Slowly add 1⅓ cups of powdered sugar and continue to whisk until it is glossy and thick, but not stiff. Add a teaspoon of lemon juice and whip to combine. Pour the glaze over the cooled cake, spreading evenly with a rubber spatula. Let dry for 24 hours.

Valerie Stivers is a senior editor of UnHerd US.

scraped.title: Natural England is killing the economy
scraped.author: Lawrence Newport
scraped.h1: Natural England is killing the economy The quango must be culled
scraped.body_text:
Tony Juniper, chair of Natural England, has overseen a regime that is anything but permissive. (JG Fox)

Tony Juniper, chair of Natural England, has overseen a regime that is anything but permissive. (JG Fox)

To govern, the old saying goes, is to choose. The modern British state, preferring not to choose, has found an alternative: referring, reviewing, consulting, meeting. Difficult decisions are handed down the chain to faceless bodies. These bodies are often led by ideologues who operate at arm’s length from accountability.

The paramount example of this phenomenon — of a British state unable to make decisions, and of a bureaucracy detached from improving the lives of people across this country — is Natural England. Established in 2006, Natural England was given the purview of protecting the natural environment in planning decisions. That is a worthy goal. But the organization has little accountability, and little incentive to take any risk or offer even a “yes”. As a result, its goal has been subsumed beneath ideological ambitions, or — even worse — the repeated spectacle of bureaucrats obstructing construction and other activity simply in order to show that work was indeed done and that every risk was indeed mitigated.

The current chair, Tony Juniper, is a former Green Party parliamentary candidate and anti-nuclear activist who was appointed by a Conservative government. Natural England was supposed to be above politics, but it is filled with activists who have been garlanded with veto power over British housing and infrastructure.

Around a year ago, LFG and others started pushing for the quango’s abolition. A month ago, the Conservatives pledged to get rid of the quango once they were back in power. Then Reform did too. And now, it appears, the Labour government may be following suit. A “sprawling web” of arm’s-length bodies, said Louise Haigh, the First Secretary of State, has become a “tax” on growth. Natural England, it seems, may finally be struck from the British state.

By Lawrence Newport

Why is this necessary? The abolition of Natural England isn’t an attack on nature, though the organization’s nice-sounding name may make you think otherwise. Rather, it is an attack on absurdity and unaccountability. As with any unaccountable body, the organization’s decisions became steadily more absurd. To take a few examples: the taxpayer has had to underwrite a £100 million for the construction of a bat tunnel to save bats along HS2 — a tunnel that is actually not, it turns out, bat-proof. We are also paying more than £700 million for a “fish disco” at Hinkley Point C, a nuclear plant under interminably slow construction. The disco is meant to deter fish by broadcasting underwater sound — but, as EDF’s own figures show, only two salmon were detected within one kilometre of the intakes over a period of two years .

These are the well-known stories of Natural England, but its strange overreach has gone much further. In a Britain where objections rule the day, the organization made itself a chief architect of newer, more complicated ways of saying “no”. In Royston, Hertfordshire, a nearly 30-year-old annual charity kite festival was ended after Natural England objected to it in 2024. Preposterously, it told the local Rotary Club that using 1% of local Therfield Heath, in the way the kite-fliers had for nearly three decades, would result in a “likely adverse impact” due — in part — to the “mowing regime” .

Natural England then suggested several alternative sites, all of which were unsuitable, including one in the middle of a “bowl” surrounded by hills, a placement guaranteeing no wind. The outcome? No money raised for charity, no families and kids out with kites, an annual tradition closed. The festival hasn’t returned.

This is far from the only example. In Hoylake, Merseyside, the local firework display, which was held to raise money for the RNLI, was canceled after Natural England objected . Specifically, it objected to moving anything across the beach by vehicle , meaning that everything had to be carried across the beach by hand. With the additional requirements that the bonfire be placed further away, and made smaller, orchestrating the event became ever more onerous. It has never run again.

Nearby, a beach is now covered in slime — because the local council has been advised that raking the beach, and using weedkiller, might be unlawful . The slime is the result of decaying beach vegetation that would previously have been cleared. 14,000 locals signed a petition asking for “amenity” space to be returned , to have their beach cleared so they could use it again. But Natural England told the council it couldn’t go ahead , and its advice continues to constrain the council from clearing the vegetation. It does so to protect the roosting land of thousands of birds — though those same birds used to roost in large numbers on the sand before Natural England’s advice changed, in 2020, so as to stop the removal of the vegetation. The swamp remains; only a slight carve-out has finally been agreed to clear some of it for lifeboats . Residents are left without a beach space. No family picnics: the slime comes first.

The list of projects that Natural England has said no to is never-ending. A theme park application was withdrawn , and a small town’s worth of housing , after the contaminated brownfield area — positioned next to the high-speed rail line in Ebbsfleet — was designated by the quango as important for wildlife including a particular species of jumping spider . After Norfolk County Council committed to build the Norwich Western Link road back in 2016, it finally applied for permission in 2024 — at which point, two days before the application was received, Natural England changed its guidance on bats , which meant the road construction would now face significant hurdles. Construction on the £274 million road was meant to begin in this year — but the thwarted council is still searching for alternative routes .

This is all to say nothing of the prospective cull of 75% of Dartmoor ponies. Earlier this year, Natural England produced new grazing guidance for farmers. The practical result of this guidance was to result in farmers having to choose between either culling their own livestock or culling Dartmoor’s ponies. Ultimately, this was going to lead to an estimated 75% of Dartmoor’s ponies being culled . Following public outcry, the organization attempted to defend itself by arguing that it was not calling for a cull at all — technically true, because it was simply the practical, obvious outcome of their new guidance. The government simply changed the rules, giving ponies a carve-out from the new grazing rules. The ponies were saved, no thanks to Natural England.

Granted, Natural England’s power is derived from overzealous environmental regulations, some of which must also be unpicked. But its interpretations of these regulations are consistently broad and repeatedly expanding. It is for this reason that what was once legal is deemed illegal — as in the case of Royston and Hoylake — and that Natural England has been so confident in bat tunnels and fish discos.

By John Rapley

An institution that once objected to the planning application for its own office is now finally facing accountability for its choices. We have allowed ministers to dodge difficult decisions for too long. SW1 has encouraged a politics of no trade-offs, of interminable proceduralism at the expensive of decision-making.

Growth isn’t something we can take for granted. It doesn’t happen automatically or by default. It requires humans acting on the world — trying something new, taking risks, and working day by day to achieve something. The world today is the result of generations of that attempt. Our ancestors dragged us out of the poverty and misery of natural existence — the brutality of high infant mortality and the devastation of plagues and famines. We have been gifted with industry, technology and possibility. We have the ability to grow those gifts — to grow ourselves —- but our status quo is one of decline.

Our current stock of politicians have chosen to maintain that status quo. They have created and deferred to a labyrinth of systems designed to remove them from the terrible business of governing. A network of quangos that pulls decisions down the chain; fleets of lawyers who advise against government decisions on the basis of ever-more widely construed “illegality”; a planning regime at the mercy of judicial review; and a world of government advisors who are so comfortably embedded that our last Prime Minister said he had given the “Island of Strangers” speech without really reading it .

None of this is because our politicians are optimizing for votes. If they were, the country would look quite different. They don’t optimize for GDP per capita — that much is obvious. Instead, they optimize for acceptability among a particular class of people: not so much elites as much as dinner guests and immediate friends. Why was Natural England given so much power? Why was a Conservative government happy to appoint an activist to chair it? Because those circles would praise them for it: the “vibes” felt right.

Abolishing Natural England does not mean that the natural environment is unimportant. Our environment is important, but so are the people of Britain. Our politicians have a duty to them: a duty to make life easier, to give people more chances to take more risks, to get bills down, to build a world wherein people want to raise children. That means removing barriers to scaling companies, having fun, and replacing or improving the decaying infrastructure of yesteryear; it means removing unaccountable decision makers, and it means forcing politicians to look at reality square-on. MPs are elected by the British people, for the British people. They must make decisions for them, and create the conditions where their lives are likely to get better. That means trade-offs, it means difficult decisions, but it also means a path to an improved place for us all to live. The British state is far from fixed. The country remains numbed by decades of decline. But the potential closure of Natural England brings hope that the tide may finally be turning.

Lawrence Newport is the CEO and co-founder of Looking for Growth

scraped.title: Jensen Huang: king of battery-farm capitalism
scraped.author: B. Duncan Moench
scraped.h1: Jensen Huang: king of battery-farm capitalism We can't escape the machine
scraped.body_text:
“We all know that this way of living is completely unhealthy.” (Chesnot/Getty)

“We all know that this way of living is completely unhealthy.” (Chesnot/Getty)

As Americans prepare for their annual Black Friday rites of debt-financed excess, the economy’s true nature has revealed itself through an even stranger event: the return of Jensen Huang. Little could better illustrate America’s two-tiered system of economic justice. The fact that Nvidia was deemed too big to face consequences for its CEO’s actions, much less fail, illustrates two things.

First, nothing has fundamentally changed since the 2008 financial crash. Second, what has changed has been a movement in the same direction that caused the crash to start with: growth based on deceit rather than actual value-added. Do the AI companies actually make money? Do they contribute new value, or merely steal it from everyone else for their enormous gain? No one seems to care. Certainly not investors, certainly not the President. But when your economy is built on sand, you can’t fire the architects of the sandcastle.

Economist Yanis Varoufakis has dubbed our present state of affairs “technofeudalism”. In this same vein, I have previously offered the alternative “hyper-feudalism”. But the Huang affair brings our grim reality into even sharper relief, for it makes clear that our present system is one where the tech giants are building a system of total dependence — without any notion, much less guarantee, of reciprocity towards the public at large.

A serf, at least, was owed something, which is more than can be said for the creature whose situation ours most resembles. The way we live now would be better labeled “battery-farm capitalism”. Think of it as a civilizational frequency, one where we all power a giant wealth-extraction machine that everyone must remain plugged into — at all times — to keep the deception of benevolence alive.

Yes, everyone will someday have everything provided for them by “machines of loving grace” — the actual title Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei used for a recent essay. This brand of soft-pedaled progressivism serves as the nucleus of how Silicon Valley and Wall Street joined forces over the last 30 years to remake the economy in a way that ensures they hoover up all the money, and all the resources, and everyone else simply accepts their station as rudderless plebs, keeping the “attention economy” afloat through the power of their addiction to social media and other forms of pointless entertainment.

By B. Duncan Moench

As they say on therapy TikTok, “when people tell you who they are, believe them.” Indeed, in a recent Wall Street Journal profile , that’s precisely what happened with Amodei. The Journal documented that Anthropic’s CEO at one point seriously floated the notion that in the employment-free economy of the future, highly immersive video games would be needed to pacify young men — and keep them from coming after their social betters in Silicon Valley, who, of course, ought to remain the rightful rulers of the economic multiverse.

Donald Trump may enable this, but, for what it’s worth, he’s no technophile futurist — as his embarrassing “everything computer” White House lawn advertisement for Tesla illustrated. Still, with all the chaos surrounding Iran and the Strait of Hormuz, in other words a tangible economic problem, Trump learned something essential. In a second-by-second attention economy, the machine cannot be turned off — even for a moment.

Trump instinctively knew that “we” — investors on Wall Street like himself — could not risk letting Nvidia and the AI-ready microchips they produce falter because LLMs have already, just as their makers hoped, become as essential to our lives as petrol-powered transport, albeit far less useful.

That suggests a far deeper transformation. The problem with talk of “late capitalism” has always been fairly simple. Today’s obscenely unequal “free market” structure isn’t collapsing. Not even remotely, at least not in terms of keeping the masses sated and distracted. Rather, what’s collapsing are the moral foundations of liberalism itself.

The AI economy and tech IPOs are killing the Protestant work ethic, and indeed the civic-mindedness on which capitalism depends. Nearly every tech “growth company” — from OpenAI to Anthropic to Tesla — is priced not on profit but on the promise of eventual trillions, and the whole advantage evaporates the moment the market decides they’re “mature”. The crash risk is, of course, familiar, but the deeper story is what price valuation-without-profit does to liberalism’s core: tying reward to productive effort. Instead of working from that basis, in the mold of both Max Weber and Christopher Lasch, our economic system now mints unprecedented fortunes through mere anticipation , teaching its ambitious young people that actual productive work is for suckers. Social media influencer culture — fed rhetorically and literally by people like Amodei — feeds into this deception: with its “branding” logic eerily symbiotic to the work pursued by the AI giants themselves.

Liberalism is a concept distinct from both democracy and capitalism. Yet in the bleak world social-media executives and tech-monopolists are erecting, liberal democracy is becoming less and less possible. To that extent, the 2020s can be understood as in-between space, one where a new form of totalitarianism is assembling itself all around us. That future may not be feudal, but it’s capitalist all the same.

By B. Duncan Moench

Marx wagered that the capitalist class would eventually push its insatiable urge for ever-more profits with ever-greater productive efficiency into the total immiseration of working people, creating an insurmountable contradiction that would bring down the liberal, post – feudal order.

A generation later Werner Sombart — the sociologist who actually made the word “capitalism” stick — asked why there is no socialism in the United States. Sombart, like the theorist Eduard Bernstein before him, pointed out that Marx — despite all the religiosity surrounding his thought — was plain wrong that capitalism was immiserating the proletariat. American socialism, he concluded, failed to appeal on the basis of the “roast beef and apple pie” abundance seen in the country’s growing middle class. It goes without saying that those days are long gone. Even Ivy League graduates stare down the grim face of unemployment today. Could it be, then, that Marx was indeed correct about the inevitable immiseration of the masses, but that the whole affair simply took 150 years longer than he anticipated?

A century after Sombart, our supply of “roast beef” is getting smaller and more expensive by the day. Yet no new heterodox political movement of any size exists. Nobody is storming anything, which suggests that the system has found something cheaper — and more efficient — than roast beef to feed us.

Nothing that happens in the modern American battery-farm offends any actual liberal-individualist principle. No one is coerced, the fruits of screen-addiction are freely offered and freely consumed. Every consumer has, in the parlance of our times, clicked “agree” several times over somewhere down the line. All our liberal formalities have stayed on the books. We still vote, we can still hire attorneys to sue, we still post dissenting opinions on publications.

Meanwhile, the creature for whom American liberties were designed for — the church-going, community-minded, God-fearing, family-oriented citizen — is in the process of going extinct. Everyone knows this, of course, and everyone is dissatisfied. And yet we remain completely unmotivated to do anything beyond what’s convenient on our hand-held devices. Battery-farm capitalism cannot stop: not just because of the relentless ATM machine it provides for those with the largest stock portfolios, but because, without it, we might cease to function as batteries for this hideous machine and start talking to each other again.

As it is, screen addiction has created a professional class wholly unwilling — and increasingly unable — to read anything other than short-form texts. A supposedly well-educated stratum of the population is entirely dependent on subscription-based LLMs to complete their professional duties or express thoughts beyond a few hundred characters. Meanwhile, our poor and working classes exhibit levels of literacy that are quickly making Mike Judge’s Idiocracy seem prescient.

Everything is getting faster, yet also infinitely dumber. The hallmarks of AI-produced writing have crept into practically all forms of communication. News stories. Substack posts. Advertisements. YouTube videos. Press releases. Undergraduate writing assignments. Peer-reviewed scholarship. You name it and inside that space the AI-driven enshittification of thought is already the norm. Within a remarkably short period of time, since OpenAI debuted ChatGPT four years ago, almost everyone with internet access has let AI do the heavy-lifting of writing and thus, thinking, for them.

In 2020, Covid-19 was dubbed the greatest virus humanity had faced in a century. Not long after, Elon Musk began tweeting about the great “mind-virus” of wokeness infecting the planet’s elites. But as dangerous viruses go, both were small fry. The greatest infection to ever face human thought is clearly our self-consuming dependence on machines to do the thinking for us. To that extent, yes, Jensen Huang had to be reinstated because the AI golden goose must continue to lay its IPO eggs. Just as important, though, he needed to be reinstated because LLMs have become a kind second brain — and a reassuringly dull one at that.

We all know that this way of living is completely unhealthy. We all know that, economically speaking, we’re getting ripped off. We all know that the people in power are utterly self-interested. But like most battery hens, even when offered a way out of our cages, we stay put because everyone else is doing the same.

B. Duncan Moench is a writer and scholar of American political culture. He also writes the Producerist Substack.
