scraped.description: On Saturday Nov. 21, hundreds of people from across North Carolina mobilized for a statewide protest in Winton, a small town where ICE plans to reopen
scraped.author: Deja Gaston
scraped.h1: How North Carolinians are fighting beyond the ballot box to stop the opening of an ICE facility
scraped.body_text:
On Saturday Nov. 21, hundreds of people from across North Carolina mobilized for a statewide protest in Winton, a small town where ICE plans to reopen a massive detention center. Buses and carpools from Charlotte, Asheville, Greensboro, Durham, Raleigh, Wilmington, Fayetteville and more converged to raise awareness about a facility that ICE is intentionally trying to hide in a remote, rural community.

The facility is owned by GEO Group – a private prison corporation notorious for abuse against detainees. If opened, it will be one of the largest on the East Coast, holding over 1,300 people, and will dramatically escalate attacks on immigrant communities in North Carolina. Currently, most people arrested by ICE are taken to facilities further south in Georgia and Louisiana, a process which takes time and resources that slow ICE’s efforts.

The protest came just weeks after North Carolinians delivered a sweeping rebuke of Trump’s mass deportation agenda at the ballot box. In a battleground state that Trump won three times, Democrat Roy Cooper defeated Republican Michael Whatley by nearly 20% to flip the Senate seat. Democrats flipped at least seven House seats, including districts newly gerrymandered to favor Republicans. They also took control of the state House and broke the Republican’s state Senate supermajority.

Since 2010, North Carolina has been controlled by a Republican dominated state legislature that has contributed to making it the worst ranked state for workers. North Carolina has the second lowest unionization rate in the country and is ranked dead last in public school funding. These unprecedented election results show that North Carolinians are fed up with a right-wing status quo and are demanding change.

The election also reflects a growing anger across the state against ICE’s attacks on immigrant communities. North Carolina has seen massive protests standing against ICE terror, with major mobilizations emerging in early 2025 and again during the summer, many of them led by the children of immigrants. When ICE and Border Patrol terrorized the state last November, we again saw mass demonstrations, shutdowns and walkouts across North Carolina. ICE violence disproportionately targeted the state’s Latin American community, whose vote shifted 34% to Democrats compared to 2024.

The midterm elections make it clear that mass consciousness has shifted, in North Carolina and across the U.S., but we cannot rely on the Democrats if we are serious about stopping ICE. History has shown us time and time again that the Democratic Party will not come to our rescue.

The Democrats incorporated “comprehensive immigration reform” into their platform in 2004, and Barack Obama promised to pass it during his first year in office. Despite controlling the House, Senate and Presidency between 2009-2011, the Democrats failed to act. Instead, the same administration deported over three million immigrants. In 2010, it was six Democratic senators who voted against passing the DREAM Act, which would have created a pathway to citizenship for millions of immigrants.

Here in North Carolina, Democratic Senator-elect Roy Cooper has so far said nothing about the ICE detention center opening in his state. Democrat Governor Josh Stein has expressed his opposition to the detention center, but said there’s nothing he can do: “The planned ICE detention center in Winton is not state-owned, and I did not approve this transaction. Like many other North Carolinians, I do not want it in our state. ICE and Border Patrol have not earned our trust.”

In fact, only three NC Democratic congresspeople have even spoken against the proposed detention center. In a recent statement , representatives Valerie Foushee, Alma Adams, and Deborah Ross wrote “We respectfully request answers on the decision to reopen Rivers and how ICE intends to uphold detainee dignity, rights, health, and safety.”

If most North Carolina Democrats will not even mention the ICE detention center being opened in our state, how can we trust them to defend our immigrant community? We need more than just statements. It is not enough for the Democrats to “respectfully request answers.” Democrats won big in North Carolina, and they will have the ability to stop ICE terror – both at the federal and state level. Now is the time to demand more from our elected representatives and to hold them to account.

North Carolina Democrats could introduce legislation overturning or weakening S.B. 153, an anti-immigrant bill passed last year that requires state police to collaborate with ICE. They could sue to delay the detention center’s opening, like in San Antonio , or introduce legislation banning private detention centers like GEO Group’s from operating in the state, like was done in Maryland .

At the federal level, Congress controls the funding for DHS, ICE’s parent agency. Democrats could use their new majority in the House and Senate to shut down the Winton detention center by cutting DHS’s funding.

But this is the bare minimum. Simply shutting down one detention center is not enough. There are nearly 70,000 people held in ICE’s concentration camps, 70% of whom have no criminal conviction. At least 57 people have already died in detention since Trump’s second term. Democrats must use their new majority to grant amnesty and full rights to all immigrants, provide a pathway to citizenship and abolish ICE – a demand supported by 48% of Americans.

The only solution to ICE terror is to build a mass movement. The racist Sensenbrenner bill, which would have made it a felony to be undocumented, was only defeated in 2006 after millions of immigrants boycotted shopping and walked out of school and work. DACA was only passed in 2012 after undocumented youth risked arrest and deportation to stage sit-ins and occupations. Border Patrol and Greg Bovino were only kicked out of Minneapolis after 100,000 people shut the city down in a general strike on Jan. 23 and then again on Jan. 30.

The Winton protest shows that the movement in North Carolina, which inflicted a massive defeat to the Trump program on Election Day, will not stop at the ballot box. That hundreds of people drove hours to a remote corner of the state to show that ICE can’t hide from the people is a powerful demonstration that North Carolinians are ready to keep fighting.

It is our responsibility to continue organizing to:

We cannot rely on politicians to stop ICE. We must build a movement powerful enough to force them to act.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

Buses and carpools from Charlotte, Asheville, Greensboro, Durham, Raleigh, Wilmington, Fayetteville and more converged to raise awareness about a facility that ICE is intentionally trying to hide in a remote, rural community.

items.title: The Bronx is ready for socialism
items.summary: Up against incumbent Ritchie Torres, his $14 million war chest and the entire political establishment, socialist public school teacher Andre Easton won nearly one in 11voters in New York’s 15th Congressional District.

scraped.title: The Bronx is ready for socialism
scraped.description: Up against incumbent Ritchie Torres, his $14 million war chest and the entire political establishment, socialist public school teacher Andre Easton wo
scraped.author: Jasper S
scraped.h1: The Bronx is ready for socialism
scraped.body_text:
Up against incumbent Ritchie Torres, his $14 million war chest and the entire political establishment, socialist public school teacher Andre Easton won nearly one in 11 voters in New York’s 15th Congressional District.

Easton, running on the “Socialism PSL” ballot line, won 8.7% of the vote and beat that mark in 144 election districts, according to unofficial results . This accounts for a total of 10,647 votes for socialism in what is known as the poorest congressional district in the United States, or as we said on the campaign trail, the most exploited congressional district.

In one South Bronx election district, more than one in four voters chose socialism. And in 123 EDs, from Mott Haven and Melrose to Belmont, Norwood and Eastchester, voters picked the socialist candidate over the Republican.

The millions behind Ritchie Torres come from the worst of the billionaire class: the pro-Israel lobby , real estate developers , and crypto and AI super PACs bankrolled by Trump-supporting megadonors .

Despite facing these odds, our campaign successfully collected 10,000 signatures to get socialism on the ballot in the Bronx in the span of 13 days. Determined not only to secure votes but also to build a lasting movement for socialism in the Bronx, we began canvassing in December 2025. By November of this year, we were holding outreach sessions from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m. daily. Our campaign secured major media coverage — from an appearance on iconic NYC hip hop radio station Hot 97 to coverage in The Guardian , The Hill , The New York Post , Al Jazeera and The Associated Press .

Through countless outreach conversations across NY-15, our campaign learned that the distrust Bronx residents have for politicians has been misrepresented as conservatism and apathy.

In reality, this distrust points to a longing for radical, system-wide change. The Bronx is ready for a whole new system: a system where working people control the economy and the government, not the billionaires. A system that actually meets the needs of the people and the planet.

We’re currently witnessing the Democrats do a victory lap.

It is true that workers across the country are right to rejoice in the fact that voters dealt a major blow to Trump and the Republican Party on Nov. 3. But we cannot forget that the Democrats are beholden, just as the Republicans are, to the billionaire agenda — funneled through lobbying groups like AIPAC, the military-industrial complex and big business. The Democrats remind us of this every time they hold majorities in Congress and fail to pass even the most basic reforms that bring us to the polls in the first place: ending the war, affordability, universal health care, defending civil rights, or stopping ICE and police violence.

Few areas of the country are as familiar with the broken promises of the Democratic Party as the Bronx. The Bronx has been blue for essentially the entire modern political era. Democrats have represented the Bronx through the landlord arson wave and the systematic burning of the borough’s housing stock in the 1970s, the rise of the drug addiction crisis in the 1980s, and mass incarceration and “broken windows” policing in the 1990s and onward that have devastated Bronx families and communities. NY-15 has been identified as the nation’s “poorest congressional district” since the 2010 Census.

Much of the Bronx’s rich legacy of radical socialist organizing, from the Young Lords, to the Black Panther Party, to the sweat equity movement, to the movement against police brutality, has been wiped from our history classes or subsumed into the nonprofit industrial complex. The Democratic Party organization of the Bronx is rife with corruption and is compromised by gifts from major corporations .

Meanwhile, more than one in three Bronx renter households is severely rent burdened, spending more than half of their incomes just to keep a roof over their heads. Nearly one in three NY-15 residents lives below the poverty line , including 41% of children. Full-time daycare for one infant costs more than a quarter of the typical Bronx family’s income , one of the highest shares of any county in the country. One in three Bronx adults has high blood pressure , the highest rate of any borough, and 15% have diabetes , while the cost of treating these conditions in our capitalist health care system pushes working families deeper into debt.

It is in this context that the Party for Socialism and Liberation ran socialist Bronx educator Easton against one of the most widely hated establishment Democratic politicians, Torres.

Our campaign sought to tear down the pessimistic narratives that exist around building working-class political power in the Bronx. These narratives are rooted in the racist biases of the political establishment and mainstream media, casting the majority Black and Brown population of NY-15 as inherently conservative and incapable of leading a movement for radical change. It is notable that shortly before the election, Trump-endorsed candidate for New York Governor Bruce Blakeman opened an outreach office steps away from our headquarters.

But as socialists, we know that Black workers have been at the vanguard of some of the most revolutionary chapters in U.S. history: from the Civil War, to Civil Rights, to the Black Panther Party, to the 2020 uprisings against police brutality.

Recognizing this legacy, our campaign turned the label ascribed to NY-15 on its head: from “the poorest congressional district” to “the most exploited congressional district.”

It is true that something is keeping the 750,000 people of NY-15 in deep poverty, but it is not the people themselves. Bronx workers produce vast amounts of wealth and resources for the financial capital of the world, the city with the most billionaires — New York City.

Bronx workers feed the city. The Hunts Point Food Distribution Center, the largest in the country, supplies about 25% of NYC’s produce, 35% of its meat and 45% of its fish . The Bronx makes the city run. Before the pandemic, more than 70% of the Bronx workforce was employed in essential or face-to-face industries. Health care is the borough’s largest private sector employer , so when the Bronx had the city’s highest COVID hospitalization and death rates , Bronx health care workers were on the front lines.

But perhaps the best-known source of wealth in the Bronx is its culture. Hip hop has grown into a multibillion-dollar industry , yet Bronx public schools are still shortchanged on arts education .

The framing of exploitation over poverty points us in the direction of the exploiters: the billionaires and the capitalist system itself. It also points to our ability to actually change these conditions ourselves — without outside intervention from philanthropists, nonprofits or politicians.

Our campaign sought to move away from expressions of cynicism and defeat. Something Easton said often on the campaign trail was the need to replace the expression “it is what it is” with “it will be what we make it.”

This sense of revolutionary optimism is what drove our field organizing. We knew that without access to corporate PAC money, our biggest obstacles would be name recognition and mass visibility.

We fought the battle of ideas block by block. When we first launched, we held a series of volunteer events that doubled as political education sessions on our platform. Our launch event packed 400 people into the historic Andrew Freedman Home. We started knocking on doors as early as December 2025. And in only 13 days, our team of volunteers successfully collected 10,000 signatures to get socialism on the ballot in the Bronx.

New York has some of the most draconian ballot access laws in the country, and they’re written to keep third-party, left-wing candidates off the ballot. An organization only earns recognized party status by hitting a vote threshold in a race for governor or president. In other words, to attain status at even the most local level, we first have to prove mass electoral success at the top of the ticket.

Those without recognized party status face major obstacles. Independent House candidates need nearly three times as many signatures as Democrats and Republicans: 3,500, compared with 1,250.

The rules are sequenced to hurt independent candidates. A signature on our petition only counts if that voter hasn’t already signed for a Democratic or Republican candidate, but the major parties get to circulate first. By the time independents can start, part of the pool is already locked up, so some of our signatures are guaranteed to be thrown out.

That’s why we set our goal at 10,000 signatures, nearly triple the requirement.

Still, with tenacity and revolutionary optimism, we collected 10,180 signatures in under two weeks. Many Bronx residents dropped their skepticism as soon as they heard the word “independent,” and younger residents in particular signed the second they heard “socialism.”

While Easton’s campaign knocked on thousands of doors, Torres was nowhere to be found, except in our mailboxes and on our TVs, where his donors’ millions paid for round after round of glossy mailers and ads.

In June, Torres won the Democratic primary with just 24,600 votes out of more than 460,000 eligible voters in NY-15. Nearly 95% of the district didn’t vote for him. Apparently, that was all the democracy he needed.

Our canvassers never once ran into anyone volunteering for the Torres campaign. We did, once, run into Torres himself, who promptly told us to go f*ck ourselves when confronted on his votes for pro-ICE legislation and the pro-Israel lobby money behind his campaign.

His district has some of the lowest voter turnout in the country, yet Torres found no time for registration drives, town halls, or even letting residents know an election was coming. But it was not only Torres who was silent. The Democratic Party and political establishment as a whole turned a blind eye to this race.

There was only one poll released shortly before the primary, and then shortly after, it was scrubbed from the internet. It revealed that Torres had a wide lead in the June Democratic Party primary for NY-15 over his challenger Michael Blake, which carried over into the primary election itself. But the same poll showed that lead vanished once voters learned he backed the war on Iran, took AIPAC money and wouldn’t fight for Medicare for All. This small study revealed that Bronx voters are open to socialist ideas and fed up with the status quo, if anyone bothers to tell them the truth.

Torres’ absence was not an oversight. It was part of a larger strategy. Torres and the Democratic Party have spent years making sure the Bronx stays disengaged and disenfranchised.

An engaged Bronx is the last thing they want. The moment Bronx residents start paying attention, they’ll start asking whether there’s a better option than decades of Democratic Party neglect, and so will every other urban district written off as a “safe seat.”

In contrast, our campaign team was on the ground nearly 24/7. Two weeks before the general election, we were running more than 20 canvassing shifts daily, out on the streets from 7 a.m. to 8 p.m., speaking with our neighbors. From Mott Haven to Van Cortlandt Park, we were building an unstoppable socialist movement that reached every corner of NY-15.

We’ve learned a lot from doing what the Democratic Party refuses to do: build a movement for free health care, clean air, more and better public housing, and fully funded schools. Build a future for the Bronx, not for the billionaires who fund and control our entire political establishment. That work didn’t end on Nov. 3. This campaign has always been an invitation to join the struggle for a socialist future.

The Bronx is ready for socialism.

The Party for Socialism and Liberation is comprised of leaders and activists, workers and students, of all backgrounds. Organized in branches across the country, our mission is to link the everyday struggles of oppressed and exploited people to the fight for a new world. Interested in joining? Click here!

items.title: Greek workers strike over cost-of-living as Mitsotakis government pours billions into rearmament
items.summary: Public and private sector workers struck across Greece against falling wages and the cost of living, as part of a growing movement of workers and youth across Europe against austerity and war.

scraped.title: Greek workers strike over cost-of-living as Mitsotakis government pours billions into rearmament
scraped.description: Public and private sector workers struck across Greece against falling wages and the cost of living, as part of a growing movement of workers and youth across Europe against austerity and war.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Greek public sector workers mounted a 24-hour nationwide strike against the conservative New Democracy government Wednesday. Called by the ADEDY civil servants’ confederation, workers in 30 labour centres and over 10 union federations in some private sector industries also participated.

The labour centres are local trade union councils, which bring together unions from all industries in a city or region, while the federations involved are national bodies that organise workers by sector. Federations representing construction workers, food, milk and beverage workers, accountants, pharmaceutical workers and entertainment workers joined the strike, as did the Press and Paper Federation. Seafarers joined, with the PEMEN, Stefenson and PENEN unions calling a 24-hour strike that kept ferries in port across the country.

Greece’s public hospitals, health centres and the EKAB ambulance service ran an emergency skeleton service. Hospital workers in the POEDIN federation and doctors in OENGE joined the strike. Ministries, regional and municipal offices, tax offices, social security services and citizens’ service centres (KEP) were disrupted, with the municipal workers’ federation POP-OTA among those taking part.

Many schools were affected as primary and secondary teachers walked out, and EYDAP water company unions joined. A court banned the OSYPA civil aviation federation from striking at the government’s request. But civil aviation telecoms staff, who guide pilots at small airports without control towers, still walked out, cancelling 32 flights at 15 regional airports.

In Athens, the metro, electric railway and tram ran only between 9 a.m. and 6 p.m., and suburban rail drivers held stoppages.

More than 70 rallies took place in over 60 towns and cities across the mainland and islands. In Athens, tens of thousands marched after gathering at Klafthmonos Square for the rally of ADEDY and the Athens Labour Centre. Thousands more organised by the All-Workers Militant Front (PAME), the trade union front of the Stalinist Communist Party of Greece (KKE), gathered at the Propylaea.

In Thessaloniki, thousands of workers rallied at the Venizelos statue before marching through the city centre.

Among those demonstrating in Athens was Dimitris, a university student nearing the end of an interior architecture degree. He also works in a furniture and model-making workshop.

Speaking to the Orange Press Agency , he explained, “The cost of living has skyrocketed, my salary runs out by the 15th of the month. We’re young, we’re entering the labour market, and we can’t support ourselves or stand on our own two feet.” Dimitris added, “We’re here to demand the basics, to be able to live with dignity. Not to be paid poverty wages, not to run out of money. Simple things, nothing extraordinary.”

ADEDY’s main demands are for pay rises to make up for lost purchasing power and the restoration of the 13th and 14th monthly salaries for public employees, which were sharply reduced to fixed amounts in 2010 by the social democratic PASOK government. They were abolished in 2012 under the New Democracy–PASOK–Democratic Left coalition government.

ADEDY estimates public servants have lost €35 billion to €40 billion in income since 2012. Including the cuts made to pensioners’ incomes, the total exceeds a staggering €50 billion. Proportionate to population, this would be the equivalent of stripping €400 billion from public sector workers and pensioners in Germany, €330 billion in France, £280 billion in Britain and more than $1.8 trillion in the United States.

Government spokesman Pavlos Marinakis said that restoring the 13th and 14th salaries would “cost €3 billion a year. We wish the money existed, but it doesn’t.” In August, the Council of State, Greece’s highest administrative court, upheld their abolition, citing “fiscal stability.”

The money does exist but is being shovelled into military spending at record levels. The strike took place as Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis presses ahead with the largest rearmament programme in Greece’s modern history, with the country a key base for US and NATO wars . ND’s 2027 budget, tabled last week, raises spending on weapons purchases to €4 billion, from €3.2 billion this year. The budget is part of a €25 billion, 12-year arms programme announced in April 2025.

The walkout is the latest in a Europe-wide wave including the November 11 one-day general strike in Spain, 24-hour stoppages in France, Italy and Greece , and mass protests in Albania, Serbia, Belgium and Portugal.

Wednesday’s strike followed the general strike in Italy last Friday against the Meloni government’s budget of war and austerity. On Monday, a nationwide mobilisation in Belgium saw widespread strikes against the De Wever government’s austerity agenda, as up to 70,000 marched in Brussels.

The determination of Greek workers and youth to fight is in stark contrast to a trade union bureaucracy desperate to hold back the growing militancy and anti-capitalist sentiment. After calling two one-day strikes earlier this year, and a limited stoppage in October, ADEDY again restricts its mobilisation to a single one-day action.

ADEDY is also to head off growing anti-war sentiment by confining its strike call to economic demands. In March, ADEDY called a rally against “the involvement of our country” in war. Its latest call, issued on November 17, lists 14 demands but says nothing about war, military spending or Greece’s role in the US-Israeli war against Iran, Israel’s genocide in Gaza or NATO’s war against Russia in Ukraine.

Greece’s largest union body, the private sector General Confederation of Greek Workers (GSEE), refused to call out its members in support of public sector workers. A survey of 6,000 private sector employees by GSEE’s own Labour Institute (INE GSEE), carried out in late 2025, found that 35.5 percent work beyond their normal hours. Of these, 34.5 percent were not paid for the extra hours, The Press Project reported.

The brutal conditions enforced on workers, including cuts in workplace safety, have led to a series of devastating deaths . Last year, the construction workers’ federation OSETEE recorded 201 deaths at work, the highest in four years, in.gr reported. Research presented this week estimated that some 3,400 deaths a year in Greece are linked to the workplace.

Since February, GSEE President Yiannis Panagopoulos has been at the centre of an embezzlement and money laundering investigation . The Anti-Money Laundering Authority froze his assets in an investigation into €73 million in state and EU funding for training programmes.

The GSEE is run by factions loyal to the main parliamentary parties. At its congress in April, the faction led by Panagopoulos, aligned with PASOK, increased its vote to 42.89 percent and its seats on the governing body from 19 to 20. New Democracy’s DAKE took eight seats.

The KKE holds a major position within this bureaucracy. Its Democratic Militant Cooperation (DAS) faction, part of PAME, came second at the GSEE congress, with 26.57 percent and 12 seats. Four DAS members sit on the GSEE Executive Committee alongside Panagopoulos.

In ADEDY, DAS is the largest faction on the 17-member Executive Committee, with five seats, against four for New Democracy’s DAKE. DAS member Nikos Vourdoubas, president of the DOE primary teachers’ federation, chairs ADEDY’s General Council.

However DAS holds no senior officer posts in either confederation, allowing the KKE to share in running both bodies while keeping its distance from their decisions.

Such was the anger at the GSEE leadership’s refusal to call strikes that labour centres across the country defied it, revealing the duplicitous role of the KKE. By early November, 23 labour centres and 11 national federations, many of them led by KKE supporters, had voted to strike. The KKE-aligned Katiousa reported that by November 23, this had risen to 29 labour centres, including the Athens Labour Centre, and 14 federations.

During the 2010–19 austerity offensive, the GSEE and ADEDY called dozens of one-day general strikes to allow workers to let off steam, while the bureaucracy collaborated with successive governments imposing ever deeper cuts. The unions assisted Syriza (Coalition of the Radical Left) into power in January 2015 and collaborated with it to the end. Imposing vicious austerity on behalf of the capitalist class , the European Union and the International Monetary Fund, Syriza never restored the 13th and 14th salaries.

The struggle against the onslaught of the ruling elite in Greece and everywhere can only be successful when organised independently of the pro-capitalist trade union bureaucracies. The International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC) urges the formation of independent, democratically controlled rank-and-file action committees in every workplace.

The class struggle in Greece must be expanded in a joint offensive with workers across Europe, uniting them across industries and borders to prepare a European general strike. Greek workers must take up this fight, as part of building an international socialist movement against capitalism and war.

Called by the ADEDY civil servants’ confederation, workers in 30 labour centres and over 10 union federations in some private sector industries also participated.

items.title: Production restarts at HABAŞ steel plant after 19 workers killed
items.summary: Workers’ lives cannot be entrusted to laws that protect companies, nor to occupational safety experts and inspectors who depend on those companies.

scraped.title: Production restarts at HABAŞ steel plant after 19 workers killed
scraped.description: Workers’ lives cannot be entrusted to laws that protect companies, nor to occupational safety experts and inspectors who depend on those companies.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
Eight days after the explosion and fire that killed 19 workers at the HABAŞ Iron and Steel plant in Aliağa, İzmir, on November 9, management restarted production without taking any serious safety measures.

A statement issued on November 18 by the Chamber of Metallurgical and Materials Engineers, part of the Union of Chambers of Turkish Engineers and Architects (TMMOB), fundamentally undermines the “accident” narrative of the company and the government.

According to the Chamber, the runways of the crane carrying the steel shell of the electric arc furnace collapsed while the shell was being replaced during maintenance. The falling crane and shell damaged the gas pressure regulation valve system and high-current cables. In the Chamber’s assessment, gas escaping from the ruptured natural gas and oxygen lines was ignited by electrical arcing from the damaged cables.

Nineteen workers were burned to death in the gas explosion and the heat wave that followed. Dozens more were injured.

“This disaster did not originate from one or more metallurgical processes,” the Chamber states. According to the statement, there was no molten metal and no water leak in the area, because production had been stopped and the work was being carried out in a cold environment.

Yet the preliminary findings of the expert panel appointed by the Aliağa Public Prosecutor’s Office, as reported by the daily Evrensel , had attributed the explosion to water leaking from the arc furnace’s water-cooled panels and coming into contact with molten steel. Responding to this, the Chamber stated: “As a matter of our professional and social responsibility, we are obliged to correct the inaccurate reports in the media that we have followed with astonishment in recent days.”

The Chamber’s statement raises a number of questions. Why did the structure supporting the crane collapse? When were the crane runways last inspected? What do the maintenance records show? Were there emergency shut-off systems, and if so, why were they not activated? Why were so many workers in the danger zone?

These questions, which directly concern the company’s management, remain unanswered. The refusal to allow a TMMOB delegation into the plant is bound up with this. According to a worker who spoke to soL , the debris was hastily cleared by workers kept on compulsory overtime, and concrete is now being poured at the blast site.

According to a worker who spoke to Evrensel , systems were started up on the morning of November 17, and production resumed at 2 p.m. The steel melt shop where the explosion occurred is not yet operating. However, coil production continues in the sheet rolling mill, subcontracted workers are working at full strength in the cold rolling mill, and some workers are being kept on overtime.

Another worker recalled that shipments did not stop even on the day of the explosion. He said that if management had its way, it would not have halted production even on that day. According to workers, the only visible change has been an increase in the number of private security guards in orange vests at the factory gates. The company’s management is protecting not the workers, but itself against the workers’ anger.

The account of a crane operator shows that production continued despite known risks and repeated warnings. Speaking to Evrensel on November 22, the operator said he had reported faults in the cranes in the crane crew’s messaging group. But the engineer in charge told him to “keep feeding the lines.” Electrical maintenance workers came two or three times, but the fault was never fixed. Meanwhile, workers continue to work beneath coils weighing 15 to 20 tonnes. The operator says he quit on the 28th day of his probationary period as a result.

According to Health and Safety Labour Watch (İSİG), at least 45 workers have lost their lives at HABAŞ facilities since 1999. Across Türkiye, at least 1,930 workers were killed on the job in the first 10 months of 2026.

In 2025, HABAŞ recorded 145 billion lira (about $2.9 billion) in net sales. It spent only 2 percent of this on labour costs, while receiving 18.2 billion lira (about $360 million) in state incentives and tax breaks the same year. According to the company’s own sustainability report, lost-time accidents among subcontracted workers rose by 118 percent in a single year.

Nevertheless, the British certification body CARES awarded HABAŞ ISO 45001 occupational health and safety certification in November 2025. According to Evrensel , the certificate was still valid at the time of the November 9 massacre of workers.

The state’s response to this preventable disaster shows that HABAŞ will not be the last unless workers intervene as an independent social and political force. The Aliağa Criminal Judgeship of Peace imposed a publication ban. Deputies of the ruling Justice and Development Party (AKP) and its fascist ally, the Nationalist Movement Party (MHP), voted down a motion for a parliamentary inquiry. Workers and supporters protesting the massacre were detained.

The Türk Metal union, which organises the plant, never once demanded that production be halted. According to workers, the return to production was presented as a decision taken with the union’s approval.

An interview given to Evrensel by academic Erhan Özşeker shows that impunity was systematic in 20 cases between 2003 and 2024, in each of which at least seven workers were killed. According to Özşeker, indictments are drawn up under the lightest category of offence, and expert reports shift the blame onto lower-level staff rather than company owners and executives.

Occupational safety expert Deniz İpek, speaking to Yeni Yaşam , stressed that the problem is not that the risks are unknown, but that production continues in spite of them. The existing pro-company Occupational Health and Safety Law also allows fatal workplace accidents to continue.

After the 2014 Soma mine disaster, in which 301 miners were killed, holding company owner Alp Gürkan was acquitted. Company chairman Can Gürkan was released after serving about five years of a 20-year sentence, while the public officials involved escaped with token sentences.

At HABAŞ, too, nine mid-level managers have been jailed pending trial, while the company’s owner, Mehmet Rüştü Başaran, was released after his detention under judicial control in the form of “house arrest.” According to reports, Başaran is serving his house arrest in his historic waterfront mansion in İstanbul’s Yeniköy district, reportedly worth 2 billion lira (about $40 million).

On average, 2,000 workers are killed on the job every year in Türkiye, and 330,000 worldwide according to International Labour Organization (ILO) figures. Workers’ lives cannot be entrusted to laws that protect companies, nor to occupational safety experts and inspectors who depend on those companies. The struggle to end workplace killings requires the independent organisation and mobilisation of the working class.

The demands raised in the statement issued on November 13 by the HABAŞ Workers Rank-and-File Committee Initiative remain fully valid. The Initiative called for building rank-and-file committees in every workplace to fight for these demands:

· An independent workers’ investigation must be carried out by elected workers, together with engineers, doctors and lawyers they trust.

· All production must be halted until the independent committee approves it as safe, and all workers must be placed on paid leave. Until the serious and imminent danger has been eliminated, workers must exercise their right to refuse work under Article 13 of Law No. 6331.

· The pro-company Occupational Health and Safety Law must be changed, and oversight by elected safety committees must be established in every workplace.

· Iron and steel and other key industries must be put into public ownership under the democratic control of the workers.

As the HABAŞ Workers Rank-and-File Committee Initiative stated, workers must fight in the knowledge that these demands can be realised only if they “unite as a class through rank-and-file committees across workplaces, industries and borders, and take power.” This requires workers to unite their struggles internationally through the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees (IWA-RFC).

Workers’ safety and well-being can be guaranteed only when production is reorganised on the basis of social need rather than private profit—that is, on a world socialist basis.

Get email updates on workers’ struggles and a global perspective from the International Workers Alliance of Rank-and-File Committees.

items.title: Timms report on PIP welfare benefit lands, but has already been eclipsed by Milburn
items.summary: Whatever balance it strikes between the two reports, both serve the same end: a vicious assault on the incomes of millions of sick and disabled people.

scraped.title: Timms report on PIP welfare benefit lands, but has already been eclipsed by Milburn
scraped.description: Whatever balance it strikes between the two reports, both serve the same end: a vicious assault on the incomes of millions of sick and disabled people.
scraped.h1: Read more
scraped.body_text:
The final report of the Timms review of personal independence payment was published on November 24. It arrived a week after Alan Milburn’s review of young people and work, whose plans to cut disability benefits for under-25s Prime Minister Andy Burnham has promised to act on quickly.

In the space of a week, the Labour government has received two reports on disability benefits that on specific issues disagree with one another. Whatever balance it strikes between them, both serve the same end: a vicious assault on the incomes of millions of sick and disabled people.

On November 17, former Labour health secretary Alan Milburn published From a Welfare State to a Working State . It proposes ending personal independence payment (PIP) and the Universal Credit (UC) health element for everyone under 25, existing claimants included. In their place would come a “Youth Allowance” paid at the under-25 Universal Credit rate of about £78 a week, enforced by a “duty to engage”. Under-25s would no longer undergo a work capability assessment for the universal credit health top-up. Instead, they would be referred within two weeks to a new youth opportunity service.

The World Socialist Web Site explained that the plan is a template for wider welfare cuts that will not stop at young people.

Seven days later came the final report of the Timms Review of PIP, led by the Minister for Social Security and Disability, Sir Stephen Timms. It was co-produced with disabled people. It too found that the PIP system is “not fit for purpose” but argued that PIP should remain a cash benefit for people of all ages, in and out of work.

The government will publish a single White Paper in early 2027, ostensibly in response to both reviews. In reality, the White Paper will generally follow Milburn’s priorities, which match those of employers and the Treasury. But this does not mean that Timms offers disabled people a defence. His report also supplies the framework for cutting PIP for claimants of every age.

Milburn told The Times that reform would not be “pain-free”. The Institute for Fiscal Studies (IFS) counts about 390,000 18–24-year-olds in England and Wales receiving health-related benefits, averaging £9,500 a year. The Resolution Foundation estimates that UC health payments and PIP currently keep 120,000 young people out of poverty. The review would cut young people’s benefit spending by £3.6 billion a year. This is less than 1 percent of projected welfare spending, but it sets a precedent for more far-reaching benefit cuts.

Joseph Rowntree Foundation (JRF) senior policy adviser Jack Evans warned that pushing young people towards jobs that don’t exist “will just leave them poorer”. Anna Bird, chief executive of the disability charity Contact, warned that large cuts could have “devastating consequences”.

An analysis by NewsCord, a UK news-comparison site, points out that the claim of 50,000 fewer people in poverty depends on 440,000 assumed new jobs. It notes that the review gives no poverty estimate for the benefit cuts on their own.

The Timms review exists because of the Labour rebellion over the 2025 welfare bill, which would have cut about £5 billion from projected disability spending. The Department for Work and Pension’s (DWP) own impact assessment estimated it would push an extra 250,000 people, including 50,000 children, into relative poverty.

More than 120 Labour MPs signed an amendment that would have killed the bill. Then Prime Minister Keir Starmer responded by guaranteeing that existing PIP claimants would not lose out. Ninety minutes before the Commons vote, Timms announced that the planned PIP changes would not go ahead until his review had concluded. The rebellion collapsed. Only 49 Labour MPs voted against the bill.

The review was never a retreat from cuts. Its terms required it to stay within the Office for Budget Responsibility’s spending forecast. The Guardian described the report as the second half of the government’s attempt to slow the growth of the disability benefits bill. PIP spending is forecast to rise from about £16 billion in 2019–20 to just over £41 billion by the end of the decade.

Timms told MPs the system requires a “fundamental reset”. At its centre is a new test of who may claim PIP, based on whether a disability brings additional costs. The report states that the benefit is not appropriate for those who incur no additional costs from being disabled. The Resolution Foundation reports that one in six of the 4 million claimants, about 666,000 people, say they have no extra costs. It estimates that ending their payments would cut up to £4.4 billion in 2029–30.

The much-praised fast track for people with severe, well-evidenced conditions covers only about 10 percent of claimants. For the remaining 90 percent, the report proposes assessments tailored to individual circumstances, replacing the current four rates of between £30.30 and £194.60 a week.

The government has accepted two recommendations straight away: the fast track and fewer reassessments for people with lifelong conditions. The rest will be “considered” alongside Milburn.

The White Paper is highly likely to include Milburn’s Youth Allowance and conditionality for under-25s. It is also likely to include tax breaks and subsidies for retail and hospitality employers, phased in “when fiscal conditions allow”. From Timms it can take an “additional costs” test and the language of “rebalancing” to cut PIP for adults.

Burnham is dealing with Labour MPs who now believe they can get away with cuts they thought socially dangerous earlier. They also feel more secure about their seats and parliamentary careers than they did under Starmer.

Before publication, several Labour MPs criticised the trailed proposals, but after Milburn addressed the Parliamentary Labour Party on November 16, the tone for many changed. Rachael Maskell called the final proposals a “sea change”.

Burnham still faces strident calls to get a grip on the benefits bill. Employers have lobbied for the review’s tax and subsidy measures. Before publication, retail, hospitality and tourism firms pledged to hire 250,000 young people over the coming years, which Work and Pensions Secretary Pat McFadden welcomed in the Commons. They will be paid for doing so. Milburn’s proposals include doubling the employer National Insurance threshold for 21–24-year-olds in retail and hospitality from £5,000 to £10,000 and paying employers £3,000 to £7,000 per hire.

Pret A Manger, KFC, Young’s and Punch Pubs pressed Chancellor John Healey to adopt the National Insurance cut. The British Retail Consortium called the measure “not only incredibly welcome, but essential”, insisting that keeping a lower minimum wage for young people was vital. The review cautions against earlier plans to raise the youth minimum wage.

In The Spectator , economics editor Michael Simmons argued the Timms report “does not go far enough”. He complained it makes no savings while the disability welfare bill heads for £120 billion. Conservative Party Shadow Work and Pensions Secretary Helen Whately called the review “a complete farce” and pledged to remove eligibility for low-level mental health PIP claims.

Anti-poverty and disability organisations spoke out against Milburn. Citizens Advice warned that young people “must not be pushed into poverty”. Turn2us said the report ignores financial insecurity as a cause of young people being out of work or education, and urged MPs to reject the cuts. The Mental Health Foundation warned against “rushed cuts or cliff-edge changes” to PIP.

Some charities have welcomed Timms. Mind chief executive Sarah Hughes said it was promising that the review recognised PIP as a cash benefit, available in and out of work. Svetlana Kotova of Inclusion London said the government should prioritise Timms’s recommendations over Milburn’s.

They are clutching at straws, as are those charities who collaborated in its production and lent it undeserved legitimacy. They are presenting a recommendation that most claimants be reassessed against an additional-costs test, within a fixed budget, as the lesser evil to Milburn. The Resolution Foundation has already put a figure of £4.4 billion on what that test could take from disabled people.

The Socialist Workers Party has made its own contribution to this deception. Socialist Worker headlined its report “Timms review: Labour forced to water down attacks on disabled people’s benefits”. It presented the review as the fruit of a retreat forced on Labour in 2025. It praised the fast track for ending humiliating repeated assessments, before stating that the review leaves room for attacks on benefits that must also be fought.

Even as Socialist Worker concedes that Labour is ideologically committed to cutting welfare spending, it promotes the illusion that the party can be pressured into defending disabled people.

A handful of union leaders opposed the cuts. As dutifully reported by the Stalinist Morning Star , these included Unison General Secretary Andrea Egan, Fran Heathcote of the Public and Commercial Services Union, and the National Education Union’s Daniel Kebede, who pledged to oppose them. This opposition will never materialise.

For the most part, the union leadership welcomed the review. Trades Union Congress General Secretary Paul Nowak called a permanent legal right to training or a job a “game-changer for young people”, asking only that the government fund its response properly. The University and College Union’s Jo Grady welcomed calls for more investment in colleges and Kebede also welcomed parts of the report.

scraped.title: Homes, Not Commodities: Flatbush Residents Fight for Justice After the Collapse - Left Voice
scraped.description: Left Voice speaks with an organizer from the Mutual Aid for Flatbush Coalition about the community's response to the deadly building collapse and the fight for accountability and the right to housing.
scraped.author: Left Voice
scraped.body_text:
Left Voice speaks with an organizer from the Mutual Aid for Flatbush Coalition about the community’s response to the deadly building collapse and the fight for accountability and the right to housing.

Left Voice

On November 11, a three-story apartment building at 1321 Flatbush Avenue collapsed into a construction excavation site in the Flatbush neighborhood of Brooklyn, killing eight workers and tenants, injuring 18 people including seven children, and displacing dozens of residents. The collapse has exposed the deadly consequences of a system that puts real estate profits ahead of the safety and well-being of working-class communities. In a predominantly Black, Brown, and immigrant neighborhood, the disaster is part of a broader pattern of gentrification, landlord neglect, and unchecked development.

In the aftermath of the collapse, residents and community members have organized to support displaced families and demand accountability. Left Voice spoke with an organizer with the Mutual Aid for Flatbush Coalition, a network of tenant associations and grassroots organizing efforts, about the response to the disaster and the fight being built in its wake.

The interview takes place amid a broader housing crisis in which the needs of working-class people are routinely subordinated to the interests of developers and landlords. It offers a look at the organizing taking place in Flatbush and the fight for a different approach to housing — one that prioritizes working-class people and communities over profit.

Left Voice: The Flatbush building collapse was not simply a random accident but was an entirely preventable tragedy. It happened in a predominantly Black, Brown, and immigrant working-class community, and reflects a larger system that puts these communities at risk. Can you speak a bit about this context?

Gentrification in New York City has been happening for many, many years. If you ask different people when they can pinpoint the start of gentrification in their neighborhood, depending on what neighborhood they’ve lived in previously, there’s a different timeline.

Especially in Flatbush, what we’re seeing is a lot of really large prewar buildings, with building lots bigger than what you would probably find in most newer buildings. It’s the same thing in Washington Heights, Harlem, and all these places that are being rapidly gentrified.

A lot of these old buildings have been deliberately left to become dilapidated as a landlord tactic to get tenants to move out. A lot of these buildings were bought up by landlords when there were different laws in place protecting rent-stabilized housing. Landlords saw this as an opportunity to invest in rent-stabilized housing stock. Then the laws changed, and in their opinion, they no longer had the incentives to fix up these buildings.

That’s why landlords have been finding other strategies to push out tenants so they can capitalize on this wave of gentrification. What we’re seeing is a lot of really old buildings in Flatbush coming down, landlords selling their buildings, intimidating tenants and asking them to leave, or not disclosing the rights tenants have to their specific units. Some landlords won’t share that tenants are actually living in rent-stabilized housing.

What ends up happening is that landlords are allowed to operate criminal operations as a business, with zero repercussions from the city. If we point to a restaurant, for example, and it doesn’t maintain its proper licenses, upkeep, or cleanliness, the city will shut it down. But when it comes to housing for multiple families, lots of people, and children, it seems like landlords get to do whatever they want.

There really isn’t enough oversight, and there aren’t any qualifications to develop on land or tear down land, potentially harming the community with whatever project you’re working on. There are no qualifications except money. That’s it. The city only needs to see money. At the site where this happened, across all of those businesses, there were multiple lawsuits involving companies that were already part of the project, but apparently that doesn’t matter to the city.

Left Voice: The community has been organizing mutual aid for families while they wait for support from the state. You’ve also talked about how the city doesn’t regulate or make sure landlords and developers produce safe housing. We’re also seeing the Mamdani administration push forward more deregulation to make this development happen more easily. Can you talk a bit about the failure of the state in this situation — both in terms of regulating landlords and developers and supporting the people impacted by the collapse?

People have to remember the timeline of this event. It happened during an election cycle, when several ballot proposals concerned accelerating construction and changing building regulations. These proposals would make it easier to fast-track development with less oversight and less community input.

The city already has a system that does not listen to tenants who advocate for themselves. Tenants go through the proper channels and document problems with the Department of Buildings (DOB) and the Department of Housing Preservation and Development (HPD), but their complaints are ignored, their cases are closed, and landlords receive small fines that are nowhere near proportionate to what they’ve done.

On top of that, the city has an interest in supporting large developments across the city. It is involved in some of these developments through so-called affordable housing programs, where landlords receive substantial tax benefits in exchange for making a portion of the housing available at certain income levels. Of course, those income levels do not necessarily reflect the incomes of people in the neighborhood.

All the grassroots groups who have been watching Mamdani, not just what he’s saying but what he’s doing, were sounding the alarm about these ballot proposals. We wanted people to consider the history and future of the city. If Eric Adams had supported these proposals, many people would not have voted yes. But because it was Mamdani, people felt comfortable doing so.

People supported Mamdani because he said he would be tough on landlords, change how things were done, and champion tenants’ rights. Yet this has been allowed to happen. This is now the second building collapse during his tenure. The first one happened with the Pfizer building in July, which could have been absolutely catastrophic. The number of deaths and the damage to property and the city could have been impossible to calculate. Yet there was no change afterward in DOB or HPD policies. Now people are dead as a result of the Flatbush collapse.

Left Voice: You’ve pointed out that money raised for families does not always reach them, leaving community and mutual aid networks to meet basic needs. What kind of organizing has been necessary?

Typically, the state has a certain procedure for how it handles emergency situations and disasters. What we’ve noticed time and time again, with Hurricane Sandy, building collapses, and fires, is that the people who benefit the most are the organizations themselves and the state.

When you actually talk to these families about the help they’ve received, it almost never matches what is being publicized. In this particular case, we set up this mutual aid fund because we already knew this would happen. We didn’t need to wait for proof to find out. We’ve raised $131,000, with the community trusting us to distribute these funds equally.

That’s one part of the effort. The other major part is our long-term advocacy plan, where we’re connecting with families directly to stay on track and stay up to date with what they need.

The agencies and nonprofits working with them right now are letting them slip through the cracks and are not giving them the direct answers they need. They want these people to just be done with. They want this whole thing to end, and they don’t care what that end result actually looks like for these families.

Left Voice: Mutual Aid for Flatbush has put forward demands including a transparent investigation, permanent housing for impacted families, and the resignation of the Department of Buildings commissioner. How were those demands developed, how are people organizing around them, and how can others support them?

The demands were created with the different groups that came together for Mutual Aid for Flatbush and discussed with families. We created these demands because we knew that achieving accountability and justice meant asking for these things. We were not going to settle for low-hanging fruit or scraps. We needed to give voice to our neighbors who had just buried their loved ones and gone through an entirely preventable tragedy.

We wanted to uplift their concerns and what they wanted, and make sure the narrative wasn’t just that they’re going to get justice or a lot of money in a lawsuit. That’s not it. We developed those specific demands because we knew we could hold our elected officials to them.

One of the demands is that nothing for profit should be erected on that site. Absolutely nothing can be built there for profit. It has to be a park, a place of reflection, a memorial.

Housing is an immediate concern. On November 30, these families are expected to become homeless. After the collapse, there were press conferences, a lot of people crying, shaking hands, and taking pictures. There was one meeting with all of the elected officials together at City Hall, on November 13. But there has not been a concrete plan for a proper temporary housing solution for these families.

We’ve been advocating for hotel stays longer than 30 days. We’re trying to confirm whether that has been approved for up to 60 days. In the meantime, we’re learning that families are being pressured to sign HPD documents under the impression that the documents will help them get an apartment or temporary home. What the documents actually direct them toward is a shelter.

Families are being misled and told that completing these forms will help their housing process, while also being told that not completing them could hurt their chances of getting an apartment. That is not true. Right now, there is no actual temporary housing option beyond a shelter.

We also learned that there is no permanent housing plan for them, or for any New Yorker if there were ever another building collapse, a fire, or anything like that. The city does not have a plan for you to get permanent housing with support from the city.

That’s concerning to us, especially because there has not been transparency around the mayor’s fund and how much money was collected for these relief efforts. Unofficial information suggests there could potentially be a million dollars in that fund.

We were asked earlier: in a perfect world, what would we want to see as the solution? Our answer was: that world exists now. This isn’t hypothetical. The resources, the money, the connections, the task force, and the staff are available. We’re genuinely confused why a socialist mayor, who has access to those resources, is choosing to make these families homeless.

People need to listen to groups like ours and to the grassroots organizations doing this work. The information and propaganda from Mamdani are wonderful. It’s delicious, it’s soothing, like chicken noodle soup for the soul. But it is empty. Every time he makes announcements, like disbanding the SRG , there’s always more truth to dig into.

People should not simply accept the positive messaging about what the city is doing. They need to understand that what the city says is happening is not necessarily the reality of what families are experiencing.

It’s up to everyone to amplify the voices of neighbors who are saying that they are not getting the help they need and do not want to be sent to shelters. We need people to stand with them.

We’re planning protests and rallies until our demands are met, including an adequate temporary housing solution and permanent housing. The families themselves are furious that the only solution being offered is a shelter and that they are being left homeless.

Left Voice: The collapse shows the consequences of treating housing as a profit-driven commodity rather than a basic human right. What is your vision for how housing should be organized?

Tenants need to control their housing.

Right now, the model is incredibly outdated and broken. We pay our own electricity and our own gas. The money we’re putting into rent is not going into anything that has to do with our housing. It has to do with lining the pockets of these landlords, and they are not investing that money back into the housing.

This whole myth and narrative that landlords aren’t getting enough money, and therefore can’t do the maintenance and upkeep, is simply false. That isn’t the purpose of them collecting the money. That’s just what people think the purpose of collecting the money is. There’s no pressure for them to actually do any of the work.

These are our homes. We don’t see homes as a commodity; we see them as a necessity. Everybody should have a home. We should have a model in which tenants own their buildings and control the funds that would otherwise go toward rent. Those pooled funds could be used more directly to meet the needs of the building. It could be similar to a co-op, but with less bureaucracy.

We could organize around what we need: “This is what we need today.” Then we could hire the proper help to support what needs to be done in the building. We could hire a licensed superintendent, licensed workers to make repairs, or a licensed company to take on major repairs.

This would also allow us to have dignity in our homes. We wouldn’t feel that we’re one job away from losing our housing. We could invest more in our homes, our relationships with our neighbors, and our communities because we have a real stake in them.

Left Voice: This year, we’ve seen communities fight back against attacks on immigrants like in the Twin Cities , as well as Los Angeles and Chicago . We’ve also seen major mobilizations against austerity and militarism around the world from France to India. On the same day as the building collapsed in Flatbush, workers and youth in Spain organized a general strike connected to the struggle for housing and against evictions. In this broader context, how should we organize and fight for our demands?

We have to put everything happening here in a country-wide and global context. Some of the money we received — $30 — came from people in Palestine, in Gaza. We have received a solidarity video from Gaza, and solidarity from people around the world for these families.

What is happening here, the pain and the efforts, and how the system works and fails people, is not far away from the same apparatus causing harm in other countries.

We need to organize what we have control over, like where our money goes. We need to have general strikes. We need to follow in the footsteps of what other countries are doing. We have so much power to starve the beast from the inside.

We need to organize a general strike of our labor. We should not be contributing to the economy right now, because we know that one day of us pulling out could throw everything into chaos.

We know our spending has a lot of power, so let’s use that. We also know that most of us are renters, and can use our efforts to organize a rent strike, whether that’s for these families or for other causes.

We can use our homes and our positions as renters to organize a rent strike together. We should have had a citywide rent strike years ago. It’s looming, and we need to build toward one.

Left Voice: Is there anything else you want readers to understand about what happened or what needs to change?

This is a warning for all of us. Most of the people impacted in this situation are Black and Brown and have different immigration situations. But the kind of violence the state perpetuates in the pursuit of profit can affect anyone. That’s what happens when when housing is tied to profit.

Nobody — and I mean nobody — whether you live in a fancy new place in Williamsburg or in the projects, it doesn’t matter what your zip code is or where you live. When it’s your time and you’re the one being screwed over, it can happen to you. What happened is not unique to them. It can happen to you if nothing changes.

What do you want to see when that happens to you? Do you want to see that there have been efforts to figure out solutions for people who have lost their housing?

We also have to remember that New York City is not immune to the effects of climate change. The city was not planned or developed to prepare for the rapid changes we are facing, even in the years since Hurricane Sandy.

We will see more people displaced. We will see more people who have lost their housing. Again, what do we want that plan to be? Nothing exists. Anything is open for conversation, because our elected officials clearly don’t think this is an important thing to be thinking about.

Interview

New York

Militant journalism, revolutionary politics.

Victor Harlan

James Dennis Hoff

AOC 2028 makes DSA's choice immediate: mobilize behind the Democrats and negotiate a platform acceptable to them, or build an independent organization to resist the Right and fight for all of our demands?

Maryam Alaniz and James Dennis Hoff

Despite flashes of brilliance, End Times Fascism by Naomi Klein and Astra Taylor doesn't offer much to help us understand the growth of the Far Right. In the face of what the book describes as an immediate apocalyptic threat, it proposes nothing more than milquetoast social democratic reforms.

scraped.body_text:
This semester, the Palestine movement at CUNY won one of their major demands: the disclosure of CUNY’s investments. So what are these investments exactly, and what can they tell us about CUNY?

Jennifer Caroley

In September, City University of New York (CUNY) Law Students for Justice in Palestine and CUNY for Palestine made headlines: they won a lawsuit over a denied Freedom of Information Law request regarding CUNY’s financial holdings. The university was required to disclose its records, an important victory for the divestment movement. We know now that CUNY holds stocks in a large number of companies benefiting from war, mass incarceration, and surveillance, as well as Israeli occupation and genocide.

Let’s take a closer look at who these companies are, what they are doing, and how exactly CUNY’s investments work.

CUNY’s investments are made either by the Board of Trustees of CUNY or through the board of trustees of one of the 20 college foundations related to the university like the Foundation for City College or the Hunter College Foundation. Endowments are a major source of capital invested by CUNY. These are a type of donation that comes with instructions from the donor on how to invest the money. Many donors also donate assets instead of money.

So why does the capitalist class donate money and assets to CUNY? How do capitalists benefit from their supposed philanthropy?

While endowments come with parameters, how exactly CUNY invests those endowments is not decided by the donors but by the Board of Trustees. The Board’s members are chosen by the governor and the New York City mayor, while those who sit on the boards of college foundations are often chosen by the members of these boards themselves. Many of the people on these boards work for companies that benefit from the genocide in Gaza and the U.S. deportation regime. For example, William Thompson, chairperson of CUNY’s Board of Trustees, is a partner at Siebert Williams Shank & Co, a company that manages bonds for companies like Lockheed Martin, Boeing, Raytheon, and Caterpillar, which are involved in the genocide in Gaza, mass incarceration, and surveillance both in the U.S. and around the world.

Another example is Michael Bosworth, member of the Board of Trustees of the John Jay College Foundation and partner at Goldman Sachs. Goldman manages a large investment fund in Israel and has holdings in Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, Boeing, and GM. CUNY holds $160,000 invested in Goldman Sachs. Another John Jay Board member, Caliph Mathis, is the CSO of S&P Global whose index funds include Boeing, GE Aerospace, Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and more. CUNY has holdings worth hundreds of thousand dollars combined in Boeing, Lockheed Martin, Raytheon, Northrop Grumman, and others.

This is beneficial for the capitalist class in several ways. The donors can deduct donations from their taxes, reducing their gross taxable income, and, in the case of asset donations, avoid the capital gains tax. Furthermore, since the end of the 1960s, taxes for the rich have been cut dramatically. The money public universities need to operate would usually be raised through taxation, not financial market investments. But by cutting taxes and handing the financial business of the university to the managerial class, the capitalists don’t just save money; they also gain power.

Political economists call this “philanthrocapitalism,” or the privatization of public goods. Essentially, these donations function as a valve for political pressure. CUNY provides upward mobility to a small portion of the working class, keeping the idea of the American Dream alive: instead of seeing the capitalist system as the exploitative machinery it is, people focus on their personal movement up the ranks of the system. At the same time, the donors can claim to play an important role in creating these possibilities for the working class, creating a narrative in which the capitalist class seems to be their friend and not their enemy.

Moreover, universities play an important role in reproducing capitalism . They educate future managers, engineers and administrators; they are centers for research, often working directly with corporations; and they are an important source of academic legitimacy for the politics of the ruling class. Mainstream economics, for example, is based on unreasonable assumptions and concepts like homo economicus while also providing economic models that justify capitalism but lack real-life applications.

Political science, meanwhile, offers the pseudo-scientific narrative necessary to justify the current policing and incarceration regime. Thus, universities provide academic authority to the politics and institutions of the capitalist class. Universities also conduct research with the military, developing the technology necessary for imperialism. Universities educate servants of capital and help sell their ideology as scientific fact.

But who exactly are these companies CUNY invests in and how are they benefitting from war and genocide, surveillance and mass incarceration? Let’s start with CoreCivic and GEO Group.

Both are private prison contractors who build, own, and manage prisons and ICE detention centers, and provide electronic monitoring devices and transportation of incarcerated people. Both provide educational courses, vocational training, and substance abuse programs, services that usually would be paid for through taxation but are now run for profit. That is important: many companies present themselves as helping people, yet the services they sell are lacking at best since they are designed to make a profit, not to fulfill the needs of people.

Another important company deeply involved in the police state, in which CUNY holds assets worth $40,000, is Axon, formerly TASER. The company known for electroshock weapons also dominates the police body camera market. While often hailed as tools for police accountability, these cameras gained notoriety for their involvement in wrongful convictions.

Other companies CUNY invests in that profit from the deportation regime and ICE are CACI International, Palantir, AT&T, Dell, and others. These companies provide ICE and the DHS with surveillance and communication technology, an incredibly important part of their infrastructure. Amentum, which manages ICE detention centers, has been cited by federal agencies over the years in over a hundred cases of fraud, employment discrimination, health and safety violations and is frequently critiqued for human rights abuses, including human trafficking and forced labor, by Human Rights Watch and Amnesty International.

CUNY also invests in weapons manufacturers like Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, L3Harris and others that make billions from weapons systems, border surveillance infrastructure as well as military vehicles and technology, war and genocide, and contracts with DHS and CBP. They design, produce and provide bombs, missiles and ammunition for the U.S. military and IDF. Their products are regularly found in Lebanon and Palestine. These companies in which CUNY is investing are the core of the military industrial complex.

Additionally, companies like Nvidia, Google or Amazon provide information infrastructure important for U.S. imperial violence, deeply interwoven with Israel’s military technological complex. One example is Google’s cloud servers, used to coordinate U.S. drone strikes, or Amazon’s data centers, providing infrastructure powering the U.S. military’s AI decision-support system. CUNY holds more than $5.3 million in these three companies.

There are also about $18,000 invested by CUNY in two of the largest commercial banks in Israel: Bank Leumi and Bank Hapoalim. Both of them finance illegal settlements in the West Bank and Jerusalem. They provide construction companies with the capital for infrastructure and housing construction projects. Until the debt of the construction companies is paid off, the banks hold “ownership” over the land in question, making them important “owners” of large amounts of violently stolen land. Additionally, they also offer loans for individuals who want to build a house or start a commercial business in the settlements. With its investments, CUNY is helping to finance the illegal seizure of land and the violence that comes with it.

CUNY does not only invest directly in these companies but also invests in equity and asset management companies like BlackRock and large investment banks like Goldman Sachs. Besides investing large sums in the companies above, both play a tremendous part in the global capitalist system because they advise national governments and banks and direct infrastructure investments around the globe. These companies have connections to the U.S. Congress through lobbying and the so-called revolving door: politicians who act in the interest of these organizations often get a well-paying position in their upper ranks after they leave politics. The current chancellor of Germany even acted as chair of the supervisory board for BlackRock’s German branch. These companies have an immense influence on our world and design it according to the needs of capital, not people.

CUNY’s involvement in the genocide in Gaza, the wars of U.S. empire, the mass incarceration and large-scale warehousing and deportation of non-citizens is clear.

Our university is complicit in the deportation regime that is tearing families apart and terrorizing our communities. It invests in companies that make money from mass surveillance in the U.S. and abroad. In companies that build bombs and missiles that tear apart the bodies of countless innocent people all over the world. Our university is complicit in the suppression of millions of people and the death of hundreds of thousands more. CUNY bears responsibility for tens of thousands of children who have to grow up without their parents, their families or communities. All in the service of capital accumulation.

At the same time, CUNY is much more than its administration, Board of Trustees, suffocating bureaucracy, and the financial support for police violence and genocide. CUNY is also tens of thousands of students, faculty and staff that organize, educate and push against mass incarceration, war, genocide, homelessness, misogyny, xenophobia, racism, queerphobia and exploitation. They create an intellectual environment that encourages questioning the state, the system and capitalism itself. This too is CUNY. There is a contradiction within CUNY: the oppressive side of neoliberal and capitalist education and genocide support, and a side of resistance and progressive change, even rebellion, and both are closely intertwined within the institution. But like all contradictions, this one cannot last, and it is our task as socialists to organize for a CUNY in service of the working class, here and beyond U.S. borders, and not the apparatus of capitalist accumulation.

CUNY
