scraped.title: Dangling from the Ivory Tower at CUNY: Higher Education Under Capitalism - Left Voice
scraped.description: Recent data about CUNY reveal the grim material reality for countless college students at all levels. These troubling figures raise fundamental questions about higher learning within capitalism.
scraped.author: Victor Harlan
scraped.body_text:
Recent data about CUNY reveal the grim material reality for countless college students at all levels. These troubling figures raise fundamental questions about higher learning within capitalism.

Victor Harlan

Last spring, a budget hearing for the City University of New York (CUNY) system in New York City revealed that an estimated 8,000 students were homeless in the last year. With approximately 20 percent of students reporting some kind of housing insecurity, ranging from difficulty paying rent to the more extreme danger of being unhoused, it is clear that students need serious material assistance. This is particularly startling in New York, where the CUNY system lauds itself as an institution accessible to the working class.

These dynamics are reflected nationwide. In 2020 , more than 1.5 million students experienced homelessness across the country, with around 42 percent living at or below the federal poverty line. Like most material hazards, more marginalized demographics, like people of color and women , experience these difficulties more acutely.

This phenomenon should also be understood as part of a broader affordability crisis, where the average cost of tuition, including at public universities, has skyrocketed by over 175 percent in the last 20 years. The cost of rent, on average, has doubled , while inflation-adjusted wages have grown at 10 to 20 percent less than worker productivity . Students are also expected to weather these hardships while U.S. taxpayer dollars are spent on imperialist war against Iran, recruitment for ICE, and insulating an ever more detached and opulent bourgeoisie.

The hazards of pursuing higher education for working-class people show that equal opportunity is a class-based myth. While it is true that anyone can theoretically pursue whatever kind of education and corresponding career that they choose (even though the One Big Beautiful Bill restricted the availability of loans for certain programs), the material ability to complete these degrees is uncertain for low-income and working-class students.

This is one of the ways the bourgeoisie enshrines and reproduces itself, creating a symbiotic relationship between the ruling class and academia. Universities legitimize the wealthy, insulating successive generations of bourgeois leadership with prestige. These leaders, in turn, fund the universities and link them to sectors of the bourgeoisie. In the past, it was understood that higher learning bore with it a deterministic social character, that it was the privilege of the wealthy and the powerful, but modern liberal republics promote a mythology of equal opportunity, and access to higher learning as a ladder of upward social mobility was a pillar of the Post-War Order.

When thousands of working-class students experience homelessness while pursuing secondary education, it is disgustingly disingenuous to say that any equality of opportunity exists. While CUNY still ranks relatively high in terms of social mobility, this is still part of a downward trend overall, especially given that tuition used to be free and higher levels of certification are increasingly necessary for advancement.

“The experiment is to be tried, whether the children of the people — the children of the whole people — can be educated; and whether an institution of learning of the highest grade can be successfully controlled by the popular will, not the privileged few but by the privileged many.” These words from Horace Webster, president of the Free Academy, which preceded the CUNY system, speak to an idea that everyone involved with CUNY is familiar with, but which doesn’t represent the material reality. If CUNY truly wants to educate “the children of the whole people,” then why is it patting itself on the back for being half the cost of the national university average when half the nation’s students live in poverty?

This “affordable” tuition, while far more accessible than other colleges, is not affordable enough to someone making minimum wage. Initiatives like the New York State Tuition Assistance Program, which provides non-repayable tuition grants to low-income students, have income thresholds lower than a full-time minimum wage income. This demonstrates a common frustration working-class students experience: being too poor to fund their studies, but evidently not poor enough to qualify for what assistance does exist.

The descent from the lofty liberal platitudes that sparkled on the newborn CUNY only highlights the sharp contradictions of today. Late-nineteenth- and early-twentieth-century planners excitedly proclaimed that quality education, made available to the whole population for free, would provide a way for the poor to ascend to an expanding middle class. Now that promise is systematically out of reach.

Higher education is not considered a right in the United States, but rather a commodity to be sold for profit. The barrier created by tuition alone is often enough to deter working-class, poor, and otherwise marginalized young people from pursuing education, but even if they can manage that, education can exacerbate their precarity. Forced to reduce their working hours, forego workplace advancement, or take less secure work in general, the basics of food, health, and shelter often fall by the wayside in pursuit of something that is understood to be a personal and social good. Add to that areas of study that require labs or field work, which tend to be the more lucrative career tracks that are emphasized, or the dilemma of having a handful of classes left to take that happen to only be scheduled when a student has to work.

Young people are taught that a secondary education is basically an essential component of social upward mobility in contemporary America, and yet society seems engineered to deter the working class from attaining it. Those who can weather the material hazards might find that a bachelor’s degree increasingly does not guarantee the security that it used to.

Various progressive slogans surround higher learning, ranging from canceling student debt to making state schools and technical programs free, but these slogans are not enough. With thousands of CUNY students living without secure housing, we should go beyond trying to convince rich people and reactionaries of progressive reforms, and instead raise demands for a revolutionary program for the university.

We can and must fight to preserve and expand the democratic rights we have, but we have to do so with a transitional strategy. Free tuition and student debt relief? Students should be paid to attend school, freeing them to focus on learning, engaging, and bringing forth the next great waves of thought. Disclosure and divestment from imperialism? The decisions and budgets of universities should be made democratically by students and workers, in direct defiance of the capitalist state.

The university should be the laboratory of a new society, where students and faculty reject the social arrangements of capitalism and reorganize based on meeting human needs, like housing for all. More urgently, the academy provides a battleground to raise the democratic demand for full rights for immigrants , where a collaborative environment of education can protect the students and faculty that make it vibrant. We must not be shackled by bureaucratic conservatism and compromise. Instead, we should tie the needs of the most vulnerable to our demands for a university under student and worker control, and treat this as part of a direct challenge to capitalism.

CUNY

scraped.h1: 161,000 People Speak Native Languages at Home, New Data Shows
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

In 2025, 161,000 people in the United States spoke Native languages at home.

That’s according to a dataset released on Nov. 20 by USAFacts, a nonprofit civic initiative that curates government data. The numbers come from the U.S. Census Bureau American Community Survey, which is based on 12 months of collected household information.

The data excludes Navajo speakers, but the organization compiled a separate dataset on the Navajo language.

44.4% of those speakers lived in New Mexico, Alaska, or Arizona. Of those, New Mexico had the largest share of Native language speakers at 18.1%.

Uplifting stories of Native traditions, language revitalization, and cultural innovation.

Alaska had the largest percentage of Native language speakers per state population, at 3.6%, followed by New Mexico at 1.4% and South Dakota at 1.1%. The top three metro areas with Native language speakers were Albuquerque, Phoenix, and Minneapolis.

The data also showed a sharp decrease in Native language speakers over the past 15 years; from 2010 to 2025, the number of people who spoke Native languages at home, excluding Navajo, decreased by 18.1%

USAFact’s Navajo language speakers dataset, also released on Nov. 20, showed that 139,000 people spoke Navajo at home in 2025. More than half of those people lived in Arizona. The Navajo language saw a similar decrease in speakers as overall Native languages from 2010-2015. During that time period, the number of people speaking Navajo declined by 19%.

scraped.h1: Washington Judge Admonished for Courtroom Comments on ‘too many acts of violence from the Native community.’
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

A Washington State Superior Court judge received an official admonishment on Friday, Nov. 20, for comments he made on “violence from the Native American community”

Mason County Superior Court Judge Monty D. Cobb made the comments on February 13, 2026, while sentencing a defendant — a citizen of the Skokomish Tribe — who pled guilty to charges of Manslaughter in the Second Degree for killing a fellow tribal citizen.

Your contribution is appreciated.

According to a document from the Washington State Commission on Judicial Conduct, before imposing the sentence, Cobb said:

“It is extremely unfortunate that I see way too many acts of violence from the Native community. It seems disproportionate. You’re not the only place. It happens everywhere, but I see way too much of it coming out of your community, and it is sad it really is.”

Witnesses who filed complaints with the Commission described hearing a gasp in the courtroom as the comments caused immediate offense. The complaints triggered an investigation.

The Commission deemed the comments reinforced negative stereotypes about Native communities and placed blame for the rates of violence it experiences as the result of historical and ongoing oppressions.

According to Commission documents, Cobb stated that he intended to acknowledge the suffering of the victim’s family. “However,” the Commission wrote. “Intention in words or actions does not override or cancel their impact on those receiving them.”

The Commission document noted that courtroom observers think Cobb “does not harbor a bias against Indigenous people or other marginalized groups, and that everyone is treated fairly in his courtroom.”

scraped.h1: ‘We’re Still Thriving’: Winnebago Tribe Siblings Bring Woodland Dancing to Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade
scraped.body_text:
Native News Online

On Thursday morning, Wambli Dolezal, 8, and his siblings, Wakiya Dolezal, 12, and Misu Dolezal, 14, all citizens of the Winnebago Tribe, will dance in a ceremony on the streets of Manhattan during one of the year’s most-watched televised events: the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade.

Wambli, Wakiya and Misu are Woodland Dancers and have all been dancing at powwows since 2020. Wambli, known as “Baby Wam,” drew attention last year when videos of his dancing at powwows and ceremonies gained traction online.

The siblings’ mother, Cassie Kitcheyan, told Native News Online that people would approach the family at powwows.

“People began to tell him how powerful his dancing was. Sometimes people would,” she said. “People are really touched by him. It feels like he represents something for us Indian people. It evokes something in people, especially the elders.”

Your contribution is appreciated.

Last summer, viral video of Wambli dancing caught the attention of Larry Yazzie, a Meskwaki dancer and founder of Native Pride Productions, which organizes the Native dancers at the Macy’s Thanksgiving Day Parade. Yazzie reached out, inviting him to dance with the group at the parade.

In last year’s parade, in a crowd of thousands, amid marching bands, motorcades, brightly colored performers, and beneath massive cartoon floats, Wambli was fearless.

“He was way out front,” Kitcheyan said. “His little feet never got tired.”

Kitcheyan has always seen that fearlessness in her son. Wambli was born prematurely and weighed just under 4 pounds when he came into the world. He spent five weeks in the neonatal intensive care unit before coming home for the first time.

“He had a really hard start to life,” she said. “And even then, people would say, ‘He’s powerful. He’s a little medicine man. He’s gonna be all right.’”

This year, Wambli’s equally talented brother and sister are joining him in the parade, where they will join eight other dancers from across Indian Country. The family launched a GoFundMe to cover travel expenses and raised more than $20,000, far exceeding their $3,000 goal.

While all her kids are gifted in Woodland dancing and have won awards at powwows, Kitcheyan said she stresses the “why” behind the dance.

“We teach them why they dance: to be good people, to dance for their elders, the mourners, for anyone who can’t dance anymore, and to be a good relative,” she said.

When the invitation was first extended to Wambli to dance in the parade, Kitcheyan was hesitant.

Her kids are raised in their culture, and Wambli attends a Ho-Chunk immersion school. She also worked as a Native studies teacher for many years and still teaches one class as an adjunct faculty member. Would dancing in the parade to celebrate a holiday she and many Native people don’t celebrate, one that perpetuates a false and damaging story about American history and Native Americans, be a betrayal? Would it put her kids in the line of fire for criticism?

After giving it a lot of thought, she asked herself: What if there were no Native people in the parade?

“I realized how powerful it would be to show that yes, despite all of this, this trauma, this genocide, we’re gonna dance at your parade,” she said. “We’re gonna show you who we are, and that in itself is powerful because we’re still here. We’re still thriving people. That’s how I got through that. Our culture is so beautiful and so strong, and we’re a living culture.”

scraped.title: Catie St. Germain and rise from insecurity to the top of the charts
scraped.description: It has only been about three years since Catie St. Germain released his first single but she has been racking up the accolades, ever since.
scraped.author: Dennis Ward
scraped.h1: Métis country singer Catie St. Germain and her journey from insecurity to the top of the charts
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

It has only been about three years since Catie St. Germain released his first single but she has been racking up the accolades, ever since.

Growing up, St. Germain says she had a front-row seat to a legendary musician and television host, crushing it on stage every night.

Her grandfather, Ray St. Germain, is a Canadian Country Music Hall of Fame inductee, who also created and hosted a nationally syndicated variety show, Big Sky Country.

However, having a famous grandfather and a very musical family did not ensure she would follow in their footsteps.

St. Germain’s mother even tried to push her in another direction.

“She didn’t have the best experience, I think doing music. The pressure of it all was a lot for her, so, she kind of steered us away. She didn’t want her kids to have to go through the hardships of the music industry and everything,” says St. Germain on the latest episode of Face to Face.

“For a long time I just didn’t think this was something in the cards for me. But I did perform, I did sing. I joined a rock tribute band and was kind of touring with them for a while but I ended up quitting and just having kids myself and thinking it was easier and better to do the 9 to 5 thing and obviously the scheduling worked better for having kids. And then I got back to it though.

“I really wasn’t fulfilled and so I decided to write my original song, The Taxman in 2023 and release that and see what would come of it and it just sparked a whole new passion for me,” adds St. Germain.

The time on the road had St. Germain feeling like she was away from her family all of the time.

Breaking out on her own was also a way to challenge herself and show some bravery.

“I’ve always been somebody who is a little bit more insecure and never would try, I didn’t want to put myself out there. Even in the family too, I would do the family shows with them but I was always the shy one, like I wasn’t the one that was out there, at all. Very shy, very timid. I had my kids and I just really wanted to show them that they could do anything they put their mind to and they can be brave and if I was going to tell them to do that, then I probably should do it too,” says St. Germain.

The reaction to that first song and following EP, Cleaning House (Or Trying) was even more incredible that St. Germain had imagined.

In the three years since then, St. Germain has sang the national anthem at the 2025 CFL Grey Cup in Winnipeg, been named one of Amazon Music’s breakthrough artists, and racked up three number one hits on the Indigenous Music Countdown.

In November at the 2026 Manitoba Country Music Awards, St. Germain was named Female Artist of the Year and took home Interactive Artist, Duo or Group of the Year, for the third straight year.

St. Germain says social media has allowed her to reach a bigger audience.

“I think too, a lot of people get to relate to me as a human, as a person and not just the music, which is really fun. Again, I just create better relationships that way and I think it entices them more to go listen to the music after that,” says St. Germain.

St. Germain’s latest single, a duet with Don Amero called Home hit the Indigenous Music Countdown on November 21.

Her next single , I Ain’t Free will be released on Nov. 27.

Dennis is Métis from southern Manitoba. After spending a decade working in TV in Alberta and Ontario, Dennis returned to Manitoba to join APTN. In 2016, he won a Canadian Association of Journalists award for his story A Soldier Scorned for APTN Investigates. In 2017, he became a host/producer for APTN National News and Face to Face.

scraped.title: AFN calls for strengthening of First Nations Clean Water Act
scraped.description: The national chief of the AFN says the Carney government’s proposed Bill C-37 falls short on health, legal and environmental protections.
scraped.author: Fraser Needham
scraped.h1: AFN calls for strengthening of First Nations Clean Water Act
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

Assembly of First Nations National Chief Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak addresses media at the start of the fall session of Parliament on Sept. 22, 2026. Photo: Keelan Jacobs/APTN.

The national chief of the Assembly of First Nations says the Carney government’s proposed Bill C-37 falls short when it comes to the necessary health, legal and environmental protections to ensure access to clean drinking water.

“Clean drinking water is a human right that has been denied for generations of First Nations families across Canada,” Cindy Woodhouse Nepinak said in a press release.

“Sadly, with Bill C-37, the federal government is still refusing to recognize the human right to water for First Nations in Canada.”

Woodhouse Nepinak was a witness before the Indigenous and Northern Affairs Committee on Tuesday, which is studying the proposed legislation.

The AFN says Bill C-37, also known as the First Nations Clean Water Act, is significantly weaker than legislation drafted by the previous Trudeau government.

Bill C-61, which did not pass because Parliament was prorogued under former prime minister Justin Trudeau, recognized First Nations access to clean drinking water as a human right, but has been weakened under the current legislation to the “progressive realization.”

It took Carney more than a year to reintroduce the new legislation.

According to the United Nations, progressive realization means that states “have a duty to respect, protect and fulfil economic, social and cultural rights,” and are “required to progressively achieve the full realization of these rights over a period of time. Regardless of resource availability, States have an immediate obligation to take appropriate steps to ensure continuous and sustained improvement in the enjoyment of these rights over time.”

The AFN also says the proposed legislation gives provinces a veto, lacks adequate protections for source water and doesn’t live up to Canada’s United Nations Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples commitments.

“We are calling on Parliament to take the time needed to work with First Nations on required improvements, clarifications and amendments to Bill C-37 that respect our rights and jurisdiction,” Woodhouse Nepinak said.

Bill C-37 has passed second reading in the House of Commons and is currently in committee.

The previous water legislation was drafted in response to a lawsuit that was settled in 2021.

That bill also included an option for source water protection but failed to pass before Parliament was dissolved for the 2025 election.

The new bill is backed by $4.6 billion in funding over five years, which the federal government describes as the single largest commitment ever made to First Nations water protection.

Indigenous Services Minister Mandy Gull-Masty has said the new legislation was written to “stand the test of time” and insists it does not weaken the protections in the previous bill.

Fraser spent the last 20 years working in both print and radio in Saskatchewan – mostly in the northern part of the province. Before joining APTN’s Ottawa bureau, he was news director for the Missinipi Broadcasting Corporation working out of their Prince Albert office. He holds a bachelor of arts degree in political science from Carleton University and a diploma of journalism from Algonquin College.

scraped.title: Nunavut’s family services minister gave ‘untrue’ statements to legislature: Bates
scraped.description: Jane Bates, Nunavut's child advocate, says the minister of Family Services has made false statements to the territory's legislature.
scraped.author: Jesse Staniforth
scraped.h1: Nunavut’s child advocate accuses minister of Family Services of delivering ‘absolutely, patently untrue’ statement to legislature
scraped.body_text:
APTN News

Stories about First Nations, Métis and Inuit peoples

APTN News

‘The very government services that are being funded to protect children are failing them. That is catastrophic,’ says Jane Bates.

Nunavut's territorial legislature. Photo: APTN

Nunavut’s child advocate says information presented to the territory’s legislature by the minister of Family Services regarding child welfare issues was “absolutely, patently untrue.”

Jane Bates, the Representative for Children and Youth Nunavut, told APTN News that Gwen Healy Akearok has on multiple occasions made false statements to the territorial legislature.

According to Bates, in a May 22 statement, Akearok said her department had “completed a full update of our standards and procedures manual, which now reflects best practices in social work with a priority focus on Inuit culture and maintaining connection to family.”

Bates said she was astonished to hear this announcement.

“I was listening to it thinking, ‘What? Hang on here,’” she said. “So I went back to them and I said, ‘You don’t have any section for children in care and you have no section for foster care. How is it that you’ve got a comprehensive standards and procedures manual?’”

More recently, Bates took issue with the way Healy Akearok handled the acknowledgment that DFS had given incorrect numbers on children in care to the media.

On Oct. 22, Healy Akearok rose in the legislature and said, “Recent public reporting has raised important questions about information previously provided by Family Services regarding children and youth receiving services. The department identified errors in the information initially provided, apologized, and supplied corrected information before publication.” Bates, who said she was the one who identified the wrong information, took umbrage at the minister’s claim that her department identified the errors itself.

“That is absolutely, patently untrue,” said Bates. “That is not what happened.”

In fact, CBC’s reporting acknowledged “Nunavut’s representative for children and youth Jane Bates, thought that figure looked suspiciously low, so CBC News asked the department for further clarity.” Bates provided APTN the text of a letter she wrote to the minister, in which she described Healy Akearok’s statement to the legislature as “factually inaccurate,” adding “your statement inaccurately attributes the identification of the error to the department and implies that it was corrected before the inaccurate information was published.” Bates also forwarded the text of Healy Akearok’s response, which read, “Thank you for your message, advice, and recommendations. At this time, after careful review, we’re satisfied with the information that was presented in the Assembly.”

“To be honest,” said Bates, “there are moments when it’s like pure dishonesty around what has been done. I have on numerous occasions caught the department telling me something that’s factually inaccurate.”

APTN has repeatedly requested interviews with Healy Akearok to discuss the issue of child welfare in Nunavut. At first, her office was open to scheduling an interview, but after several follow-ups, we’ve received no response.

APTN also reached out to Premier John Main, who told APTN News InFocus in May that the territory recognized the need for improvement and was “committed to making improvements” to the child welfare system. His office did not reply to our requests for an interview.

‘If I’m being perfectly honest, I’m angry’ Allegations of dishonesty are far from the only source of frustration for Bates, who said the DFS has sat for years on recommendations she’s made for its improvement since 2020. “If I’m being perfectly honest, I’m angry,” Bates told APTN.

In September, Bates tabled her 2025-26 annual report. It noted a series of worsening circumstances, such as the fact that reports of sexualized violence jumped from eight events in 2024-25 to 22 events in 2025-26, though it added, “The Department of Family Services’ reporting of critical injuries also remains problematic, and the figures provided cannot be considered accurate or reliable.”

Bates told APTN that the unwillingness of the department to implement changes is deepening an already longstanding crisis in child protection.

“I’m angry that the department has not made significant change [or] improvement — this is now the fifth report,” she told APTN. “There was one in 2011, 2014, and then in 2023, of course, the report that declared that child welfare was a crisis in Nunavut. And then now we fast-forward to 2025: there were no significant changes again.”

APTN recently reported on the text of notes for an excoriating presentation Bates delivered to the Nunavut Legislative Assembly, in which she alleged the territorial Department of Family Services was failing so dramatically that the department assigned to protecting Nunavummiut children was actually complicit in harming them.

Bates acknowledged to APTN that she had prepared the notes and stood by their messaging.

In that presentation, Bates threatened to ask the Nunavut Court of Justice to compel the department to heed the recommendations that have been overwhelmingly ignored since she began in her position.

“Child welfare in Nunavut is the single biggest issue that needs to be addressed facing children, youth, and families,” Bates said, “and the very government services that are being funded to protect children are failing them. That is catastrophic.”

She noted there are currently over 400 children in care, with as many as 80 placed in care outside the territory, yet the department knows neither where all the children in their care are located, nor even how many children it is responsible for.

“The injustice that is currently occurring,” Bates said, “the violation of rights of children, youth and their families is egregious — egregious.”

Like this since the beginning

Bates began her role as Representative for Children and Youth in 2019 and said her most recent annual report and her address to MLAs in September were not the first times she’s flagged serious concerns in the DFS.

“I issued a letter to the Department of Family Services about my intense concerns about what I was seeing in January of 2020,” she recalled. “It was less than six months into my appointment. And again, it’s the same message: ‘There are significant concerns in data collection. There are significant concerns around the safety of children in the care of the director.’”

Bates said she didn’t make specific recommendations, but raised her concerns about information collection, DFS conduct in investigating child-protection matters and other issues of child safety. These were, eventually, the concerns she flagged formally, and has continued to flag.

Referring to the damning Nov. 3 report by the auditor general into Nunavut child welfare, which found among other things that “the department [of Family Services] still could not consistently demonstrate that the basic safeguards intended to protect children [in their care] were being followed,” Bates said what was in the report was nothing new.

“It’s the same message. And it’s really disheartening. These are all some of the recommendations the Representative for Children and Youth Office has actually made to the department dating back to 2022.”

DFS lacks basic infrastructure

Bates describes the problems at the heart of the failing department as complex, and not resolvable either by firing existing staffers and replacing them, or by hiking salaries to attract as much talent to the department as possible.

Her plan for fixing DFS, rather, would begin with a full audit of all the communities in Nunavut in order to begin to develop a proper figure for the number of open cases involving children, comparing open cases with those that have been closed, and assessing the functioning of the process.

“My understanding is the department did an audit, if you will, of about 1,400 files,” she said. “So that’s been done fairly recently. And I have requested the report on that to say, ‘What happened with this? Tell me what the outcome was.’” She said she has not yet received that information.

Regardless, Bates returned to a single fault that she sees as a root of many failures in the department: the lack of a comprehensive standards and procedures manual.

The DFS, she said, “lacks what I would call basic infrastructure or a basic foundation. The family wellness division doesn’t have a comprehensive standards and procedures manual that governs children in care.”

Such a manual is not optional, Bates underlined. Comprehensive standards and procedures manuals are the road-maps organizations working with children in care are supposed to use to carry out their operation.

“That’s your starting point,” Bates said. “Then you have to ensure that once you implement those standards and procedures, that your supervisors and managers are ensuring that the frontline social workers are maintaining those standards.”

Bates said Nunavut’s DFS lacks specific standards and procedures for children in care, despite having more than 400 children in care. She said they lack separate documentation setting up standards and procedures for foster care. “There’s no program description [to clarify] this is the program, this is what it does, and here are the standards, i.e. the expectations, that help us fulfill our obligations under the legislation,” Bates said.

“There is not a foundation on which the department is practicing child welfare or delivering child welfare services. You have to have infrastructure. You have to have a foundation. You don’t build a house from the roof down.”

Against starting from scratch

Bates noted she had told the department, following the auditor general’s 2023 report, that there was no need to reinvent the wheel by developing their own standards and procedures manual.

She said she told the DFS that many jurisdictions across Canada (such as the Northwest Territories, whose protocols are online ) have already developed standards and procedures that the DFS could adopt, which she framed as far preferable to the extreme demands of developing such a document from nothing.

“You don’t need to create your own as you go,” she said she told DFS. “You don’t need to start from scratch. And I would recommend that you don’t do that because it’s a lot of work. Turn to First Nations who are delivering child welfare, who have standards and procedures, and build from those. Let’s build on expertise.

“But the department has chosen to write their own standards and procedures.”

One aim for a comprehensive standards and procedures manual, Bates said, was to determine what kind of operational model the department will rely upon.

“From my perspective, and certainly working in a First Nation environment and Inuit environment, generally most child welfare agencies are moving towards a child-centered, family-focused approach, which means families are very much involved. They’re in the driver’s seat in relation to decision-making about their children, that family group conferencing,” she explained.

“What we see in our work and our reviews is that once children enter into the care of the director, families… they disappear.”

In September 2024, the department released the Ilagiitsiarniq Family Wellness Action Plan which outlines priorities for the department. But both Bates and the auditor general have told APTN that the plan doesn’t contain concrete actions to fix the problems with which the department is struggling.

Reliable data systems

Children in the care of the DFS, Bates said, are the department’s legal responsibilities, and she argued the most basic level of taking responsibility is knowing who is in DFS care and where they are.

The Nov. 3 auditor general’s report found “The department did not have a single, reliable source of information on how many children were in care or where they were placed, affecting both child safety and service planning.”

“This is about having good data systems,” said Bates. “You have to collect adequate data on your children. So this is about having a system in place. They have Matrix [data processing system]. It was implemented roughly three years ago. It should be able to collect that data, but it requires people to input the data into it.”

Nonetheless, the auditor general’s Nov. 3 report found the DFS relied on “a manually compiled list of children in care as the most accurate source of reporting information” rather than on the new Matrix system because employees had neither fully adopted Matrix nor become proficient in using it.

The auditor general found errors in the Matrix system were caused by delayed filing by social services workers or confusion about how to input information.

“The root cause of these realities continued to be a lack of staff capacity and chronic turnover challenges faced by the department,” the report noted.

But Bates rejected the idea that there is inadequate staff or that turnover is preventing DFS employees from getting used to using the Matrix system.

“The natural reaction is to assume it’s misappropriation of funds, or typically what you hear from the department is ‘This is a staffing issue,’” she said. “Staffing may be a component of it, but there are staff that are not using the Matrix system. There are staff not following the standards and procedures that are currently in place. Lack of comprehensive standards related to the department’s services contributes to a lack of clarity.”

Bates cautioned against presuming the DFS’s problems are all caused by staffing issues.

“It doesn’t account for the fact that there are staff currently in place that are not following standards related to investigations,” she said. “There are standards in place that are simply not being followed, yet there are staff available to do so.”

Training and oversight

While Bates predicted those outraged by various auditor general’s reports on the failing DFS might call for firings, she was uncertain changing or losing staff would help more than it would hinder the department.

“Certainly in the 2023 auditor general report,” she recalled, “there was a change in deputy ministers. They went to standing committee in September of 2023. The premier made the decision to change deputies, which is problematic in and of itself because often what happens is you’re starting from scratch again. You lose that corporate knowledge. And there really needs to be a focus on accountability.”

She argued the current situation with the Matrix system — and other issues in DFS — could potentially be resolved with further training.

“You need to understand how to do a proper investigation,” she said, “and there’s also oversight. When I talk about oversight, I mean supervisors. Supervisors need to ensure that they are supporting the social workers completing the work, that they are meeting standards and procedures, that they are falling in line with what the legislative requirements are. And then supervisors are in turn to be supervised by managers.”

Yet DFS, she said, “is not a department that is open to oversight.”

The Child and Family Services Act is Nunavut’s legislation governing child welfare, through which the Department of Family Services derives its power.

“What I conveyed to the standing committee was that this is all about follow-through and holding the Department of Family Services accountable. And everyone has to take responsibility to do that. That means bringing people to standing committee and asking for evidence — not statements that ‘things have been done,”’ she said.

“When you say that you’ve done ‘this,’ show ‘this’ to me. Prove it to me.”

An easy set of fixes?

Bates said improving the system seemed to her a simple-enough process.

“The fix is not that far away,” she said. “It’s not out of reach. And it’s not particularly difficult.”

DFS would seem to concur. The department has agreed to all or nearly all recommendations suggested by the office of the auditor general of Canada, as well as recommendations suggested by the child advocate.

“They agree,” Bates said, “and then they state the issue is follow-through.” DFS has failed to implement the overwhelming majority of recommendations it agreed to, in some cases dating back to 2011.

She added that following the auditor general’s damning 2011 and 2014 reports, which included recommendations to which DFS agreed, the department appeared before the Standing Committee on Oversight of Government Operations and Public Accounts.

“They basically, publicly said, ‘We have fulfilled these recommendations.’ But when the auditor general came in 2023, they found that that, in fact, did not occur.”

Bates alleged the DFS operates in a unique manner unlike other government departments.

“When issues are raised to our attention at the Representative for Children and Youth Office related to other departments, I can tell you our experience is very different than when we deal with the Department of Family Services,” Bates said.

“If an issue is raised with another department, we have a protocol that requires us to contact the department and say, ‘This concern has been raised to our attention, and we’re going to do a review of this.’ And the response from the other departments is very quick, and they say, ‘Whatever you need, we’ll get it to you.’ That is not our experience with the Department of Family Services.”

Lack of empowered oversight

Bates argued, as she did in her presentation to MLAs, that the most pressing issue for DFS is its lack of independent oversight, especially striking in a department that has been consistently found in assessments over more than a decade to have remained unable to reach basic standards it has set for itself.

“From the [perspective of the] Representative for Children and Youth Office,” Bates said, “we see significant failure in terms of oversight. From the front line right up to a fairly high level, there’s no one compelling people to say, ‘You’re not following standards,’ or ‘You’re not meeting the legislation.’ And when you don’t have this kind of oversight happening within your system, you’re bound to see a situation that we currently see.”

At present, she said, the DFS develops, reviews, approves and implements all its own standards and procedures. This includes deciding whether to accept and enact recommendations from outside agencies.

Recommendations from the auditor general of Canada, Bates said, or from her own office, are never more than suggestions, and are not legally binding on the family services department.

Nor, she says, is there any consequence to DFS employees in failing to follow through on implementing recommendations on how to fail Nunavut’s neediest children less often than they are currently doing.

“There is a consequence on the human level,” Bates noted. “It directly impacts the service to children, youth and families. And what we’ve seen is children and youth are being left at risk.”

Jesse joined APTN as a producer after 16 years as a print and web journalist. During seven of those years, he covered the Cree Nation of Eeyou Istchee for community newsmagazine The Nation. Jesse’s writing on Indigenous issues has also appeared in Canadian Geographic, the Toronto Star, the Rover, The Eastern Door, Metro, and the Huffington Post.

scraped.body_text:
After the Cree word for grandmother was added to the Oxford English Dictionary, a knowledge keeper says its spelling and how its defined leaves out key parts of its history

Amy Romer, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

Kôhkom (grandmother) Elsie Paul was nervous about posting her first TikTok.

The young people Paul worked with at the Kohkum Kisewatisowin Society encouraged her to share her teachings online. Paul had established the society to pass on Cree language and teachings after being punished for speaking Cree at a day school in Saddle Lake.

“You could probably reach 500 people in one day,” her oskâpêw (helper), Kathy Hamelin, told her.

“Oh my,” Paul, who was 77 at the time, replied.

It was December 2021, and the COVID-19 pandemic was still keeping people apart. Hoping to reach more young people in the amiskwaciwâskahikan (Edmonton) community, Paul decided to try something new.

From her kitchen, the Cree-Métis knowledge keeper from Treaty 6 territory could share her culture with people beyond her immediate circle.

Ping! Her phone chimed.

Ping!

“I don’t know why this one keeps pinging,” said Paul.

“I bet it’s your TikTok,” Hamelin replied.

Within an hour, Paul’s first video, a 21-second clip of her dancing the Red River jig in her kitchen, had racked up 2,000 views. By the end of the day, that number had climbed to 12,000.

Paul couldn’t believe so many people had watched it.

“That many people around the world,” Hamelin laughed.

Paul soon became known as the #technokokum , with some of her videos reaching 350,000 views.

Her time on TikTok was relatively brief, ending when she retired in late 2022. But the response to her videos showed how far a Cree kinship term could travel, reaching people far beyond the communities where it originated — with comments like “thank you for being everyone’s kokum” and “I can smell the smudge and tea through the screen.”

In June 2026, kokum — an anglicized spelling of the Cree word kôhkom — entered the Oxford English Dictionary (OED).

According to the OED, it’s the first kinship term from an Indigenous language in “Canada” to be added to the dictionary.

For Danica Salazar, a lexicographer and the executive editor for “World Englishes” at Oxford Languages, the addition reflects a shift in how Indigenous Languages are represented in English.

“There’s something quite anthropological about most of our early evidence for these words,” she said in an interview with IndigiNews.

Words like muskimoot (bag or sack), shaganappi (rawhide strip, from pîsâkanâpiy) and pemmican (dried meat and berries, from pimîhkân) are all anglicized Cree words already recorded in the OED.

Those earlier entries often reflected the objects and cultural practices that outsiders encountered and documented.

“Kokum,” on the other hand, is the first example of a word rooted in the familiar relationships and everyday lives among Indigenous communities in “Canada.”

Salazar believes the addition reflects a growing influence of Indigenous communities on the English language, as their words circulate beyond the accounts of anthropologists and other outside observers.

“So that’s really interesting because you can really see the more direct influence of Indigenous languages on English,” she said, “without the third party involvement.”

But for Hamelin, the word’s inclusion raised another question: what happens to a word’s meaning once it’s recorded in English?

To be considered for inclusion in the OED, a word must have an established presence in the English language

Oxford Languages , part of Oxford University Press, uses a vast digital collection of texts, known as a corpus, containing billions of words gathered from across the internet. Software helps lexicographers follow the ebb and flow of language, tracking which words are gaining momentum, how often they’re used, and by whom — whether in particular regions, communities or fields of study. When lexicographers noticed “kokum” appearing more frequently in “Canadian” English, they flagged it for further research. They found evidence of its use dating back to 1973, when Métis writer Maria Campbell published her memoir Halfbreed , about growing up in Saskatchewan.

Hamelin remembers the impact Halfbreed had when it was first published.

“Everybody read that book,” she said. “It’s where a lot of people were introduced to that word.”

For Salazar, this first citation was particularly meaningful: rather than someone writing about an Indigenous community and the words its members use, it was a person from the community using the word herself.

Later examples traced “kokum” through newspapers and books, and eventually into social media and everyday vernacular.

But the word was also circulating in Indigenous artistic and cultural spaces. In 2019, the Cree Literacy Network shared Kokum Rap , a collaboration featuring “power-poets and power-kokums” including Campbell, Louise Bernice Halfe-Sky Dancer , Rita Bouvier , and Zoey Roy .

Salazar sees the word’s increasing visibility as part of a broader shift in the public acceptance of Indigenous languages and cultures. Words that were once discouraged, if not prohibited, are now increasingly celebrated.

“A grandmother can be on TikTok and call herself a techno kokum, and everybody thinks that’s great,” she said.

Although Hamelin is “thrilled” to see the word recognized by the OED, she takes issue with its spelling — “kokum” — and the dictionary’s definition of it as “a grandmother” or “one’s grandmother.”

“It’s kôhkom,” Hamelin — who is a kôhkom herself — asserted.

“’Kokum’ doesn’t mean anything. All the meaning is lost.”

But the OED records how words are adopted into English, including changes to their spelling, pronunciation and meaning. Its etymology of “kokum” also acknowledges the Cree spelling, kôhkom, which it translates as “your grandmother.”

Hamelin says even that translation doesn’t tell the whole story.

“That’s what it has come to mean,” she said.

In Cree, Hamelin explained, kinship terms change depending on whose relative someone is speaking about.

If she were talking about “your grandmother,” it’s kikôhkom, said Hamelin.

The language distinguishes between one’s own grandmother, another person’s grandmother, or the grandmother of someone being discussed.

Those distinctions are part of a much broader understanding of kinship.

She recalled a teaching the late Henry Luboucan shared with her about the origins of kôhkom. He connected the word to ohkomimâw, which Hamelin understood as meaning “leader.”

In the teaching Hamelin described, kôhkoms held the authority to question and veto family decisions made by okimâwak (chiefs), particularly those affecting the community’s political or economic life.

“It’s so much deeper than just grandmother,” she said.

You don’t have to have children of your own to become a kôhkom, either. Your siblings’ children can make you one, too. And there’s a saying. The more kôhkom’s you have, the richer you are.

“So if you have 10 kôhkoms, you’re a millionaire,” chuckled Hamelin. “People don’t understand because of the disconnection from our language and culture.”

These relationships carry responsibilities for care, guidance and passing knowledge between generations. Hamelin worries that much of this understanding has been weakened by the disruption of families and languages through the residential “school” system and the Sixties Scoop .

“A lot of people forgot how to say the words,” said Hamelin. “So they anglicize them without even knowing the full meaning.”

“If I’m talking to you about my grandmother: ninôhkom. If I’m asking you about your grandmother, I say kikôhkom. And if I’m asking you about that person’s grandmother, I’d say ôhkoma,” said Hamelin.

For Hamelin, that history is part of why she believes the OED has a responsibility to represent the word’s origins accurately, given its authority and the millions of people who rely on the dictionary as an authoritative source.

“But I’m not at all surprised,” she said of what she considers an inaccurate entry.

Salazar, however, described the OED’s role differently.

“It’s there to tell the story of the language,” she said. “We’re basically just following usage rather than dictating it. So we’re documenting it, recording it, studying it, rather than influencing it.”

Yet the question of a dictionary’s influence is difficult to separate from its own reputation. On its website, the OED describes itself as “widely regarded as the accepted authority on the English language.”

Unlike many other English dictionaries, the OED is a “historical dictionary.” Its entries trace the development of words through documented examples of their use, sometimes spanning centuries.

But that written record is itself shaped by colonialism, which imposed written forms of documentation while suppressing Indigenous languages.

The OED’s earliest documented use of “kokum” therefore dates only to the 1970s, despite the word’s much longer history.

“Obviously, we cannot go back in time and listen to what people say. So it could very well be that if we could do that, we would have a much earlier date than 1973,” said Salazar.

The distinction between a word’s earliest recorded appearance in English and its history within Cree is especially important here. The dictionary’s written citations can establish when a word appeared in sources available to its researchers, while a word’s full history is often carried through oral teachings and community knowledge.

Salazar said the OED sometimes consults local language experts when researching words from other languages, but such consultations are uncommon.

“Only when information is missing,” said Salazar. “There was enough in the text for ‘kokum.’”

For “kokum,” OED etymologists drew on three online resources: the Online Cree Dictionary , the Dictionary of Moose Cree , and the East Cree Dictionary .

While the Online Cree Dictionary translates kôhkom as “your grandmother,” the Dictionary of Moose Cree lists ohkomimâw as “grandmother,” with ohkom as the stem and kôhkom meaning “your grandmother.”

Salazar acknowledged that words borrowed from historically oral languages should be traced through oral histories, not solely through written records. But she also pointed to the practical constraints of this approach, arguing that information must be recorded in some form to be accessible to researchers.

Audio recordings, she added, are relatively recent technologies in the history of languages. This reliance on recorded evidence, however, risks overlooking oral transmission itself as a knowledge system, through which language and its histories are passed down across generations.

Salazar said the OED is also hoping to introduce “moshum” — the anglicized spelling of môshom (grandfather) — in the near future.

That kinship word, like “kokum,” also appears in Halfbreed . But it doesn’t appear in literature as often as “kokum,” and so it didn’t make it into the 2026 round.

Hamelin believes the difference in their visibility may also reflect the impact of colonization on Indigenous men, including incarceration and premature death.

“The majority of our men die an early death or spend most of their lives incarcerated,” she said.

Hamelin stressed that mosômak (grandfathers) are valued just as much as kôhkomak (grandmothers).

“The mosômak deserve recognition,” she said. “I’ll look forward to seeing it in the dictionary.”

Despite her concerns about the dictionary entry, Hamelin said she doesn’t mind kôhkom becoming a more general word for grandmothers.

She recognizes that, for people separated from their languages, even an anglicized word can connect them to their families and cultures.

“It’s a way of preserving the language for people who don’t know it,” she said. “That small piece of language and culture keeps them anchored.”

Amy Romer, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

scraped.h1: May we all have a kôhkom — or a kokum
scraped.body_text:
After Oxford English Dictionary adds ‘kokum’ to its lexicon, IndigiNews publisher Eden Fineday reflects on her language — and her granny

Eden Fineday

●

●

In my 20s, I used to travel regularly from California, where I was attending university, to Saskatchewan to visit my family on the rez.

My granny, Irene Fineday, lived in a little red house on Sweetgrass Reserve, now called Sweetgrass First Nation .

Back then, in the 1990s, my cousin Etley also lived with her. Etley took care of her. Every day, she would brush her hair, cook her meals and generally do her bidding. She would drive granny into town for her appointments.

I only reconnected with my Sweetgrass family at the age of 14. Until then, I had lived with my white mother and my two white siblings in “Vancouver,” far away from my father and his side of the family.

I was told as a child that I was Native, so I understood it on an intellectual level, but I did not understand what it actually meant. Growing up, I was hungry for connection to my culture, but I had no one close to me who could teach me.

Once I was in touch with my Cree family, I began to visit at least once per year.

Whenever I landed in Saskatoon, I would pick up a rental car and get on the road to the rez. It was about an hour and a half from the airport to my granny’s little red house.

On the way, I always stopped in North Battleford and picked up some fried chicken. I would arrive on Sweetgrass with my offering, and my granny, my cousins, and whatever extended family was visiting would feast with me.

Sometimes, I would take my granny and my cousin Etley out for a meal. On one such occasion, at a chain restaurant in North Battleford, a waiter came to our table to take our order.

“What can I get you, kokum?” he asked my granny Irene.

I was taken aback.

I had never heard someone non-Indigenous use a Cree word like that. In fact, until that moment, I’m not sure I had ever heard the word. I called her granny. I felt a wave of gratitude wash over me – both for him making an effort to respect my grandmother, and for teaching me the word.

Wow! I thought. This white guy knew a Cree word. Not only that, but he used it to communicate something important — that my granny was indeed his kokum.

All kokums are everybody’s kokums in public.

My granny was an understated person. She didn’t have big, instantaneous reactions.

Once, I accidentally lit a frying pan on fire while I was cooking her some bacon. I yelled about the fire and the smoke, grabbed a cloth to wrap around the handle, ran to the front door with the frying pan, opened the door and the screen door, and threw the entire contents of the pan out into the snow off the side of the porch — while she watched me out the corner of her eye, barely looking up from her game of solitaire on the kitchen table.

I’ve come to learn this non-reacting is part of our culture. So my granny didn’t jump for joy when this waiter addressed her the way he did. But her eyes twinkled and I could see that she was clearly tickled pink.

The waiter also didn’t make a big deal of it. I think they both understood Cree ways of communicating. She placed her order.

That moment has always stuck with me. I think of it often, especially when I’m learning Cree. I hadn’t heard the word kokum very often growing up.

Even my Cree cousins on Sweetgrass called my grandmother “Granny” in my presence. Others, the ones she had raised, called her “Mama.”

There were different names for her, depending on who was speaking and their relationship to her. I wonder now how much of that was simply family habit, and how much came from the pressure to speak English.

I’ve been reflecting on this because I was moved last month when I learned that the Oxford English Dictionary had added the word “kokum” in June.

It’s a version of the proper Cree word, kôhkom. Lots of people spell it without the diacritics or the letter H, both of which are actually instructions for how to pronounce the word phonetically.

These widely accepted variety of spellings also serves a useful function — it shows us that, unlike kôhkom, which means “your grandmother” in Cree, kokum is an anglicization of the word, and the meaning has shifted a bit. Spelt in this way, it’s used to just mean “grandmother.”

In the past, my family may have felt pressured to use English words to describe their own family members.

Now, they can use a Cree word proudly, and if anyone tells them they should be speaking English, they can tell them that they are using English, too.

Living languages change, and that’s a beautiful thing. They grow to encompass the lived realities of the people speaking them.

Cree people have been forced to speak English for centuries. Now, there’s a tiny piece of reciprocation, a small acknowledgement of our worldview, which feels big.

“Canada” is a nation made of European culture on Indigenous Peoples’ lands. This country is a co-creation.

As we continue to move toward truth, toward reconciliation, my wish is that this small act leads to more understanding.

May more “Canadians” become aware of the many languages spoken on the sacred land under their feet.

May understanding grow from this.

May they learn more about the People, too and the beautiful cultures contained in our languages.

May we all have a kôhkom. Or a kokum.

Eden Fineday

scraped.description: Kalli Van Stone’s debut poetry collection welík't is informed by a decade of learning nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín

scraped.h1: From bending time to 16 names for a berry — a poet finds inspiration in her ancestral languages
scraped.body_text:
Kalli Van Stone’s trilingual debut collection welík’t is informed by a decade of learning nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín

Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

●

●

While exploring nsyilxcn (syilx language) and Secwepemctsín (Shuswap language) dictionaries, Kalli Van Stone (Spyu7) found herself drawn to words that held concepts she couldn’t find in English or Latin dictionaries.

In nsyilxcn, for example, she came across a word for the bending of time, which inspired her two-line poem “sumix kaʔɬis medicine power iii.”

These teachings opened up new worlds for Van Stone, which she began exploring through poetry.

Her debut poetry collection titled welík’t — meaning “sparkle” in Secwepemctsín — was published by Nightwood Editions in September.

The collection is divided into three sections: “nsyilxcn,” “english poems with indian names,” and “secwepemctsín.” Translations accompany her poems, alongside her own artwork.

Van Stone, who is syilx and Secwépemc from the north end of Okanagan Lake in “B.C.,” began reclaiming her ancestral languages a decade ago. This collection grew out of that work.

Across the collection’s 77 poems, Van Stone writes about personal experiences, the lives of her ancestors and the differences between her languages.

“They’re meant to be kind of shorter, more musical phrases, and then to kind of highlight any cool curiosities I find in the language,” she told IndigiNews.

Van Stone is particularly drawn to words in nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín that “challenge the Western concepts of time and personhood,” as well as those that speak to spirituality and ceremony.

Finding new words that displayed inspiring concepts brought up feelings of excitement and fulfilment for Van Stone. She references the nsyilxcn word kʷu ksq́ʷiɬq́ʷɬt, which translates to “you do wonders.”

Dictionaries are only one place she looks for inspiration. Van Stone also draws on things she’s heard throughout her life, returning to them later when she sits down to write.

“Mostly, it’ll just be like something cool I’ve heard throughout my life, and I’ll kind of tuck it away and then expand on it later in my own time,” she said.

“Or I find something really cool in the dictionary, or just in other documents or videos, and I’ll be like, ‘Whoa, there’s so much in that one sentence,’ and then I’ll kind of make my own thing.”

Writing in languages she’s still learning has, in part, shaped her aesthetic as a poet.

“I thought it was a really cool challenge to make something beautiful using some of the limitations I have. I know enough to do something creative, but it also makes it more simple, very stripped down to core ideas,” she said.

“I don’t let it stop me if I don’t have the words.”

There is also a musical quality to this brevity. In some of her poems, Van Stone experimented with call and response, drawing on musical traditions from her communities.

In the notes accompanying her poem “nt̓aʔlils,” Van Stone draws a parallel between a drumstick striking a drum and a dancer’s feet striking the earth. She relates these movements to syilx teaching about working through different emotions.

Van Stone has found similarities between nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín, both members of the Salishan language family.

“Our languages are sisters, so I love that there are so many ways where they kind of converge into each other, and then I was really interested in where they’re different,” she explained.

“Then we have really similar but still distinct music styles and a lot of our seasonal round is really similar, so that’s why it just felt so nice to learn both and do both and embrace all my ancestral sides.”

Working between nsyilxcn, Secwepemctsín and English brought its own challenges, particularly when translating and finding words that could convey what she wanted to express.

In “sixteen names of síyaʔ,” Van Stone lists 16 nsyilxcn names for the Saskatoon berry, compared with three English and Latin names. She connects that difference to the relationships her people have developed with the plant over thousands of years. She writes:

ʔupnkst uł taq̓mst skwists iʔ síya sixteen names of siyaʔ

síyaʔ sx̌wetl’x̌wítlaʔst wusxenílheml̓x t’et’k̓’ílhmel̓x t’et’íkwt’ekwt spep’aʕts’álak̓w slhk̓ilhp slhak̓ skw’lkw’lk̓in sk̓w’ets’k̓w’ets’wiʔhálhaʔk̓ sk’ek’sálhaʔk̓ siʔílhp siyíya lhek̓’alhpákst lexwús kt’etíkws

how many names? there are sixteen names

síyaʔ serviceberry saskatoon berry Amelanchier alnifolia

“Over time, you just spend so much more time and relationship with these plants and the different conditions they need to grow, the places they are,” she explained.

“We aren’t commodifying the plant as much, so it’s not like someone’s trying to claim it and it gets named and then we’re done with it. Over 1000s of years in the same place, [we] found all these different ways to call the plant.”

Van Stone took language courses that gave her a foundation for writing her poems. The connections she made in those classrooms also became an important part of her learning.

She also turned to the language and culture department in her father’s community, where she could reconnect with others who had grown up there.

Learning her languages has brought Van Stone closer to her ancestors and the histories of places connected to her family.

In “t ̓ík ̓naʔ flood,” she explores the history of a flooded reserve and the feelings of displacement she had experienced while visiting the area, even before learning what had happened there.

“I don’t like going there, and then it was like, ‘oh, it makes so much sense,’” she said.

Her family came from the area, and the poem became a way to explore her relationship with a place she found difficult to visit:

tík naʔ flood

i trace back before there was me my mom’s dad’s dad’s dad’s dad’s dad

i trace back before the border when we went back and forth as we pleased

i trace back before you flooded our village, the trout village before your hydroelectric dam on ntxʷitkʷ when we were from the lakes when we knew true power when we weren’t extinct

i trace back before we were baptized before the french and the jesuits came when we had Indian names

Groslouis, Grandlouis, born at inninkameep Aloysius, Ludovicus, renowned warrior, became our latin name

Paul Louis, npaupaukʷikn, a gambling name, born to.ma.as 1852 who went to live on Okanagan Indian Reserve #1 when he married Mary Anne daughter of Newilliskut, “Nouhiliskut” granddaughter of Quihammiken

Pierre Louis Benjamin Louis Clarence, Mike Louis mom me

She describes the poem as “trying to use art as a way to connect with some of those places that are harder to be in,” while also asking, “How do you relate to that place now, generations later?”

After drafting her poems, Van Stone turned to others for help refining them. Some were people she’d met in language classes, giving her a chance to reconnect and learn how their knowledge of the languages had developed since they’d studied together.

Much of the writing itself, however, happened independently.

“I mostly do a lot of my stuff alone just because it is […] kind of an emotional process or an internal kind of reflection,” she said.

More people across “B.C.” are learning their First Nations languages. According to the 2022 Report on the Status of B.C. First Nations Languages , the number of language learners increased by 3,106 between 2018 and 2022, bringing the total to 17,103.

While Van Stone notes that more people are learning their language, it can still be difficult to find people who are willing to contribute translations.

“It can be, kind of, a little bit lonely,” she said about the process.

“Sometimes it’s hard to find a group of people that want to do that together or support making creative work in [the language].”

She is not yet fluent in nsyilxcn and Secwepemctsín, but believes using the languages is important regardless of fluency.

“If we’re too scared to speak, then it’s like residential school again. We should be supported in learning, and then expressing ourselves and saying difficult things,” she said.

With all the topics covered in her collection, which include the impacts of day and residential “schools,” and her own educational experience discussed, it made the creation of welík’t a delicate process.

“Sometimes people just aren’t ready to hear those things, but I think it’s important to express ourselves,” she said.

In “Higher Learning in the Valley of the Shadow of Death,” Van Stone writes about experiencing racism on a university campus. She felt the experience needed to be included in the collection.

“It had to go somewhere because those things happen,” she said.

Van Stone also questions the lack of support Indigenous students can encounter in higher education, particularly when they’re already doing work connected to their communities.

Throughout the creation of welík’t , Van Stone faced many challenges, from difficult translations to finding publishers willing to publish a trilingual book.

“It was a challenge to find a cool publisher that wanted to work with me and lay it out in new ways and kind of be creative with how it looks on the page,” she said.

Van Stone speaks positively about the increasing presence of language in communities, including building names and signs.

“That’s what I want: our language to be everywhere,” she said.

She has also encountered people who are hesitant to pronounce unfamiliar words, something she hopes will change as the languages become more visible and familiar.

“I want to help break through that into something else, where it’s not so jarring for people.”

Creating a poetry collection which centres Indigenous languages is another avenue for people to see what can be done in the language.

With welík’t , she hopes to show other language learners what they can create, even while they’re still developing their fluency.

“We feel pretty safe in our own circles, but sometimes it’s hard to break further and go into new kinds of realms with our language or to talk about it in artistic ways,” she said.

“So it felt good to put [ welík’t ] out there.”

Alongside the poems, Van Stone included photographs and artwork, some depicting the cultural items and places that inspired her writing. Among them are images of root-digging tools such as pića, knapped arrowheads and knives made by her brother, stemelqín (Eric Van Stone).

“I really pushed for having some of my pictures in there, and different art that I’ve made because sometimes the poems are in response to a cultural item or a place, or a cool image,” she said, adding that digital images are also featured in welík’t .

She’s already thinking about how to experiment further, including with the call-and-response forms she explored in the collection.

“I like experimenting now, a bit more, for maybe a future collection or something,” she said.

Beyond writing, Van Stone sings, dances, and creates performance art, and has begun incorporating poetry and cultural tools into her performances.

Some of those performances have featured the pića (root-digging stick) and other tools pictured in welík’t .

“I’m hoping to fuse performance, visual art, and poetry together. That’s my fun time right now,” she said.

Dionne Phillips, Local Journalism Initiative Reporter

Dionne is Secwépemc on her father’s side and has Nuxalk and Cree roots on her mother’s side. She currently resides in her home territory of the Xats̓úll First Nation. Dionne started her journey of becoming a storyteller as a mentee with Indiginews. Now, she is excited to use the knowledge she learned to tell the stories from all over Secwepemcúl’ecw.

And yet, I have hope for journalism because of the work we’re doing at IndigiNews.

At IndigiNews, we embody tâpwêwin — the Cree value of integrity and responsibility in truth-telling. We are committed to our independent, Indigenous-led newsroom rooted in community, accountability, and relationality. We believe storytelling is a sacred fire that connects our pasts, presents, and futures through the storytellers in our Storytelling Lodge . IndigiNews creates space for Indigenous journalists, storytellers, Knowledge Keepers, and communities to gather, learn, and share stories that matter.

As a registered charity, we are building a fire that allows our work not just to ignite but to thrive. Rather than relying on advertising or corporate acquisition, IndigiNews is sustained by people like you who believe Indigenous stories are important for the future of our communities.

Your support is making a real difference.

Our community of supporters, our Firekeepers , make it possible to grow our newsroom, publish award-winning journalism, train emerging Indigenous journalists through initiatives like the ReFocus Photojournalism Fellowship, and publish trustworthy stories that serve our communities across the country. Every story we publish helps fill in gaps left by mainstream media and ensures Indigenous perspectives are represented with care, accuracy and respect.

But there is still more work to do.

As the media landscape becomes more and more uncertain, community support is as necessary and essential as it’s ever been. Every new Firekeeper helps protect the independence of our newsroom and strengthens journalism that is accountable to our many and varied communities over corporations.

That’s why we’re inviting you to become a Firekeeper.
