scraped.title: How many Native people are missing or murdered in California? The state still can’t say - ICT
scraped.description: Newsom vetoed a statewide program, calling it duplicative of existing efforts. Advocates say families turn to social media and grassroots groups instead of police.
scraped.author: Melanie Henshaw
scraped.h1: How many Native people are missing or murdered in California? The state still can’t say
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Melanie Henshaw ICT + CalMatters

In 2020, California legislators ordered the state Department of Justice to find out how many Native Americans and Alaska Native people in California are missing or have been murdered, and what more the state could do to report and find them.

Janet Bill, director of the department’s Office of Native American Affairs and the chairwoman of the Picayune Rancheria of the Chukchansi Indians, told an Assembly budget subcommittee in April that the report was “in the final stages of internal review.” Seven months later, there still is no report. In an unsigned statement sent by email, the Department of Justice said the report is now expected this winter.

The state set aside $5 million in 2021 for the study and for a tribal assistance program meant to help law enforcement agencies and tribal governments navigate overlapping jurisdiction on tribal lands. About $1.2 million of that remained unspent as of February, according to a document prepared for the same subcommittee. The department did not say what is in the report, what delayed it or how the money was spent.

In September, Gov. Gavin Newsom vetoed Senate Bill 891 , the third attempt in as many years to create a Missing and Murdered Indigenous Persons Justice Program within the department. The program would have supported investigations, served as a liaison between families, tribal governments, and law enforcement and required the department to annually report the number of cases to the Legislature.

In his veto message, Newsom pointed to existing efforts, including the Feather Alert system for missing Indigenous people and roughly $35 million in grants to tribes for their own programs.

“This historic investment highlights the need for sustained action — and California’s continued commitment — to confront the disproportionate violence facing Native communities,” Newsom wrote . “While well-intentioned, this bill disregards those efforts and creates a new, unfunded program that is duplicative of the work already underway.”

Amid what federal agencies and Indian Country recognize as a nationwide crisis , homicide was the fourth-leading cause of death among Native American and Alaska Native men and boys ages 1 to 44 and the sixth-leading cause among Native American and Alaska Native women and girls in the same age group in 2023, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

California has no statewide office dedicated to missing and murdered Indigenous people and no official count of cases.

Assembly Bill 3099 , was meant to change that. It required the state justice department to determine the scope of the problem, identify barriers to reporting and investigating cases and recommend changes, including legislation, after consulting with tribal governments, law enforcement and courts.

The law was written by Assemblymember James Ramos , a San Bernardino Democrat who is Serrano and Cahuilla and a lifelong resident of the San Manuel Indian Reservation. Ramos did not respond to a request for an interview.

The Legislature funded the work in 2021, and the department described it as a five-year effort. In January 2024, a department official told the Assembly Select Committee on Native American Affairs that the report was due in 2025.

The Weekly · Free, every Thursday

The stories that mattered most across Indian Country, chosen by ICT's newsroom. Want regional or powwow news? See all our newsletters

Part of the delay may come down to the very problem the study was meant to measure. A 2024 Senate analysis noted that a lack of data on crimes in tribal jurisdictions kept the department from completing the report. That year, the state passed Assembly Bill 2695 , which for the first time requires law enforcement agencies to collect and report data on crimes on tribal lands.

“(The Office of Native American Affairs) has raised concern about the lack of accurate statistical data and is actively collaborating on viable solutions,” Isaac Bojorquez, a specialist in the office, told the same budget committee in March 2025.

The final report will contain recommendations on how law enforcement agencies across the state can protect Indigenous communities, according to the unsigned justice department statement.

Lacking a state count, lawmakers and advocates at times rely on outside data. State officials frequently say California ranks fifth in the nation for the number of cases based on a 2018 study of 71 U.S. cities by the Seattle-based Urban Indian Health Institute.

The Sovereign Bodies Institute, a Humboldt County nonprofit, also tracks cases. A 2020 analysis by the group identified 165 missing or murdered Indigenous women, girls and Two-Spirit people across the state since 1900, and its data shows about 18 new cases a year.

Official records offer little help. Missing Indigenous people may appear in the federal National Missing and Unidentified Persons System, known as NamUs, in the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children’s records and in a California version of the search tool. But tribal affiliation is not searchable in the national center’s records or the California tool, and the state justice department did not respond when asked if it has a separate internal search system.

Until 2018 , tribal affiliation could not be searched in NamUs, according to the federal Department of Justice. Without a system designed for Indigenous cases, investigators and researchers have trouble tracking them, especially because databases don’t record tribal affiliation in the same way.

Federal death data also undercounts American Indian and Alaska Native deaths. Coroners and law enforcement officials often fail to collect information on people’s Indigenous identity, according to lawmakers and advocates. Because death certificates often list Native people as another race, usually white, the CDC estimates the actual death rate for American Indian and Alaska Native people nationally is about a third higher than reported.

The state’s main response has been to award money for tribes.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Since 2023, the Board of State and Community Corrections has awarded about $35 million in three rounds of competitive grants for tribal programs on missing and murdered Indigenous people. The programs include victim services, programs to reduce risk to human trafficking, support for domestic violence victims and connecting with people at high risk, like youth in foster care.

Only federally recognized tribes can apply. California has 62 tribes that are not federally recognized, according to the governor’s office, and it does not maintain an official, single state recognition process.

The state has also given the justice department money to work on individual cases. The 2024 budget included $5 million in one-time funding for the department to help identify and investigate cases and to act as a liaison between tribal governments, families and law enforcement.

Some local and county law enforcement agencies have formed partnerships with nearby tribes to help in missing and murdered persons cases, and the department’s office of Native American Affairs sometimes works with tribal departments on cases.

Sen. Sabrina Cervantes , a Riverside Democrat, has carried bills to create the justice program three years in a row. In 2024, Assembly Bill 2279 passed the Legislature and was vetoed and last year’s Senate Bill 4 passed the Senate but was held in committee. This year’s version, sponsored by the Yurok Tribe, also made it through the Legislature before Newsom’s veto.

Cervantes has said that although the state has expanded its efforts to curb the crisis, a statewide office focused on collecting data, working with families and tracking cases across jurisdictional boundaries is still missing.

Cervantes pointed to data from the Sovereign Bodies Institute showing that the overwhelming majority of missing and murdered Indigenous children in Southern California are girls, and that law enforcement responded in only a few cases.

“Murdered and missing Indigenous people were a serious issue that wasn’t being fully addressed,” she said to CalMatters/ICT.

Advocates, like Norm Sands, cofounder of Way Of The Sacred Mountain, an advocacy group for Native women, who is of Apache and Yaqui descent, says distrust between tribal communities and law enforcement, a complicated jurisdictional picture and limits on tribal police authority have deepened the crisis.

“The families feel completely alone — and they often are,” he said.

Lawmakers removed a proposed statewide task force on missing and murdered Indigenous people that would have been led by the California Highway Patrol, from Ramos’ separate Assembly Bill 31 in August. The law Newsom signed in September made permanent a program giving some tribal police officers state peace officer authority.

Teyana Viscarra, the organization’s other cofounder, who is of Piro-Tewa Pueblo, Apache and Kumeyaay descent, said confusion over which agency is responsible for looking for a missing Indigenous person makes reporting harder and adds to families’ stress.

“The families feel powerless,” she said. “They’re intimidated by law enforcement and an overly complex system.”

Families often turn first to social media and other groups to search for missing relatives since that’s a network they trust, she said.

“We’re resisting erasure,” Viscarra said. “Our public officials need to be held accountable for holding the first peoples of this land in dignity and honor.”

Meanwhile, the justice department now says the report California ordered six years ago will be released this winter.

This story is co-published by CalMatters and ICT, a news partnership that covers Indigenous communities in California.

scraped.description: Kansas Rep. Sharice Davids traveled to Michigan to stump for Sean McCann – and assist in his victory
scraped.author: Amelia Schafer
scraped.h1: Native lawmaker helps Native candidate make history
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Amelia Schafer ICT

The longest-serving Indigenous woman in the U.S. Congress thinks more Native people should be national lawmakers.

So she went on the road to campaign for other Indigenous candidates and met with largely untapped voter blocs: Indigenous people. “Native representation in Congress matters,” said Rep. Sharice Davids of Kansas. The Democrat represents the state’s 3rd Congressional District.

In Michigan she found success, helping elect Sean McCann, a citizen of the Citizen Potawatomi Nation, as the first Native to represent Michigan in Congress.

“Traveling across the country, meeting with tribal leaders, and campaigning alongside folks like Congressman-elect Sean McCann was a powerful reminder of how far we’ve come,” Davids, a citizen of the Ho-Chunk Nation, told ICT in a statement. “Sean is a dedicated family man and proven problem-solver who listens to his community, and I couldn’t be prouder to welcome him to Congress as the first Native American to represent Michigan.”

Davids campaigned with McCann in Michigan, aiming to visit with Indigenous leaders and communities across the state’s 4th Congressional District.

The Woodlands · Free, monthly

On-the-ground stories from Wisconsin, Minnesota, Michigan, Iowa, Illinois, Indiana and Ohio, from ICT's North Central Bureau. See all our newsletters

As a result of this historic outreach, McCann flipped the district for the Democrats, something that hadn’t happened since 1933.

“Our communities deserve a real seat at the table when decisions affecting our families and tribal nations are made,” said Davids, who won her bid to stay in office for a fifth term on Election Day. “That’s why I’ve been so focused on electing more Indigenous leaders who bring lived experience and common-sense leadership to Washington.”

Representatives from the Citizen Potawatomi Nation expressed their joy in seeing McCann win his election.

“His election as Michigan’s first Indigenous member of Congress is a significant milestone that reflects the growing presence and contributions of Native people in all levels of government,” said Citizen Potawatomi Nation Vice-Chairman Jason Smalley in a statement to ICT. “I had the opportunity to meet with Sean several times during his campaign and was impressed by his willingness to listen, learn, and engage on issues important to tribal nations and Native communities.”

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

Indigenous people make up roughly 2.6 percent of the population of Michigan’s 4th Congressional District, according to the U.S. Census Bureau data . And three federally recognized Potawatomi bands possess tribal trust land in the district: the Pokagon Band, Match-e-be-nash-she-wish Band and Nottawaseppi Huron Band.

During the campaign, McCann and Davids attended a round table with tribal leaders hosted by the Match-e-be-nash-she-wish Band, which was attended by representatives from the Nottawaseppi Huron and Pokagon bands.

“Outreach has been really important to me, and I just look forward to strengthening those tribal ties from here on out, and I’m excited about it,” McCann told ICT .

The roundtable discussions allowed for the two legislators to hear directly from local tribal leaders’ about their concerns, McCann said, adding that they plan to address those issues in January.

“From our perspective, Native issues are not red or blue,” Smalley said. “They are issues that require understanding, meaningful dialogue, and informed action. Tribal sovereignty, economic development, healthcare, education, infrastructure, and public safety affect Native citizens regardless of political affiliation. We look forward to working with leaders from both parties who are committed to advancing solutions and strengthening the government-to-government relationship between tribes and the United States.”

Amelia Schafer is ICT's North Central Correspondent based in Milwaukee, Wisconsin. Schafer covers MMIP, Indian Gaming and business for ICT. She is of Wampanoag and Montauk-Brothertown Indian Nation descent.... More by Amelia Schafer

scraped.description: Former Obama administration official brings nearly two decades of federal policy experience to the Senator-elect’s office
scraped.author: Daniel Herrera Carbajal
scraped.h1: Mary Peltola taps Alaska Native woman as chief of staff
scraped.body_text:
ICT

Daniel Herrera Carbajal ICT

Mary Peltola has named Raina Thiele as her chief of staff as she prepares to be sworn in as Alaska’s first Native American senator.

Thiele, Dena’ina Athabascan and Yup’ik, served as a senior political advisor on Peltola’s Senate campaign following four years as the senior advisor for Alaska affairs and strategic priorities at the Department of the Interior when Deb Haaland, Laguna Pueblo, served as Interior secretary during the Biden administration.

The Weekly · Free, every Thursday

The stories that mattered most across Indian Country, chosen by ICT's newsroom. Want regional or powwow news? See all our newsletters

Thiele also served for seven years in the executive office under President Barack Obama where she served in the Office of Management and Budget before becoming associate director of the Office of Intergovernmental Affairs and Public Engagement. She also worked as a liaison for tribal nations during the Obama administration.

Donors made this story possible.

A $10 monthly donation keeps Native journalists on stories like this one.

“I’m honored to have this opportunity to continue serving my home state in a new capacity,” Thiele said in a statement. “Senator-elect Peltola has always put Alaska first, and I look forward to helping her build a Senate office that reflects that commitment and delivers for Alaskans across the state.”

Peltola, a Democrat, highlighted Raina’s experience working in two different presidential administrations.

“As we build an office equipped to address the unique needs of Alaska, I’m confident that Raina will help us hit the ground running on day one,” Peltola said.

Thiele was born and raised in Alaska. Her family hails from Pedro Bay Village. She is a graduate of Yale College and the Harvard Kennedy School of Government.

scraped.description: Premiering Dec. 4, ‘Bank on Her’ will give three business owners an opportunity to pitch their ventures to a panel of industry experts.
scraped.author: Odafe Oghen
scraped.h1: Kandi Burruss is putting Black women entrepreneurs in the spotlight with new OWN competition series
scraped.body_text:
Premiering Dec. 4, ‘Bank on Her’ will give three business owners an opportunity to pitch their ventures to a panel of industry experts.

Kandi Burruss is stepping into a new hosting role, and this time, she’s helping women turn their entrepreneurial ambitions into reality.

The Grammy-winning singer, entrepreneur and television personality is set to host “Bank on Her,” a new business competition series coming to OWN next month. The series will give three entrepreneurs the opportunity to pitch their businesses, defend their strategies and compete for what the network describes as a potentially game-changing financial investment.

According to PEOPLE , OWN announced the series on Tuesday, Nov. 24, as part of its slate of new original programming to close out the year. “Bank on Her” will premiere Friday, Dec. 4.

The competition will feature three businesses: 1010 Wine and Events, owned by the Jones Sisters; Urban Comfort Foods, founded by Jinell Singletary; and Black LA Food Tour, founded by Daisy Miles.

Burruss will be joined by business panelists Raquel Graham and DonJuan Clark, who will evaluate each entrepreneur’s vision, strategy and potential for growth.

According to the show’s official synopsis, the competition offers participants national exposure, expert mentorship and a “transformative cash investment” that could help take their businesses to the next level.

The new hosting gig represents another chapter in Burruss’ television career following her 2024 departure from “The Real Housewives of Atlanta.” After 14 seasons on the Bravo reality series, Burruss stepped away to pursue other creative opportunities, including acting.

Since leaving the franchise, she has appeared in Broadway productions of “& Juliet” and “Chicago,” as well as television projects including “Reasonable Doubt” and “The Chi.”

“Bank on Her” is not the only new project OWN has planned. The network is also introducing “OWN Spotlight: One of One,” an anthology series celebrating eight remarkable Black women and their personal and professional journeys.

The series will launch in 2027, with a preview episode featuring CNN anchor Abby Phillip airing Dec. 11.

For Burruss, “Bank on Her” offers a different kind of reality television spotlight: one centered on business ownership, ambition and the possibilities that can come when entrepreneurs get the resources and exposure they need to grow.

scraped.title: A historic 68-member Congressional Black Caucus is coming to Washington. Meet its 18 new faces
scraped.description: The Congressional Black Caucus credits Black voters, particularly those across the South, with fueling its historic growth.
scraped.author: Gerren Keith Gaynor
scraped.h1: A historic 68-member Congressional Black Caucus is coming to Washington. Meet its 18 new faces
scraped.body_text:
The caucus credits Black voters, particularly those across the South, with fueling its historic growth.

The Congressional Black Caucus just got a lot bigger.

The powerful group on Capitol Hill, known as the “conscience of the Congress,” announced that, come January, its membership will be its largest since the Congressional Black Caucus was founded in 1971.

“The Congressional Black Caucus today announced it will enter the 120th Congress with a historic 68 members, marking the largest membership in the Caucus’s history,” the caucus said in a press release.

“The incoming Congress will also bring the largest class of new members ever welcomed into the CBC. The historic 68-member caucus will include 62 members of the U.S. House of Representatives and six members of the U.S. Senate, reflecting the growing representation and influence of Black leadership in Congress.”

Black candidates dominated in districts and states across the country in this month’s 2026 midterm elections. U.S. Rep. Yvette Clarke (D-N.Y.), chairwoman of the Congressional Black Caucus, noted that those critical wins are thanks to Black voters who showed up in high numbers at the polls.

“Despite the odds and repeated efforts to diminish the power of Black voters, Black representation has grown in Congress,” Clarke said in reference to Republicans redrawing election maps that diluted the voting power of Black and brown communities.

She continued, “Our historic growth is a testament to the power of Black voters, particularly across the South, who refused to be relegated to second-class citizenship.”

Clarke says the influential caucus, whose members will lead some of the House majority’s most powerful committees, is committed to delivering results for the voters who elected them, including lowering the cost of living, holding the Trump administration accountable, and defending “fundamental freedoms and the hard-fought progress of the communities we serve.”

The CBC leader, whose term as chairwoman ends in January, added, “Our charge is clear: to lead boldly, deliver results, and ensure that no community is left behind.”

Ahead of the swearing-in of the new Congress, here are the 18 new faces of the Congressional Black Caucus:

U.S. Rep.-elect Melat Kiros (D-Colo.) will represent Colorado’s 1st Congressional District. The 29-year-old is not only the second member of Gen Z but also the first female Gen Zer to enter Congress. Kiros, an attorney who worked as a barista to pay for her student loans, made history in the 2026 midterm election as the first Black woman elected to Congress to represent Colorado. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America and Working Families Party, Kiros is one of the 11 Democrats who voted against the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries as the next House Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives.

U.S. Delegate-elect Robert C. White Jr. (D-D.C.) will represent the District of Columbia. His entrance into Congress marks a generational change for D.C., which had been represented by the legendary Congresswoman Eleanor Holmes Norton, who retired at 89 after holding the non-voting U.S. territory seat for 35 years. White, 44, is an attorney and has served on the D.C. Council since 2016.

U.S. Rep.-elect Oliver Gilbert III (D-Fla.) will represent Florida’s 24th Congressional District. He is succeeding the retiring U.S. Congresswoman Frederica Wilson. The 54-year-old is an attorney and former Miami-Dade County commissioner and mayor of Miami Gardens.

U.S. Rep.-elect Jasmine Clark will represent Georgia’s 13th Congressional District. She is filling the seat that is currently held by U.S. Congressman Everton Blair, who became the first openly gay Black congressman from the South. Blair temporarily held the seat that was left vacant after the death of U.S. Congressman David Scott earlier this year. Clark, 43, is a former member of the Georgia House of Representatives and a clinical professor.

U.S. Senator-elect Juliana Stratton will serve as Illinois’ junior senator and will become the second Black woman elected to the Senate from Illinois. She is succeeding the retiring U.S. Senator Dick Durbin. Stratton is the former lieutenant governor, elected in 2018 as the first Black woman to hold the office. Stratton, 61, previously served in the Illinois House of Representatives.

U.S. Rep.-elect Donna Miller will represent Illinois’ 2nd Congressional District. The former Cook County commissioner is succeeding U.S. Congresswoman Robin Kelly after her unsuccessful bid for the U.S. Senate. Miller, 61, is no stranger to Washington, D.C. She is a graduate of the DC’s famed HBCU, Howard University.

U.S. Rep.-elect La Shawn K. Ford will represent Illinois’ 7th Congressional District. He is succeeding the retiring U.S. Congressman Danny Davis, who has held the seat since 1997. Ford, 54, previously served in the Illinois House of Representatives.

U.S. Rep.-elect Adrian Boafo will represent Maryland’s 5th Congressional District. He is succeeding the retiring U.S. Congressman Steny Hoyer. Boafo, a 32-year-old child of Ghanaian immigrants, previously served in the Maryland House of Delegates. He represented Prince George’s County, one of the nation’s wealthiest majority-Black counties. Boafo is the first millennial to represent the district.

U.S. Rep.-elect Donavan McKinney will represent Michigan’s 13th Congressional District. He defeated incumbent Democratic Congressman Shri Thanedar for the seat representing parts of Detroit in Wayne County. McKinney, 34, previously served in the Michigan House of Representatives. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America, McKinney is one of the 11 Democrats who voted against the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries as the next House Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives.

U.S. Senator-elect Scott Colom will serve as the junior senator representing the state of Mississippi. After defeating incumbent Republican U.S. Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith, Colom will be the first African American to serve in the U.S. Senate since the Reconstruction Era in the 1870s. Colom, 43, is also the first Democrat to represent the Magnolia State since 1982. Colom previously served as a state District Attorney for the 16th Judicial District of Mississippi and was nominated by President Joe Biden to serve as a federal district judge.

U.S. Rep.-elect Darializa Avila Chevalier will represent New York’s 13th Congressional District. She notably defeated incumbent U.S. Congressman Adriano Espaillat in the primary in the overwhelmingly Democratic district that covers parts of upper Manhattan, including Harlem, and the Bronx. The 32-year-old activist and organizer previously served as an investigator at the public defender legal organization, Neighborhood Defender Service of Harlem. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America and Working Families Party, Chevalier is one of the 11 Democrats who voted against the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries as the next House Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives.

U.S. Rep.-elect Raymond E. Smith, Jr. will represent North Carolina’s 3rd Congressional District after defeating incumbent Republican U.S. Congressman Greg Murphy, flipping the seat from red to blue for the first time since 1995. The 65-year-old Army veteran previously served in the North Carolina House of Representatives.

U.S. Rep.-elect Cyril Johnson will represent North Carolina’s 6th Congressional District. Jefferson defeated Republican incumbent U.S. Congressman Addison McDowell in the general election. Jefferson, 34, previously served on the High Point City Council and later was elected the city’s youngest mayor.

U.S. Rep.-elect LaKesha Womack will represent North Carolina’s 14th Congressional District. She defeated incumbent Republican Congressman Tim Moore in the general election. The 49-year-old Alabama native moved to North Carolina in 2016 to support Hillary Clinton’s presidential campaign and has lived in the state ever since. Womack is an ordained minister and author who previously worked in community financial development.

U.S. Rep.-elect Chris Rabb will represent Pennsylvania’s 13th Congressional District. Rabb secured the nomination in the overwhelmingly Democratic-leaning district after Democratic Congressman Dwight Evans declined to run for re-election. Rabb, 56, previously served in the Pennsylvania House of Representatives. A member of the Democratic Socialists of America and Working Families Party, Rabb is one of the 11 Democrats who voted against the nomination of Hakeem Jeffries as the next House Speaker of the U.S. House of Representatives.

U.S. Rep.-elect Frederick Douglass Haynes III will represent Texas’s 30th Congressional District. Haynes is succeeding U.S. Congresswoman Jasmine Crockett, who declined to run for re-election to instead seek the U.S. Senate seat in the 2026 election. Ironically, Haynes, 66, is Crockett’s pastor in Dallas, where he serves at Friendship-West Baptist Church. In 2023, Haynes succeeded the Rev. Jesse Jackson as CEO of the Rainbow/PUSH Coalition. However, Haynes stepped down from the position three months later.

U.S. Rep.-elect Colin Allred will represent Texas’ 33rd Congressional District. Unlike the other incoming members of the Congressional Black Caucus, Allred is not new to Congress. He previously represented the 32nd Congressional District before Texas’s congressional maps were redrawn. The 34-year-old former congressman served three terms in the U.S. House before leaving office for an unsuccessful bid to unseat U.S. Senator Ted Cruz in 2024. The former NFL player and civil rights attorney sought the U.S. Senate again in 2026, before dropping out before the primary election after Rep. Jasmine Crockett entered the race.

U.S. Delegate-elect Janelle Sarauw will represent the U.S. Virgin Islands, succeeding longtime Delegate Stacey Plaskett, who was elected the first Black female governor of the U.S. territory. The 41-year-old St. Thomas native will make history as the first openly LGBTQ person to represent the U.S. Virgin Islands. Prior to being elected to Congress, Sarauw served as a member of the U.S. Virgin Islands Legislature. She is the granddaughter of Ivan Buchanan, former Speaker of the National Assembly of Saint Kitts and Nevis.

scraped.title: In an era of book bans and DEI rollbacks, the Free Black Women’s Library is thriving
scraped.description: Inside the Free Black Women’s Library and what it takes to sustain it in an era when it couldn’t be more integral.
scraped.author: Kay Wicker
scraped.h1: In an era of book bans and DEI rollbacks, the Free Black Women’s Library is thriving
scraped.body_text:
Inside the Free Black Women’s Library and what it takes to sustain it in an era when it couldn’t be more integral.

On any given day in Brooklyn, the sounds emanating from a local library could be that of strummed banjos, peals of laughter during a comedy show, singles using books as wingmen, applause during lively book talks, lifelong friends meeting again for the first time, or the discovery of the life and legacy of some of literature’s most integral voices. Such is life at the Free Black Women’s Library , where OlaRonke Akinmowo, a Brooklyn-born interdisciplinary artist and set dresser, has spent over a decade stewarding the literary works of some of literature’s most influential Black women writers.

Eleven years after establishing the library with just 100 books, Akinmowo, who spoke with theGrio on Tuesday, Nov. 24, is entering a new chapter with the launch of the library’s first fellowship, with plans to digitize its collection, and dreams of moving into a larger space.

“Hopefully what’s next is more growth, more expansion,” she gushed.

At a time when there is growing urgency around preserving Black literature, history, and culture, the Brooklyn native is aware of how integral her mission is. Born out of a desire to celebrate Black womanhood rather than just lament the circumstances under which so many Black women exist, the Free Black Women’s Library has, in a sense, become a living embodiment of many of the Black radical feminist texts on its shelves through its expansive mutual aid and community focus.

“If I had known how important this project would become, I think I would have been intimidated by starting it,” she admitted.

A post shared by Rebeka @ NYC for FREE (@nyc_forfree)

The Free Black Women’s Library came to the artist in 2015 as she was theorizing about how to continue doing something meaningful to impact Black women while navigating what felt like burnout after years of more conventional organizing. It started as a mobile library, and has since grown to a storefront in Bedford-Stuyvesant that houses a collection of more than 5,000 books by Black women and nonbinary writers. Instead of a traditional library card and check-out system, the Free Black Women’s Library runs on a trade setup where visitors leave a title in order to take a title that they can either bring back for another trade or are free to keep.

The community can also partake in everything from adult literacy classes and herbalism workshops using herbs grown in the library’s own backyard to picking up gently used clothing from its free store or even stocking up on menstrual supplies from its period pantry.

When the founder was getting the library off the ground in the latter half of the 2010s, Black literature was enjoying something of a renaissance. Black women were dominating bestseller lists as Black stories were increasingly making their way to the big and small screens, and diversity, at least on the surface, was something many of the country’s leading cultural institutions were striving toward. A decade later, amid a widespread backpedal on diversity, equity, inclusion initiatives, book bans, and debates on how history can be taught in schools, the Free Black Women’s Library couldn’t be more necessary.

“I’m glad I didn’t realize it at the time,” she continued, adding, “Because it is so critical right now for us to preserve, protect, and actively defend these books and these stories and Black women’s stories.”

What comes to mind for the literary enthusiast is the extremely apt, famous Kurt Vonnegut quote, “The death of a library, any library, suggests that the community has lost its soul.”

A divestment in Black literature, she said, “robs us of our own possibility and our own potential. It’s so important for us to see and feel and read about worlds outside of ourselves and beyond ourselves, especially written by Black women.”

She continued, “There is so much possibility and imagination and encouragement and motivation that’s found within our books and within our stories.”

A post shared by OlaRonke (@thefreeblackwomenslibrary)

Sustaining the library over the years has required a combination of what Akinmowo described as “blood, sweat, and tears,” the generosity of others, and getting creative about generating revenue. She now sells merch with the library’s logo and other designs, including tote bags and apparel bearing the likenesses of some of her favorite Black women. There’s also been crowdfunding efforts and Patreon, and she spends a portion of virtually every week applying for grants.

Among those who have shown the library some love recently is Drew Barrymore, who in 2022 had her as a guest on her daytime talk show and gifted the artist laptops. Today, those laptops are being used by community members to apply for jobs and Medicaid, among other things, with two social workers on hand. Breakthroughs like that are part of what keeps her going.

Even though it’s become a labor of love at times, what sustains the librarian is how much life the Free Black Women’s Library has managed to cultivate under its roof. She’s welcomed back folks celebrating a friendiversary after having met there and witnessed writers discover their voices in community workshops. She’s seen the start of an artist’s journey, or someone discovering there are writers already out there on the same wavelength.

Now, the founder, who suspects the library may have outgrown its current digs, is giving more thought to how it might outlive her. The newly launched Dottie Fellowship , which will usher in the library’s first paid position, pays homage to Dorothy Porter Wesley , the pioneering Howard University librarian whose work collecting and preserving Black history continues to serve generations of scholars.

She’s also exploring an expansion of the library’s digital reach, hopefully to a global audience through an app, which is a prospect that has the bibliophile excited, especially for someone who still gets a kick out of putting people onto books by Black women they might otherwise never have encountered. Despite the cultural backlash and the increasingly urgent nature of her work, that aspect of running the library hasn’t lost any of its novelty.

“Witnessing people’s awe and fascination and excitement when they see the wide range of work that has been put out into the world, written by Black women,” she said. “That’s really exciting to me.”

scraped.title: Where Will ESSENCE Fest Go After Leaving New Orleans?
scraped.h1: ESSENCE Fest and New Orleans Have Broken Up. So, Where Does the Black Internet Want It to Go Next?
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

After 33 years in New Orleans, ESSENCE Festival of Culture is looking for a new home, and these cities could be next.

By

Shellie M. Scott

Published

A general view of the crowd during the 2026 ESSENCE Festival of Culture® (Photo by Paras Griffin/Getty Images for ESSENCE)

After more than three decades of Black joy set against the French Quarter, the ESSENCE Festival of Culture and the city of New Orleans have officially split, leaving the timeline looking at a major shakeup. The festival launched a thousand girls’ trips, forged traditions that outlasted presidencies, and generated an estimated $1.31 billion between 2022 and 2025 , according to the festival’s ROI report. The parting comes amid stalled contract talks and friction over unpaid local vendors, local reports including Fox 8 Live noted. But the breakup has the Black internet wondering: where will Black America’s homecoming go next?

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

New Orleans allowed 88,000 people to move seamlessly between festival experiences in 2026. Whichever city steps up next needs deep hospitality infrastructure, major transit hubs, and multi-venue capacity to pull off an event of this scale without losing the vibe. Here are the cities leading the conversation for ESSENCE Fest 2027.

In a recent interview with WWL-TV , New Orleans Mayor Helena Moreno referenced ESSENCE Fest’s interest in moving to Atlanta while discussing the breakdown in talks with the city. Fresh off hosting matches during last summer’s 2026 FIFA World Cup, Atlanta’s ability to handle large crowds, hotel surges and transportation access is part of its appeal. As @iamkingwilliams put it, “We have actually more in Atlanta [Labor Day] weekend than they do at Essence Fest July Fourth.”

But not everyone is sold on trading Bourbon Street for Peachtree. “Bringing Essence Fest to Atlanta is the most terrible idea I’ve heard this quarter…,” @guavaa_x wrote on Threads. “You cannot vibe and make organic connections driving forty minutes in traffic to the next venue. It’s not cohesive. NEXT.”

With walkability a plus, Detroit has already pulled off welcoming a major crowd with the 2024 NFL Draft, and it is set to host the NCAA Men’s Final Four in 2027. “ESSENCE Fest in Detroit would actually be the perfect alt,” @djohsoxo wrote on social media. “Atlanta, Houston & DC already got too much goin on, let’s spend our Black a– dollars there for once.” The Motor City has the convention space, concert venues and casinos to make it work, but transportation is a question. The People Mover elevated rail loop stays downtown and the QLINE streetcar covers just 3.3 miles of Woodward Avenue.

Hotel space is a concern, too. As @dailydetroit posted, “the big challenge w/ Essence Fest in Detroit (and events like it) is hotel rooms within a couple mile radius, everything else we have. This is why you’re seeing new hotels get built (~1,600 rooms on their way).”

Houston and ESSENCE have history. The festival relocated to H-Town in 2006 after Hurricane Katrina forced it out of New Orleans. Now, two decades later, the city is in talks to bring the cultural homecoming back to Texas for 2027. With its experience hosting the festival and its convention, hotel and entertainment infrastructure, Houston could make a compelling case for a reunion.

However, some Houston residents, like TikToker @Crysie, are calling for a hard pass due to reasons like traffic and overcrowding. “We don’t need it here in Houston at all,” Crysie said. “Find somewhere else to go,” she added.

D.C.’s world-class museums, including the National Museum of African American History and Culture and many cultural attractions, could give festival-goers plenty of reasons to head to the nation’s capital. D.C. offers elite public transit and undeniable Black cultural cachet, but could it deliver an ESSENCE-sized nightly concert without sending the crowd out of town?

Capital One Arena seats more than 20,000 , while the larger Northwest Stadium is in Landover, Maryland. Threads user @shakenbayke put the concern bluntly: “Y’all forget there’s a concert every night after the fest? Folks gon leave the city and head out to Fed Ex?”

On TikTok, creator Mack Julión encouraged ESSENCE Fest to head north. “You cannot have a serious conversation about Black culture in America without mentioning Chicago,” he said, noting the Windy City as the birthplace of Soul Train, Harold’s Chicken and the rise of the Obamas.

Chicago has a vast transit system, hotels, world-class food, beaches, and a stadium-scale concert option in Soldier Field, right off of Lake Michigan. But not everyone in the Chi is rolling out the welcome mat. “It’s folks saying Essence Fest should come to Chicago and Chicagoans like hell nah lmao,” @oksomik wrote on Threads. @iseeisaid’s added, “We are booked, we are full, and no thank you!”

Meanwhile, New Orleans isn’t wasting any time mourning the relationship. Mayor Moreno revealed that the city is already planning to get boo’d up with a brand-new July 2027 music festival of its own.

scraped.title: Tyrie Howse’s Family Demands Justice After GA Teen Was Fatally Shot By Police – The Root
scraped.h1: Tyrie Howse’s Family Demands Justice After GA Teen Was Fatally Shot By Police
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

Ben Crump is working with Tyrie Howse’s family as the Georgia NAACP calls for transparency and an independent review of the teen’s fatal shooting.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Screenshot from Facebook

Civil rights attorney Ben Crump is joining a Georgia mother’s fight to find out how her 16-year-old son ended up dead after an encounter with a Henry County police officer. Tyrie Howse was supposed to meet his mother at a Stockbridge Krispy Kreme. Instead, that November evening has now drawn national attention and renewed demands for the release of police body camera footage.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

“Just show us the video,” Crump said during a Nov. 24 press conference in Atlanta, emphasizing that the central question is whether the officer’s use of deadly force was justified.

Howse was shot and killed on Nov. 3 in the Krispy Kreme parking lot. According to the Georgia Bureau of Investigation (GBI) , an officer approached Howse and another 17-year-old at the scene. That’s when investigators said the older teenager handed Howse a handgun before Howse ran away. The officer pursued him, ordered him to drop the weapon, and fired when he allegedly failed to comply. A gun was reportedly recovered at the scene.

Crump, alongside attorneys Harry Daniels and Gerald Griggs, is calling on authorities to allow Howse’s mother to see the footage of her son’s final moments. He also challenged officials to stop withholding the video and give the grieving family the answers they deserve.

RELATED : Ben Crump Raises New Questions After Nolan Wells’ Funeral as Witness Accounts Continue to Conflict

“I fail to understand why the most dangerous thing in America to police seems to be young Black people running away from them,” he continued.

The family’s attorneys say witness accounts paint a different picture. According to them, Howse was unarmed and running away when the officer shot him. Attorneys have also said photographs show he sustained a gunshot wound to the back of his head. They say eyewitness accounts and video they have reviewed raise serious questions about the official narrative.

Howse was an honor-roll junior at Woodland High School who dreamed of becoming a pediatric nurse, according to his family. His mother, Taneshia Puckett, described a young man with ambitions, a promising future and a family who expected him to come home.

The growing calls for transparency have now gained support from the Georgia NAACP and its Henry County branch. Georgia NAACP leaders are demanding a meeting with the GBI, preservation and release of body-camera footage, and an independent, impartial review of the shooting, Fox 5 Atlanta reported . State NAACP President Gwenette Westbrook stressed that accountability must accompany public trust in law enforcement.

The Henry County officer involved remains on administrative leave while the GBI conducts its investigation. The agency is expected to submit its findings to the Henry County District Attorney’s Office for review.

Meanwhile, Howse’s family continues to wait for answers. Their demand is straightforward: transparency, accountability and the opportunity for a mother to see what happened to her son.

Funeral services for Howse are scheduled for Nov. 28 at Divine Faith Ministries in Jonesboro, Georgia.

scraped.h1: Still Making Headlines! What Past Root 100 Honorees Are Up To Right Now
scraped.body_text:
Black News, Opinions, Politics and Culture

From career milestones and major awards to headline-making moments, see how these Black trailblazers continued making history throughout 2026.

By

Phenix S Halley

Published

Ledisi performs onstage during The Root 100 2024 Gala at The Apollo Theater on December 05, 2024 in New York City. (Photo by Jason Mendez/Getty Images for The Root), Mayor of Birmingham, Alabama Randall Woodfin attends the 2018 The Root 100 gala at Pier Sixty at Chelsea Piers on November 8, 2018 in New York City. (Photo by Jim Spellman/Getty Images), Gayle King attends the 2025 The Root 100 Gala at Gotham Hall on December 03, 2025 in New York City. (Photo by Dia Dipasupil/Getty Images)

It’s no secret that Black politicians, athletes, leaders and entertainers honored on The Root 100 annual list always make their mark, but the story doesn’t stop there! For 17 years, The Root 100 has celebrated the Black visionaries, cultural icons and changemakers shaping conversations, breaking barriers and influencing generations.

To view this video please enable JavaScript.

From award-winning legends like Misty Copeland and groundbreaking journalist Abby Phillip to cultural icons and game-changing leaders like Jasmine Crockett and Al Roker, these trailblazers continued making moves in 2026. Now, we’re checking in on where they are, celebrating the wins, the milestones and moments that keep their names in the conversation.

Abby Phillip joined The Root 100 in 2025, celebrating her influential journalism and contributions to conversations about politics, power and representation.

Abby Phillip has continued commanding the political conversation as CNN’s “NewsNight” anchor. In 2026, she also appeared at the Library of Congress National Book Festival, bringing her work on Jesse Jackson and Black political power to readers. Phillip and her husband, Marcus Richardson, welcomed their second child, son Maxwell Elias Richardson, in October following an IVF journey.

Birmingham Mayor Randall Woodfin joined The Root 100 in 2018, earning recognition for his leadership and commitment to creating new opportunities for residents of one of America’s most historic Black cities.

Randall Woodfin is still putting Birmingham first! In November 2025, the mayor officially began his third term, continuing his work to revitalize the city’s neighborhoods, expand educational opportunities and strengthen economic development. Through initiatives like Birmingham Promise, he’s also keeping his focus on creating pathways to college and careers for the next generation. His mission to build a stronger Birmingham is far from finished!

Misty Copeland joined The Root 100 celebration in 2023, honoring her groundbreaking career and lasting impact on ballet and Black representation.

Misty Copeland has never been content with simply breaking barriers; she’s determined to make sure others can walk through them, too. In 2026, the ballet trailblazer added a new distinction to her résumé, joining the Metropolitan Museum of Art’s Board of Trustees while continuing her advocacy for greater access to dance.

Texas Rep. Jasmine Crockett hit the Root 100 red carpet in 2024, celebrating her fearless leadership and growing influence in American politics.

RELATED : PHOTOS: The Root 100 Gala Is Back! Take a Look Back at Last Year’s Best Moments

The Texas congresswoman spent 2026 keeping the pressure on Washington , championing voting rights and civil rights while continuing to challenge political power with the sharp tongue and fearless approach that have made her a force in the national conversation. With her exiting Congress come January, her future is limitless… and you can bet that The Root will be following along for the ride!

Marc Lamont Hill brought his signature blend of journalism, scholarship and cultural commentary to The Root 100, celebrating his influence as an educator, author and outspoken voice in conversations about race, politics and social justice.

Marc Lamont Hill smoked this!📍 pic.twitter.com/1wLxmBRqCq

Marc Lamont Hill is taking the conversation from the classroom to the page and the podcast studio! In 2026, the CUNY professor expanded his literary legacy with the release of “Schooling Against the Prison: Education, Imagination, and the Promise of Abolition,” examining the relationship between education and the criminal justice system… And that’s all on top of becoming a fan favorite on the “Joe Budden Podcast,” one of the biggest platforms in the U.S. Whether he’s teaching, writing or challenging the status quo, Hill isn’t slowing down.

Leslie Odom Jr. brought his star power to The Root 100 in 2023, celebrating his award-winning career on Broadway and beyond.

Some roles are career-defining. Others become part of your legacy. For Leslie Odom Jr., Aaron Burr is both. In 2026, the Tony Award winner returned to the role that helped make him a Broadway sensation, bringing his celebrated “Hamilton” performance to London’s West End and introducing a new audience to the magic.

Tamron Hall joined The Root 100’s celebration of Black achievement, bringing her celebrated journalism career and commitment to storytelling into the spotlight.

Tamron Hall continues making moves in daytime television! In September 2026, the Emmy-winning journalist returned for season eight of her nationally syndicated talk show, continuing to bring heartfelt conversations, celebrity interviews and stories that matter to audiences. She’s also preparing to share more of her personal journey in her upcoming memoir, “Bet on Yourself,” arriving in January 2027.

Nikole Hannah-Jones joined The Root 100 in 2019, earning recognition for her groundbreaking investigative journalism and her work documenting the history of racial inequality in America.

Nikole Hannah-Jones is continuing to shape conversations about race, history and democracy. In 2026, the Pulitzer Prize-winning journalist remains a leading voice through her work at Howard University and the legacy of her groundbreaking “1619 Project.” She’s also expanding her cultural footprint with a new venture, North Star Books + Bar, a Brooklyn bookstore and gathering space celebrating Black literature, artistry and community.

Gayle King brought her signature warmth and journalistic excellence to The Root 100, celebrating her influence as one of America’s most recognizable media voices.

Gayle King isn’t going anywhere! In 2026, the veteran journalist renewed her CBS News contract, reaffirming her place at “CBS Mornings” after 14 years on the show. She also continues her work with Oprah Daily and SiriusXM, proving there’s plenty more storytelling ahead.

Deanté Kyle joined The Root 100 community of influential voices, bringing his distinctive perspective and passion for amplifying Black culture.

Deanté Kyle took his “Grits & Eggs” podcast from truck-stop conversations to national recognition. He’s grown to over 612,000 followers on Instagram and 244,000 subscribers.

Kamala Harris has spent her career making history, from serving as California’s first Black woman attorney general to becoming the first woman, first Black American and first South Asian American vice president of the United States. Her place in The Root 100 community reflects a political career that has helped reshape American leadership.

Kamala Harris is continuing to make her presence felt beyond the White House. In 2026, the former vice president relaunched her political organizing platform as Headquarters, an initiative focused on engaging and mobilizing the next generation of voters and activists. She’s also returned to the campaign trail, supporting Democratic candidates ahead of the midterm elections while keeping her own political future in the spotlight. Whatever comes next, Harris is making it clear that her public service journey isn’t over.

Ledisi took the stage at The Root 100 in 2024, bringing her powerhouse vocals and unmistakable presence to a celebration of Black excellence and cultural influence.

Ledisi is taking her talents to Broadway! In 2026, the Grammy-winning singer stepped into her first principal Broadway role as Tallulah Clarke in “Wanted,” while earning another Grammy nomination for her Dinah Washington tribute album, “For Dinah.” From music to musical theater, Ledisi continues expanding her artistic legacy.

Don Lemon joined fellow influential journalists at The Root 100 in 2025, celebrating his career and impact on American media.

Despite being arrested and federally charged with conspiring to violate someone’s constitutional rights and violating the FACE Act, journalist Don Lemon continues to build his independent media empire, with more than 1.25 million YouTube subscribers and over 10 million followers across platforms. He also earned a spot on the 2026 Out100 for his journalism and visibility as a Black gay media personality.

Filmmaker Ava DuVernay joined The Root 100’s celebration of Black excellence, earning recognition for her groundbreaking work behind the camera and her commitment to telling stories that challenge, inspire and reshape the cultural conversation.

Ava DuVernay is once again bringing history into focus. In 2026, the award-winning filmmaker unveiled “14th,” a new documentary examining the history and ongoing significance of the 14th Amendment. The project follows the legacy of her acclaimed documentary “13th,” continuing her exploration of race, justice and American history. Set to premiere on Netflix in December, “14th” marks another powerful chapter in DuVernay’s career as a filmmaker committed to stories that matter.

Kecia Lewis brought decades of Broadway excellence to The Root 100, celebrating a remarkable career dedicated to storytelling and theatrical excellence.

Kecia Lewis is taking her talents from one iconic production to another. Fresh off her Tony-winning run as Miss Liza Jane in “Hell’s Kitchen,” the Broadway veteran stepped into a new chapter in 2026, joining an all-star cast featuring Kerry Washington, Dominique Fishback and Kara Young in “The Whoopi Monologues” at Lincoln Center Theater. More than four decades into her career, Lewis is still finding new ways to command the stage, and audiences are taking notice.

Pastor Jamal Bryant attended The Root 100 in 2025, where his leadership and commitment to empowering Black communities took center stage.

Jamal Bryant took the fight for Black economic power straight to the checkout line. The Atlanta pastor helped lead the Target boycott, which began in protest of the retailer’s rollback of diversity initiatives. Bryant called the campaign a victory, pointing to its impact on corporate accountability and Black consumer power. But he’s not putting his activism on sale anytime soon! His next chapter includes building economic opportunities and generational wealth in Black communities.

Chlöe Bailey celebrated her growing musical legacy at The Root 100 in 2022, marking another milestone in her evolution as an artist.

Chlöe Bailey is making it clear that she’s not interested in being boxed into one sound, one era or one expectation. Between her “Resurrection” project with Timbaland and a holiday release of her own in 2026, the singer continued flexing her musical range and giving fans plenty of reasons to keep her on repeat.

Al Roker joined The Root 100’s celebrated lineup, bringing decades of broadcasting excellence and a legacy of service to the spotlight.

Rain, shine or a packed morning-show schedule, Al Roker remains a familiar face Americans can count on. But the beloved broadcaster’s impact reaches well beyond the weather desk. In 2026, he marked 30 years on “TODAY” and continued his philanthropic work, earning recognition at Citymeals On Wheels’ annual Power Lunch for his commitment to giving back.

Jon Batiste took the stage at The Root 100 in 2023, celebrating his extraordinary musicianship and contributions to Black American culture.

Jon Batiste is giving the classics a distinctly Black American remix, and the results are music to our ears. In 2026, the eight-time Grammy winner released three new piano projects: “Black Mozart,” “Monk Meditations” and “Monk Movements,” reimagining the work of musical legends through his own creative lens. He also stepped behind the microphone to narrate “American Amazon,” a PBS documentary celebrating the landscapes, wildlife and cultural richness of the American South.

scraped.title: ‘Pull Your Gun!’: Amazon Driver Goes Head-to-Head with Couple Who Picked the Wrong Day to Mess with Him
scraped.description: A Black Amazon delivery driver recorded a tense confrontation with a couple walking their dog after an argument over his route took a threatening turn.
scraped.author: Grace Jidoun
scraped.h1: ‘Pull Your Gun!’: Amazon Driver Goes Head-to-Head with Couple Who Picked the Wrong Day to Mess with Him
scraped.body_text:
A Black Amazon delivery driver recorded a tense confrontation with a couple walking their dog after an argument over his route took a threatening turn.

Delivery drivers have enough holiday madness to navigate without being yelled at by people in the very neighborhoods they’re delivering packages to.

One Black Amazon driver filmed a heated encounter with a couple who were walking their dog along his route.

Instagram user @otmlostfiles_ wrote in the caption of his Reel that he had 180 stops that day, not counting multi-location stops.

During his route, he said he had to “whip around” the couple because they were walking in the middle of a narrow, residential street.

He alleged the couple cussed at him, prompting him to stop and confront them. A full-fledged dispute soon broke out.

He told the couple, “I’m not your kid, so don’t cuss at me. Simple as that.”

The exchange quickly devolved after the unidentified man reached into his pocket as if he were about to pull a gun.

“Pull your gun, pull it,” otmlostfiles_ challenged the man as the woman told her companion to take a photo of the license plate on his Amazon truck.

“There’s no license plate, goofy. Goofy, what the —- is wrong with ya’ll?” he shouted.

In a move one viewer called “crazy work,” the woman kept telling him to “go away!” even as she moved closer and closer.

Her male companion stood behind her, smirking, as she continued arguing with the driver and eventually said she was going to call the police.

Shared on Nov. 23, just days before Black Friday, the video drew an outpouring of support for the driver.

“Imagine targeting an Amazon truck??? I leave them snacks, cold water, and wave at them. They work hard,” one Instagram user wrote.

Many people echoed that sentiment.

“It’s an Amazon driver. What in the world are they bothering him for?” one viewer asked.

Another person chimed in, “People really think they can just harass!! Dude working, making his deliveries, and it takes an ignorant individual to involve himself!!”

Otmlostfiles_ has not provided an update on whether police responded or whether the man was carrying a weapon.

No weapon is visible in the footage.

A post shared by JAMAICAN STONER 🅿️🇯🇲 (@otmlostfiles_)

scraped.title: Chris Rock Reveals Why Watching Terry Crews with His Own Family Convinced Him He Could Play His Father
scraped.description: Chris Rock knew Terry Crews could act, but one moment on set convinced him Crews was the right man to play Julius on “Everybody Hates Chris.”
scraped.author: Danielle Jones
scraped.h1: Chris Rock Reveals Why Watching Terry Crews with His Own Family Convinced Him He Could Play His Father
scraped.body_text:
Chris Rock knew Terry Crews could act, but one moment on set convinced him Crews was the right man to play Julius on “Everybody Hates Chris.”

“Everybody Hates Chris” is arguably one of Chris Rock’s most successful projects.

​The series follows a Black teenager named Chris who lives with his parents and two siblings in a Bedford-Stuyvesant, Brooklyn apartment.

It’s no coincidence that Rock and the main character, played by Tyler Williams James, share the same first name, as the show is loosely based on the comedian’s childhood growing up in the same neighborhood.

The series ran for seasons between 2005 and 2009.

​Rock tapped “Martin” star Tichina Arnold to play his no-nonsense mother, Rochelle Rock, while “White Chicks” actor Terry Crews portrayed his hardworking and easygoing father, who juggled multiple jobs.

​Rock previously detailed that he knew he wanted Arnold to play his mom and had to fight for that after the network suggested they hire a biracial woman to play his mom instead.

​As for Crews, Rock told GQ in a Nov. 24 interview that watching how Crews handled fatherhood in real life is what got him the job to play his on-screen father.

​He said , “Terry Crews is great. I met Terry Crews — it’s funny, we were auditioning fathers for ‘Everybody Hates Chris,’ and looking at a bunch of actors, and I was filming ‘The Longest Yard’ at the time, so I was doing two things at once.”

​The 61-year-old said he would even watch auditions on the computer, trying to find the perfect Julius. But then came Crews.

​“One day Terry Crew’s family comes to the set,” the 61-year-old said. “He’s got like seven kids, dude. Him and his wife have been together for like 30 years, they’re high school sweethearts. And I watched this man interact with his family, and I was like, ‘Oh, he’s playing the dad.’”

Rock was referring to the set of “The Longest Yard,” where both actors appeared.

Crews and his wife Rebecca have been married for 37 years. They share a blended family of five children: four daughters and one son.

The eldest child, Naomi, is Rebecca’s eldest daughter from a previous relationship. Crews adopted Naomi after he and Rebecca married in 1989.

​Rock continued, “I knew he could act, I knew he was funny just from ‘White Chicks,’ but when I saw him interact with his family, I was like, ‘And you’re hired.’”

​Fans reacted to Rock’s recollection of choosing Crews to play his father online.

​One person said, “Chris Rock saw something in him that an audition couldn’t show.”

​A second fan paying Crews a compliment said, “That’s why Terry Crews was so believable as Julius. He wasn’t just acting like a dad.”

​Another person who enjoyed Crews performance said, “Julius will forever be one of the greatest TV dads.”

​Crews also shared his experience of booking Julius while filming 2005’s “The Longest Yard.”

​In a 2024 interview on “Club Shay Shay,” he said , “He saw me, and my wife, and my two kids, out there in Santa Fe, New Mexico, when we was filming ‘The Longest Yard’ and he was watching. That’s the thing – you got to remember everybody is watching.”

​Crews remembered Rock approaching him on set to tell him that he had something for Crews. But he wouldn’t initially tell Crews what the thing was.

​“I go home the script for ‘Everybody Hates Chris’ is literally on my doorstep. I open that up, he’s like ‘I want you to play my dad.’”

​After the show ended in 2009, they brought back an animated version in 2024 called “Everybody Still Hates Chris.” It continued where the original show left off.

Both Crews and Arnold returned to reprise their roles, but sadly the show ran for only one season.

scraped.title: Duffy’s Return to Reality TV While Running U.S. Transportation Draws Scrutiny Ahead of Congressional Grilling Over Airport Chaos
scraped.description: Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will soon face Congress to discuss a number of issues including the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.
scraped.author: Yohance Kyles
scraped.h1: Duffy’s Return to Reality TV While Running U.S. Transportation Draws Scrutiny Ahead of Congressional Grilling Over Airport Chaos
scraped.body_text:
Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy will soon face Congress to discuss a number of issues including the FAA’s nationwide ground stop.

Secretary of Transportation Sean Duffy remains under fire following a nationwide airport shutdown that left thousands of travelers stranded.

President Donald Trump handpicked Duffy, 55, for his inner circle, and the two have more than politics in common: both know their way around a reality TV set.

Congress confirmed the “Real World” alum in January 2025 to oversee the nation’s interstate transportation system.

Duffy oversaw the Federal Aviation Administration’s ground stoppage on Nov. 13. The FAA halted U.S. air travel for more than four hours before reopening the airspace later that day.

All departing traffic across American airports stopped due to caution. Initially, Duffy mentioned that a “communication issue” impacted Air Route Traffic Control Centers.

Within hours, Duffy and other members of the Trump administration provided conflicting explanations for the inconvenient suspension of flights.

Duffy insisted the outage resulted from pre-existing equipment malfunctions. By contrast, Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin claimed new upgrades caused the disruptions.

Both Cabinet members came off as overwhelmed in dealing with the crisis. Mullin looked disheveled during last week’s congressional hearing, where lawmakers questioned him about using a government-funded plane to take his niece to a college football game.

Officials have since pulled him from public appearances, amid whispers of a betting pool over how long Trump will wait before firing him.

Duffy and FAA Administrator Bryan Bedford will face Congress next week over the Nov. 13 nationwide flight grounding, according to Politico.

Lawmakers demand answers about the outage and plans to prevent another disruption. They will also face questions about Duffy’s $50 billion air traffic overhaul proposal, which has drawn bipartisan skepticism.

Meanwhile, scrutiny of Duffy’s leadership has brought renewed attention to his past on a classic reality television show.

Before becoming transportation secretary, he raised his stock in Republican circles by serving in the House of Representatives from 2011 to 2019.

Walking the halls of Congress was not the Wisconsin native’s earliest introduction to the spotlight. He first appeared on TV screens as part of the cast of “The Real World: Boston.”

The sixth season of MTV’s “The Real World” premiered in 1997, featuring 25-year-old aspiring lawyer and his conservative views.

In 1998, Duffy returned to the network for “Road Rules: All Stars,” the precursor to “The Challenge” series. He met his future wife, current Fox News host Rachel Campos-Duffy , on “All Stars.”

“Real World/Road Rules Challenge: Battle of the Seasons” then began airing in January 2002. Duffy again made his way back to the small screen with a game-winning appearance.

Duffy choosing to leave his reality television past behind him upon arriving in Washington would be expected.

However, Duffy fully embraced having cameras follow him and his family for a brand new peek into his life. Campos-Duffy, 55, and their nine children were along for the ride.

“Great American Road Trip,” starring the Duffys, arrived on the Department of Transportation’s YouTube channel in April. They visited seven states over six episodes.

Critics slammed Duffy for being out of touch. Questions about whether taxpayers footed the bill arose as well. As backlash mounted, the former Ashland County District Attorney pushed back.

“Production costs were paid for by the Great American Road Trip Inc., not taxpayers. Zero taxpayer dollars were spent on my family,” he tweeted in May.

Duffy insisted that neither he nor his family received compensation for the show. The message also included him bragging about his tenure leading the Department of Transportation.

“Under my leadership, DOT has become the most responsive, productive, and transformational in its history,” Duffy boasted. He then took a shot at the previous TransSec, Pete Buttigieg.

Duffy continued, “Modernizing air traffic control, hiring 20% more controllers annually than my predecessor, moving grants at record speed, and removing illegal truck drivers from the road.”

Plus, Campos-Duffy tweeted , “All production costs were paid for by the non-profit, The Great American Road Trip, Inc. No one in my family – including my husband – were paid to do this.”

Some of the corporations listed as sponsors for “The Great American Road Trip” included Boeing, Toyota, Shell, United Airlines, Lyft, and Royal Caribbean Group.

The fact that Duffy’s Transportation Department regulates many of those companies raised alarms for possible corruption, an issue voters named as a top concern in the midterm elections.

“Sean Duffy is as corrupt, incompetent, and lazy as his boss, Trump,” an X user expressed. Another person renamed Duffy’s YouTube series “The Great American Rip-off.”

Similarly, a poster wrote, “This is a serious conflict of interest.” Trump’s entire team caught heat when someone declared, “The priorities of this administration are so out of whack.”

Younger social media users might not have realized that the federal official who oversees national transportation policy and aviation safety came from reality television.

“The world is a stage. I can’t take this government serious. I knew he looked familiar. Sean Duffy was on the reality series called ‘The Real World,’” an X poster shared.

That led to a reply that read, “Central casting… DJT says it all the time!”

Trump, also a former reality star, has not been shy about wanting photogenic, attractive people representing his administration.

Given that Trump’s decade-long run on “The Apprentice” reality show helped launch the real estate mogul’s polarizing rise to political power, many of his detractors view the “central casting” requirement as the epitome of the president’s misplaced priorities.

Duffy’s FAA shutdown troubles put Trump’s hiring decisions under scrutiny. Trump has already fired several Cabinet members during his second term.

The White House reportedly formed a special team to prevent further airport outages.

However, Duffy’s time on “The Real World” and as a producer of “The Great American Road Trip” did little to prepare him for an emergency that disrupted millions of travelers for days.

I’ve been talking for months about how Sean Duffy spent seven months filming a reality show while still getting paid for being The Transportation Secretary and now we find out that his sponsors for the show are all Companies his department oversees and regulates. pic.twitter.com/S0Lo3iPHqB

Subscribe To The ABS Newsletter — Get our stories in your inbox.

We hope this story was worth your time. For over 14 years, Atlanta Black Star has stayed Black-owned and independently run. We didn't get here by waiting on ad budgets that were never built to prioritize us. Our readers did that.

Corporate support for Black media has always been thin. Outlets like ours get roughly 1% of the $170 billion spent on U.S. advertising each year, and that margin is shrinking further as advertisers walk back the DEI-linked commitments they made in 2020. That's the backdrop. It's not why we're asking.

The wider picture isn't any steadier. Newspaper ad revenue has fallen more than 80% since 2005, and local newsrooms are closing at a rate of roughly two a week nationwide. When outlets go under, it's rarely the ones built to center a Black perspective from the ground up that get to stick around.

We know a request for support isn't why you came here. But without readers choosing to fund this work directly, the depth of reporting we can do at home and abroad shrinks along with everyone else's. If you're not in a position to give, that doesn't change how much we value you as a reader.

If you are able to, a recurring contribution does more for us than a single one-time gift, because it lets us plan the next investigation instead of just the next invoice. It takes about 30 seconds, no long form, no account. Thank you for continuing to support independent journalism and freedom of the press.
