scraped.title: A Memphis Pastor’s Vision for His Neighborhood Takes Root
scraped.description: The Rev. Marlon Foster sees farming as a way to tackle food insecurity in one of the city’s food deserts.
scraped.author: HoneyRose Smith
scraped.h1: A Memphis Pastor’s Vision for His Neighborhood Takes Root
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

MEMPHIS, Tennessee – Cherrese Cooper-Holmes says that when she saw her son pull a fresh carrot out of the ground at a South Memphis micro-farm, the moment changed her life.

The family lives in a neighborhood with no full-service grocery stores. In one of the city’s food deserts, the Green Leaf Learning Farm’s culinary program became a lifeline to better eating for Cooper-Holmes’ family. Processed foods have been replaced with fresh fruits and vegetables, meals, and even cooking classes.

“I did not know there was such an amazing difference between farm-raised organic and conventional grocery store food,” Cooper-Holmes said. “The quality is totally different!”

Micro-farms like Green Leaf are critical to the growth and revitalization of areas like South Memphis, residents say. Memphis has also consistently ranked as the city with the highest crime rate per capita, with crime largely situated in the South Memphis area . Most residents only have the options of corner stores, which primarily sell processed foods. Many of these stores are also located on blocks where gang violence is rampant.

Yet, one longtime resident believes that developing a healthier lifestyle and deeper connection with the surrounding land is a step toward improving the community’s myriad challenges.

Founded in 2010, the farm is the vision of the Rev. Marlon Foster. As the founder and CEO of youth and community development organization Knowledge Quest, his main goal was to address the needs of the surrounding neighborhood. As a result, it helps the community return to what he remembers when he was growing up.

The soil of South Memphis holds a rich history, Foster said. “We are really trying to return to who we are.”

As Memphis fights food insecurity, Foster sees the micro farms as one solution. A micro-farm is an agricultural infrastructure typically located in an area that is self-contained generally in 5 acres or less.

Foster believes that Knowledge Quest’s framework can help alleviate some of the blight occurring in the city. It’s based on three pillars: education, community and economic development, and food security. These pillars are manifested through its Learning Farm, Container Cafe, an upcoming organic market, and community partnerships.

The nonprofit is leaning into the third pillar by working to see how agriculture can help nurture community development, Foster said: “Our number one support system is really from community residents.”

The farm sits on Jeanette Place in the Soulsville area of South Memphis, and is the only USDA-certified organic farm in the area. But a few miles away sit buildings ravaged by neglect and age. They once housed the area’s finest examples of Black entrepreneurship and creativity, Foster recalled.

Following increased drug use in the 1970s and ’80s, the landscape of the neighborhood began to deteriorate, shifts that let drugs run rampant and left families impoverished.

The answer to revitalizing South Memphis lies in the same roots of the neighborhood he grew up in, Foster said.

He has lived all 54 years of his life in the city, long enough to see corner stores turn into “crack houses” and poverty infest a once thriving area.

“I see the former glory and I see the drug activity, the gang activity, the dogfighting rings, that’s the temporal thing,” Foster said. He likened it to a small rung on the ladder of the history of the area.

As his idea for a farm began to take shape in 2010, that same year Memphis was named the “Hunger Capital of the United States” by the Food Research and Action Center .

The need was already crystal clear. A study conducted by FRAC determined that 26% of people in the Memphis metro area could not afford to buy their own groceries. Many depend on organizations such as Mid-South Foodbank to get meals for the families. Green Leaf and Mid-South have partnered with the The Mid-South Regional Food System Plan to “increase awareness and access to long term food access and sustainability.”

Still, it was an incident in 2011 that fueled Foster’s efforts even more. One day, as children were studying on the farm, there was gun violence across the street, no more than 300 feet away.

The incident encouraged Foster and other community members to join together to turn the housing and empty lots where the shootout occurred into something that would benefit the community. There is now a deli and market for the community, as well as a college dormitory, where students at LeMoyne-Owen College can reside to study agriculture hands-on. The organization has also obtained 30 lots.

“We need to really do something positive with this housing,” Foster said. He recalls that the shootout led to an intentional effort by the nonprofit to continue to develop the neighborhood’s assets.

LEFT: Potted plants grown by the students of Knowledge Quest. Each popsicle stick has the name of a student who helped grow the plant. RIGHT: Foster said he sees micro farms as one solution to food insecurity in Memphis. (HoneyRose Smith)

Knowledge Quest extended the farm’s resources by opening this market for residents. On Oct. 30, Knowledge Quest hosted a grand opening of its Organic Market in the neighborhood. Foster said the idea for the market was inspired by the fresh produce markets and grocery stores he remembers growing up.

“There was a deli that was so clean, you could eat off the floor,” Foster recalled.

Through Knowledge Quest, he has plans to bring a clean and bright grocery store back to the neighborhood, just like when he was young.

At the market, there are plans for Green Leaf Learning Farm to provide quality meats, cheeses, and produce. Foster hopes to recreate the secure nature of a community grocer, reviving the resource South Memphis lost years ago.

“Its incredible and amazing,” said Cooper-Holmes when she learned of the plan for a market. “To me it is a prayer that has been answered.”

The ethos of Foster’s initiatives is that the community members play active roles in improving their lives and environment. During the farm’s 16-year existence, children who once learned at the farm are now leading classes and paying it forward.

For Tamia Townsend, life as a chef is like a full-circle moment. As the current sous chef and manager of the Culinary Program & Container Cafe, she now works alongside the people she taught when she was a young adult.

“I love giving back to my community and watching it blossom,” Townsend said.

She has been a part of the Knowledge Quest since she started middle school in 2011. She was a student in their afterschool program, and began the culinary academy when she became a high school student.

“It was always a learning place for me,” Townsend said. “It was an opportunity for me to make something out of my life.”

Prior to participating in the culinary academy at the Green Leaf , she wanted to become a nurse. Learning farm opened her eyes to a world of possibilities within culinary and nutritional science.

Townsend said she fell in love with the open learning environment between the students and the teachers at Greenleaf. This educational framework allowed the students to participate in activities of their personal interest, and fostered her love of cooking.

A few years into her culinary career, Townsend answered a call from her mentor at Green Leaf Cafe. She had an offer: return to Greenleaf, this time as a teacher instead of a student.

“It was no doubt in my mind to come back,” Townsend said. “Why not be a light in somebody else’s life, how Knowledge Quest was a light in my life.”

She now uses this light to serve current students and families within the South Memphis neighborhood. She sees it as a chance to put back into her community, giving children the same opportunities she was once gifted.

Students take their education home to teach their families how to properly cook and preserve produce and encourage them to change their eating habits. They’ve also spoken with the mayor and other city officials to request more funding to support efforts at Greef Leaf.

“You have to be the start of the change,” Townsend tells her students, urging them to imagine a world their generation can create by continuing the work of those before them.

Cooper-Holmes, the mother of three children, first learned of Knowledge Quest’s resources in 2016 after she heard a representative speak on a neighborhood panel. Soon after, she was invited to the farm and participated in a cooking demonstration. Since then, her family has been reliant on the resources provided by Green Leaf.

Cooper-Holmes has not only seen healthy behavior in herself, but her children as well. With the help of the farm, her family has now started its own backyard garden. She says her children now love carrots. With the market on the way, they will get the chance to find tasty vegetables at a grocery store once again.

This holiday season, Cooper-Holmes and other community members will continue to benefit from the farm. Cooper-Holmes looks forward to incorporating produce from the farm’s harvest in her holiday dinners for her family. Additionally, Townsend plans to help the children at Green Leaf cook greens for the community’s Harvest Festivals.

“Anything we do, we want to be a good benefit for the body and soul,” Townsend said.

scraped.title: Where to Find Black-Owned Bookstores Across the U.S.
scraped.description: From books to puzzles and stationery, these shopping destinations also serve as gathering places in communities across the country.
scraped.author: Alecia Taylor
scraped.h1: Where to Find Black-Owned Bookstores Across the U.S.
scraped.body_text:
Capital B News

Read them in Seen & Heard, our free, twice-weekly newsletter.

This story was originally published in December 2025 and has been updated.

Black-owned bookstores across the country continue to offer spaces and access to books that you may not find on the shelves of chain bookstores.

Despite a fire and an economic downturn forcing some brick-and-mortar shops to go strictly online , Black-owned bookstores are pushing through and open for business.

Larger corporations like Amazon and Target sometimes may sell books at a lower price compared to independent bookstores. Yet, Black owners told Capital B they can offer customers so much more: places to gather and a sense of community.

The following are Black-owned bookstores to add to your shopping rotation, including recommendations from Capital B readers, and some of the stories behind them.

Call & Response in Chicago

The mission of Call & Response is pretty simple: normalize books by Black and authors of color, said Courtney Bledsoe, who opened shop in Chicago in May 2024.

“There is an entire world of literature out there,” Bledsoe said. “Be it science fiction, fantasy, romance, literary fiction, nonfiction and [children’s] graphic novels … there’s an entire world out there that is waiting for everybody. My goal is to normalize all of that.”

Bledsoe said when she first opened the bookstore in Hyde Park — a neighborhood that is 40% white and 28% Black, according to state data — some customers realized all her books featured people of color. They immediately walked out. Bledsoe said this shouldn’t be the case. People should normalize reading books that center groups that aren’t just white people.

Instead of pre-ordering your books from chain bookstores such as Barnes & Noble, Books-A-Million, or Amazon, Bledsoe said she is encouraging people to pre-order from indie bookstores like her own. Her shelves are stocked with books that are in high demand, not just across the country, but from her community as well.

For those in the area, Bledsoe said she curates community events that she refers to as a “third space” for customers to get to know their neighbors. She wants people to get to know their local community as well as they know the characters in the books they’re reading. Bledsoe and her customers come up with ideas for the events: They hold silent book clubs, open mics, local author events, and fundraise for children living in the Palestinian territories.

While she loves what she does, she said she’s faced some challenges being a Black woman who owns a small business. Customers sometimes will ask if her store will price-match Amazon, Target, and other big corporations (she doesn’t) or come in with their own preconceived notions about her identity as a Black woman.

Still, Bledscoe shows up to serve her community. She has only one part-time employee at Call & Response.

“It’s been a pleasure to just be able to be that space for people,” she said. “I always say that this is kind of a judgment-free zone when it comes to literacy and reading.”

If you’re not sure what book to get someone, Bledscoe said shoppers can ask bookstore employees for recommendations.

There are other items you can purchase that aren’t books at her store: Black-themed crossword puzzles, Apostrophe Puzzles (a Black-owned puzzle company), candles, stickers, journals, and stuffed animals for the little ones.

Call & Response is on Bookshop , and Libro fm , the audiobook alternative for Audible, which is owned and operated by Amazon.

More Black-owned bookstores in the Midwest:

Grand Gesture Books, Portland, Oregon

Katherine Morgan used to sell books at another independent bookstore, and she said she felt the absence of Black folks and other people of color in the romance genre.

Morgan used to work in the romance section, which led her to open her own independent bookstore in downtown Portland, Oregon. She said her store focuses on the people who are often overlooked in romance books.

“It’s so important to highlight people’s identities because it helps them learn more about themselves,” Morgan said. “It helps them discover what it is that they deserve in a romance themselves, whether that’s on the page or in real life.”

Thinking back to when she was a child, Morgan said she doesn’t remember Black people as the main character in romance books. It wasn’t until she was around 26 that she read a popular Black romance book by Jasmine Guillory.

“When you don’t see yourselves represented in a genre where it’s important that everyone gets a happily ever after,” she said, “it makes you convinced that you don’t deserve that, or that something is actually wrong with you, and it’s not that at all.”

Books are how Morgan said she discovered she was queer later on in life. She said queer representation is also important at her store, where she has two large bookcases dedicated to just LGBTQ romance.

Grand Gesture Books doesn’t just bring representation from the page, Morgan said they bring representation in real life, too. She said while her store can’t compete with Amazon’s prices, she can build connections with the community and her customers to adjust her inventory to meet demand.

The store held an all-day wedding ceremony in partnership with a local county in Oregon where judges were able to officiate weddings. Among the shelves as the couples stood together, she said her bookstore became a hub for real-life romance.

If you’re not into physical books, Morgan said folks can still shop for other gifts such as stickers, and cases for e-readers.

Grand Gesture is also on Bookshop .

More Black independent bookstores to shop on the West Coast :

Marshall’s Music and Books in Jackson, Mississippi

If you’re feeling radical and you’re in the South, stop by Marshall’s Music and Books, one of the oldest bookstores in the country. It has been open for 87 years — and counting.

The shop has moved only two times since its opening in 1938, said Maati Primm, the current owner. For decades, the bookstore’s home has been located on Farish Street in Jackson, Mississippi, where Primm said gentrification is taking over.

Primm said with Mississippi’s ongoing attacks on diversity initiatives , she’s seeing more Black families come into her shop to access books and parts of history that are no longer taught in schools.

“We have a large collection of Black history and Black culture books,” she told Capital B. “That was something that hadn’t been done before I got here, and so that is something that has been added.”

Primm said she feels like education has become illegal in her state when it comes to teaching Black people about their history. But she said that is not going to stop her and her community. Instead, Primm said patrons are asking questions: “Why is it you don’t want me to know my history? What is in my history that threatens the status quo?”

That’s why she has a wall dedicated to important faces in Black literature — some of whom are from Jackson, like young adult author Angie Thomas. Thomas’s book The Hate U Give , which was turned into a feature film in 2018, was challenged in several public libraries and schools across the country.

Marshall’s has items other than books such as dashiki’s, bracelets, Bible and spiritual literature churches can purchase in bulk, Primm said. As of right now, she said, customers can shop only in the store.

More bookshops to support across the South :

Obodo Serendipity in Stratford, Connecticut

Obodo Serendipity Books started as a pop-up bookshop at a local coffee shop and has blossomed into a bookstore in Stratford, Connecticut. Since its opening in September 2024, it has made connections with its surrounding community through events.

“After realizing how receptive the community was to supporting a pop-up shop randomly twice a month, I felt like a brick and mortar was more of a possibility,” said the bookstore’s owner, Nikkya Hargrove. “It was a viable option for our town.”

While business booms during months like Black and Women’s History as well as Pride, Hargrove said she wants to remind folks that independent bookstores have to keep the lights on 365 days a year and keep the shelves stocked.

The store got started with the help of the community and Honeycomb Credit, a peer-funded loan platform that invests in minority-owned small businesses. Hargrove fundraised $32,000 to help with start-up costs.

Hargrove is also a published author and editor-in-chief of the Stratford Crier , a local newspaper. She said the store is situated in a community still reeling from the impacts of redlining. She has spent the past year working on marketing to different neighborhoods by partnering with business owners to sell books at their stores.

Hargrove has a volunteer who helps her at Obodo Serendipity. Despite being the only full-time employee, the bookstore still hosts monthly author events and a middle grade book club that lets the young readers come up with their own discussion points.

The community outreach doesn’t just stop at bookish events. Obodo Serendipity also offers yoga classes, and partners with cultural services in Connecticut, an organization that provides job training for those with mental disabilities such as autism. For about six weeks, members of the organization work with Hargrove to gain experience.

You can find Obodo Serendipity on Bookshop to purchase books. Other gifts such as stationary items and non-book items are sold only at the store.

Loyalty Books in Washington, D.C.

Some indie bookstores can focus on Black romance, but Hannah Oliver Depp, one of the co-owners at Loyalty Books, said they wanted to highlight communities that are on the brink of erasure in the nation’s capital.

“I really wanted to be able to serve the communities that I’d grown up with, and be able to wholeheartedly say whatever I wanted to say, and support whatever causes we wanted to support and represent the community,” said Depp, who uses they/she pronouns.

Washington, which earned its nickname “Chocolate City” for being a majority Black city, is seeing a decrease in Black residents. In the 2000s, the Black population declined by 58,000 while the white population increased by upward of 80,000, according to a report by the DC Fiscal Policy Institute, a source for data in the Washington area.

This bookstore doesn’t just highlight Black voices, Depp said; it highlights voices from all marginalized communities, such as authors who are disabled, as well as books featuring characters of color.

As someone who is Black, queer, on the spectrum, interracial, and an adoptee, they said it only felt right to bring their intersectionalities as a symbol to Loyalty Books, which is located in Petworth in Northwest D.C.

In the windows of the store are the Pride flag, a Black Lives Matter sign, Free DC signs, and the slogan “None of us are free until all of us are free,” in support of Palestinians.

In a recent social media post , Depp said that the store’s windows have been vandalized several times. However, this only led her to use this as momentum: last week, 10% of the store’s earnings are going to Free DC as well as individual fundraisers for people who are on the ground in Gaza.

“Instead of silencing us, all that did was empower us to do something we’re not normally able to do as a small business and financially put our money where our mouth is,” they said. “I try to exist as a place that points out how all these interconnections work.”

Loyalty Books started as a pop-up shop in 2018. After seeing the support of the bookstore during pop-ups and online , Depp opened a physical bookstore in 2019, before the start of the COVID-19 epidemic.

As businesses closed and people stayed home in 2020, Depp moved all bookstore events online, but she said the community continued to support. The online effort was spearheaded by Christine Bollow, who worked then as the programming lead. Bollow, who is Filipino and a member of the disabled community, later joined as a co-owner of Loyalty Books.

Bollow helps plan large community events and partnerships with D.C. Public Library and as well as the bookstore’s participation in Awesome Con, the annual comic-con event in D.C.

Loyalty books also has other booksellers who help the owners curate their inventory through book recommendations and events. When walking through the bookstore, there are even note cards with staff suggestions for books.

There are also stickers that they create with the bookstore logo that customers can stop in and purchase. Customers can purchase audiobooks and gift cards on their site and on Bookshop .

More bookstores in the D.C., Maryland, Virginia area

More bookstores on the East Coast

Black publishers, authors and booksellers have banded together to create resource centers on where and how to find Black independent bookstores.

The African American Literature Book Club , founded in 1998 by Troy Johnson, has a website dedicated to information about Black authors and books.

The Black Bookstore Coalition was founded by two bookstore owners, Ramunda Young of MahoganyBooks and Kalima DeSuze of Café Con Libros, in the height of the COVID-19 pandemic. The site features not only Black-owned bookstores, but also features monthly bestselling books by Black authors throughout the diaspora.

Alecia Taylor is the national education reporter at Capital B. More by Alecia Taylor

scraped.title: Kenyan communities take on Nigerian billionaire’s $16 billion refinery project as court adjourns hearing
scraped.description: Environmental science and conservation news
scraped.h1: Kenyan communities take on Nigerian billionaire’s $16 billion refinery project as court adjourns hearing
scraped.body_text:
If you liked this story, share it with other people.

Around 40 community representatives gathered early in the morning on Nov. 24 at a county assembly hall in Lamu, a town on an island off Kenya’s coast, to virtually witness a court hearing. The case pits residents against the Dangote group, owned by Nigerian billionaire Aliko Dangote. The conglomerate plans to build an oil refinery on lands where the residents claim they have lived for generations.

With an estimated cost of $16 billion and a reported production capacity of 700,000 barrels per day , the East Africa Petroleum Refinery, if it goes ahead, would be the largest in Africa.

However, some residents appear not to have been informed of the project beforehand. Because they do not hold formal land title deeds, the government is asking them to leave, the community representatives said. “We want information,” Mzee Hilal Suleiman Ali, an elder from the indigenous Mvinjeni community who attended the hearing, told Mongabay. “We are not opposed to the project, but we want to be included, and above all, we want to keep our land.”

On Sept. 30, Dangote held a groundbreaking ceremony attended by several African heads of state.

The November hearing was held at the Environment and Land Court in Malindi, around 200 kilometers (125 miles) from Lamu along the Kenyan coast. Because traveling to attend in person would be too expensive, the communities witnessed the proceedings remotely using a phone. Their lawyer, who was present with them, participated in the hearing virtually.

After several hours, the judge announced an adjournment on procedural grounds.

“We would prefer to adjourn the hearing until Dec. 15, by which time you will have brought us the documents,” the presiding judge, Jane Onyango, told the plaintiff’s lawyer. As the complaint was filed by email, the judge required that it be submitted in person in Nairobi, with copies for all the parties concerned, before the case can proceed.

In the room, one could feel the frustration among the community representatives growing.

“It seems like they are trying to delay the process and discourage us from filing a complaint,” Daniel Mwaniki Mwangi, a farmer and resident of Lamu county, told Mongabay. “The government should not abandon its people. We have filed a court case, we will not abandon it, and we will follow through with it.”

George Wakahiu, the plaintiffs’ lawyer, remained optimistic about the situation. “It is nothing. I’ll go to Nairobi and do what they are asking for,” he said, adding that: “[T]he National Land Commission is now coming to the ground to see who is affected. They have now agreed to talk to the people. Before, they refused to talk to the people, so I am optimistic that there will be a discussion and everything will be sorted out.”

Banner image: George Wakahiu, the lawyer representing community members, pleading remotely before the Environment and Land Court in Malindi, seen here alongside members of the affected communities.

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) sits at the center of the global race for the critical minerals needed for advanced technologies ranging from medical equipment and military hardware to electric cars and industrial batteries. items.title: King tides bring record coastal flooding to California
items.summary: The highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping occurred in both San Diego and Los Angeles today, beating the records set just last month.

scraped.title: King tides bring record coastal flooding to California » Yale Climate Connections
scraped.description: The highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping occurred in both San Diego and Los Angeles today, beating the records set just last month.
scraped.author: Jeff Masters
scraped.h1: King tides bring record coastal flooding to California
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

The king tides of November clobbered California during the morning high tide on Nov. 25, bringing the highest coastal water levels in over a century of record-keeping to both San Diego and Los Angeles , beating records set just last month. Monterey also had its highest water level on record (since 1973), Santa Monica , its second-highest (since 1933); Point Reyes , its fourth-highest (since 1975); Alameda , its sixth-highest (since 1939); Humboldt , its fifth-highest (since 1977); and San Francisco , its ninth-highest (since 1897). Oregon also got into the act, with Charleston , located about 100 miles north of the California border, experiencing its second-highest water level on record (since 1970), and South Beach , its eighth-highest (since 1967). Of the top-10 water levels on record for California’s three largest coastal cities, 60% are now from 2026 (see yellow-highlighted entries in Fig. 1).

Get news for people who love the planet. Sign up for our newsletters for the latest weather updates, tips, and inspiring stories

The high-water records occurred during weather usually unfavorable for setting such records: clear skies, light winds, and above-average surface pressures. But this week marks the arrival of the king tides, when the elliptical orbit of the moon brings it closest to the Earth, resulting in the highest tides of the year.

This is one of the most extreme marine heatwaves in North American history. Over 1,000 miles of ocean is running 5°C (9°F) or more above normal, from central Baja California all the way up to Eureka on California's North Coast. This marine heatwave is unprecedented in every… pic.twitter.com/shky3NJPFw

The other key factor: a very strong El Niño event that brought record-warm water to the coast, resulting in local sea level rise. Sea surface temperatures more than 5°C (9°F) above average are present along most of the California coast. That’s substantially boosting sea levels because water expands as it warms. And with the king tide and El Niño-driven warm water arriving at a time when human-caused sea level rise has substantially boosted water levels, we now have a recipe for record flooding in the absence of a storm.

While today marks the peak amplitude of the astronomical high tides from this king tide event, Thanksgiving Day water levels will also be very high, likely setting top-10 water level marks all along the California coast. In southern California, a long-period west swell arriving Wednesday night will worsen flooding and persist into Thursday. In San Diego, this swell will generate large breaking waves of 6-8 feet on Thursday, with 10-12-foot sets on exposed west-facing beaches. Santa Barbara is expecting breaking waves of 15-22 feet, and Los Angeles and Malibu are expecting 6-11 feet. A High Surf Advisory is in effect for most of Southern California.

Growing signs of active winter storm pattern developing in California during Dec. And embedded within that are early indications of a potentially very strong storm that could affect central & southern CA next Mon/Tue w/very heavy rain, strong winds, & thunderstorms. Stay tuned.

While the tides will be gradually decreasing through next week, we need to keep an eye on a strong Pacific storm predicted to hit central California on Tuesday, Dec. 1. Models are predicting that this storm will bring strong southerly winds, very low surface pressures, and heavy rain to the coast – conditions ideal for generating a significant storm surge, as explained in my post Monday, What’s causing major coastal flooding in California?

We’re not done with king tides after this week: The December 23-25 and January 21-22 full moon periods will have king tides similar in magnitude to this week’s (see the Bluesky post by Daniel Swain below to see the timing and severity of the coastal flooding severity). With this winter’s El Niño event not yet at its peak, the record-warm water by the coast isn’t going anywhere soon, and may spread farther north to the coasts of Oregon, Washington, and British Columbia, increasing coastal flooding odds there.

There will be multiple episodes of major coastal flooding in CA this winter. Substantial impacts are likely even without storms, but worst case scenario would involve overlap with strong storm. Fortunately, Nov event lacks major storm–but that luck may not hold through Dec-Jan.

Meanwhile, the U.S. East Coast has its own coastal flooding concerns. As documented in our post from yesterday that we’ve now updated , a powerful Thanksgiving Day nor’easter will slam areas from the Outer Banks of North Carolina to Long Island, New York, with coastal flooding, heavy rains, and high winds. Numerous power outages, road closures, and flight delays are expected. At least two stations — Cape May, NJ, and Chincoteague Inlet, VA — are predicted to see all-time record coastal flooding.

Irene Sans contributed to this post.

scraped.author: Bob Henson, Jeff Masters
scraped.h1: Un “Nor’easter” durante el Día de Acción de Gracias traerá vientos huracanados, lluvias torrenciales y niveles del agua cercanos a máximos históricos
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Como si estuviera programada para coincidir con las festividades, la tormenta del noreste (nor’easter) más intensa de la temporada hasta ahora azotará la costa este de Estados Unidos desde la noche del miércoles hasta el jueves 26 de noviembre, Día de Acción de Gracias. Dos potentes sistemas de baja presión en los niveles superiores de la atmósfera se fusionarán mientras giran uno alrededor del otro. Debajo de ellos, una poderosa baja presión en superficie se intensificará rápidamente a medida que avance hacia el noreste cerca de la costa. Esta tormenta coincidirá con una superluna casi llena y un extenso corredor de vientos provenientes del océano, lo que elevará el nivel del mar hasta valores que normalmente solo se observan cada 10 a 15 años. En algunos lugares, podrían acercarse a máximos históricos.

Para la mañana del martes, ya se habían emitido avisos de inundaciones costeras en el noreste de Carolina del Norte, Virginia, Delaware y Nueva Jersey. Los fuertes vientos también podrían derribar árboles y derribar tendidos eléctricos, incluso en zonas alejadas de la costa.

Aunque no sufran inundaciones directamente, millones de personas a lo largo del densamente poblado corredor de la autopista interestatal 95 enfrentarán lluvias intensas y vientos fuertes con ráfagas mientras se reúnen para celebrar el feriado. Las precipitaciones podrían acumularse rápidamente entre 1 y 4 pulgadas (25 a 102 mm) en las zonas costeras y cercanas al litoral, desde Carolina del Norte hasta Maine. Se pronostican vientos sostenidos superiores al umbral de tormenta tropical (39 mph o 63 km/h), con ráfagas generalizadas de 50 a 60 mph (80 a 97 km/h) tierra adentro y velocidades aún mayores en la costa. Estas condiciones afectarán los Outer Banks durante la noche del miércoles y se extenderán hasta las costas de Nueva Inglaterra el jueves.

Los fuertes vientos podrían impedir que vuelen los enormes globos característicos del Desfile del Día de Acción de Gracias de Macy’s en Manhattan. De ocurrir, sería la primera vez en 55 años que los famosos globos no participarían. Las regulaciones municipales prohíben el uso de globos grandes cuando los vientos sostenidos superan las 23 mph (37 km/h) o las ráfagas superan las 34 mph (55 km/h).

Valoramos mucho tus perspectivas, por lo tanto, queremos que nos mandes tus preguntas sobre el cambio climático y sus efectos.

Un aspecto favorable es que esta tormenta se desplazará rápidamente, avanzando desde las proximidades de los Outer Banks hacia Nueva Inglaterra durante el jueves. Otro factor importante es que no se producirá una tormenta extremadamente fría a finales de noviembre. Cualquier episodio inicial de nieve o hielo durante el jueves probablemente se limitará a las zonas más elevadas de la cordillera de los Apalaches, así como a sectores del interior de Nueva York y del norte de Nueva Inglaterra.

Entre la noche del jueves y el viernes, la parte posterior del sistema de baja presión en altura, cada vez más frío y consolidado, podría generar una franja relativamente estrecha pero intensa de nevadas desde el “Cinturón Agrícola del Maíz” (Corn Belt) hasta los Apalaches centrales. Las nevadas más abundantes probablemente se producirán en el sureste de Canadá. Para comienzos de la próxima semana, la tormenta debería ser un recuerdo lejano, ya que se pronostican temperaturas superiores a los 60 °F (16 °C) incluso en zonas tan septentrionales como Nueva Jersey.

¡No podemos hacer este trabajo sin ti! Aproximadamente el 83 % de cada dólar que donas se destina directamente a pagar a nuestro equipo de reporteros, editores, meteorólogos y productores de radio. El otro 17 % cubre este sitio web, computadoras portátiles, un sistema de nómina y otros gastos similares necesarios para nuestro trabajo.

Un episodio breve pero intenso de inundaciones costeras, concentrado alrededor de la pleamar del jueves, podría afectar a miles de residentes de zonas próximas al litoral, con algunos de los niveles de agua más altos jamás registrados.

Los factores que contribuyen a esta situación, enumerados de mayor a menor influencia, son:

Incluso en la región de Hampton Roads, en el sureste de Virginia, donde las inundaciones son cada vez más frecuentes y graves, esta podría ser una tormenta memorable. Dejando de lado los huracanes, una de las tormentas invernales de referencia por sus inundaciones en la costa este de Estados Unidos fue la tristemente célebre “Tormenta del Siglo” de 1993, que avanzó desde el golfo de México hasta el extremo sureste de Canadá a mediados de marzo. Aquel gigantesco sistema causó más de 300 muertes y daños por un valor superior a 5.000 millones de dólares, expresados en valores de 1993. No se espera que la tormenta de esta semana iguale, en términos generales, aquel acontecimiento histórico y mortal.

“Esta podría ser una tormenta histórica en el sureste de Virginia, con niveles de agua que se acerquen a los registrados durante eventos tan destacados como el Huracán Chesapeake-Potomac de 1933, el Huracán Isabel de septiembre de 2023 y el Huracán Irene de agosto de 2011”, señaló Hugh Cobb, meteorólogo jubilado del Servicio Meteorológico Nacional. Cobb creció en la región y trabajó como responsable de ciencia y operaciones en la oficina del NWS en Wakefield, Virginia, antes de dirigir la División de Análisis y Pronóstico Tropical del Centro Nacional de Huracanes.

Almost exactly two months after the Delmarva coast suffered severe beach erosion during a powerful nor'easter, another one is on the way for Thanksgiving. Full story: https://t.co/iDFsp43KMk pic.twitter.com/K3IovG6JtL

El clima está cambiando y nuestros periodistas están aquí para ayudarte a comprender lo que está pasando. ¡Suscríbete a nuestro boletín informativo y nunca te pierdas una historia!

A continuación se presentan algunos de los niveles máximos de agua previstos para el jueves en las localidades incluidas en las vigilancias de inundaciones costeras emitidas el martes por la mañana. Las cifras representan la altura total pronosticada, en pies, sobre el nivel medio de bajamar inferior (MLLW, por sus siglas en inglés), una referencia utilizada para medir las mareas. En muchas zonas expuestas al océano, las grandes olas se superpondrán a estos niveles elevados del mar.

*En Chincoteague Inlet, el nivel previsto superaría el récord anterior. **En Atlantic City, el nivel pronosticado sería el décimo más alto desde que comenzaron los registros en 1911. ***En Cape May Harbor, también sería el décimo más alto desde 1965, situándose apenas 0,4 pies por debajo del nivel registrado durante el Huracán Sandy en 2012. La contribución de la marejada ciclónica sería de 2,4 pies.

El Servicio Meteorológico Nacional advierte que, cuando se alcanzan los niveles previstos de inundación grave, el agua comienza a provocar daños estructurales y anegamientos generalizados en las carreteras. Las viviendas y los negocios vulnerables pueden sufrir daños severos a medida que el agua supera estos umbrales. Numerosas carreteras pueden volverse intransitables y algunos vecindarios podrían quedar aislados. Las aguas de inundación también representan un peligro para cualquier persona que intente atravesarlas a pie o en vehículo.

Las inundaciones costeras provocadas por esta tormenta podrían resultar especialmente problemáticas en los Outer Banks de Carolina del Norte. Durante septiembre y octubre, las tormentas costeras destruyeron tramos de la carretera NC-12, la única vía que conecta esta vulnerable cadena de islas barrera con el continente, lo que provocó cierres durante un total de 15 días. La tormenta del noreste de septiembre produjo el quinto nivel de agua más alto desde que comenzaron los registros en 1979 en el mareógrafo de la NOAA ubicado en Duck, en el sector norte de los Outer Banks. La erosión causada por aquella tormenta obligó a cerrar la carretera NC-12 durante cinco días y a establecer un servicio de transbordadores de emergencia hacia el continente por primera vez desde 2013.

El Servicio Meteorológico Nacional pronostica que la carretera NC-12 podría sufrir el desbordamiento del agua del mar durante la pleamar de las 7:00 a. m. del miércoles, y que ese desbordamiento sería probable durante la pleamar de las 8:00 a. m. del jueves, Día de Acción de Gracias. Los niveles del agua previstos para ese momento serían superiores a los del 19 de octubre, cuando el avance del mar sobre la carretera causó graves daños y obligó a cerrarla durante diez días. El martes por la mañana, la carretera mantenía abierto un solo carril en la zona dañada, mientras la arena seguía acumulándose sobre la calzada. El Departamento de Transporte de Carolina del Norte trabaja activamente para reforzar las dunas que protegen la carretera y colocar sacos de arena.

Sigue nuestro canal de WhatsApp y suscríbete a nuestro canal de Youtube .

La tormenta del noreste de septiembre provocó el derrumbe de varias viviendas. Según informó Island Free Press , la playa de la costa nacional protegida de Carolina del Norte quedó cubierta por una cantidad considerable de restos de escaleras privadas de acceso a la playa, plataformas de madera, componentes de sistemas sépticos y escombros de madera y metal procedentes de las viviendas. La playa tuvo que cerrarse debido a que los desechos humanos provenientes de los sistemas sépticos destruidos contaminaron el agua. Las tormentas del noreste de septiembre y octubre provocaron el colapso de 16 viviendas. Antes de esos episodios, otras 32 casas habían caído al océano a lo largo de los Outer Banks entre 2020 y febrero de 2026. En total, 48 viviendas se derrumbaron entre 2020 y octubre de 2026.

Durante el próximo invierno, cabe esperar que varias tormentas intensas del noreste afecten la región del Atlántico medio de Estados Unidos. Las probabilidades de que la carretera NC-12 sufra múltiples episodios de desbordamiento e interrupciones hasta la primavera de 2027 parecen elevadas.

Esta nota fue traducida por Irene Sans .

scraped.author: YCC Team
scraped.h1: Low-interest loans help Vermont towns recover from devastating floods
scraped.body_text:
Yale Climate Connections

Transcript:

In July, 2023, heavy rain unleashed catastrophic flooding across much of Vermont. Then, a year later to the day, it happened again.

For hard-hit cities and towns, the expense of clearing debris and repairing roads and other infrastructure was staggering. And in some small municipalities, the cost far exceeded their entire annual budget.

Gaughan: “And so caused an issue where they, in select cases, were pushing up against the amounts that their banking relationships would lend to them.”

Michael Gaughan is executive director of the Vermont Bond Bank, which stepped in to help.

The state created the bond bank in 1970 to help cities and towns access low-interest financing for infrastructure.

Gaughan: “For over 50 years, we’ve had the backs of our communities in Vermont.”

In response to the flooding, the bond bank launched a municipal climate recovery fund that offers low-interest loans to help cities and towns rebuild.

Gaughan says the fund has helped municipalities across Vermont cover critical costs while they wait for FEMA reimbursements.

This fall, Indiana’s bond bank launched a similar program after floods there. And other bond banks across the U.S. could follow suit as climate change fuels more extreme weather.

Reporting credit: ChavoBart Digital Media

scraped.title: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’? - Carbon Brief
scraped.description: In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.
scraped.author: Carbon Brief Staff
scraped.h1: Media reaction: Who is to blame for COP31 ‘failure’?
scraped.body_text:
COP31 came to a dramatic close last weekend when a coalition of nations rejected the proposed “Antalya pact”, citing its failure to mention fossil fuels.

The tense final moments and lack of a much-anticipated “pact” have sparked extensive media coverage around the world.

Many commentators have rushed to label the COP31 outcome a “ failure ”, questioning what it means for the future of the UN climate process and a “ divided world ”.

There has been much finger-pointing, with some outlets attributing COP31’s “collapse” to “ oil-rich nations ”, while others blame Europe’s “ reluctance ” to provide more climate finance.

While it is not accurate to say there was “ no agreement ” at COP31, the media response demonstrates the complexity of the divergent views on display at the Antalya conference.

In this article, Carbon Brief draws together media reactions from around the world to show the diversity of responses to the COP31 outcome.

COP31 ended without agreement on a proposed “Antalya pact”, which had been pushed by the Turkey-Australia presidency.

The final text was rejected by at least 32 countries, including the EU, the UK and some climate-vulnerable countries, in chaotic scenes as the talks overran by two days.

An Irish Times editorial said the outcome was an “unprecedented ending of a COP without any agreement or roadmap forward”.

This view, while commonly expressed in the media, is incorrect.

As veteran “COP-watchers” explained for an article on CB Connect , the summit reached agreement on many decisions, even though the presidency’s “cover decision” failed.

Referring to the rejection of the cover decision, Melbourne University climate researchers Prof Jacqueline Peel and Prof Kathryn Bowen wrote in the Conversation that “these texts have always been add-ons to the formal negotiation process”.

Membership

They noted that there was “progress in a few areas” at COP31, including negotiations on supporting a just transition via a “phased approach” and “improving alignment in climate adaptation”.

For a full overview of what happened at COP31 – both inside and outside the negotiations – see Carbon Brief ’s “key outcomes” article.

In the aftermath of COP31, commentators have critiqued decisions made by the presidency. An editorial in the Hindu noted that “usually, cover texts evolve as a final synthesis of deliberations”, but said the COP31 leadership “thought it fit to push for a cover text early in the proceedings”.

Australian “president of negotiations” Chris Bowen has also faced criticism over how he managed competing interests at the summit. An editorial in the climate-sceptic Australian said:

“One thing is clear: Chris Bowen, who presided over Australia’s $150m investment in the conference, has some explaining to do. International reporting has raised questions about Australia and Turkey, the two nations that co-hosted the summit. Some negotiators have criticised their handling of the talks.”

Free fortnightly newsletter

Similarly, climate-sceptic journalist Graham Lloyd wrote in the Australian that “globally, Bowen has embarrassed himself and diminished Australia’s reputation”.

For Australian news outlet Crikey , journalist Royce Kurmelovs said that Bowen “tried to run the world’s climate talks the way Labor [Australia’s ruling party] runs climate policy at home: quiet, pragmatic and without mentioning fossil fuels”, adding that “in Turkey, it didn’t work”.

A commentary by journalist Xu Luyi in Chinese financial news outlet Caixin said that future COP presidencies should “distinguish achievable implementation measures from ambitions that lack a coalition capable of delivering them”.

Separately, an editorial in the National – a UAE state-owned English-language daily newspaper – said “the next UN secretary general needs to restore the art of diplomacy”.

In media coverage, much of the blame for the perceived failure of COP31 has been placed on oil-producing nations – particularly with the final cover decision draft containing no mention of fossil fuels.

Even before the summit had finished, Panama’s minister of environment Juan Carlos Navarro warned that the COP process was being “held hostage by the petroleum mafia”.

After the talks had closed without a deal on the Antalya pact, a Guardian editorial said that responsibility lay with “petrostates resisting a transition away from fossil fuels”, along with a lack of climate finance . The “fossil-fuel backsliding” was being led by a “Saudi-Russian coalition”, it said.

A Bloomberg editorial also noted that the omission of fossil fuels from the decision text came “amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil fuel producers”. A Times editorial described oil-rich nations, “led by Saudi Arabia”, as the “culprits” for the lack of an agreement, because they “insisted on dropping a reference to phasing out hydrocarbons”.

In the i newspaper , David Shukman, a former BBC News science editor, described a “deception” at the “heart” of the COP process:

“This pattern of lobbying by oil-rich nations has become increasingly blatant and aggressive over more than three decades.”

Despite signing up to the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) at the 1992 Earth Summit in Rio de Janeiro, the participation of the “oil-rich minority” has been “in name only”, wrote Shukman:

“At more than a dozen of the UN’s giant conferences, I’ve seen for myself the tactics of trench warfare and how well they’ve worked. It’s why fossil fuels remain so dominant and why the climate is turning so hostile.”

Writing for the Guardian , University College London’s Prof Bill McGuire warned that the COP process had been “deeply compromised” by the “major fossil-fuel producers”. For Al Jazeera , York University’s Prof Ilan Kapoor added that “fossil-fuel power operates well beyond the conference hall”.

( Reuters reported that, according to negotiators from Europe, small-island states, Latin America, Asia and Africa, Saudi officials had “regular access” to the summit’s presidents, “allowing them disproportionate influence”.)

In Australian outlet Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s Prof Michael Jacobs wrote that since “transitioning away from fossil fuels” language was included in COP28 , fossil-fuel producers “have been determined to ensure the phrase would never be used again”.

Nick O’Malley, national environment and climate editor for the Sydney Morning Herald , noted:

“The tension between the action the world knows it must take on climate change and that which a handful of oil-rich nations will allow it to take has been growing for years.”

At the summit itself, shortly after rejecting the cover decision on behalf of the EU, Irish environment minister Darragh O’Brien told Agence France-Presse that the talks had been “hijacked by some oil states”.

The Backchannel substack collated reactions from negotiators and observers. Among them, Dr Mary Robinson – former president of Ireland – warned of the “disturbing politicised attacks on [climate] science from those still clinging to fossil fuels and looking to sabotage climate action”.

In contrast, an editorial in the National loosely described a failure of the talks to “bridge divisions over fossil-fuel language, carbon capture and adaptation finance in the final draft”. It added:

“Unfortunately, the gap between countries – major emitters, energy producers and the more vulnerable nations demanding accessible funding – proved too wide to close.”

Much of the commentary about developed countries’ role at COP31 focused on the EU and the UK blocking the final “Antalya pact”, due to its lack of language about fossil fuels.

A cover-decision text without such language was “vehemently opposed by dozens of countries, including the EU delegation strongly led by [Irish] minister for climate Darragh O’Brien”, according to the Irish Times .

Similarly, an editorial in the UK’s Times concluded that “several countries, including the UK, rejected a draft omitting the not insignificant matter of winding down fossil-fuel use”.

Peter Prengaman, climate news director for the Associated Press , wrote that the EU and its allies “were no longer willing” to leave out fossil-fuel language. (He noted that “top polluter” the US was not present at the summit.)

Other media outlets took a more balanced approach to the role of developed nations at COP31. A Guardian editorial concluded:

“European governments’ objection to fossil-fuel backsliding by a Saudi-Russian coalition was right, but they were wrong to rule out fresh EU funding for developing countries’ climate action.”

Reflecting on the need for “funding to help the poorest countries adapt to global warming”, an editorial in Le Monde noted that “the most developed nations have been reluctant to increase their contributions, despite their historic responsibility for CO2 emissions”.

An editorial in the Hindu stressed:

“It stands to reason that developed countries, which have committed to providing climate finance in recognition of their historical emissions, make good on past promises to shoulder the cost of the carbon emissions that are responsible for warming.”

Writing in US outlet Drilled , reporter Rishika Pardikar noted that “wealthy countries like Japan, the UK and Canada…largely aligned with the EU in opposing support mechanisms for developing countries like long-term finance, adaptation finance and just transition”.

Climate campaigner John Gibbons wrote in the Irish Examiner that the EU was “right to reject” carbon capture and storage in the COP31 outcome, but accused O’Brien of “cosplay[ing] at being a progressive climate leader”, despite Ireland’s poor climate record.

Many developed countries were not particularly vocal at COP31, and an editorial in Japan’s Yomiuri Shimbun lamented a general “low level of interest in and low priority given to global warming”. The editorial concluded:

“It is hoped that Japan will continue to fulfill the practical roles expected of it and contribute to the international community in ways unique to Japan.”

Equity, historical responsibility for climate change and a need for finance have all been portrayed at the centre of developing countries’ positions at COP31.

A comment in the Hindu said that “India’s insistence on historical responsibility, climate finance and adaptation belongs at the centre of any credible plan to cut emissions”.

It added that India had played a “constructive role” to “provide bridging language” in texts on adaptation and the just transition work programme.

Down to Earth noted that “India has referred to historical responsibility in submissions at previous climate summits, but rarely with the emphasis evident” at COP31.

Harjeet Singh, strategic adviser to the Fossil Fuel Non-Proliferation Treaty Initiative , told Radio France Internationale that those who criticise India’s opposition to fossil-fuel phaseout “need to acknowledge that there has been a lot of mistrust between India and developed countries”.

Other developing countries also held firm, particularly on the issue of finance.

Kenya’s the Star said the country had “drawn a firm line” at COP31 and would not “back down until an acceptable deal is secured on climate finance”. The outlet added that the country had “ruled out walking away from the negotiations”.

Inter Press Service , a global south-focused news agency, noted that the “deadlock” at the talks leaves COP32 host Ethiopia “to pick up the pieces”.

An editorial in the Mexican newspaper La Jornada called the failure to reach consensus “suicidal”, adding:

“The conflict is far more complex than a mere opposition between the global north and south, or between hydrocarbon producers and consumers.”

Indeed, some developing countries sided with developed countries in blocking the final passage of the Antalya pact.

The Fiji Times reported that Fiji “held the line in the final negotiating rooms”, joining the EU, the UK and several other Pacific countries in “refus[ing] to endorse a weakened compromise that avoided to mention fossil fuels [sic]”. It added:

“Yet standing on principle carries heavy practical consequences…COP31’s breakdown is a sobering reminder that, while Fiji must keep fighting in global arenas, its sharpest shield remains regional solidarity and rapid, resilient action at home.”

Major Chinese news outlets largely portrayed China as a constructive participant in the COP31 negotiations, a defender of multilateralism and an active advocate for international climate cooperation.

State news agency Xinhua reported that “China acted responsibly and advanced the conference process, earning widespread recognition from all parties”.

State broadcaster CCTV similarly said that the “international community recognised the positive role China played in addressing climate change”.

People’s Daily , the official newspaper of the Communist Party of China, reported that China played a “constructive role” in building consensus and promoting cooperation. It quoted COP31 president Murat Kurum as saying that China was a “key participant” in the multilateral climate process and that its support was “crucial to the summit”.

State news agency China News Service said that China demonstrated “ability to act” amid divisions at COP31, highlighting China’s participation in negotiations and initiatives on international cooperation in carbon credits and its climate actions in the global south.

Financial newspaper 21st Century Business Herald said that the Chinese delegation “actively participated in negotiations across all agenda items” and highlighted China’s efforts to advance practical cooperation on climate change.

Three of China’s main state media outlets, Xinhua , CCTV and People’s Daily , covered the COP31 outcome.

Xinhua said that climate multilateralism “moves forward under pressure” as COP31 concluded without a deal.

Citing Chinese experts, Shanghai-based outlet the Paper reported that China, the African group and south-east Asian countries were among the parties “willing to accept a compromise [deal] to uphold multilateralism, despite being dissatisfied with the draft text”.

CCTV reported that, although COP31 ended without adopting an “outcome document”, this did not mean international climate action had “come to a halt” or that previously agreed climate agreements and international promises would “automatically become invalid”.

State-run newspapers China Daily and the Global Times both published editorials on COP31.

China Daily argued that the COP31 “impasse” underscored the “need to strengthen multilateral cooperation”. It continued that China was “committed to addressing the climate crisis through real action.”

The Global Times editorial, meanwhile, responded to criticism that China was “unwilling to take the lead”. It said:

“With its own climate governance arrears unpaid, how can western media expect China to ‘pick up the tab’?”

Regarding China’s role at COP31, several western news outlets’ coverage focused on its approach to climate diplomacy, trade and the proposed final agreement.

Ahead of the summit’s conclusion, Reuters cited diplomats and observers in reporting that China’s envoys to COP31 stuck to the country’s “accustomed low-key playbook”.

The Financial Times reported that China used the climate talks to “complain about tariffs on EVs and green energy products”.

On the final day of the summit, the Guardian said that China was among the parties that “did not object to the deal”.

Bloomberg also reported that while Chinese diplomats maintained a “relatively low profile”, its “world-leading” companies featured in China pavilion events.

Bloomberg continued:

“at a United Nations climate conference that was low on delivery and high on dysfunction, China’s clean-technology companies showed that some aspects of the green transition are persevering despite geopolitical tensions.”

In the aftermath of COP31, many commentators have called for a reform of the COP process.

The European Commission is “drawing up plans to overhaul the UN climate summit process, warning that the current negotiating system risks becoming ineffective because a single country can block an agreement among nearly 200 parties”, according to Euronews .

Many other commentators shared the view that the COP process must be reformed.

Marco Lambertini, convenor of the Nature Positive Initiative, said in Reuters :

“We must be clear: reform remains essential. COPs are cumbersome, expensive, bureaucratic, environmentally unfriendly and frustratingly slow. The consensus rule – adopted in the climate and nature conferences – allows a handful of countries to dilute ambition in the main plenary deliberations. Too often, fossil fuel and agrochemical lobbies interfere with negotiations and obstruct progress. This must change.”

Similarly, York University’s Kapoor said in Al Jazeera that the current system results in “an international forum in which the most reluctant participants can limit what everyone else is allowed to say, let alone do”.

The Associated Press ’ Prengaman wrote that “reforms floated over the years include shortening the conference from its current two weeks, limiting it just to delegates and reducing its overall size”.

The Independent ’s climate correspondent, Nick Ferris, said the “collapse” of the talks “represents a shocking nadir in the history of COPs”, adding that “the process requires urgent reform”.

Similarly, Pilita Clark, the Financial Times associate editor and business columnist, said “the disaster that was the climate gathering in Antalya should prompt overdue reform”.

Justin Worland, a senior correspondent at Time , likened this year’s summit to the 2009 COP in Copenhagen. He added:

“Following the defeat, negotiators went back to the drawing board and created the architecture that led to the Paris Agreement. Today, there’s another opportunity for reinvention.”

(For more on COP reform, see Carbon Brief ’s interviews with 16 experts on the topic.)

While many editorials lamented the failure of COP31 to agree on the Antalya pact, there were various articles that highlighted a more positive view.

In the Guardian , Dr Bill Hare , chief executive of Climate Analytics , wrote that COP31 was “a line in the sand moment, a victory for multilateralism as countries stood up to the big fossil fuel producers and said no”.

He continued:

“The [cover decision that parties] rejected barely recognised the catastrophic climate emergency we’re facing, let alone signalled a definitive move away from fossil fuels.”

Others shared the view that numerous countries rejecting the cover decision due to its failure to mention fossil fuels could be seen as a significant moment of pushback.

In an interview in Le Monde , Prof Johan Rockström , director of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research in Germany, said that it is “better to have this kind of crisis and to do something good with it, rather than having a watered-down agreement”. He added:

“It will have a very positive signal: It means that the world is taking risks seriously. The world is taking science seriously.”

An editorial in Bloomberg stated that COP31 should “serve as a call for action”, pushing like-minded governments to continue working together to make progress. It added:

“The outcome at COP31, discouraging as it was, strongly suggests that much of the world remains committed to fighting climate change. More than 100 governments, led by the EU, opposed a final declaration that – amid pressure from Russia, Saudi Arabia and other fossil-fuel producers – omitted any reference to the transition away from fossil fuels.”

In Reuters , columnist Antony Currie wrote that the failure to adopt the cover decision could in fact be “healthy”. Elsewhere, in Inside Story , the University of Sheffield’s r Jacobs argued that “this COP’s failure might have been what the world needed”.

scraped.body_text:
Following the close of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, Carbon Brief’s journalists answered a range of questions in a CB Live panel discussion.

COP31 came to a dramatic conclusion nearly 50 hours after its scheduled close – making it the longest COP in history.

Less than 24 hours later, Carbon Brief published its 21,000-word summary , capturing everything that happened in the negotiations, the cover decision and more.

This includes the “Antalya pact”, proposed by the joint Turkish-Australian presidency, being rejected in the final hours of the summit by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable nations.

There was some progress at COP31, including an agreement on the adaptation fund, as well as a raft of announcements within the “action agenda”.

Carbon Brief journalists – who followed every detail of the summit on the ground in Antalya and remotely answered a range of questions, including those sent ahead of time by CB+ members on CB Connect .

These covered climate finance, China, the “just transition mechanism”, the potential for COP reform and much more.

The discussion was moderated by Carbon Brief’s senior policy editor Dr Simon Evans and featured the following journalists:

scraped.title: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya - Carbon Brief

scraped.author: Carbon Brief Staff
scraped.h1: COP31: Key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at the UN climate talks in Antalya
scraped.body_text:
The COP31 climate talks in Antalya, Turkey, failed to agree on a “pact” that – despite making no clear reference to fossil fuels or adaptation finance – had contained strong signals for oceans.

The “Antalya pact” took up much of the two weeks of negotiating time in Turkey, only to be rejected during the closing plenary by the EU, the UK and several climate-vulnerable countries.

Several countries expressed their regret during the plenary that significant work on advancing ocean-climate action would be lost.

The COP ran nearly 50 hours over time, but did not end with substantive outcomes on several key topics.

For the second year in a row, negotiations on agriculture and food security broke down and will now have to resume next year.

Food-systems advocates were, however, heartened by the explicit inclusion of “agroecology” in a decision within the “just transition work programme”.

Ocean-conservation groups noted an increased focus on ocean-climate links at this year’s COP, but said COP31 did not live up to its promise of being a “blue COP”.

There was also scant new funding for food systems and nature, with just a handful of small pledges to ocean initiatives and two newly announced contributions to the Tropical Forest Forever Facility .

Here, Carbon Brief analyses all of the key outcomes for food, forests, oceans and nature at COP31 – both inside and out of the negotiating rooms.

(See Carbon Brief’s coverage of food, forests, oceans and nature at COP30 , COP29 , COP28 , COP27 and COP26 .)

The final draft of a COP31 “cover decision” was rejected by at least 32 countries during a chaotic – and, at times, acrimonious – closing plenary in Antalya.

Other recent COPs have issued cover decisions, setting a firm precedent .

However, many parties remained unhappy about the existence of the cover decision, the process by which it was put together and the impact it had on time for other negotiations.

Ultimately, parties did not find consensus on the text, particularly around the removal of any reference to fossil fuels and the lack of concrete climate-finance targets.

The cover text was one of the places in the negotiations where ocean advocates were hoping to see ocean-climate linkages highlighted.

Marine Lecerf , head of international policy at Ocean & Climate Platform , told a press huddle:

“What we’re really asking for right now is to make sure we can recognise ocean-based interlinkages…We’re not asking for a new mandate. We are asking for acceleration of the work that is already undertaken.”

The first draft of the cover decision, published on 16 November, was a compilation of all the issues that parties had put forward for inclusion. It was accompanied by a short “ presidency note ” explaining that all elements were still in play, including whether or not they should appear in a final text.

This lengthy first draft had 21 references to the ocean, including recognising the impacts of climate change, support for ocean-observing systems, encouraging parties to strengthen ocean-climate action and a multi-year plan for the “ ocean and climate change dialogue ”, which occurs annually at the Bonn intersessional meetings in June.

Regarding that draft, Steven Guilbeault , former environment minister of Canada, told Carbon Brief:

“I don’t see why the elements that are in the cover decision right now on oceans should be controversial or problematic to any nations. If you’re serious about fighting climate change, there’s nothing in this text regarding oceans that should be problematic for you.”

( Earth Negotiations Bulletin reported that Russia opposed mentions of the ocean in the cover text during the ocean ministerial consultation.)

The next iteration of the text, on 19 November, retained many of the ocean elements, albeit with less detail than the first draft. The second text also removed references to post-2028 ocean work and a proposed high-level ministerial ocean dialogue.

In the end, oceans had 19 mentions in the rejected Antalya pact.

During the final plenary, Fiji’s Dr Sivendra Michael – co-chair of the ocean and climate change dialogue – appealed to the COP31 president to “humbly consolidate” the consensus on ocean as a “standalone ocean decision” and “directly submit” ten paragraphs with no objections in text as a “way to preserve” work done.

Lynda Tabuya, Fiji’s environment and climate change minister, said:

“The ocean-climate nexus is undeniable. We, the people of the Pacific, are deeply indebted, as the ocean is our home, our identity and it is what connects us. There is no climate action without ocean action. We hope this is not lost today and that parties will please consider keeping the ocean text alive.”

Other aspects of the natural world garnered significantly less attention in the cover text.

The final decision failed to mention the Brazil-led roadmap on deforestation , although it was “welcome[d]” in the initial draft . (See: Deforestation .)

Mentions of the “critical role” of forests in carbon storage, food security, biodiversity and community adaptation were also stripped from the text between the first and second iterations.

The final Antalya pact – that was rejected – did, however, retain wording on deforestation agreed by countries in the global stocktake at COP28 in Dubai.

The same draft also “recognises” the role of nature-based solutions and ecosystem-based approaches as “essential climate solutions” – although many experts reject the former term and warn that its vagueness leaves it open to deliberate misuse.

The final draft cover decision “emphasised the importance” of nature, forests, the ocean and other ecosystems as “natural infrastructure for resilience”, while “recogni[sing] that they play a critical role as sinks and reservoirs of greenhouse gases”.

Experts, however, were concerned that this language preceded a paragraph “welcoming” carbon dioxide removal, even if it “stressed” that these methods – that include tree planting – “should ensure environmental safeguards and respect the rights of Indigenous peoples”.

None of the iterations of the rejected cover decision mentioned COP17 , the biodiversity summit held in Armenia, which concluded just 10 days before COP31 started. Nor did they mention the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework (GBF), a landmark pact sealed in 2022 to reverse biodiversity loss by 2030.

When Carbon Brief pointed this out to Guilbeault – a key architect of the GBF – in an interview on 17 November, he vowed that he would try to make the case to ministers to get these aspects added in.

One observer told Carbon Brief that the “toxic” nature of discussions over the need for closer “ synergies ” between climate and biodiversity summits could explain the lack of mentions in the cover decision.

Despite this, they said the rejected pact did “underline” the “urgent need to address, in a comprehensive and synergetic manner, the interlinked global crises of climate change, biodiversity loss, desertification and land and ocean degradation”.

Adopting such language would have represented positive progress, the observer added.

Although the first draft of the cover decision referenced “food” twice – in the context of food security – both of these instances were removed in the subsequent draft. The rejected final cover decision draft mentioned “food security” four times.

Membership

However, observers told Carbon Brief that a mention of “food” or “food systems” in the cover decision was not a priority for them. Teresa Anderson , global climate-justice lead at ActionAid , said:

“What we often find is that getting references or language to things in the cover decision doesn’t really play out as impacts on the ground and it’s more effective to push a meaningful agenda in a negotiation space.”

For the second year in a row, negotiations on the Sharm el-Sheikh joint work on agriculture (SJWA) collapsed without parties reaching an agreement.

SJWA is where formal negotiations around climate change and agriculture take place under the UNFCCC .

Part of SJWA’s mandate is to synthesise information about work being done in the agricultural space – under both the UNFCCC and other international bodies – in an annual report.

SJWA also held two workshops – one on holistic approaches to agriculture and one on “means of implementation”, usually taken to mean finance – where countries and other partners could share their experiences, as captured in summary reports.

At COP31, parties were meant to discuss the conclusions of these reports and, time permitting, decide on the future of the agricultural workstream under the UNFCCC. (The four-year mandate of SJWA was set to end at COP31.)

Work “moved very slowly” in the first week, said Oliver Camp , senior policy and implementation specialist at the Global Alliance for Improved Nutrition . He added:

“It took a really long time to get into any substantive conversation.”

Ahead of the summit, many observers were hopeful of agreeing a text that recognised agroecology as beneficial for humans, climate and biodiversity.
