scraped.body_text:
Egyptian author and former political prisoner Abdelrahman ElGendy speaks about his new memoir, Huna .

Honest, paywall-free news is rare. Please support our boldly independent journalism with a donation of any size.

This year’s annual National Book Award ceremony in New York City was marked by the notable absence of nonfiction winner Abdelrahman ElGendy, after the Trump administration denied the Egyptian author entry into the United States. ElGendy’s debut, Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , chronicles his arrest and over six years of imprisonment, alongside his father, following arrest at a protest against the military dictatorship of Egypt’s President Abdel Fattah el-Sisi. After his release from prison in Egypt, ElGendy obtained an MFA in the United States but was forced to flee once again — this time from the U.S. to Europe — for fear of being targeted by immigration authorities over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations.

“It was a gutting thing to not be able to attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising,” ElGendy tells Democracy Now! about being barred from receiving the National Book Award in person. “[I] have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love.”

We speak to ElGendy about the weaponization of the visa process, in both the U.S. and Egypt, “as a form of transnational repression,” his arrest and imprisonment beginning at the age of just 17, and the Egyptian government’s ongoing repression of free speech, including its attempted closure of the independent news outlet Mada Masr , whose lawyers were in court today appealing its shutdown.

“ Mada carries so much of the archive of our revolutionary history … so to erase it is to erase an archive,” says ElGendy, whose early writings were smuggled out of prison and first published in Mada Masr . “The current Egyptian military dictatorship [is] a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before.”

This is a rush transcript. Copy may not be in its final form.

AMY GOODMAN: This is Democracy Now! , The War and Peace Report . I’m Amy Goodman.

We are currently awaiting an Egyptian court decision on whether the closing of Mada Masr , the independent newspaper in Egypt, will stand. We’ll go to Cairo when we hear.

But right now we’re going to turn to what happened in the last few weeks here in this country, in New York, where we are. Novelists, essayists, poets and other writers from around the world took to the stage at the 77th annual National Book Awards ceremony in New York City last week. The winner of this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction, Egyptian author Abdelrahman ElGendy, though, was notably absent from the event, after the Trump administration denied his U.S. visa application, blocking him from entering the United States.

ElGendy’s debut book is called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming , and chronicles his more than six years of imprisonment in Egypt following his arrest at the age of 17, alongside his father, during the crackdown on protests after the military coup led by Abdel Fattah el-Sisi in 2013. He and his father were in their car, and Abdelrahman was taking a picture.

This is the moment the prize for nonfiction was presented by panel chair Robert Warrior.

ROBERT WARRIOR: It’s my distinct honor to announce that this year’s National Book Award for Nonfiction goes to Abdelrahman ElGendy for Huna .

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor, Helen Thomaides, then took the stage and read a statement written by ElGendy.

HELEN THOMAIDES: If you’re listening to this, then a years-long dream of mine has come true, and I’m not there to live it with you. Years ago, in my prison cell in Egypt, I used to fantasize about writing a memoir. I would slip under a bright red duvet my mother had bribed the guards to let through, and imagine that everything happening to me would one day end up in a book, that the guard’s baton was battering not my ribs but those of the book’s protagonist, that the slap was landing on the protagonist’s face, not mine. I was the author, concerned only with how to render on the page the torture my body was enduring. The scribbles on a smuggled page became a potential essay, the essay a potential published article, the article a book. I’d imagine that book winning an award, and deliver fictional acceptance speeches under Mama’s duvet, fleetingly unincarcerated. Today, that dream should have come full circle, but like so many of the circles ruptured in my life, it will remain unfinished, broken by an oppressive regime with a fascist ideology whose concentration camps stand ready to swallow the bodies it deems undesirable.

AMY GOODMAN: That was Abdelrahman ElGendy’s editor Helen Thomaides reading Abdelrahman’s words after his memoir Huna won the National Book Award just last week. Ahead of the ceremony, Abdelrahman wrote a piece in The New Yorker magazine. It’s headlined “I Am a 2026 National Book Award Finalist. The U.S. Denied My Visa.”

Abdelrahman ElGendy wrote much of the book while in the United States, where he came two years after he was released from prison in Egypt. He studied at the University of Pittsburgh, where he obtained an MFA in creative nonfiction. Then, in April 2025, following the Trump administration’s widespread targeting of pro-Palestine voices, including international students and academics, Abdelrahman ElGendy decided to flee the U.S., fearing he’d be next, that he’d be detained and possibly deported back to Egypt over his criticism of Israel’s war on Gaza and U.S.-Egypt relations. At the time, he wrote in The Nation magazine, quote, “I was a political prisoner in Egypt. I didn’t want to become one again in America,” unquote.

For more, we’re joined now by Abdelrahman ElGendy from Europe, where he lives now.

Abdelrahman, I just want to congratulate you on this remarkable book, which I’ve just finished. And I had the joy, flying back from Turkey, the U.N. climate summit, of listening to your book, the audio book, which you read in your own words. The magnificence, the power, the pain of this book cannot be underestimated. I want to thank you so much for sharing your life with us, Abdelrahman ElGendy. Thank you for joining us.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Thank you. Thank you so much, Amy. Thanks for having me and for these kind words. Thank you.

AMY GOODMAN: So, we are awaiting word right now about whether Egypt will be forced to reopen Mada Masr , a place where you actually, I think, published your first words. You wrote throughout your six years in prison. But talk about — well, first, start with the title, and talk about what it meant to win the National Book Award in the United States, the place you wanted to stay, to be in exile, to be protected, but could not reenter for the award ceremony.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. Thank you. I mean, of course, it was a gutting thing to not be able to, you know, attend the ceremony. But it was also unsurprising. You know, we all know how this U.S. administration is now trying to keep everyone who criticizes policies out, especially when it comes, you know, to our region, especially when it’s around Palestine. You know, and if you’re a citizen of another country that doesn’t, you know, need a visa, they don’t want you. They just detain you at the point of entry at the airport. But if you do, like in my case, they just deny you, you know, at the embassy.

And I just — yeah, they love repeating the idea that the visa is, you know, a privilege and not a right. This is kind of the mantra that they keep, you know, repeating to everyone. But, yeah, this, I think, is just intentional distraction from the most important point here, which is that the visa process is being weaponized, and has been now for a while, as a form of transnational repression, which we’re very familiar with in Egypt, as well, because the Egyptian state also uses this form of transnational repression, you know, denying us certain paperwork and stuff like that to punish you for political speech and to keep certain bodies that you deem undesirable outside. So, same for the U.S. So, the visa denial itself being weaponized in that way is the issue, not the fact that the, yes, consul office can deny or approve, etc. So, I think this should be, yeah, the headline, really.

But it was also, like, very sad, I think, in a way that is very specific to my personal journey, you know, as a — this is not new to me. As a kid, you know, I worked my whole life to earn a scholarship to study engineering at this great school that my family couldn’t afford at the time. And then I was arrested on the eve of my first day as a freshman. This is — I speak about this in the book — before I get to live this dream. And then, when I was released in 2020, it happened straight into COVID in 2020. And I started, like, when the lockdown was being lifted, and I started slowly rebuilding community. Because of my writing with Mada Masr , actually, because I continued writing with Mada post-prison, word kind of circulated. Relatives who were well connected told me that my name is being kind of floated again for rearrest. And eventually, I was forced to flee Egypt because of that writing with Mada Masr . And since then, you know, I’ve never been able to share a room with Egyptian readers of my work, except accidentally in exile, you know, when we’re all, like, kind of shunned away from Egypt together. So I’ve had to do it from a distance.

And now, you know, this book, which I imagined writing from prison, which I wrote, you know, throughout my time in the U.S., and then, just as I was about to graduate from my MFA in the U.S., which this book was the graduation, the thesis for — right? — you know, I was forced again to temporarily leave for safety concerns of ICE targeting, as you mentioned, because of my political writing and pro-Palestine activism on campus. And so, I had to graduate from my MFA remotely, as well, witness that moment, you know, be celebrated remotely by people in the room that I was unable to be in. And I wanted to bring my family over to the U.S. to have that graduation ceremony, that prison denied us in Egypt, and we were deprived of that again.

I couldn’t do a U.S. book tour. And now the book, you know, has made it all the way into that room of the National Book Award. And, you know, to have labored for so long my whole life to get to this point, only to again and again and again be forced to witness it all from afar and detached from the people I love who have witnessed this journey, it is gutting. But in a way, it is also just the story of my life. This is not new.

And still, I think I need to redirect all this back, you know, to Egyptian political prisoners, because as I said in my speech, a life that I’m living right now beyond prison, in which my dreams could even be crushed in this way, that was the dream back in prison. I dreamed of a day when I have these, like, unincarcerated people problems. But there are 60,000 political prisoners, you know, who don’t even have the luxury of such precarity, that at least opens into possibility, right? So, I think, yeah, I always want to redirect it to them. I am blessed, no matter what, like, everything that happened that was very sad and gutting and everything. But I always try to put that in relation to people back home behind bars in Egypt, my friends, Ayman and everyone else still behind bars. I’m still blessed to have these problems. Yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: Tell us why you named the book Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming .

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, I mean Huna , huna is the Arabic word for “here.” And it was inspired by a popular Arab protest song, “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which means “We Will Remain Here.” And I first heard that song, you know, up close on my third night in detention. We were in this, like, military camp in the middle of the desert, very excruciating physical conditions, where 68 of us were crammed into a tiny room, piled on top of one another. There were some people that were shot and wounded, so it was very heavy. My father was with me at the time. He was dying.

And then, out of nowhere, the guards finally allowed in the homemade food our families had brought to the gate. So, our families would come every day; they’d be sent back. But that day, they just brought in the food. And then, for the first time since the arrest, we had a taste of home.

And then something very magical happened. We just began to sing. The mood got lighter, and we began to sing. And one of the songs was “Sawfa Nabqa Huna,” which goes, “We will remain here until the pain subsides. We will remain here. The melody will sweeten.” And, you know, we sang together, and I started feeling those chills on my arms. You could feel that everyone in the room was entering this sort of visceral moment together.

And I found myself thinking, fascinated, that I didn’t want to remain here. Like, who wants — you know, none of us wants to remain here. We couldn’t wait to escape this room fast enough. My father was dying. We were being tortured. People were shot. So, what was this huna ? What was this “here” that we were so touched by, that we were all actively choosing to inhabit together? What were we entering?

And I think I would say my book — if I would kind of put it in one line, I’d say it is a six-year pursuit of this huna , like the question of what it means to inhabit a space that is designed to erase you in body, in language, in your very sense of personhood, and still find ways to be. So, I try to trace, you know, that sense of nonphysical hereness and witness, that repeatedly saves me from being wholly conquered by prison.

And you also mentioned the becoming part, which is important to me, because I was arrested — I think sometimes that gets lost, the fact that I was arrested at 17 years old. So, to me, this is not just prison and revolution. It is also becoming, because I say this is a coming-of-age story. And so many people come to this political awakening that I had, you know, in high school age. They start getting politically agitated or involved. And to me, it happened that I went into prison in those formative years. So, my whole history of activism was two months — right? — after the Rabaa massacre until October 6, and then I was arrested. So, incarceration, in a way, was this school in which I was thinking about the world and my positionality inside it.

So, I was just politically activated before I went into prison, and I went into prison with all those agitated questions that were so unsettled for me. I was so angry. I carried so much rage at the military dictatorship, the police state. And I felt like I had a moral compass. But it was mostly motivated not by, you know, theory or intellectual thought or engaging with political theory. It was just rage at seeing certain injustices and wanting to intervene and be part of removing them or restoring justice. So, to me, that was — you know, I see people massacred, a military dictatorship. I think, “These things are wrong, and I don’t want to be on this side. I want to be on the other side that is against them.”

But in prison, I get into a more, I think, sophisticated approach. In prison, I think you have — you know, you have nothing more than time, and you sit down, and you just question everything. And I think prison forces you to confront so many not only political questions, but also very existential questions, you know, about what it means to be here, to be human, to be in relation to other humans, to your own father, to your friends, your mom, and what kinds of obligations does that carry.

So, every day, I was encountering new things that agitated me even more, and that were forcing me, you know, to think. You’re beaten. You’re tortured. You’re being beaten by those batons every day. You see your father hit. Everything around you radicalizes you and makes you think, you know, “I cannot afford to look away from these things. I don’t have the luxury of looking away from these questions,” because the batons are beating me every single day. I just cannot not think about them and my relationship to them and to other people fighting them, and whether I think of them, again, as allies or even political enemies. So, momentarily in prison, I have to align with factions that, you know, I don’t align with politically. It forces me to think about these questions. Like, in my cell, I don’t agree with you politically. I’m very aggravated by you. But we step up outside the cell, and the same police officers are beating us. So, what does that mean in terms of, you know, allyship, mobilization, working together? So, yeah, all those questions at 17, you wouldn’t be thinking about, I think. But I couldn’t afford not to, because my survival depended on grappling with them in prison.

AMY GOODMAN: I mean, this is also a story of a father and son, a mother and son, a brother, a cousin. Talk about how you were first detained with your dad. And it’s a relationship that carries throughout the book. I mean, you go from being a son to being your dad’s protector, to having to separate from your father. My goodness, I mean, you were arrested at the age of 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah. One thing I always like to bring up about this is, one of my dear friends, when she read the manuscript of the book for the first time, before it was published, she told me, “Do you know what this book is?” And I told he, “What?” And she said, “This is a love letter to Baba.” And I found that very moving, because I do think this is one of — at least one of the things that this book is, because, you know, my father was apolitical. Like, he wasn’t even involved in politics. And I was a very hot-headed teenager. I really wanted to be on the streets. I was very — again, I was — I had this awakening, and I was attending protests very — you know, every single day, maybe three protests, you know, in the morning, in the afternoon and in the evening. And they tolerated — my parents tolerated that for a while.

But then, on October 6, that was a particularly dangerous day. This is the Armed Forces Day. And protesters wanted to break into Tahrir Square. And because of its symbolic value, you know, revolutionary value, the police would get very brutal when people attempt to even approach Tahrir Square. Up until today, it’s a very heavily securitized area. And so, what happens, the arrangement is my mother forced my father to basically come chaperone me, you know, to this protest, to look out for me and make sure that I don’t get harmed or arrested, which, you know, doesn’t work out as planned, obviously.

So, we go there. I start shooting a video. I’m, like, speaking enthusiastically. I leave the car. He yells at me to come back, so I go back inside. I shoot from the window. And then I don’t notice there are two plainclothes officers standing right next to the window, who kind of, from my commentary, kind of deduce that I’m aligned with what’s happening. So, they, you know, pull the door open. They wrench me out. They start beating me, take my phone. And then my father comes, and he starts trying to wrench me away, you know, from their arms. And then they end up arresting him, as well. So, my father gets arrested just because, you know, I made him be in that space, which, of course, we can always argue that it’s a structural issue, it’s a state’s issue. But guilt, you know, doesn’t — it doesn’t work like that. And so, my — the whole six year begins from that kind of inciting incident and that guilt. It’s a very guilt-ridden story, you know, toward my father.

And we’ve always, my father and I, struggled, I think, to express affection to one another. There’s also commentary about Arab masculinity in the book a lot, and specifically father-son relationships. So, we struggled to do that, and I think we carried so much and so many unsaid things inside both of us. And through prison, it was very difficult to communicate, because you’re used to seeing your father as this protective figure, right? And then, in prison, you suddenly realize he is helpless, he cannot protect you. And in a way, he does his best to protect me in all those small ways in prison, of course, but in the bigger scheme of things, he cannot get me my freedom, right? And I cannot get him his freedom. And, you know, the state loves to weaponize love, the Egyptian state, any fascist state, really. So, in prison, they used that against us. They hurt my father to get to me. They hurt me to get to him, and so on. So it was a very difficult situation.

But what I also try to explore in the book is the avenues that opened up once my father and I were not only father and son in prison. I suddenly started seeing him in all those other kind of roles. He was also a prisoner in relation to the state, a prison cellmate or, you know, a prison mate to other prisoners, which was both difficult, but I think also opened up different avenues of communication between us, because sometimes, I don’t know, we’d have a fight in the cell, and we’d fight together with — like, against people and be aligned with one another, and I think, “Oh, my father and I are co-conspirators now.” There’s that first scene in the book where we do this. And through the night, my father, for the first time ever, he rests his hand, you know, on my back and leaves it there through the night. And I remember that being one of the first instances in my life where he touches me in that way.

So, when he read the book after, you know, it was published — I gave him the Arabic. I wrote it in Arabic. It’s coming out in Arabic, and he read the Arabic version. And again, he doesn’t — he was so struck, I think, by the intensity of the love, because I couldn’t express it to him verbally. So, he just said, “You know, I understand so many things much better now,” and then went on to, like, fact-check the entire book, because that’s his — you know, his language of love. So, eventually, I think this is just the sweetest, I think, closure that could have happened to this harrowing experience that we shared together. And if he was the only reader, you know, of this book, if this was the only thing to come out of it, that would have been enough for me.

AMY GOODMAN: And, of course, he gets out before you and then tries to get you out, and ultimately does, based on the fact that you were arrested at 17.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yeah, and it is — I was wrongly tried — wrongfully tried as an adult instead of a minor. And this is — again, throughout the book, you come across the absurdity and arbitrariness, you know, of the Egyptian state. I was 17 at the time of arrest, two months shy of 18, right? So I had two months to turn 18. And then, the officer that arrested me breaks my ID, or both of our IDs, delivered us to the police station. And just so randomly, because of that, I get processed as an adult, and then I just keep getting processed as an adult throughout. In the prosecution, my lawyer ends up, you know, submitting appeal after appeal. None of them gets looked into, because we’re in Egypt. We get tried as this package deal, right? All of us together in a mass trial.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman, I want to continue this conversation after the show, but I want you to stay with us, because we’re going to go to Cairo right now.

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: OK, yeah, yeah.

AMY GOODMAN: This story doesn’t end, and I want you to be a part of it. We’re going to Cairo, Egypt, where an appeal was just heard in the case against Lina Attalah, the editor-in-chief of Egypt’s leading independent news outlet Mada Masr , for operating an unlicensed website, they’re saying, though she’s been operating it for years. Late last month, she was fined $50,000 or to shut down Mada Masr , following an expedited trial where her lawyers were denied time to prepare a defense, call witnesses or submit documentation. Lina Attalah is also facing charges for publishing so-called false news, that could lead to her imprisonment. We’re going right now outside the court to Hossam Bahgat, founder and director of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights, part of Mada Masr ’s legal team, just outside the courthouse. And I want Abdelrahman to respond to what you report to us. Do we have a decision from the court whether Mada Masr can be reopened, Hossam?

HOSSAM BAHGAT: Thank you, Amy, for having me.

No, I mean, the defense team finished their oral pleadings and submitted the requests. The court has adjourned the session, and we should get a decision on this final appeal by the end of today. I mean, the good thing is that at least it looked more like a courtroom and more like a normal trial today compared to the absurdity that we saw in the first instance. Unfortunately, though, we don’t have any signs that there is an intent to look fairly at the situation, the position of Mada Masr . Today, the lawyers not only challenged the decision to convict Lina and shut down Mada Masr —

AMY GOODMAN: You’re breaking up.

HOSSAM BAHGAT: — and confiscate all its —

AMY GOODMAN: Hossam, you’re breaking up, but I want to tell people you can go to see our interview with Lina Attalah that I did with Anjali Kamat just as she was facing all of this, and also you can go to democracynow.org to see our visit to Mada Masr when we were in Egypt. I want to give Abdelrahman ElGendy the last word, though. You thank Lina Attalah and our former producer Sharif Abdel Kouddous for being able to find a way to get your words out of prison. Ultimately, you would smuggle them out. Is that right?

ABDELRAHMAN ELGENDY: Yes, absolutely. I began writing in that way, smuggling my words out in prison. And I think you just — you know, once you, as a political prisoner, get a taste of that magic of being able to smuggle your language out to the world, and then receive the world’s language back in response, you just cannot stop. And Mada were the first place to, you know, offer my words a home, is how I thank them. And they feature in the book, as well, because Mada , you know, they sent me wanting to publish, you know, some of the things that I smuggled out, and ever since I had this relationship with them, I published six more pieces with Mada Masr from prison. And that was important to me.

I think that the project of the current Egyptian military dictatorship is — it’s a frantic project of erasure of everything that has to do with the revolution, and it’s an insistence on erasing every trace that would allow people to remember that revolution has happened, that this rupture has happened before. It was possible, and therefore it is possible. And they don’t want it to be a thinkable or imaginable thing anymore.

And I think Mada Masr is a huge part of that. I cannot understand or speak about the campaign against Mada Masr , you know, divorced from the idea of this more bigger project of erasure of the Egyptian state, because Mada carries so much of the archive, you know, of our revolutionary history. It is the place that people like me, in prison and after prison, can go write in. It is the place where, you know, Alaa El-Fattah, who published “Graffiti for Two People” with Ahmed Douma. It is the place that speaks about prison letters and communication. And so, to erase it is to erase an archive. And also, it is to erase the more, I think, intimate and dangerous thing, is we go to Mada Masr to feel less alone, to remember, you know, that we were many, and therefore we are many still today. We have not been — you know, as Alaa says, we have not been fully defeated. And that, to me, is important. Maybe we’re not — maybe we are defeated in a way, but not wholly, not fully.

AMY GOODMAN: Abdelrahman ElGendy, I want to thank you for being with us and for this incredible memoir. It’s called Huna: A Memoir of Revolution, Prison, and Becoming . It has just won the 2026 National Book Award for Nonfiction, and we’ll link to your New Yorker and Nation pieces. That does it for our show. I’m Amy Goodman. This is Democracy Now!

scraped.title: The Trump administration is racing to overhaul the National Park Service
scraped.description: A Park Service employee said top officials are “hell-bent on pushing this through before the new Congress.”
scraped.author: Dan Friedman
scraped.h1: The Trump Administration is Racing to Overhaul the National Park Service
scraped.body_text:
The National Park Service logo at Joshua Tree National Park in Twentynine Palms, California. Mario Tama/Getty

The Trump administration plans to begin a reorganization of the National Park Service in early December, in what critics call a rushed bid to overhaul the agency before congressional Democrats taking power next year can stop them.

According to an internal Park Service planning document obtained by Mother Jones , the agency is set to launch what it calls a “realignment” during the week of December 7. The document, a communications plan for the overhaul last updated on November 18, says that the agency will announce the overhaul via an “all-employee message” from acting NPS director Jessica Bowron.

Nonprofit groups tracking NPS’ plan, and Park Service employees, believe the agency’s rapid timeline reflects an attempt to race ahead with the reorganization before Democrats who are critical of the effort can enact legislation blocking it.

An NPS employee with knowledge of the agency’s planning said that senior NPS officials “are hell-bent on pushing this through before the new Congress.”

Under the plan, the Park Service would shift how it runs more than 400 park units, which include large national parks along with historic sites, to what it calls a “hub and spoke” system. That entails centralizing management powers in larger “hub” parks that would oversee smaller “spoke” units, replacing the current system where all the park units report directly to a regional office.

In NPS Washington headquarters, the agency plans to streamline 10 directorates into six: “Infrastructure; Resource Stewardship; Visitor Experience; “Law Enforcement Safety & Health; Community Engagement; and Comptroller,” according to a NPS realignment summary that is among materials Mother Jones reviewed.

Even internally, NPS hedges on the sensitive topic of firing employees. The agency’s communications plan urges spokespersons to repeat the message that: “No relocations or reductions in force are anticipated as a result of this realignment, at least in the short term (not counting voluntary reassignments).”

But the plan says that the realignment will address agency shortcomings including “duplicative work,” raising the prospect that the reorganization will eventually entail significant layoffs.

The Washington Sun reported the agency’s reorganization plans in September. But NPS has tried to keep a tight lid on the details of the effort, including its timing.

The agency’s communications plan outlines an effort to minimize public information about the effort. “Public messaging will focus on the purpose of the realignment, continuity of mission delivery, and continuity of park operations, and must be approved by the NPS and DOI Communications before release,” the plan says.

Interior Secretary Doug Burgum, who oversees the Park Service, has been pushing to overhaul the agency. Burgum has consolidated its functions in Washington, including centralizing control of communications under political appointees in the Interior Department. And he has already overseen a more than 20 percent reduction in the Park Service’s staff, mostly achieved so far through a voluntary resignation program and attrition.

Interior, which is also attempting to reorganize the Fish and Wildlife Service, has sought to lay off thousands of employees, but has been largely stymied so far by federal courts. The department has also cut funding for national parks. The Park Service this year also redirected park entrance fees relied on by parks to fund regular maintenance to Washington to pay for beautification efforts and the garish celebrations organized by the White House in connection with the country’s 250 th anniversary.

The Park Service’s plans face opposition from outside groups and from Democratic lawmakers. Rep. Chellie Pingree (D-Maine), who is in line to chair a House Appropriations subcommittee that controls funding for the Interior Department, recently told Mother Jones that she is considering language that would block the the Park Service from reorganizing “without congressional approval.”

Rep. Jared Huffman (D-Calif.), who is expected next year to chair the House Natural Resources Committee, which oversees the agency, has indicated that he opposes Burgum’s plans for the Park Service and other Interior agencies, arguing that the secretary’s various plans are all aimed at easing a path to handing over national land to private industry.

The Trump administration does not appear to have run its plans by Congress. A congressional aide on Wednesday told Mother Jones that the Park Service has so far not contacted the House Natural Resources Committee to set up a briefing on the realignment effort.

The Park Service did not respond to questions on Wednesday.

items.title: Defense Contractors Are Pouring Millions Into Donald Trump’s Vanity Projects
items.summary: No industry is doing more to bankroll Donald Trump’s garish self-celebrations and personal projects than defense contractors. Led by Lockheed Martin, the largest federal contractor, top defense companies—Boeing, RTX (formerly Raytheon), Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, Palantir, and Amazon—have together put up more than $40 million, and counting, for the projects and events for which Trump […] No industry is doing more to bankroll Donald Trump’s garish self-celebrations and personal projec...

scraped.title: Defense contractors are pouring millions Into Donald Trump’s vanity projects
scraped.description: Congressional Democrats are gearing up to take on “one of the most egregious areas of grift” in the US government.
scraped.author: Dan Friedman
scraped.h1: Defense Contractors Are Pouring Millions Into Donald Trump’s Vanity Projects
scraped.body_text:
Some of the same companies that got billions in Pentagon contracts this year donated millions to Trump's parties and construction projects. Mother Jones illustration; Kent Nishimura/AFP/Getty; Getty

No industry is doing more to bankroll Donald Trump’s garish self-celebrations and personal projects than defense contractors.

Led by Lockheed Martin, the largest federal contractor, top defense companies—Boeing, RTX (formerly Raytheon), Northrop Grumman, General Dynamics, Palantir, and Amazon—have together put up more than $40 million, and counting, for the projects and events for which Trump has tapped corporate donations. Those causes include the White House ballroom, his idiosyncratic celebration of the country’s 250th anniversary, the military parade held last year on Trump’s 79th birthday, and Trump’s 2025 inaugural committee.

The gifts are just one part of a larger display of fealty by corporate America to Trump. But the defense titans’ donations are notable because they came as the companies were lapping up massive federal contracts.

In June 2026—about eight months after its donation to the ballroom fund—Lockheed won $44 billion in new multiyear federal weapons contracts . Most of those contracts were for missiles—though one $86 million contract sks the company to co-develop a “directed-energy laser weapon.” A few weeks after one big award to Lockheed was announced, Trump revealed that the company had agreed to pay about $5 million to help construct a new helipad at the White House, in order to prevent the new Marine One helicopters from damaging the South Lawn grass.

After donating to Trump’s ballroom fund, Palantir won more than $1 billion in new government work, and Amazon won $256 million, according to an analysis by Public Citizen. Those new awards came on top of substantial existing Pentagon business for those firms.

“A one-time donation that boosts the ego of Trump and lets him fulfill his interior design dreams could pay off for years and years to come.”

No evidence has emerged showing that any of these companies won their contracts in explicit exchange for funding Trump’s pet projects. But the nexus between large donations and contract awards creates the appearance that big contractors feel pressure to support Trump’s controversial endeavors to ensure they can compete for federal awards, especially when their competitors are also kicking in.

“That kind of money always gets you an open door, so you can make your case,” said political scientist Bill Hartung, who studies the arms industry at the Quincy Institute. “[Trump is] transactional—it’s like if you haven’t ponied up, you’ve taken yourself out of the game or diminished your chances.”

The president’s acolytes are now raising funds for new endeavors, including a plan to plant 500 statues of famous Americans near the National Mall, as well as Trump’s presidential library in a Miami skyscraper. But after routing the Republicans in the midterms, Democratic lawmakers are clamoring to use their impending subpoena power to investigate whether the Trump administration has created what lawmakers call a “pay-to-play ” system for federal contractors. Contractors may have to decide if continuing to support the lame-duck president’s pet projects is worth the scrutiny.

A Palantir spokesperson told Mother Jones that “Palantir has not and will not discuss jobs, payments or gifts of any kind in exchange for contracts.” None of the other companies mentioned in this article responded to requests for comment.

In June 2025 , tanks and armored personnel carriers, along with troops dressed in colonial garb, paraded down Constitution Avenue as Trump looked on from a reviewing stand. The president, on his 79th birthday, got the military parade he’d pined for since his first term, in an event nominally celebrating the Army’s 250th birthday.

Boeing, Lockheed Martin, and General Dynamics were among listed sponsors of the parade, reportedly putting up $35,000 to $75,000 apiece. Amazon, Boeing, Lockheed, Northrop Grumman, and Palantir were also among the official sponsors of America250, a congressionally chartered organization that organized the event as one of various celebrations for the country’s 250th anniversary.

The defense firms backed the MAGA-style parade around the same time they stopped sponsoring Pride parades. Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman and other defense firms, which had helped fund the pro-LGBTQ events each year for about a decade, cut off support in 2025.

Planned or not, the contractors’ decision to drop Pride events and sponsor the military parade signaled their allegiance to Trump in his bid to impose power over American culture.

And they quickly began putting more significant funds behind that stance, egged on by a Trump political apparatus that shifted from fundraising for campaigns to vanity projects.

Defense firms, including Lockheed, Boeing and Northrop Grumman , became sponsors of Freedom 250, a White House-affiliated public-private partnership, as it hosted events like a day of prayer on the National Mall, the Great American State Fair , and a night of UFC fights under a giant steel claw on the White House lawn on Trump’s 80th birthday.

“[Trump is] transactional—it’s like if you haven’t ponied up, you’ve taken yourself out of the game or diminished your chances.”

RTX this year filed a lobbying disclosure report detailing a $1.5 million donation to Freedom 250. The company was among a handful of corporations that filed such reports, suggesting those firms considered spending on the anniversary events part of their efforts to influence the Trump administration. Most of the organization’s reported donors, however, did not disclose their contributions. Freedom 250, which used taxpayer funds along with corporate donations to fund those events, has declined to detail its donors.

Freedom 250 was one of various nonprofits set up by Trump aides to raise corporate money for projects that appear to be personal priorities for the president. Even before Trump took office, Lockheed, Boeing, and Palantir CEO Alex Karp each gave $1 million to Trump’s 2025 inaugural fund. RTX gave $500,000. These donations were part of the nearly $240 million the committee raised .

Defense firms made especially big contributions to Trump’s ballroom. The most notable ballroom donation may be the $25 million that Nvidia reportedly coughed up while its CEO was successfully pressing the White House to loosen restrictions on selling its chips to China. But Lockheed Martin and Palantir also donated $10 million each to the ballroom effort while pursuing federal contracts, according to The Washington Post . Amazon gave $5 million.

Those donations were solicited by a Trump fundraising apparatus that pivoted from his 2024 campaign to other projects, with many asks made by Meredith O’Rourke, a fundraiser for Trump’s super PAC MAGA Inc.

In late 2025, O’Rourke began fundraising for Freedom 250. The Wall Street Journal has reported that she keeps Trump up to date on donations to his favored projects, and made clear to prospective contributors that donations are important to the president, using phrases like “the boss wants this money.” Democrats have keyed in on O’Rourke’s role, arguing that she and Trump appear to have shaken down contractors with an implied or actual threat to their federal business.

“The fundraising operation that President Trump reportedly directs” to fund his pet projects and celebrations “reeks of potential corruption and the potential for quid pro quo politics,” Sen. Elizabeth Warren (D-Mass.); incoming chairman of the Senate Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, Sen. Richard Blumenthal (D-Conn.), and incoming House Oversight Committee Chairman Rep. Robert Garcia (D-Calif.) wrote in a recent letter seeking information from O’Rourke.

O’Rourke did not respond to questions.

What are these companies getting for their money?

Federal spending is expected to top $800 billion is 2026, with military and defense contractors receiving at least half of that money, according to the Government Accountability Office. The Trump administration is expanding the pie by increasing the Pentagon’s overall yearly budget past $1 trillion, and through its war against Iran, which has cost US taxpayers at least $48 billion.

In 2026, as the US depleted its missile stockpiles in the Middle East, the Defense Department initiated dozens of new multiyear contracts—mostly for interceptor missiles and missile components —with the very same companies that donated to Trump’s ballroom and birthday events. These contracts, collectively, are worth hundreds of billions of dollars.

Lockheed Martin is the largest beneficiary, but other firms are making out well. Boeing in March 2025 was awarded a $20 billion initial contract to build the nation’s next-generation fighter jet. That jet, still under development in a recently constructed warehouse in St. Louis, is called the F-47. Its name—a departure from standard Air Force nomenclature that was chosen in part to honor “the 47th president’s pivotal support”—makes it a bit of a Trump vanity project, too.

RTX signed agreements with the Pentagon in February to accelerate production of five types of missiles for an undisclosed price. Then, the company was awarded a $441.6 million contract to manufacture more missiles in April; a spot among 12 companies selected to propose Golden Dome missile-defense prototypes in May; and, in October, $6.3 billion to spend up to seven years building yet more interceptor missiles. In the third quarter of 2026 alone, RTX secured Pentagon contracts worth almost $59 billion —more than double the $23 billion in Pentagon contracts they received over the same period in 2025.

Even absent any explicit link between contributions and favorable treatment by federal agencies, critics say the wave of large gifts creates an appearance of corruption. Government contractors seem, at least, to believe it’s in their interest to make major financial contributions to Trump’s agenda.

“A one-time donation that boosts the ego of Trump and lets him fulfill his interior design dreams could pay off for years and years to come,” said Julia Gledhill, a Pentagon budget analyst with the Stimson Center. The contractors, Gledhill said, “can spend a little and get a lot in return.”

Finding causal relationships between any one donation and one contract is not often possible, she said. But the pattern is hard to miss.

Defense contractors certainly donated to presidential projects before the Trump era. Obama’s second inaugural committee took donations of similar amounts from Lockheed Martin, Northrop Grumman, and Boeing, too. But prior presidents didn’t build monuments to themselves like Trump has, Quincy’s Hartung said.

And Trump’s willingness to construct vanity projects creates a new channel of influence. “[Contractors] used to mostly stick with the bread-and-butter contributions, some dark money, funding think tanks to make arguments they agree with,” Hartung said. “But now Trump has sort of opened up this new territory…and they’re almost competing to do it.”

But with a Democratic House and Senate, these cycles of vanity-project donations and defense contract deals look increasingly vulnerable to inspection come January. “The potential for crackdown on very loose contracting policies is ripe in this moment, which is exciting,” said Savannah Wooten, a Pentagon budget reduction advocate at Win Without War. “This is one of the most egregious areas of grift in our government.”

Various Democrats have recently announced plans to look into contractor donations to Trump projects in the next Congress.

Rep. Jim Himes (D-Conn.), the top Democrat on the House Intelligence Committee, told the New York Times last week that his committee would examine whether defense contractors had been “promised anything,” or “threatened” in exchange for their donations.

Democrats on the House Natural Resources Committee recently instructed defense contractors and other firms that funded Trump projects to preserve records for an expected investigation next year.

These investigations appear set to become a key point of conflict with the Trump administration. Trump recently issued an executive order that purports to bar contractors from sharing information with Congress without White House permission. That’s a legally dubious claim that nonetheless highlights the administration’s intention to shield its dealings with those companies from congressional scrutiny.

Trump is not done raising money for his pet projects. O’Rourke is reportedly pressing donors to help pay for the president’s plans to replace the East Potomac golf course and construct a massive statue garden near the Jefferson Memorial, along with his planned presidential library in Miami.

Trump has reportedly mulled redirecting leftover inaugural funds to his library. According to the Wall Street Journal , he even persuaded Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick to donate $25 million to the library, a gift that may have helped Lutnick hang on to his job.

Trump has also suggested he might seek corporate funding for the so-called Triumphal Arch he wants to plant in a traffic circle in front of Arlington National Cemetery. Trump, along with Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin, has ludicrously claimed the arch will serve a military function. Trump has said the structure will house “drones” and “snipers” and serve as an ammunition depot. Experts have dismissed those claims, which appear aimed at persuading judges hearing legal challenges to the plans to grant deference on national security grounds.

But if defense contractors are going to support a Trump vanity project, why not one that he claims will be in part “a top grade Military Complex” ? The arch, along with other ongoing projects, could test whether, with Trump diminished by his midterm repudiation and Congress poised to aggressively investigate, top defense firms will continue bankrolling Trump’s whims.

scraped.title: Your not-so-friendly neighborhood turkeys will have their revenge
scraped.description: In suburbs around the country, wattled warriors are turning the tables on unsuspecting Americans.
scraped.author: Nick Lund
scraped.h1: Your Not-So-Friendly Neighborhood Turkeys Will Have Their Revenge
scraped.body_text:
A wild turkey in Michigan, June 2026.. Joseph Weiser/Zuma

This story was originally published by Slate and is reproduced here as part of the Climate Desk collaboration.

In suburbs across America, marauding bands of young males, hormones boiling, are stalking our quiet streets—and attacking unsuspecting citizens without warning.

For Lili Korbuly-Johnson, it happened in late December, when she was taking out her compost. The assailant appeared beside her on the sidewalk, first following closely, then physically pushing against her. Her screams had no effect, so she sprinted across the icy street in St. Louis Park, Minnesota, and managed to get herself on the other side of a car that had slowed down to help. “If you go now, you can outrun him!” the driver yelled to her, and she bolted back to her condo before collapsing in a shaking heap.

“Being attacked by a wild turkey is as close as one can get to being attacked by a velociraptor.”

She felt genuinely scared, but also a little bit foolish. The cause of her panic wasn’t a bag snatcher or a snarling dog. It was a bird: a wild turkey.

She was set upon again a few months later by, she believes, the same repeat offender. This time she stood her ground, whacking him with her purse until he fled the scene.

Korbuly-Johnson is only one victim in a recent nationwide outbreak. Turkeys will take on anyone, from schoolchildren in Wisconsin to 83-year-olds in California . Bike riders aren’t safe, nor pregnant women , nor even hustling AI entrepreneurs : “I got attacked by a turkey at a train stop. Here’s what it taught me while building my startup.”

Turkeys have harassed UPS drivers in Connecticut , the USPS in Ohio , and Amazon drivers in New York . They’ve taken on cops in Georgia and Wisconsin , even getting a Bay Area woman out of a speeding ticket .

Some individuals become local legends, like “ Kevin ” from Massachusetts, “ Gladis ” and “ Gregory Peck ” from Minnesota, and “ Gerald ” from California, who terrorized Oakland residents for five months in 2020. (A wildlife capture professional posed as a “frail, old woman,” Gerald’s favorite target, to lure him in.) To be clear, turkey attacks aren’t fatal, but they are dangerous. These avian aggressors can weigh upward of 25 pounds, and they can flap, jump, and peck in what can be a relentless and maniacal pursuit. Male turkeys—called “toms”—grow spikes of hard keratin on the backs of their legs that they use to battle each other. These “spurs” are also effective on people, sometimes drawing blood and prompting trips to urgent care .

“Why is this Thanksgiving staple suddenly turning the tables on us?”

“Turkeys, all modern birds, are literally dinosaurs,” says Steve Brusatte, paleontologist and author of The Story of Birds: A New History From Their Dinosaur Origins to the Present . “So if you live in the United States, being attacked by a wild turkey is as close as one can get to being attacked by a velociraptor.”

These run-ins can also inflict psychological wounds. “I feel like it’s pathetic to have PTSD from going up the hill to do your recycling,” Korbuly-Johnson told me of her close call in Minnesota, “but I’m still scared.”

For a while she carried a broom for protection when she went outside, and when she’s out with her husband and they see turkeys, she has him menace around like Bigfoot to protect her from the birds. “I wish they didn’t scare me,” she said. “I wish I could say that they don’t scare me.”

And yet, when she was interviewed by the local news, the resulting story attempted to straddle the line between serious and silly. The reporter discussed the growing number of altercations involving turkeys in greater Minneapolis to a soundtrack of plucking strings and humming kazoos.

Wild turkey attacks are happening all over the country, but most of us don’t know why they’re increasing or how to feel about it. So I decided to call up the experts—animal handlers, scientists, historians, and injured parties—and talk turkey: Why is this Thanksgiving staple suddenly turning the tables on us, and what, if anything, can we do about it?

To understand why this epidemic of turkey-on-human violence is happening now, it’s important to first understand the perpetrators’ checkered history. After all, the national turkey takeover is surprising, considering that only a century ago the species was nearing extinction.

The wild turkey rebound began after World War II, when state wildlife agencies began reintroduction programs.

Turkeys have been in North America for millions of years. They’re the largest bird in the group Galliformes, or landfowl, which also includes dozens of species of quail and pheasant, and more. While there were once several different species of turkey, today there are just two: the resplendent ocellated turkey ( Meleagris ocellata ) of Central America, and Meleagris gallopavo , our neighborhood wild turkey . Although its range was until recently limited to parts of what is now Mexico, the eastern half of the United States, and southern Quebec and Ontario, it has now also been introduced across much of the American West and has taken up residence in every U.S. state except Alaska.

The reason people have spread wild turkeys around is also one of the reasons they were almost exterminated from the face of the earth: They’re delicious. Thanks to their large size, tasty meat, and relative abundance, wild turkeys were a dietary staple of many Native Americans. They were first domesticated by the Mayans in what is now Mexico an estimated 2,000 years ago, and it was these birds that made their way to Europe on Spanish ships in the 1500s. They became immensely popular livestock across the continent, so much so that domestic turkeys made a return trip to their native lands with English colonists in the 1600s.

Today there are roughly 450 million domestic turkeys kept around the world, and though their numbers are dwarfed by that of chickens (the domesticated version of Asia’s red junglefowl, or Gallus gallus ), they are one of the most numerous birds on earth. Though they’re the same species as their wild relatives—these distant cousins do, occasionally, interbreed—the domestic population has been bred to emphasize the parts humans love, with the result being enormous breasts and juicier legs. These features have disadvantages for the turkeys, however, leaving many domestic birds so fat they’re unable to fly , or even breed . Still, that’s not to say that the wild turkey isn’t good eating: It remains a common game bird, with a leaner, darker meat and more intense flavor.

But while domestic turkeys, bred by humans, boomed, wild populations cratered. Though the wild birds always had a special place in the minds of Americans (many of us know the famous story of Ben Franklin suggesting that the wild turkey, “a Bird of Courage,” be the national symbol over the “Coward” that was the bald eagle), they were driven to the brink of eradication by the twin forces of habitat loss and the new human neighbors who were gobbling them up.

“Predators in suburbs may just have a broader menu of options, buffering their impacts on wild turkeys.”

The effects were felt first in the populous New England states, where in some areas up to 80 percent of the turkey’s forest habitats were cleared for agriculture in the 1800s. The species was completely extirpated from Massachusetts, Connecticut, Maine, and Vermont by the mid-1800s and hung on in other states only in remote outposts. It’s thought that it reached its low point in the 1930s, when only about 30,000 birds remained in the wild.

But it wasn’t too late. The wild turkey rebound began after World War II, when state wildlife agencies began reintroduction programs that trapped turkeys from remaining strongholds and relocated them to states with regenerating forests and new restrictions on hunting. Turkeys flourished, and today there are estimated to be more than 6 million of them in the US—a tremendous conservation success story. Their comeback was thanks in large part to a new kind of emerging habitat, one that provided the turkeys with a host of advantages: the suburb.

“Suburbs typically offer a mix of woodlots and openings,” says Doug Little of the National Wild Turkey Federation, “and this mix of habitat, along with backyard bird feeders being prevalent, can offer abundant food sources throughout the year.” The suburban bounty includes a high abundance of insects needed by turkey chicks in the spring and summer, Little says, as well as fruit like dogwood berries and heavy seeds like acorns and beechnut for turkeys to fatten themselves on in the fall and winter.

Plus, though there are predators in the suburbs, they’re too busy eating other stuff to concern themselves with prey as imposing and fearsome as the turkey. Sure, raccoons and opossums will raid nests and eat turkey eggs, and larger predators, such as hawks, owls, foxes, and coyotes, may snack on baby turkeys, or even the occasional adult. But suburbs also serve up easier meals, such as mice, rats, rabbit, and pet cats, not to mention the leftover goodies from our garbage cans. “Predators in suburbs may just have a broader menu of options, buffering their impacts on wild turkeys,” Little says.

This is only part of the “human shield hypothesis,” advanced, when it comes to turkeys, by Michael Chamberlain, a professor at the University of Georgia and founder of the Wild Turkey Lab research project. “There’s a growing awareness in the academic world that wildlife species are adapting to urban and suburban areas, and they’re very likely drawing benefits like reduced predation, high availability of resources, protection from hunters,” he says.

In a recent study , Chamberlain and his co-authors found that female turkeys who nested near human activity—areas that also had fewer predators—had better survival rates. “As you continue to see suburban sprawl, particularly in the Northeast, turkeys are essentially protected in those areas, and they’re not hunted and they’re not persecuted at all and they’re very productive,” Chamberlain says. “I think these problems [of rampaging posses of turkeys] are going to grow through time.”

So that’s how turkeys came to rule America’s suburbs, but why are they bothering to attack humans?

Horny young males are, as in so many species, a big part of the problem.

Gallinaceous birds like turkeys are famous for their complex mating displays, in which males compete for the attention of females by dancing, strutting, and fluffing themselves up. For wild turkeys, this means much more than just fanning their tails. To impress females and prove their dominance to each other, males in breeding condition grow a series of accessories, including beards (a cluster of long, coarse feathers protruding from their chests), long wattles dangling from their necks, and warty caruncles on their heads—all of which are crowned by the snood, a fleshy protuberance that sprouts from the area just in front of their eyes.

Most of the time, the snood simply hangs foppishly over their faces, but when turkeys become excited, their snoods become engorged with blood and become erect. (Perhaps this feature helps compensate for their phalli, which are minuscule.) In other words, a male wild turkey is built to impress the ladies, and he takes this task very seriously.

And no such stud is complete without his wingman. Wild turkeys engage in what’s known as polygynous-promiscuous mating, which means that although there’s a group of males that hang around with a group of females during the breeding season, usually just one of the males gets to mate with the females. However, even though there’s a pecking order, with one dominant male, the other males in the group protect him because it’s their flock at stake. “They all sort of operate together,” says Chamberlain. “There’s three or four or five of them. They’ll strut or they put their tails up in the air, or fan their wings towards the ground, or gobble at the same time, and so they’re functioning as a breeding group, even though only one gets to mate.”

Often, male turkeys in such a troop are related as brothers or half brothers. Though that may sound like an odd setup for us, it works out for all the toms. The nondominant males support the dominant male (“ like a backup singer ,” as one researcher put it), and they chase away potential rivals, giving the alpha male more time to focus on breeding. In return, since they’re related to the alpha, the nondominant birds benefit indirectly by passing on some portion of their DNA. These betas may not get kids of their own, but they get nieces and nephews.

Still, it’s not as if the nondominant birds are thrilled about it. “A lot of these nondominant birds are just biding their time,” says Chamberlain, waiting for the day when they can have the rule of the roost. They need to be prepared to swoop in if something happens to the head of their brotherhood, and so they’re still coursing with testosterone and ready for a fight throughout the spring. That’s when these other confrontations happen, Chamberlain says. “So they see a reflection or a human being, or they walk by a car and they see an image in the window, and they get extremely aggressive, because they’re wired to be that way in the spring.”

Walking around towns, “turkeys “lose their fear of humans and become aggressive to protect what they now see as their territory.”

And while gang activity from nondominant males explains most of the spring incidents—if you read the news, you’ll find that the majority of the stories are from March , April , and May —it’s not the only reason turkeys lash out. The other reason isn’t unique to wild turkeys at all but is a familiar story wherever man meets beast: People just get too close.

“What we’re seeing with wild turkeys isn’t unlike what we’re seeing with many wildlife species that live close to humans,” Chamberlain says. “They’re tolerant until they’re not.” It’s the same story in suburbs across the country with elk or deer or alligators : people and animals struggling to share the same space. Chamberlain thinks that Lili Korbuly-Johnson’s wintertime flap in Minnesota may have been one of these kinds of encounters, in which she unwittingly entered the turkey’s personal space and the turkey reacted combatively.

Wild turkeys are somewhat unusual among suburban creatures, though. Elk and alligators are not common backyard visitors, and most other animals—deer, foxes, coyotes, raccoons, opossums, rodents, bats, etc.—are either nocturnal or generally shy around humans. Not wild turkeys. They strut around in broad daylight, right through parks and yards and other places humans like to call their own. It’s hard to imagine another species that we’d tolerate in such proximity, especially if they were as unruly as turkeys can be.

But the fact is, we like turkeys. If you saw a turkey trotting around your neighborhood, you’d probably be more likely to snap a photo for your group chat than freak out. So far, even towns with turkeys that have been known to cross the line have had a difficult time taking action.

The poster city of America’s seemingly contradictory relationship with wild turkeys might be Phoenix, Oregon. Wild turkeys aren’t native to Oregon, but they were introduced by hunters in the early 1960s. They were successful— approximately 45,000 wild turkeys live in Oregon today, and thousands are hunted each year—but some birds found refuge in cities and towns that provided plenty of food but no threat from hunters. Phoenix was one of those towns.

“You’ll have a couple strutters, and then a bunch of bully jakes operating like a New York or Los Angeles gang—they’re like a little turkey MS-13.”

There, turkeys “lose their fear of humans and become aggressive to protect what they now see as their territory,” says Hadassah DeJack-Reynolds, executive director of the Tikkun Olam Farm Sanctuary, which has offered to help with what has become a headache for many in town. This spring, the birds began getting feisty, chasing schoolchildren and motorists and leaving one woman who was out for a jog with a bloodied hand . People were afraid to leave their homes, and town officials decided it was time to act.

The mayor collaborated with a local wildlife trapper on a plan to bait and trap the birds, then transport them to a meat processing facility for eventual donation to a nonprofit organization. Officials scheduled a City Council meeting to approve the plan and end the saga of the bullies … until almost everyone spoke against it. Despite all the harassment, people liked having the birds around. The turkeys were spared.

DeJack-Reynolds says that residents’ feeding the turkeys is the main reason the animals are getting so comfortable in Phoenix. “Residents will put food out for them because they enjoy having them in their yard,” she says. “I understand that people are naturally drawn to these beautiful birds and want to engage with them,” but “feeding and interacting with them is what can ultimately cost the turkeys their lives.” The town instead passed an ordinance in early September “restricting the feeding and attracting of wild animals.”

Towns looking to fight back against the turkeys do not have many options. Culling wild turkeys, even in “humane” ways and when the meat supports needy citizens, as was proposed in Phoenix, is not generally a popular solution. Towns all over the country have banned the intentional feeding of wild turkeys, and many more discourage it, but it’s difficult to be completely effective unless you also ban the feeding of songbirds (which ordinances like Phoenix’s do not), since bird feeders can easily but unintentionally provide food for turkeys.

“I don’t hide my fear that well, and I try not to look in their direction.”

Hunters are more than happy to lend a hand. Official wild turkey hunting seasons exist in 49 states—every one that has a viable turkey population—and hunters kill an estimated 690,000 wild turkeys each year. Turkey hunting is permitted in many suburban jurisdictions if strict regulations are followed and when personal permission is obtained when hunting on private property. “You only need 10 or 12 yards when you’re bow hunting,” says Blaine Cardilli, a writer and longtime hunter from Maine. “You can set right up in someone’s backyard or garage.”

Most of the turkeys he’s seen going berserk are young males—“bully jakes,” as they’re known—scrambling for their place on the social ladder. “You’ll have a couple strutters [dominant males], and then a bunch of bully jakes operating like a New York or Los Angeles gang—they’re like a little turkey MS-13—and they’ll come in and challenge them.”

Hunters are eager for towns to allow them to help out with problematic suburban turkeys, in part because while turkey numbers are fairly steady as a whole, they’re decreasing in rural areas. Experts point to a number of potential causes for the declines, especially the continuing loss of hardwood forest habitat and excess hunting (especially early in the spring, which may throw off turkey social hierarchies). A labor-intensive but widely satisfactory way forward is trapping turkeys from suburban areas and sending them to the country. In Texas, for example, hundreds of turkeys have been transported from states as far away as Maine and released into the large swaths of habitat in the eastern part of the state.

But for most suburbanites, the best option may be to just learn to live with their feathered neighbors. The vast majority of the time, the turkeys peacefully go about their business and inspire much more than they frighten. (I’ve personally seen dozens of kids stand in open-mouthed awe as the harmless resident flock at the Gilsland Farm Audubon Center , where I work, parades past in full regalia.) And for those certain months when turkeys might be looking to cause trouble? The advice from Michael Chamberlain, of the Wild Turkey Lab, sounds similar to counsel you’d give anyone about navigating around others in a suburban environment: “Let them be. Don’t need to go out of your way to avoid them, and don’t go out of your way to get close to them.”

It’s practical guidance, though perhaps too late for people who’ve been on the receiving end of a turkey attack, like Lili Korbuly-Johnson, who remains haunted by her ordeal. “I don’t hide my fear that well, and I try not to look in their direction,” she says. “It’s annoying as hell.” Still, just like many American towns, she doesn’t have an answer to the growing turkey threat. “I know they have a right to be where they want to be,” she says. “I just wish I could convey that they should stay on their side and we’ll stay on ours … or else you’ll become dinner.”
